survey_notes: Sec. 12 (Speech) and Sec. 5 (halting policy). The loop sits in the connector over audio-encoder features, not inside the LLM, so it adds depth to the audio branch only. The Fixed-4 control is iso-architecture, which isolates halting from looping; no non-looped parameter-matched control is reported (inference from the baseline list).

title: CALR: Continuous Anchored Latent Reasoning via Render-of-Thought Compression
relevance_reason: Sequence-axis continuous latent reasoning; no shared block iterated in depth.
one_sentence: Anchors continuous visual latent reasoning to answers and derivations with a parallel-to-autoregressive curriculum; reaches 63.8% against 37.8% for Render-of-Thought on GSM8K-Aug with Qwen3-VL-4B.
key_contributions: Diagnosis that continuous latents influence answers but collapse content while discrete latents are bypassed
Functional anchoring with latent-mediated answer supervision
Parallel-to-autoregressive curriculum

setup.model_sizes: Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct main; also Qwen3-VL-2B and 8B, LLaVA-Mistral-7B
setup.loops_train: not applicable
setup.baselines: RoT, Coconut, CODI and others
setup.benchmarks: five mathematical reasoning benchmarks incl. GSM8K-Aug

claims.claim: Large gain over a comparable continuous latent method under matched latent budget.
claims.evidence_quote: unified autoregressive CALR achieves 63.8% versus RoT’s 37.8% accuracy with 32 continuous latents each, a 26.0-point gain.

survey_notes: Sec. 13 (Sequence-axis latent reasoning), comparison only. Priority 3.

title: What Matters for Latent Reasoning with Flow Matching
relevance_reason: Latent reasoning with flow matching in a learned latent space; its related work places looped models as the 'vertical' family.
one_sentence: Recipe for flow-matching latent thoughts probed against five requirements (useful, diverse, explainable, refinable, efficient); reaches 97% of explicit CoT accuracy at a quarter of its latency on arithmetic benchmarks.
key_contributions: Five requirements for a latent thought with a probe for each
FLaRe training recipe
Latency test against explicit CoT and prior latent methods

setup.model_sizes: VAE from Llama-3.2-1B and 3B; flow model Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct
setup.train_tokens_or_data: GSM8K-Aug
setup.loops_train: not applicable
setup.baselines: Coconut, CODI, KaVa, PCCoT, LaDiR
setup.benchmarks: GSM8K, GSM8K-Hard, SVAMP, MultiArith

claims.claim: Flow-based latent reasoning reaches near-CoT accuracy at lower latency.
claims.evidence_quote: while reaching 97% of the accuracy of explicit CoT at a quarter of its latency.

claims.claim: Authors classify looped models as one family of latent reasoning that applies the same layers over a fixed number of slots.
claims.evidence_quote: keep the number of slots fixed and apply the same layers over them several times, so the reasoning becomes an iterative computation within the hidden states

survey_notes: Sec. 13 (Sequence-axis latent reasoning and diffusion-style latents), comparison only. Their taxonomy 'horizontal / vertical / parallel' is a useful cross-reference to the survey's three recurrence axes.

title: Enhancing Long-Video VLM Embeddings with Query-Aware Streaming Latent Reasoning
relevance_reason: Clip-by-clip recurrent memory tokens for video embeddings; no shared block iterated in depth.
one_sentence: Clip-by-clip recurrent memory tokens for video embeddings; no shared block iterated in depth.
survey_notes: Out: recurrence over clips (time), no depth-looped shared block.

title: Continuous Memory Machines
relevance_reason: Nonlinear RNN with internal ticks and a shared memory Transformer; recurrence over time and ticks, positioned as a memory RNN, not as a looped Transformer.
one_sentence: Extends the Continuous Thought Machine with matrix-valued short- and long-term memory updated by a shared Transformer at every internal step; improves maze action accuracy from 88.8% to 96.3% at a 10M budget.
key_contributions: Separate short- and long-term matrix memories with a shared memory Transformer
Beats memory-augmented baselines on algorithmic and in-context tasks
Preserves CTM interpretable attention on mazes

setup.model_sizes: 10M parameter budget for maze task; 500K budget for other ablations
setup.train_tokens_or_data: algorithmic, in-context learning, maze, ImageNet-100 tasks
setup.loops_train: 50 internal steps on mazes; 25 on images
setup.baselines: CTM, CMM-LSTM, Transformer, RMT, other memory networks
setup.benchmarks: copy, recall, sort, 39x39 mazes, ImageNet-100

claims.claim: On 39x39 mazes the CMM beats the CTM at a 10M budget.
claims.evidence_quote: increasing action accuracy from 88.8% to 96.3% and full maze accuracy from 37.4% to 61.6%.

claims.claim: Maze solving iterates the model over internal steps on the same input.
claims.evidence_quote: The model processes the maze over 50 internal steps, producing a full route prediction at each iteration.

limitations: Nonlinear recurrence restricts training parallelism; extra hyperparameters; memory Transformer applied at every step.
survey_notes: Sec. 13 comparison (memory RNNs with internal ticks, CTM lineage); borderline with recursive reasoning in Sec. 11 because ticks reuse parameters on the same input. Kept adjacent because the paper frames itself as a memory RNN.

title: Loop the Loopies!
relevance_reason: Large-scale looped MoE LMs (20B-A2B, 6B-A0.6B) pre-trained from scratch with per-layer recurrence and compute-matched baselines.
one_sentence: Introduces layer-loop recurrence (each MoE layer applied twice before the next) plus a wall-clock-matched width/depth recipe; Loopie-20B-A2B overtakes a reproduced Qwen3-like 30B-A3B after about 600B tokens at matched step time.
key_contributions: Layer-loop (per-layer repeat, L1 L1 L2 L2 ...) vs model-loop (whole-stack, as in Ouro/Huginn), with a controlled ablation favoring layer-loop on MoE backbones.
Loopie Recipe: halve stored layers, loop each twice, spend activation-memory headroom on doubled microbatch and wider/deeper stored model, select config by measured optimizer-step time.
Large-scale post-training (supervised pre-training on 2T tokens + math RL) producing Loopie Thinking models.

setup.model_sizes: Loopie-20B-A2B (D=2304, L=27 stored layers, R=2) and Loopie-6B-A0.6B (18 layers, D=1536); 128 experts, top-8; scaling ladder 0.10B-0.70B Loopie vs 0.15B-1B baselines
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Stage 1 approx 2.28T tokens (4 epochs of approx 570B Nemotron-CC-v2-HQ; intro says 3T), Stage 2 annealing 1.26T; Sec. 4.3 says 3.5T pre-training tokens; SPT 2T tokens
setup.loops_train: 2 (layer-loop)
setup.baselines: Reproduced Qwen3-like 30B-A3B MoE trained on 800B tokens at matched step time; model-loop ablation; N x layer vs N x loop; public reasoning models (Qwen3-30B-A3B Thinking, Nemotron 3 Nano, Nemotron Cascade 2, Ouro Thinking)
setup.benchmarks: 8-benchmark average (ARC-C/E, BoolQ, CSQA, HellaSwag, MMLU, OBQA, WinoGrande); post-training: MMLU, BBH, IFEval, AIME 24/25, AMC, LiveCodeBench

instantiation.k_R: 1 layer per loop unit, 27 (20B) / 18 (6B) such units in sequence (per-layer loop)
instantiation.injection: none stated (plain residual; each layer re-applied to its own output)
instantiation.sharing: strict tie within each layer's 2 applications
instantiation.train_tokens: approx 2.28T stage 1 + 1.26T annealing (paper also states 3T and 3.5T in different places) + 2T SPT

claims.claim: At matched measured optimizer-step time (not matched theoretical FLOPs) and the same 800B tokens, Loopie-20B-A2B overtakes a vanilla Qwen3-like 30B-A3B after about 600B tokens.
claims.regime: iso_train_flop (wall-clock matched; Loopie has about 1.42x the nominal block FLOPs) + iso_data
claims.evidence_quote: after roughly 600 billion tokens of pre-training, Loopie-20B-A2B overtakes the compute-matched baseline and maintains a consistent advantage thereafter.

claims.claim: Compute matching is by measured step time; the looped model performs more nominal computation per token than the reference.
claims.evidence_quote: The models are not matched by their theoretical FLOP counts. Loopie performs more nominal computation per token, but the additional work is offset by the higher realized efficiency.

claims.claim: Layer-loop (per-layer repetition) beats model-loop (whole-stack repetition) on MoE backbones at the same parameters and FLOPs, but only after about 1.2T tokens; model-loop leads early.
claims.evidence_quote: layer-loop initially trails model-loop slightly on downstream benchmarks. However, it overtakes model-loop after approximately 1.2 trillion training tokens and improves more rapidly thereafter.

claims.claim: The advantage over wall-clock-matched vanilla MoE baselines persists across a 4-rung scaling ladder (0.15B to 1B baseline parameters).
claims.evidence_quote: Across all four rungs, Loopie consistently outperforms its compute-matched vanilla counterpart. More importantly, the gap does not vanish as model size increases.

claims.claim: Marginal benefit of extra loops decays fast under fixed pre-training compute; R=2 chosen; the N x layer vs N x loop figure is not compute-matched for N=2.
claims.regime: iso_param vs iso_effective_depth (N x stored layers), authors caveat compute mismatch
claims.evidence_quote: when comparing N × looping against N × stored-layer scaling, the marginal benefit of recurrence is largest at R = 2. We therefore choose R = 2 for the Loopie Series.

claims.claim: Post-trained Loopie-20B-A2B is competitive with public MoE reasoning models trained on far more tokens (cross-model comparison).
claims.evidence_quote: Loopie is pre-trained on only 3.5T tokens, whereas Nemotron 3 Nano and Nemotron Cascade 2 are each trained on 25T tokens drawn from the same pre-training data source.

limitations: No systematic study of inference-time compute; post-training limited mainly to math and code; no comprehensive ablation of supervised pre-training; only a Qwen3-30B-A3B-like base architecture; compute matching is by measured wall-clock, so FLOP-level conclusions depend on the hardware/parallelism setup; N x layer vs N x loop comparison not compute-matched at N=2; inconsistent total pre-training token counts (3T, 2.28T, 3.5T) in different sections.
survey_notes: Key datapoint for the compute-regime audit: first looped LM claiming a win over a non-looped baseline at matched training compute, but matched by measured wall-clock (via activation-memory savings enabling doubled microbatch), not FLOPs (Loopie uses about 1.42x nominal block FLOPs). Explicitly argues Ouro-2.6B x4 should be compared to a 10.4B model and Huginn-3.5B x32 to a 112B model. Topology contrast: per-layer loop (adjacent reuse) vs whole-stack model-loop (Ouro, Huginn); this aligns with Takase and Kiyono's (2104.06022) finding that sharing pattern matters and with MoEUT's grouping, and is the opposite choice to Huginn's sandwich whole-core loop. Uses only R=2 and no input injection, contrasting with Huginn's 32-step injected recurrence. Model-loop wins early in training (crossover at about 1.2T tokens), so short-horizon ablations would reach the opposite conclusion.

title: Solve the Loop: Attractor Models for Language and Reasoning
relevance_reason: Weight-tied refinement module solved to a fixed point with implicit gradients; LM pretraining up to 770M vs parameter-matched Transformer and looped Parcae.
one_sentence: A non-recurrent backbone proposes an output embedding; a small weight-tied attractor module refines it to a fixed point (Anderson solver, one-step implicit gradient), beating parameter-matched Transformers and Parcae at 140M-770M with constant training memory.
key_contributions: Fixed point placed in tied output-embedding space, warm-started from the backbone proposal (not zero/noise), with persistent additive proposal injection.
One-step implicit-gradient training: constant memory in iterations and 25-31% fewer training FLOPs than Parcae at the same Tmax.
Equilibrium internalization: after training, decoding the backbone proposal with zero solver steps is near the converged quality.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: FineWeb-Edu; 11.2B / 29.6B / 61.6B tokens for 140M / 370M / 770M (Table 9, as parsed); ablations 1B tokens
setup.loops_train: solver-determined, max 64 (140M, 370M) or 32 (770M) forward iterations
setup.loops_test: adjustable; peak at T=1, T=0 near converged
setup.baselines: parameter-matched Transformer, Parcae (prelude-core-coda looped LM with mean recurrence 8), DEQ, HRM, TRM
setup.benchmarks: val PPL, Lambada PPL, CORE, CORE-Extended; Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard

instantiation.T_train: until relative residual < tolerance or Tmax (64 / 64 / 32)
instantiation.T_test: same solver; tolerance and Tmax adjustable at inference
instantiation.injection: persistent additive injection of backbone proposal y0: T(y_t + y0)
instantiation.sharing: strict tie in attractor module

claims.claim: At matched parameters, data, optimizer and schedule, Attractor Models beat both a standard Transformer and the looped Parcae on perplexity and downstream accuracy at 140M-770M.
claims.regime: iso_param + iso_data (Attractor uses more FLOPs than the Transformer, fewer than Parcae)
claims.evidence_quote: all models are matched in parameter count and trained with the same data budget, optimizer, and learning-rate schedule as the Parcae baselines; the only change is the recurrent block.

claims.claim: Convergence-based stopping plus one-step implicit gradients give 25-31% lower training FLOPs than Parcae at identical Tmax and near-constant memory in loop count.
claims.regime: iso_param + iso_data; FLOP comparison vs looped baseline
claims.evidence_quote: our solver typically converges below ε in well under Tmax steps, so the realized depth during training is lower despite identical Tmax , yielding 25–31% lower training FLOPs across scales.

claims.claim: Persistent proposal injection is necessary: initialization-only injection makes the fixed point proposal-independent and few tokens converge; additive injection beats concatenation.
claims.evidence_quote: When the proposal is used only for initialization, ỹt=0 = ỹ0 and ỹt+1 = Tθa (ỹt ), the recurrent update no longer depends on the input after the first state.

claims.claim: Warm-starting the solver from the backbone proposal beats zero or Gaussian-noise initialization (contradicting the random-init choice of Huginn/Parcae).
claims.evidence_quote: Starting the attractor solve from an uninformative state, either zero or Gaussian noise, substantially degrades both quality and convergence.

claims.claim: Equilibrium internalization: the backbone readout with no solver steps matches or beats Parcae at 8 recurrent steps.
claims.evidence_quote: Concretely, our 140M model at T = 0 (no solver) matches or improves Parcae 140M at T = 8 recurrent steps; the same pattern holds at 370M and 770M.

claims.claim: On Sudoku-Extreme/Maze-Hard, Attractor Models improve with scale while TRM collapses at 27M.
claims.regime: iso_param vs TRM; unmatched vs frontier LLMs
claims.evidence_quote: TRM is the strongest tiny baseline at 7M, achieving 74.7% and 85.3%, but (counter to the goal of scaling) collapses to 0% on both tasks when scaled to 27M parameters.

survey_notes: Modern DEQ descendant for LMs: it reframes the sandwich template as backbone (prelude) + small attractor core + no coda, with the fixed point in output-embedding space. Contradicts Huginn/Parcae on initial state (informative warm start beats zero/noise) and agrees with Huginn on persistent injection (init-only injection fails). Its equilibrium internalization (T=0 is near-converged) cuts against the test-time-compute-scaling story of Huginn: the recurrence acts mainly as a training-time regularizer/teacher. Appendix tables give Parcae's configuration (prelude/core/coda 2-2-2, 4-4-4, 6-6-6, diagonal injection, mean recurrence 8, truncated backprop depth 4, Poisson sampling) usable for the instantiation table, flagged as second-hand.

title: Scaling up Test-Time Compute with Latent Reasoning: A Recurrent Depth Approach
relevance_reason: Canonical prelude-core-coda recurrent-depth LM (3.5B, 800B tokens) with randomized loop counts and test-time depth scaling.
one_sentence: Pretrains a 3.5B prelude (2) / recurrent core (4) / coda (2) LM on 800B tokens with random-noise initial state, per-step concatenation injection and log-normal-Poisson loop counts; accuracy improves with test-time iterations up to about 32-64.
key_contributions: Template P -> R^r (with injection of e each step, s0 random) -> C, with sandwich normalization and a concatenation adapter, trained with r sampled from a heavy-tailed log-normal Poisson and truncated backprop through the last 8 iterations.
First open recurrent-depth LM at billion scale with released weights, code and data; documents failed runs (collapse of recurrence) without the final norm/init/adapter setup.
Zero-shot inference features enabled by recurrence: KL-based per-token early exit, KV-cache sharing across iterations, continuous CoT via warm-starting the state, self-speculative decoding.

setup.model_sizes: 3.5B, shape (2,4,2), h=5280; small ablation models (1,4,1), h=1024
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 800B tokens of public data, heavily code/math; non-recurrent baseline 180B tokens
setup.loops_train: r sampled from log-normal Poisson (mean about 33, median 29), backprop through last k=8
setup.baselines: non-recurrent twin trained to 180B tokens in same setting; public open models (Pythia, Amber, OLMo 1/2, StarCoder2)
setup.benchmarks: ARC, HellaSwag, MMLU, OBQA, PiQA, SciQ, WinoGrande, GSM8K (CoT), MATH (Minerva), MathQA, MBPP, HumanEval, MT-Bench

instantiation.T_test: chosen by user (1-64), or per-token KL-based exit
instantiation.injection: concatenation adapter A: R^2h -> R^h on [s_i; e], applied at every step (additive s+e works equally at small scale)
instantiation.sharing: strict tie of the 4-layer core
instantiation.loop_policy_test: fixed user-chosen r or zero-shot KL-threshold early exit

claims.claim: Random initial state plus injection of the embedded input at every step stabilizes recurrence and promotes path independence; injecting only at the start would not be stable.
claims.evidence_quote: injecting the latent inputs e in every step (Bansal et al., 2022) and initializing the latent vector with a random state stabilizes the recurrence and promotes convergence to a steady state independent of initialization

claims.claim: Additive injection works for small models but concatenation works best at scale; a timestep-conditioned core harms extrapolation; added diffusion-style noise did not help.
claims.scale: small ablation models; 3.5B for the adapter observation
claims.evidence_quote: While re-incorporation of initial embedding features via addition rather than concatenation works equally well for smaller models, we find that concatenation works best at scale.

claims.claim: A core block conditioned on the step index breaks path independence and extrapolation.
claims.evidence_quote: a core block that takes the current step as input (Peebles and Xie, 2023), but find that this interacts badly with path independence, leading to models that cannot extrapolate.

claims.claim: At scale, the first runs (parameter-free norms, no embedding scale, additive adapter) collapsed: the model learned to ignore the recurrence, so perplexity was the same at 1 or 32 iterations.
claims.evidence_quote: this training run is not able to leverage test-time compute effectively (right plot), as validation perplexity is the same whether 1 or 32 recurrences are used.

claims.claim: Against a non-recurrent twin trained on the same 180B tokens, the recurrent model is much better on harder tasks (ARC-C, GSM8K), with similar recall tasks; parameter/FLOP matching of the twin is not stated.
claims.evidence_quote: In direct comparison of both models at 180B tokens, we see that the recurrent model outperforms its baseline with an especially pronounced advantage on harder tasks, such as the ARC challenge set.

claims.claim: Test-time recurrence improves reasoning benchmarks up to compute equivalent to a 50B-parameter model; comparisons are to public models trained on other data.
claims.evidence_quote: We show that the resulting model can improve its performance on reasoning benchmarks, sometimes dramatically, up to a computation load equivalent to 50 billion parameters.

limitations: Single large run on an unablated data mixture, learning rate never cooled down, only 47000 steps; non-recurrent baseline only to 180B tokens and its size matching not stated; main comparisons to public models trained on different data; training FLOPs comparable to a 32B transformer.
builds_on: Deep thinking (Schwarzschild et al., 2021; Bansal et al., 2022)
survey_notes: Defines the survey's template: e = P(x), s0 ~ N(0, sigma^2), s_i = R(e, s_{i-1}), p = C(s_r). Design choices that other papers contest: (a) random initial state (Attractor Models 2605.12466 find zero/noise init worse than warm start from backbone proposal); (b) no step conditioning (Huginn says it breaks extrapolation; other works use step embeddings); (c) concatenation vs additive injection depends on scale; (d) truncated BPTT k=8. Compute regime: test-time scaling claims are unmatched (vs public models); the only controlled comparison is iso-data vs a 180B-token non-recurrent twin of unstated size. Loopie (2607.16051) argues Huginn-3.5B x32 should be compared to a 112B-parameter model at matched pre-training compute; Huginn itself states its training FLOPs are close to a 32B transformer (different accounting).

title: MoEUT: Mixture-of-Experts Universal Transformers
relevance_reason: Shared-layer (UT) language model with MoE FFN and MoE attention, layer grouping and peri-layernorm; parameter- and MAC-matched against dense Transformers up to about 1B.
one_sentence: MoEUT repeats a group of G (2-4) non-shared fine-grained-MoE layers (sigma-MoE FFN + SwitchHead attention) about 8-9 times with peri-layernorm; it slightly beats parameter-matched dense Transformers on C4 perplexity with fewer MACs, up to 1B parameters.
key_contributions: Solves the UT parameter-compute ratio problem by making the shared layers MoE in both FFN and attention, so parameters can be matched to a dense model without proportional compute.
Layer grouping: recurrently stack a group of G non-shared layers (ABAB...), G=2 optimal at 244M; AABB ordering is almost as bad as no grouping.
Peri-layernorm: no layernorm on the main residual path, only before linear layers feeding sigmoid/softmax, addressing residual-norm growth in shared layers.

setup.model_sizes: 44M to 1040M parameters
setup.train_tokens_or_data: C4, SlimPajama, peS2o, The Stack; batch 64 x context 1024 for 10^5 steps (total tokens not stated)
setup.loops_train: typically 8 or 9 recurrent steps of a G=2-4 layer group
setup.baselines: parameter-matched pre-layernorm dense Transformers with same d_model and n_layers; non-shared sigma-MoE; SUT (with and without ACT)

title: Lessons on Parameter Sharing across Layers in Transformers
relevance_reason: Systematic comparison of how M unique layers are reused across N layers (sequence vs cycle vs reversed cycle) against Universal Transformer-style full sharing.
one_sentence: Relaxes Universal-Transformer sharing by using M unique layers for N>M layers with three assignment patterns; at equal parameters these are faster than a widened UT and match or beat it in MT, ASR and LM.
key_contributions: Three reuse patterns for M unique layers in an N-layer stack: SEQUENCE (adjacent repeat, AABB), CYCLE (ABAB), CYCLE(REV) (ABBA-like final reversal).
Shows full one-layer sharing (UT) needs wider layers to match parameters and trains about 2x slower; partial sharing with more, thinner layers is faster and better.
Best pattern depends on normalization/task: CYCLE(REV) best in Post-LN MT; SEQUENCE best in Pre-LN ASR and WikiText-103 LM.

title: Deep Equilibrium Models
relevance_reason: Infinite-depth limit of a weight-tied, input-injected layer solved by root finding with implicit gradients; direct ancestor of fixed-point looped LMs.
one_sentence: Replaces an L-layer weight-tied sequence model z_{i+1}=f(z_i; x) by directly solving z*=f(z*; x) with Broyden root finding and implicit-function-theorem gradients, matching Transformer-XL/TrellisNet perplexity on WikiText-103 with up to 88% less training memory.
key_contributions: Formulates weight-tied deep sequence models with input passthrough as fixed-point problems; forward via quasi-Newton root finding, backward via implicit differentiation with constant memory.
Theorem: stacking multiple DEQs adds no representational power over a single DEQ.
Instantiates DEQ-Transformer (weight-tied Transformer-XL-style) and DEQ-TrellisNet; competitive WikiText-103 perplexity at equal parameters with 80-88% memory reduction, but slower runtime.

title: Adaptive Computation Time for Recurrent Neural Networks
relevance_reason: Origin of learned halting: a weight-shared state transition iterated a variable, learned number of times per input with a ponder cost; adopted by Universal Transformers and later looped LMs.
one_sentence: Adds a sigmoidal halting unit to an RNN so it performs a learned, input-dependent number of shared-weight state updates per input step, combined by a mean-field halting distribution and regularized by a ponder cost; large gains on synthetic tasks, little on character LM.
key_contributions: Halting distribution from cumulative sigmoid halting probabilities with threshold 1 - epsilon and a remainder term; outputs and states are halting-weighted mean-field averages (deterministic, differentiable).
Ponder cost (N(t) + R(t)) weighted by a time penalty tau to trade accuracy against computation.
Shows dramatic gains on parity, logic, addition and sorting, and interpretable ponder allocation (more steps at word/sentence boundaries) on Hutter Wikipedia character prediction.

Its LM finding (little gain on character LM) foreshadows later negative evidence for learned halting in LMs, e.g. MoEUT 2405.16039 attributes most of SUT's LM deficit to ACT. Universal Transformers adopted ACT per position; later LoopLMs (Ouro, MoR) use learned exit gates/routers instead. Note the explicit iso-parameter design rationale, which is the same decoupling of parameters from compute that the survey treats as the third scaling axis.

title: Allocating Recurrent Compute in Looped Language Models
relevance_reason: Component-level looping: repeats only the Gated DeltaNet token mixer within each layer, compared with no-loop and full-block loop at matched params and tokens.
one_sentence: MixerLoop repeats each Gated DeltaNet mixer T=4 times while running the dense FFN once; at 15M it beats full-block looping on CORE, at 110M it keeps 41.5% of full-loop's gain with 45.9% fewer backbone projection FLOPs.
key_contributions: Operator-selective recurrence: loop the stateful linear-attention mixer, not the FFN (A^T F per layer vs (A F)^T).
Iterative Transport Rank (ITR) and marginal ITR via a context-off intervention, measuring whether later mixer passes add distinct, non-negligible, beneficial readout changes.
Matched comparison of NoLoop, MixerLoop and FullLoop (LT2-style) with same unique params, data order and processed tokens.

title: The Topological Trouble With Transformers
relevance_reason: Position paper arguing feedforward depth (including depth recurrence) cannot do unbounded state tracking; offers a taxonomy of recurrent transformers by recurrence axis and token-to-step ratio.
one_sentence: Argues transformers push evolving state deeper with each input step and eventually exhaust depth; depth recurrence alone does not fix this, so step-wise (cross-token) recurrence or coarse-grained recurrence is needed; gives a recurrence-axis x tokens-per-step taxonomy.
key_contributions: Topological argument: in a feedforward transformer, state representations shift upward in the layer stack with each new token, so tracking is limited by depth.
Taxonomy of recurrent transformers by recurrence axis (depth, step, both) and ratio of input tokens per recurrence step (>1, =1, <1).
Research directions: enhanced state-space models and coarse-grained recurrence.

claims.claim: Feedforward transformers exhaust their depth on state tracking because state representations move deeper with each input step.
claims.evidence_quote: feedforward models push evolving state representations deeper into their layer stack with each new input step, rendering information inaccessible in shallow layers and ultimately exhausting the model’s depth.

claims.claim: Depth recurrence (looped transformers) does not by itself remove the upward drift of state across input steps.
claims.evidence_quote: state representation still shifts upward due to the parallel propagation of activation across steps t, regardless of how deep the transformer is made to be with recurrent depth (Figure 1b).

claims.claim: Proposes a two-dimensional taxonomy: recurrence axis and input tokens per recurrence step.
claims.evidence_quote: We characterize architectures along two dimensions: recurrence axis and input tokens per recurrence step. The axis can be depth alone (Figures 5b,c,d), in step alone (Figure 7), and in both depth and step (Figure 6).

limitations: No experiments; argument is schematic; examples of state-tracking failures are anecdotal model traces.
survey_notes: Useful for the design-space section as an external taxonomy: places looped transformers / UT / RINS in the 'depth axis, ratio > 1' cell, distinct from step-axis recurrence (linear attention, Mamba) and both-axis models (continuous thought). Its claim that depth recurrence cannot fix state tracking across tokens is a theoretical caution against over-claiming for LoopLMs; contrast with works that report state-tracking gains from looping (theory group papers).

title: Looping Beyond Twice: A Scalable Recipe for Looped Mixture-of-Experts
relevance_reason: Whole-stack looped MoE LM with per-loop routers, residual scaling, gated embedding re-injection and a looping residual; near-iso-FLOP and non-iso-FLOP loop sweeps 100M-1.7B.
one_sentence: Diagnoses curse-of-depth variance growth and expert-selection collapse in looped MoE; LOOM fixes them with residual scaling, convex embedding re-injection, loop-specific routers and an EMA looping residual, scaling to 9-12 loops and winning at near-iso-FLOP with 5 loops at 700M.
key_contributions: Two failure modes of deep looped MoE: residual variance growth across loops and routers choosing nearly the same experts each loop.

Recipe: residual branch scale gamma = lambda / (H sqrt(M)), re-injection h0^t = (1 - g_t) h^{t-1} + g_t x with g_t = lambda / (t sqrt(M)), per-loop routers over shared experts, EMA looping residual, segmented backprop (K=3).
Near-iso-FLOP protocol: increase loops H while shrinking top-k so per-token cost H(6+3k) stays about constant.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: FineWeb-style pretraining; 10B tokens (700M iso-FLOP), up to 60B tokens (1.7B)
setup.loops_train: H = 1-12 (iso-FLOP sweep H up to 6)
setup.baselines: non-looped MoE (same parameters), unstabilized looping, embed-inject-only, residual-scale-only

Different matching methods (top-k shrinking vs wall-clock vs stored-layer reduction) may explain the disagreement. Design-space evidence: per-loop routers = step-conditioned routing with shared experts (contrast with Huginn's warning that step-conditioning hurts extrapolation, though LOOM does not test extrapolation). Embedding re-injection here is a decaying convex mix, unlike Huginn's concatenation adapter.

title: Gated Recurrent Transformers: Expressive Depth through Recurrent Modulation
relevance_reason: Prelude-core-coda looped LM with GRU-style elementwise update gate conditioned on state, prelude output and noise; compared to MoR, Ouro, RRT, Huginn-style sampling under isoFLOPs and isoPARAMS.
one_sentence: GRT brackets a shared core iterated R times with prelude/coda and blends each core output into the state through a learned elementwise gate conditioned on state, prelude output and noise; matches GPT-2 Small at iso-FLOPs with about a third of the parameters.
key_contributions: Update h_r = g ⊙ h_{r-1} + (1 - g) ⊙ B_shared(W_proj[h_{r-1} + noise, h_pre]) with gate bias initialized to +4 (near-copy at start).
Unified isoFLOPs and isoPARAMS evaluation at three GPT-2 scales against MoR, heavy-tail Poisson (Huginn-style), Ouro and Relaxed Recursive Transformers retrained under one recipe.
Uniform depth sampling gives emergent early exit (about 92% accuracy at half the recurrences) without auxiliary losses.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: about 9.8B tokens per run (20,000 steps)

setup.benchmarks: validation loss; ARC-C/E, BoolQ, HellaSwag, LAMBADA, OBQA, PIQA, WinoGrande

Gating is an alternative injection/state operator to Huginn's concatenation adapter; state noise at every step echoes Huginn's random init (Huginn reported diffusion-style per-step noise did not help, GRT finds it worth 0.018 nats: a mild contradiction). Key regime finding: at iso-FLOPs dense still wins at 354M/774M with standard tokens, while at iso-params looping wins, consistent with Loopie's argument that iso-param wins do not imply compute efficiency.

title: DiscoLoop: Looping Discrete Embeddings and Continuous Hidden States for Multi-hop Reasoning
relevance_reason: Whole-stack looped transformer whose inter-loop state adds a gated soft decode-then-encode embedding channel; symbolic two-hop reasoning and 440M pretraining vs vanilla loop and PonderLM.
one_sentence: Finds that vanilla looped transformers decode the bridge entity after loop 1 but pass a hidden state misaligned with its token embedding; DiscoLoop adds a gated soft decoded-embedding channel between loops, fixing two-hop OOD generalization and slightly improving 440M pretraining.
key_contributions: Mechanistic diagnosis: looping fixes depth-local fact storage but leaves a representation mismatch between the post-loop hidden state and the clean bridge-token embedding; a training-free realignment nearly closes the gap.

DiscoLoop recurrence: H~(k+1) = H(k+1) + alpha(k) ⊙ RMSNorm(Phi(H(k+1))), where Phi is a temperature-softmax over LM-head logits mapped back through the embedding matrix; alpha is fixed or a d+1-parameter learned gate.
Gains on symbolic and synthetic-language two-hop tasks (ID and OOD) and on 440M/20B-token pretraining vs vanilla loop and PonderLM.

setup.model_sizes: small models for symbolic tasks; 440M for pretraining (d=1024, 24 layers)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 20B tokens of FineWeb-Edu:FineMath 6:4 for pretraining; synthetic two-hop datasets
setup.loops_train: K loops (4 for pretraining)
setup.baselines: vanilla looped transformer (same f_theta), non-looped transformer with K untied copies (FLOP-matched, more params), PonderLM
setup.benchmarks: two-hop ID/OOD accuracy; ARC-C/E, HellaSwag, LAMBADA, PIQA, RACE, SciQ

instantiation.injection: gated additive soft-embedding channel alpha ⊙ RMSNorm(sum_v p_v(h) W[v]) added between loops (no raw input re-injection)
instantiation.sharing: strict tie

claims.evidence_quote: the first loop often makes the correct bridge entity nearly perfectly decodable, yet the corresponding hidden state remains poorly aligned with the bridge token embedding.

claims.claim: On synthetic-language two-hop data, DiscoLoop reaches near 100% ID and about 95% OOD accuracy, the vanilla loop about 90% ID but fails OOD, and the FLOP-matched non-looped model about 40%/20% ID and about 0% OOD.
claims.regime: iso_param (vs vanilla loop) and iso_infer_flop (vs non-looped, which has more params)
claims.evidence_quote: DiscoLoop reaches near 100% ID accuracy and around 95% OOD accuracy, while the vanilla looped transformer reaches around 90% ID accuracy but fails OOD, especially in the reverse format.

claims.evidence_quote: DiscoLoop obtains the best average score, improving over the vanilla Loop baseline from 49.3 to 50.5, and also outperforming PonderLM’s average score of 49.8.

numbers.quote: All models share the same model backbone as Zhu et al. [2025c] with hidden dimension d = 1024, 24 layers, loop step 4, and tied input-output embeddings.

survey_notes: State-carrying design point: injects a discrete (vocabulary-projected) channel between loops instead of re-injecting the raw input embedding (Huginn) or carrying only continuous states (Ouro). Sits between continuous-state looping and PonderLM's embedding-only recurrence. The non-looped baseline is FLOP-matched with more parameters (K untied copies), so 'looping beats non-looped' on two-hop holds at iso-FLOP/iso-effective-depth for this synthetic task. Gains in real pretraining are small and single-seed.

title: Sparse Growing Transformer: Training-Time Sparse Depth Allocation via Progressive Attention Looping
relevance_reason: Component-level looping of selected high-entropy attention heads, grown deep-to-shallow during pretraining; compared with block-level looping at matched params and tokens.
one_sentence: SGT progressively adds recurrence during training only to high-entropy attention heads, starting from deeper layers and growing toward shallower ones; it matches or beats static block looping while adding 1-3% instead of 16-20% training FLOPs.
key_contributions: Analysis: high-entropy heads act as semantic integration hubs; layers mature deep-to-shallow during training.
Training-time structural sparsity: entropy-guided, staged growth of attention-head looping (loop depth up to Kmax per selected layer), FFN applied once.
Theory that concentrating recurrence on high-entropy components speeds convergence; experiments at 573M and 1.2B with LLaMA-style models.

title: Random Recursive Models
relevance_reason: Recurrent-depth model that samples which of L shared layers to apply at each of T steps; evaluated on image classification and reasoning puzzles, not language modeling.
one_sentence: RRM keeps a pool of L learned layers and, at each of T recursive steps, samples one uniformly with replacement per example; it matches or beats fixed-order baselines with 50-75% fewer parameters and supports depth changes and Monte Carlo inference.
key_contributions: Random layer order: up to L^T possible layer sequences instead of a fixed recurrent order.
Depth T adjustable at test time, including beyond training depth, without retraining.
Monte Carlo inference and probabilistic test-time scaling over sampled layer sequences.

title: A Dual-Path Architecture for Scaling Compute and Capacity in LLMs
relevance_reason: Hybrid layer with a per-layer looped (K-times shared) sublayer in parallel with a wide once-applied sublayer, gated per token; iso-FLOP comparisons against pure-loop and pure-wide controls.
one_sentence: Each block runs a deep sublayer looped K times with shared weights in parallel with a wider once-applied sublayer, combined by dense per-token gates; at two iso-FLOP budgets the best mix beats both pure-loop and pure-wide controls with fewer parameters than pure-wide.
key_contributions: Separates compute (sequential looped updates) from capacity (wider FFN parameters) within a layer; ratio alpha sets the FFN FLOP share of the deep path.
Deep path output is a learned halting-style weighted combination of all intermediate loop states (router on state and normalized step index).
Interpretable gates: function words and lexical content go wide; punctuation, symbols and arithmetic tokens go deep.

title: SCORE: Replacing Layer Stacking with Contractive Recurrent Depth
relevance_reason: Replaces stacked layers with one shared block iterated under a relaxed (Euler/Krasnoselskii-Mann) contractive update; LM evidence only at nanoGPT/Shakespeare scale.
one_sentence: SCORE iterates a single shared block with the relaxed update h_{t+1} = (1 - dt) h_t + dt F(h_t) (dt = 0.5 or 1/K), improving convergence on GNNs (ESOL), MLPs and small nanoGPT models with fewer parameters.
key_contributions: Contractive residual recurrence as an explicit Euler step of dh/dt = F(h) - h, i.e. a static residual gate.
Comparison of Euler, Heun, Midpoint and RK4 updates; Euler gives the best cost/performance trade-off.
Applies the same recurrence to GNNs, dense nets and Transformers.

setup.model_sizes: small (nanoGPT on Shakespeare; nanochat 5-minute challenge)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: ESOL; Shakespeare (Gutenberg); nanochat autosearch
setup.loops_train: K fixed
setup.baselines: stacked layers; 0.5 residual at every stage (skip05)
setup.benchmarks: ESOL RMSE; nanoGPT validation loss

instantiation.injection: none; convex relaxation between previous state and block output
instantiation.sharing: strict tie

claims.claim: The relaxed update with step size dt controls contraction and stabilizes iterated application of the shared block; dt = 0.5 and dt = 1/K both work.
claims.evidence_quote: The parameter Δt therefore directly controls the magnitude of the update and can induce a contractive behavior when F is Lipschitz-bounded. In practice, this stabilizes the iterated application of the shared block

claims.claim: Replacing stacked decoder blocks with SCORE steps gives competitive nanoGPT performance with fewer parameters (small-scale evidence).
claims.evidence_quote: Transformers: replacing stacked decoder blocks with recurrent Euler residual steps using a shared block yields competitive performance on nanoGPT with a smaller number of parameters.

limitations: Only tiny language-model experiments (Shakespeare, 5-minute nanochat runs); no FLOP-matched comparisons; mostly qualitative claims about convergence speed.
survey_notes: Normalization/state-update design point: a fixed convex relaxation between loops (Krasnoselskii-Mann iteration), related to LOOM's residual scaling (2610.01153), GRT's learned gate (2608.15062) and Parcae's spectral-radius-bounded injection. Weak LM evidence; cite only as a design variant.

title: LSTM-UT and Recurrent-Depth Transformers on Cellular Automata
relevance_reason: Compares state-carrying mechanisms in recurrent-depth transformers (current state only, CoTFormer expanding cache, LSTM-gated cell) on synthetic cellular-automaton tasks; no LM pretraining.
one_sentence: On Rule 30 cellular automata and delayed recall, a block UT carrying only its current state extrapolates in depth better than CoTFormer's expanding cache; a new LSTM-gated UT (bounded gated cell state) improves both depth extrapolation and recall.
key_contributions: Controlled comparison of three state-carrying designs: Block UT (current state), CoTFormer (current state + expanding KV cache of earlier repeats), LSTM-UT (bounded gated cell).
Interventions show CoTFormer's depth failure comes from the interaction of state and retained history, and that it does not select the requested cached block in delayed recall.
LSTM-UT as a bounded gated-memory alternative.

title: Universal YOCO for Efficient Depth Scaling
relevance_reason: Partial recursion: only the shallow sliding-window self-decoder of a YOCO decoder-decoder is looped, keeping a single global KV cache; MoE 10B-A1.3B trained on 300B tokens.
one_sentence: YOCO-U loops the first half (Self-Decoder, sliding-window attention) of a YOCO model T=3 times and keeps a single global KV cache for the cross-decoder, giving lower loss than YOCO at matched training FLOPs and better data efficiency.
key_contributions: Restrict recursion to shallow efficient-attention layers so extra iterations add only local-window KV cache, preserving YOCO's constant global KV cache and linear prefill.
Scaling comparison vs non-recursive YOCO at equal training FLOPs and equal steps (10B total / 1.3B active MoE, 300B tokens).
Dense 1.3B comparison against Universal Transformer, RINS, ParScale and standard Transformer.

claims.claim: Restricting recursion to shallow efficient-attention layers avoids the KV-cache growth and overhead of whole-network looping as in the Universal Transformer.
claims.evidence_quote: While UT applies recursive computation to the entire network, leading to redundant overhead and potential optimization difficulties, YOCO-U restricts the recursion to the shallow self-decoder modules.

title: Tying the Loop -- Tied Expert Layers in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
relevance_reason: Component-level partial loop: expert FFN weights tied across groups of consecutive MoE layers with per-layer routers and attention; controlled ablation of which components can be shared, including MoEUT-style full tying.
one_sentence: Ties MoE expert weights across groups of g consecutive layers while keeping routers, attention and norms per-layer; at g=4 this cuts total parameters by up to 52% with negligible loss change on OLMoE/Qwen3/DeepSeek-style MoEs up to 7B, and untied 2+2 prelude/coda matter most.
key_contributions: Expert tying as a partial loop (shared FFN experts, distinct attention/routers) with a one-line HuggingFace implementation and tied-parameter LR scaling.
Component ablation: untying attention matters an order of magnitude more than untying routers; a 2+2 untied prelude/coda is the single largest gain; MoEUT-style full tying is clearly worse.
Heterogeneous width expansion: reinvest saved parameters into more experts in tied layers, beating the untied baseline at iso-parameters.

Supports the sandwich template (untied 2+2 prelude/coda) over MoEUT's fully recurrent stack. Note this is not looping in the compute sense (same FLOPs as the untied MoE), so it is a parameter-sharing result, not a recurrent-depth scaling result.

title: How to Loop MoE: Flatten the Experts, Untie the Attention
relevance_reason: Sandwich looped MoE with shared experts/routers and per-pass attention; studies how to distribute experts over layers and passes at fixed expert parameters and compute.
one_sentence: At fixed expert parameters and expert compute, Foil flattens a looped MoE core (fewer layers, more experts per layer, more passes) and gives each pass its own attention while sharing experts and routers; the most flattened (64 experts, 1 layer, 16 passes) ends 0.012 nat below the (8,8,2) baseline at 100B tokens.
key_contributions: Shape (E experts per layer, D layers in looped block, L passes) design study with expert params and per-token expert calls held fixed.
Untied attention per pass (experts and routers shared), adding parameters but no compute; yields more balanced and confident routing.
Design guidance: looping and widening expert layers amplify each other; routing confidence tracks healthy expert use better than load balance; use more experts per layer and more passes.

Favors many passes (up to 16) at fixed compute, contradicting Loopie's R=2 choice (different matching: Foil fixes expert calls, Loopie matches wall-clock).

title: LoopMoE: Unifying Iterative Computation with Mixture-of-Experts for Language Modeling
relevance_reason: Sandwich looped MoE LM with iteration- and token-conditioned adaptive norm, compared to a vanilla MoE at identical total params, per-token FLOPs and active attention/FFN ratio at 3B and 9B.
one_sentence: LoopMoE (2 prefix + 2-layer MoE block x4 + 2 suffix) uses IterAdaLN (affine norm params from iteration index and token state) and rebalances MLA ranks vs expert sizes so it can be matched to a vanilla MoE in total params, per-token FLOPs and active ratio; gains grow from about 1 point (3B) to about 3 points (9B).
key_contributions: IterAdaLN: replaces RMSNorm with adaptive norm conditioned jointly on a sinusoidal iteration embedding and the per-token hidden state, breaking weight-sharing symmetry.
Capacity balancing: adjust MLA Q/KV LoRA ranks and expert hidden size, then expert count, to restore the attention-to-FFN active ratio and total parameters of a well-tuned vanilla MoE.
Strictly matched head-to-head evaluation vs vanilla MoE (same total params, per-token FLOPs, data order) at 3B/200B tokens and 9B/300B tokens.

setup.model_sizes: 3B and 9B total (MoE)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Dolma3Mix; 200B tokens (3B), 300B tokens (9B)
setup.baselines: vanilla MoE with matched totals and FLOPs; dense and dense-loop baselines at token-matched checkpoints
setup.benchmarks: MMLU, HellaSwag, PIQA, WinoGrande, TriviaQA, RACE, BBH, GSM8K, MATH (ARC in ablations)

instantiation.injection: none: re-injection removed; h0 = h_pre then pure recursion, iteration signal through IterAdaLN

claims.evidence_quote: Across nine downstream benchmarks, LoopMoE’s average improvement over its matched vanilla MoE increases from over 1 point at the 3B scale to approximately 3 points at the 9B scale.

claims.claim: Re-injecting the prelude output at every step (Huginn/Parcae-style) suppresses iteration-to-iteration differentiation; LoopMoE removes it and uses pure recursion from h_pre.
claims.evidence_quote: re-inject the prefix output hpre additively at every step, requiring an ill-defined h0 at the first iteration and allowing a constant hpre to dominate the residual stream, thereby suppressing iteration-toiteration differentiation.

claims.claim: Dense loops cannot be matched to a non-looped baseline on both parameters and FLOPs; MoE makes this possible.
claims.evidence_quote: Iterating a dense block multiplies compute without altering parameters, which makes it impossible to simultaneously match a non-looped baseline on both axes.

numbers.quote: Our main 3B LoopMoE comprises 6 unique layers, organized as 2 prefix layers, a 2-layer block that is recurrently applied for 4 iterations with shared weights, and 2 suffix layers, which yields an effective depth of 12 layers.

numbers.what: Token budgets
numbers.quote: all our 3B models consume an identical 200B-token subset of this corpus under the same document ordering and packing configuration, while the token budget for 9B models is 300B tokens.

numbers.quote: For MoE layers, we adopt top-k routing with k = 6 together with a shared expert strategy following (Dai et al., 2024)

survey_notes: One of the cleanest iso-param + iso-FLOP + iso-data looped-vs-non-looped comparisons in the corpus (made possible by MoE). Contradicts Huginn/Parcae/LOOM on input injection: LoopMoE argues per-step re-injection suppresses iteration differentiation and removes it, whereas Huginn argues it is needed for stability/path independence and LOOM ablates it as necessary. Uses step conditioning (iteration index via IterAdaLN), which Huginn reported harms extrapolation; LoopMoE does not test extrapolation beyond K=4. Positive scaling trend from 3B to 9B rests on single runs.

title: Hyper-SET: Designing Transformers via Hyperspherical Energy Minimization
relevance_reason: Recurrent-depth (single shared layer) transformer derived from iterative hyperspherical energy minimization; evaluated on Sudoku and vision, not language modeling.
one_sentence: Derives attention, feedforward and RMSNorm as steps of energy minimization on the hypersphere, yielding a one-layer recurrent-depth Transformer (Hyper-SET) that matches or beats standard and energy-based Transformers on Sudoku and image tasks and extrapolates in iterations.
key_contributions: Top-down energy-based derivation: symmetric attention and feedforward with RMS normalization as iterative optimization steps with shared parameters.
Recurrent-depth instantiation with one set of shared parameters; variants (linear attention, gated FF) and learnable step sizes.
Depth-wise LoRA adapters per iteration as a relaxed-sharing scaling extension.

title: Chain-of-Experts: Unlocking the Communication Power of Mixture-of-Experts Models
relevance_reason: Component-level looping inside each MoE layer: the shared expert pool is applied C times sequentially with a per-iteration router and inner residuals, at fixed compute vs standard MoE.
one_sentence: Chain-of-Experts iterates each MoE layer's experts C=2 times with an independent router per iteration and inner residual connections (splitting the same number of experts across iterations); at fixed compute it lowers math validation loss from 1.20 to 1.12 vs standard MoE.
key_contributions: Intra-layer expert iteration with per-iteration routers, keeping total experts used per token per layer unchanged.
New scaling axis: 2x expert iterations matches 3x expert selections (width) with 17.6-42% less memory than other scaling strategies.
Ablations: removing iteration-specific gating or inner residuals significantly hurts.

title: VersatileFFN: Achieving Parameter Efficiency in LLMs via Adaptive Wide-and-Deep Reuse
relevance_reason: Component-level FFN reuse: a depth path loops the same FFN a token-specific number of times (Gumbel-softmax controller) alongside a width path of virtual sub-experts from the same FFN; compared to k-loop FFN baselines.
one_sentence: Replaces each FFN with a shared base FFN used two ways: virtual sub-experts (width) and a token-adaptive recursive loop (depth, up to Lmax), fused by a difficulty-aware gate; at 354M-1.21B it beats fixed k-loop FFN baselines at equal parameters.
key_contributions: Width-versatile path: mixture of sub-experts carved from one shared FFN, no extra parameters.
Depth-versatile path: same FFN applied a token-specific number of loops chosen by a Gumbel-softmax controller.
Difficulty-aware fusion using the expected loop count as a token-difficulty proxy.

title: Zero Token-Driven Deep Thinking in LLMs: Unlocking the Full Potential of Existing Parameters via Cyclic Refinement
relevance_reason: Head-tail decoupled cycling of middle layers (sandwich) with a learnable-key zero-value token per layer whose attention guides early exit; from-scratch and fine-tuned (GPT-2, OPT) small LMs.
one_sentence: ZTT keeps the first and last layers unshared and cycles only middle layers, adding per-cycle zero tokens (trainable key, zero value) from a pool whose attention mass signals layer importance and triggers early exit; it recovers most of a 6-layer model's accuracy with 3 layers' parameters.

Shows the benefit is largely due to convergence.

Across prefix-sum, mazes, visual reasoning, image classification, optimization and graph tasks, AA strongly correlates with accuracy at many more test iterations than training.

limitations: Gains are at equal parameters, not equal compute; scale details not extracted.
survey_notes: Supports the Topological Trouble argument (2604.17121) empirically: depth-only recurrence (Ladder) helps LM perplexity at equal parameters but does not solve state tracking; recurrence over time does. Early (2021) iso-param looped-LM evidence.

title: Neural Parameter Allocation Search
relevance_reason: Learned cross-layer parameter sharing under a fixed parameter budget (Shapeshifter Networks); generalized sharing without fixed-depth recurrence, so not looped in depth.
one_sentence: Defines Neural Parameter Allocation Search (training a network under an arbitrary fixed parameter budget) and Shapeshifter Networks, which learn where and how to share parameters across layers, covering low-budget compression and a high-budget regime that adds capacity without increasing inference FLOPs.
key_contributions: NPAS task: arbitrary parameter budget decoupled from architecture.
Shapeshifter Networks: learned grouping of layers into shared parameter pools with generated layer weights.
Evaluated on nine architectures across four tasks including ImageNet and transformers.

setup.model_sizes: various (nine architectures)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: ImageNet and other tasks incl. transformers
setup.baselines: hand-crafted sharing (UT/ALBERT-style), compression methods
setup.benchmarks: task accuracy at given parameter budgets

claims.claim: Existing sharing methods rely on hand-crafted strategies and many identical layers; SSNs learn where and how to share for any parameter budget, including a high-budget regime adding capacity without more inference FLOPs.
claims.evidence_quote: NPAS covers both low-budget regimes, which produce compact networks, as well as a novel high-budget regime, where additional capacity can be added to boost performance without increasing inference FLOPs.

numbers.what: Venue
numbers.quote: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2022 N EURAL PARAMETER A LLOCATION S EARCH Bryan A. Plummer*†, Nikoli Dryden*‡

venue: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2022

Also covers the title-only assignment entry 'Shapeshifter Networks: Cross-layer Parameter Sharing for Scalable and Effective Deep Learning' (same paper, earlier title).

title: TextNCA: Neural Cellular Automata for Language Modeling via Hierarchical Local Attention
relevance_reason: Iterated weight-shared local-attention LM (neural cellular automaton) with hierarchical stages; analytical probe of what iteration contributes in LM.
one_sentence: Hierarchical TextNCA (three stages of shared-weight windowed attention iterated T_s times) does not match a parameter-matched Transformer on WikiText-103 at 30M; most of its behavior comes from the narrow-to-wide window schedule, with iteration adding a bounded benefit peaking at T_s=4.

setup.model_sizes: about 30M
setup.train_tokens_or_data: WikiText-103, 60k steps
setup.loops_train: T_s per stage (optimum 4); random T_s variant
setup.baselines: Transformer-6L, Transformer-12L, non-iterating sliding-window Transformer with same schedule
setup.benchmarks: perplexity

claims.claim: At about 30M parameters the hierarchical iterated model is worse than parameter-matched Transformers.
claims.evidence_quote: The model does not match a parameter-matched Transformer at this scale (Hier-TextNCA $60.3$ vs.\ Transformer-6L $52.8$ and Transformer-12L $44.7$ PPL)

claims.claim: Iteration adds a bounded benefit with an optimum at T_s=4 and U-shaped degradation beyond; the GRU gate and per-step embeddings are required, and random T_s training gives an inference knob at higher PPL.
claims.evidence_quote: Iteration adds a smaller bounded benefit on top of the schedule, with a clear optimum at $T_s{=}4$ and a U-shaped degradation beyond it.

numbers.what: PPL: Hier-TextNCA vs Transformer-6L vs 12L
numbers.quote: The model does not match a parameter-matched Transformer at this scale (Hier-TextNCA $60.3$ vs.\ Transformer-6L $52.8$ and Transformer-12L $44.7$ PPL)

title: UniPool: Learning Expert-to-Layer Ownership from Brief Global Access
relevance_reason: MoE expert-to-layer allocation learned from a brief global shared-pool phase; experts are shared across layers only transiently (UniPool-Full keeps a global pool), no recurrence in depth.
one_sentence: Gives every layer its own router over one global expert pool for a short phase, then locks a disjoint expert-to-layer allocation; lowers held-out loss vs vanilla MoE at equal expert budget and FLOPs from 182M to 1.5B; keeping the global pool also helps with fewer expert parameters.

claims.claim: Same expert budget and routed FLOPs: learned allocation lowers loss by 0.024-0.037 vs vanilla MoE across scales up to 1.5B.
claims.evidence_quote: With the same expert-FFN budget and routed expert FLOPs, this recipe lowers held-out loss relative to vanilla MoE by 0.024-0.037 across five dense-equivalent scales from 182M to 1.5B

claims.claim: A globally shared expert pool across layers (UniPool-Full) beats vanilla MoE with only 50-66.7% of its expert parameters.
claims.evidence_quote: Keeping full-pool access throughout training (UniPool-Full) also improves over vanilla MoE at four scales and outperforms it with only 66.7% (182M) to 50% (469M and 650M) of its expert parameters.

survey_notes: Cross-layer expert sharing without recurrence; related to Expert Tying (2606.16825) and Foil (2609.35751): a shared expert pool across depth is parameter-efficient. Not a loop.

title: Write Back the $Δ$: Revisiting the Same Tokens with Fresh Representations
relevance_reason: Feedback of deeper residual increments to earlier layers (a second synchronous pass = depth recurrence; streaming variant feeds subsequent tokens).
one_sentence: ReFlux writes the depth increment (difference between deeper and earlier residual states) back to earlier layers via a learnable feedback graph; synchronous feedback (two passes) lowers perplexity on ten corpora and improves accuracy 2.1-2.3 points; streaming feedback keeps most gains at 1x backbone FLOPs.

claims.claim: Feeding back the depth increment (not the full state) is a better recurrence signal; synchronous ReFlux reduces perplexity and improves accuracy, up to 4.7 points on multi-hop reasoning.
claims.evidence_quote: synchronous ReFlux consistently reduces perplexity across ten language-modeling corpora, and improves accuracy by 2.1–2.3 points, with gains reaching 4.7 points on multi-hop reasoning.

claims.claim: Streaming feedback to subsequent tokens keeps most gains at the base model's theoretical backbone FLOPs.
claims.evidence_quote: Streaming ReFlux further retains most of these gains while preserving the base model's 1x theoretical backbone FLOPs.

numbers.what: Synchronous cost
numbers.quote: Synchronous execution performs two passes and therefore incurs roughly 2× prefill and decode cost; Original Recirculation has similar accounting.

survey_notes: State-passing design point: inject the depth delta (increment) of a previous pass into earlier layers, a history injection variant; streaming variant turns depth recurrence into cross-token recurrence (cf. Topological Trouble 2604.17121 on step-axis recurrence).

title: Reproducing Recurrent Transformers: The CoTFormer
relevance_reason: Reproduction study of CoTFormer (weight-tied repeats with attendable intermediate states) plus algorithmic OOD tests.
one_sentence: Reproduces CoTFormer perplexities within confidence bounds, finds reserved first/last layers alone are not more parameter-efficient on perplexity, observes training-time reorganization of repeat-state attention, and finds no OOD gain from more loops on a shifted-start counting task.

setup.model_sizes: 24-layer middle block x5 with reserved layers (2 -> 21x5 -> 1); small algorithmic models
setup.train_tokens_or_data: OpenWebText2 (40k-60k steps); shifted-start counting; p-hop induction
setup.loops_train: n_repeat 2, 3, 5
setup.baselines: Block Universal Transformer, standard Transformers
setup.benchmarks: perplexity; OOD accuracy

claims.claim: Base CoTFormer perplexity results reproduce exactly within confidence intervals.
claims.evidence_quote: Ours represents a single-seed evaluation showing per-batch 95% confidence intervals. ∆ values fall within these boundaries, confirming exact reproducibility.

claims.claim: More loop depth did not improve OOD extrapolation on shifted-start counting for BUT, CoTFormer or Transformers.
claims.evidence_quote: Increasing loop depth did not improve extrapolation under teacher-forced sequence prediction, suggesting that models may rely on positional shortcuts rather than an iterative counting procedure.

survey_notes: Independent reproduction supports CoTFormer's perplexity claims but not a reasoning/extrapolation benefit from looping on a counting task; complements LSTM-UT 2609.19521 (same group of authors) which finds CoTFormer's cache hurts depth extrapolation. Original CoTFormer is 2310.10845 (group b).

title: Rethinking Parameter Sharing as Graph Coloring for Structured Compression
relevance_reason: Cross-layer parameter sharing for compression chosen by a Hessian-based coloring criterion; no added depth/compute.
one_sentence: Casts cross-layer sharing as a coloring function over layers and selects sharing groups by projecting perturbations onto the Hessian's low-curvature subspace; outperforms heuristic sharing at higher compression.

claims.claim: A second-order geometric criterion selects sharing groups that beat heuristic sharing strategies at higher compression ratios.
claims.evidence_quote: Across diverse architectures and tasks, Geo-Sharing consistently outperforms state-of-the-art heuristic sharing strategies, achieving higher compression ratios with smaller accuracy degradation.

survey_notes: Compression-oriented sharing (which layers share), relevant only to the 'how much is shared' axis; not looped.

title: Learning Fine-grained Parameter Sharing via Sparse Tensor Decomposition
relevance_reason: Compression of transformer MLPs by cross-block shared basis plus sparse layer-specific projections; no recurrence.
one_sentence: FiPS factorizes concatenated MLP weights across a group of blocks into a shared basis and sparse per-layer projections (SVD init, reconstruction training), compressing ViTs by up to 33% (<1% loss) and LLMs by up to 20%.

claims.claim: Cross-block shared basis with sparse layer-specific projections compresses ViTs and LLMs better than SVD baselines at matched compression.
claims.evidence_quote: FiPS compresses Vision Transformers (ViTs) by up to 33% with less than 1% top-1 accuracy loss on ImageNet-1k, and by up to 57% when combined with fine-tuning.

survey_notes: Relaxed sharing for compression (shared basis + layer-specific sparse factors); boundary case of the sharing axis, not looped.

title: The Uncanny Similarity of Recurrence and Depth

title: Relaxed Recursive Transformers: Effective Parameter Sharing with Layer-wise LoRA
relevance_reason: Converts pretrained LLMs into looped (CYCLE-tied) models and relaxes tying with per-iteration LoRA; defines the LoRA-relaxed sharing axis.
one_sentence: Initializes a looped block from a pretrained LLM (Stepwise/Average/Lower), uptrains on up to 60B tokens with distillation, adds per-loop LoRA deltas (SVD-initialized) to interpolate between tied and full models, and proposes continuous depth-wise batching with early exit.
key_contributions: Recursive Transformer: CYCLE tying of a block of L/B layers looped B times, initialized from a pretrained dense model (Stepwise best for strict tying, Average best with LoRA)
Relaxed Recursive Transformer: iteration-specific LoRA modules on all shared linear weights, initialized by truncated SVD of residuals; rank interpolates between recursive and vanilla
Continuous depth-wise batching + early exit; simulated throughput gains up to 2.66x

title: PonderLM: Pretraining Language Models to Ponder in Continuous Space
relevance_reason: Re-invokes the whole LM s times per token, feeding back a probability-weighted embedding; a whole-stack loop with a vocabulary-space bottleneck, pretrained at up to 2.8B/300B.
one_sentence: PonderLM runs the full LM repeatedly within one token step, turning each predicted distribution into a top-K weighted embedding that is residually added to the original input embeddings; PonderPythia trained on 300B Pile tokens beats official Pythia at equal parameters and data.
key_contributions: Pondering loop: state passed between iterations is the expected token embedding under the model's own prediction (top-K=100), accumulated onto the original input embeddings
Pretraining from scratch on GPT-2, LLaMA and Pythia architectures (405M-1.4B and Pythia suite to 2.8B on the full 300B-token Pile)
Ablation at 70M against hidden-state feedback, projected hidden state, looped Transformer and pause tokens at equal extra steps; randomized steps [1,10] yields test-time scaling

Headline Pythia comparisons are iso-param/iso-data but cost about 4x forward compute at s=3, so 'surpasses Pythia-6.9B' is not compute-fair; the TinyLlama comparison is unmatched. title: Intern-S2-Mobius: Foundation Model with Decoupled Knowledge and Reasoning
relevance_reason: Shares one global FFN 'Memory' (MoE-partitioned) across all layers with per-layer attention Reasoners and describes latent recurrence, but the text never specifies a loop count, iteration rule or tied block; component-level cross-depth sharing.
one_sentence: Mobius decouples knowledge (a single globally shared, MoE-partitioned FFN memory) from reasoning (attention Reasoners) so every layer can query all knowledge; a 7B-A1B model from scratch matches a Transformer with 62.6% of the data, and a Qwen3.5-35B conversion gives ~4x end-to-end speedup via shorter CoT.
key_contributions: Global shared FFN knowledge pool (horizontal concatenation of FFNs, block-wise MoE partition at scale) accessed by all attention layers: 'backward residual connection'
Training-from-scratch 7B-A1B comparison vs Transformer on 1TB tokens; continual pretraining of Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on 1TB tokens plus SFT and RL
Claims of dynamic latent reasoning and multi-token (MTP) drafting, with shorter CoT driving end-to-end throughput

claims.evidence_quote: Mobius also scales computation through latent recurrence, but performs each update over only a few layers while retaining access to the full shared Memory.

title: Recursive Inference Scaling: A Winning Path to Scalable Inference in Language and Multimodal Systems
relevance_reason: Compute-matched comparison of 59 parameter-sharing/recursion signatures; finds recursing the first half of the network (A^r B) best.
one_sentence: Under matched parameters and training FLOPs, RINS (split the model into equal halves A,B and apply A r times before B) beats 55+ sharing variants including MobileLLM's repeat-all-over and Huginn-style AB^rC, improves scaling exponents, and with stochastic depth plus linear adapters is no-regret.
key_contributions: Signature/degree taxonomy of recursive architectures and a training-FLOP-matched sweep (59 models, 300M/600M) where recursive models see fewer tokens
RINS (A^r B) wins; optimal r grows with training compute; fitted data scaling laws show better exponent and asymptote
Stochastic RINS (binomial number of rounds) with per-r linear output adapters (<1% params) is no-regret at 1x inference; KV-cache sharing variant; gains in SigLIP but not in supervised ViT

Directly contradicts MobileLLM's preference for repeat-all-over at >1B scale (gains vanish under FLOP matching). title: PonderNet: Learning to Ponder
relevance_reason: Probabilistic halting for any recurrent step function (incl. UT-style transformers); the standard learned-exit objective reused by later LoopLMs.
one_sentence: PonderNet makes halting a Markov process with per-step conditional halting probabilities, trains on the expected loss over all steps plus a KL to a geometric prior, and samples the halt at test time; it beats ACT on parity extrapolation and uses fewer steps than UT on bAbI.
key_contributions: Halting as a generalized geometric distribution over steps, with exact, unbiased, low-variance gradients (vs ACT and REINFORCE)
Loss = expected per-step reconstruction loss + KL(p_n || truncated geometric prior lambda_p) that encourages exploration rather than minimal steps
Train/test asymmetry: unroll until cumulative halting probability exceeds 1 - epsilon in training, sample Bernoulli halts at evaluation

setup.loops_test: sampled halting per step, optionally capped at N

'Steps' in the bAbI comparison is a count reported by the authors, not FLOPs.

title: Can You Learn an Algorithm? Generalizing from Easy to Hard Problems with Recurrent Networks
relevance_reason: Weight-tied recurrent residual block between an encoder and head, trained on easy problems and unrolled longer at test; foundational easy-to-hard loop extrapolation evidence (vision/algorithmic, not language).
one_sentence: Recurrent ResNets (encoder, 4-layer weight-tied block iterated, conv head) trained on small prefix-sum, maze and chess instances solve larger/harder instances by running more iterations at test time, outperforming feed-forward nets of equal effective depth.
key_contributions: Easy-to-hard 'logical extrapolation' protocol with datasets of quantifiable difficulty (prefix sums, mazes, chess puzzles)
Recurrent vs feed-forward models matched on effective depth (only difference: weight sharing) show recurrent models extrapolate better
Test-time extra iterations improve accuracy on harder problems; per-iteration outputs resemble sequential algorithms; confidence used to pick the output iteration

setup.model_sizes: fully convolutional ResNets, 512 internal channels (mazes, chess); parameter counts not stated
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 32-bit prefix sums (test 40/44-bit); small mazes (test large); 600,000 easy chess puzzles (rating < 1,385)
setup.loops_train: fixed iterations (e.g. 10 for prefix sums, 20 for mazes)
setup.loops_test: more iterations than training; output taken from the iteration with highest confidence
setup.baselines: feed-forward ResNets of comparable effective depth (no weight sharing)
setup.benchmarks: accuracy on harder prefix sums, larger mazes, harder chess puzzles

claims.claim: At equal effective depth (recurrent vs feed-forward differ only by weight sharing), recurrent models extrapolate better to harder instances.
claims.evidence_quote: In fact, the only difference during training between a feed-forward and recurrent model of the same effective depth is that the weights are shared between the residual blocks in the recurrent models.

claims.claim: Adding test-time iterations lets recurrent models solve harder problems: maze models trained with 20 iterations exceed 70% on large mazes with 5 extra iterations.
claims.evidence_quote: models trained with 20 iterations can achieve upward of 70% accuracy on large mazes using 5 additional iterations at test time.

claims.claim: The gain is not just receptive-field growth: feed-forward models with the same receptive field as 16-iteration recurrent models are much worse on longer prefix sums.
claims.evidence_quote: This makes it clear that the increase in accuracy of recurrent models does not simply occur because the receptive field grows with added iterations

numbers.quote: 600,000 puzzles of difficulty rating less than 1,385 are used for training, and testing is performed on

limitations: Vision/algorithmic tasks only; outputs can degrade after extra iterations (pixels flip in mazes); chess gains are modest; output iteration selected by confidence; no adaptive halting.
venue: 35th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2021).
survey_notes: Lineage: early easy-to-hard recurrent-depth evidence; uses an encoder-core-head sandwich (k_P=1 conv, k_R=4-layer block, k_C=3 conv for prefix sums) with plain residual state and no input injection. Shows extrapolation is real but unstable after extra iterations (maze pixels flip), foreshadowing the overthinking problem studied in LMs (e.g. 2609.36636 knowledge degradation). Regime: iso-effective-depth (recurrent has fewer params).

title: MoRE: Mixture of Reused Experts
relevance_reason: Cross-layer sharing of MoE expert pools between adjacent layers with per-layer routers and depth embeddings; not iterating a block, but a sharing-axis design between MoE and MoEUT.
one_sentence: MoRE ties expert pools across groups of R adjacent layers (A-A-B-B), keeping per-layer routers and attention and adding a learnable depth embedding before routing; it beats DeepSeek-v3-style MoE, dense and MoEUT at matched parameters and FLOPs from 114M to 1.15B.
key_contributions: Reuse blocks: R adjacent layers share a 2N expert pool, enlarging routing combinations without extra parameters and allowing the same expert at consecutive depths
Learnable per-layer depth embedding added before routing so shared experts know their depth
Matched-parameter, matched-FLOP and matched-expert comparisons with paired bootstrap significance; block (consecutive) sharing beats non-aligned and random sharing

setup.model_sizes: 114M-1.15B (Small/Medium/Large)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: about 6.55B C4 tokens, context 1024, batch 64; FineWeb for generalization
setup.baselines: DeepSeek-v3 MoE, Qwen3MoE, Mixtral, dense (FLOP-matched), MoEUT
setup.benchmarks: C4 validation perplexity; OLMo3 downstream suite

claims.claim: At matched total parameters and FLOPs per forward pass, MoRE has lower perplexity and stronger downstream accuracy than standard MoE, dense and MoEUT baselines.
claims.evidence_quote: MoRE consistently achieves lower perplexity and stronger downstream performance than standard MoEs and state-of-the-art weight-sharing architectures at matched compute and parameter budgets

claims.evidence_quote: Block sharing achieves the lowest PPL (18.71), outperforming both Non-aligned (18.82) and Random sharing (18.83), the latter of which averages around the performance of the DeepSeek baseline.

limitations: Main backbone only to 1.15B, other backbones to 114M; ~6.55B tokens; optimal R at larger scale unknown; MoEUT configuration had to be adjusted to approximate matching.
survey_notes: Hybrid on the sharing axis: shares FFN experts only between adjacent layers (like Takase-Kiyono SEQUENCE sharing) with step/depth embeddings; claims to beat MoEUT under its own protocol (same C4 recipe as MoEUT), which contrasts with MoEUT's claim of beating parameter-matched MoE/dense. Agrees with ALBERT/RINS that what is shared and where matters (block > random). Depth embedding here is a step-conditioning signal, cf. timestep debates (Huginn vs 2609.36636).

title: CART: Context-Anchored Recurrent Transformer -- A Parameter-Efficient Architecture with Learned Stability
relevance_reason: Prelude/shared-core/coda looped LM where the core cross-attends to a KV anchor computed once by the prelude, with an LTI stability gate; reports careful negative results.
one_sentence: CART computes K,V once from a P-layer prelude (MLA) and has a shared core cross-attend to that frozen anchor for R loops with a sigmoid LTI gate; at ~1B tokens it loses to parameter-matched dense baselines and extra test-time loops hurt.
key_contributions: Once-computed KV anchor: shared-weight core cross-attends causally to prelude K,V rather than re-injecting the prelude state additively or by concatenation
Sigmoid-gated LTI residual h <- sigma(a)*h_in + f(h) guaranteeing spectral radius < 1; learned rho settles in [0.79, 0.83]

Two-stage single-GPU study (64 configs at ~49M tokens, 36 configs at ~1B tokens) showing short-run hyperparameter rankings reverse, prelude depth beats loop count, and loops lose to dense at parameter parity

setup.model_sizes: d in {256,512,768,1024}; ~75M stored parameters at d=1024 (125M for R=10 config)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Stage 1: 3,000 steps (~49M tokens); Stage 2: 30,500 steps (~1B tokens), seq len 1024
setup.loops_train: fixed R in {2,4,6,8} (Stage 1), {6,8,10} (Stage 2)
setup.loops_test: variable R tested at inference on best d=1024 model; more than trained degrades
setup.baselines: 7-layer Dense (stored-parameter parity ~75M), 12-layer Dense (effective-parameter parity ~105M), 17-layer FLOP-matched Dense
setup.benchmarks: WikiText perplexity; HellaSwag, LAMBADA, PIQA

claims.claim: At d=1024 the looped CART loses to a dense model with the same stored parameters by 1-2% and to a dense model with the same effective parameters by ~10%.
claims.evidence_quote: loses to a parameter-matched Dense baseline by 1–2% on stored-parameter parity and by ∼ 10% on effective-parameter parity.

claims.evidence_quote: running more iterations than trained consistently degrades performance on HellaSwag, LAMBADA, and PIQA, a clean negative result for test-time compute scaling under our recipe.

claims.evidence_quote: Stage 2 finds R=6 best at d ≥ 512 and R=8 best at d=256 – flipping all four per-scale predictions.

numbers.quote: a 7-layer Dense matching CART's stored parameter count (∼ 75M) and a 12-layer Dense matching CART's effective parameter count at R=6 (∼ 105M).
