Agrees with 2609.36636 and RINS that unshared prelude depth matters. Methodological warning: short screens mis-rank loop counts.

title: Ouroboros: Dynamic Weight Generation for Recursive Transformers via Input-Conditioned LoRA
relevance_reason: Retrofits a pretrained LLM into prelude / one looped layer / coda with a hypernetwork that generates per-step, input-conditioned LoRA modulation and a gated recurrence.
one_sentence: Ouroboros keeps 17 of Qwen2.5-3B's 36 layers (8 prelude, 1 looped layer, 8 coda, all frozen), loops the middle layer N times with a Controller that outputs per-step diagonal modulations of frozen SVD-initialized LoRA bases, plus an identity-biased gate; training loss improves but held-out loss does not.
key_contributions: Controller hypernetwork (mean-pooled hidden state + step embedding) producing input-dependent diagonal modulation of 7 LoRA targets per recurrence step
Frozen LoRA bases initialized by SVD of removed layers' weight residuals; gated recurrence biased to 88% retention plus per-step LayerNorm
Ablation vs static per-step LoRA over depths 1-16 and ranks 8-64; honest report of no held-out improvement

setup.model_sizes: Qwen2.5-3B pruned to 17 layers; 9.2M trainable parameters
setup.train_tokens_or_data: FineWeb-edu (token count not stated)
setup.loops_train: fixed depths N in {1,4,8,16}
setup.baselines: unmodified 17-layer pruned baseline, static per-step LoRA (RingFormer/Relaxed-Recursive style)
setup.benchmarks: training loss; held-out loss on 12 passages

claims.claim: Against equivalently sized static per-step LoRA, the input-conditioned Controller gives lower training loss at all depths and ranks (largest gap 1.44 at depth 1).
claims.evidence_quote: yet outperforms equivalently-sized static per-step LoRA by 1.44 loss points at depth 1 and remains ahead across all tested depths (1, 4, 8, 16) and ranks (8, 32, 64).

claims.claim: Gated recurrence is essential: recursive layer application without the gate makes the model strictly worse.
claims.evidence_quote: We also find that gated recurrence is essential: without it, recursive layer application makes the model strictly worse.

claims.claim: Gains are in-distribution only: on held-out text the Controller does not beat the 17-layer baseline.
claims.evidence_quote: on held-out text, the Controller does not yet improve over the baseline, a limitation we attribute to frozen downstream layers

numbers.what: Training loss reduction vs 17-layer baseline
numbers.quote: O UROBOROS reduces training loss by 43.4% over the unmodified 17-layer baseline, recovering 51.3% of the performance gap caused by layer removal.

numbers.what: Trainable parameters
numbers.quote: O UROBOROS system adds 9.2M trainable parameters (0.6% of the base model).

numbers.what: Prelude/recurrent/coda split of Qwen2.5-3B
numbers.quote: For Qwen2.5-3B (L = 36), we use P = 8, R = 18, C = 8, retaining 17 of 36 layers.

limitations: Only training-distribution gains; no held-out improvement; frozen prelude/coda; no downstream benchmarks; token budget not stated.
survey_notes: Represents 'dynamic generated weights' on the sharing axis (input-conditioned per-step LoRA via hypernetwork), beyond static per-step LoRA (Relaxed Recursive, RingFormer). Weak evidence: training-loss only, no held-out gains, so treat as a design proposal. Supports gating as necessary for deep recursion (cf. CART's LTI gate 2606.01495). The PDF carries a NeurIPS 2023 template footer, so venue is left null.

title: Looped Transformers with Source-Centered State Evolution
relevance_reason: Proposes a new state-passing/injection rule for looped Transformers: evolve deviations from a once-computed input anchor with a zero-deviation mask, instead of additive source re-injection.
one_sentence: SCSE computes an input-conditioned anchor h* once, recurs only on the deviation from it with a mask making the anchor an exact fixed point (removing the 'zero-deviation forcing bias' of additive injection), and lowers perplexity across loop depths versus additive-injection, tuned and step-conditioned shared-block baselines up to 139.2M parameters.
key_contributions: Identifies a source-driven degree of freedom (zero-deviation forcing bias) created by additive input re-injection in looped Transformers
Source-centered recurrence in anchor coordinates with a zero-deviation mask: exact anchor invariance by construction while nonzero deviations drive computation
Controlled comparisons against looped, tuned-adapter, capacity-matched and sinusoidal step-conditioned baselines; training with loop depth sampled uniformly in 1-8, evaluation to T=48

setup.model_sizes: 22M, 50M, 95.6M, up to 139.2M parameters
setup.train_tokens_or_data: WikiText-2, WikiText-103, direct web-corpus pretraining (token counts not stated in extracted text)
setup.loops_train: loop depth sampled uniformly from {1,...,8}
setup.loops_test: fixed T in {4,8,12,16,24,32,48} and adaptive stopping
setup.baselines: additive-injection looped Transformer, tuned adapter, recurrent-step-conditioned adapter, parameter-matched unshared controls
setup.benchmarks: WikiText perplexity, held-out web text, LAMBADA, adaptive-depth evaluation

claims.claim: SCSE attains lower mean perplexity than the looped baseline and stronger capacity-matched/tuned adapters at every evaluated loop depth (22M, WikiText-103).
claims.evidence_quote: The capacity-matched and tuned adapters are substantially stronger than the looped Transformer baseline, yet SCSE attains lower mean PPL than all three baselines at every loop depth reported in Appendix Table 5.

claims.claim: Sinusoidal recurrent-step conditioning is a strong baseline at 50M (151.1 to 125.7 PPL at T=8) but SCSE remains best at every depth (123.1 at T=8, 156.4 at T=48).
claims.evidence_quote: At this scale, SCSE attains the lowest PPL among the compared sharedblock methods at every measured loop depth, reaching 123.1 at T = 8, 135.5 at T = 24, and 156.4 at T = 48.

claims.claim: The theory shows the forcing bias of additive injection can be harmful, neutral or beneficial; SCSE fixes it to zero for exact anchor invariance.
claims.evidence_quote: Our theory shows that the zero-deviation forcing bias is a design degree of freedom whose task effect can be harmful, neutral, or beneficial

numbers.what: Step-conditioned adapter vs looped baseline at 50M (T=8, T=48)
numbers.quote: The adapter improves the looped Transformer baseline from 151.1 to 125.7 PPL at T = 8 and from 178.9 to 160.1 at T = 48.

numbers.what: Training loop-depth range
numbers.quote: We call T ≤ 8 the training loopdepth range and T > 8 extra-loop evaluation.

numbers.what: Largest shared-block comparison
numbers.quote: context lengths from 128 to 1024, and shared-block comparisons up to 139.2M parameters, SCSE improves the controlled recurrent quality frontier.

limitations: Small models (<=139.2M) and small corpora; perplexity-only quality frontier; perplexities rise with extra loops for all methods.
survey_notes: Injection-operator design entry: replaces additive I(s,e)=s+W e with anchor-relative deviation recurrence (fixed point at anchor), related to fixed-point/DEQ views. Shows step conditioning helps a plain looped model substantially at 50M (supporting 2609.36636, contrasting Huginn's warning) but is beaten by SCSE. All evidence at <=139M on perplexity.

title: Reshape and Recur: Improving SSMs with Input Reshaping and Depth Recurrence
relevance_reason: Depth recurrence (periodic weight tying, AAAAAA/ABABAB/ABCABC) applied to SSM stacks on time-series classification/regression; not language.
one_sentence: Loops SSM blocks across depth with periodic tying patterns (period m in {1,2,3,6} for L=6), optional block-wise supervision and a prediction-change stopping rule, matching independent 6-block SSMs with 5.3-5.9x fewer parameters on time-series tasks; input reshaping is a complementary gain.
key_contributions: Periodic depth-recurrence family AAAAAA/ABABAB/ABCABC/ABCDEF for four SSMs (LRU, S5, LinOSS, LrcSSM)
Final-layer vs block-wise loss supervision and an adaptive stopping rule on relative prediction change
Input reshaping (concatenate or re-chunk time steps) as an orthogonal improvement

setup.model_sizes: small SSMs; fully shared variant has 5.3-5.9x fewer parameters than 6-block baseline
setup.train_tokens_or_data: six time-series benchmarks (input dims 6-63, sequence lengths 400-50,000) incl. Heartbeat, MotorImagery, SCP1/2, Worms, PPG-DaLiA
setup.loops_train: fixed L=6 block applications
setup.baselines: independent 6-block SSMs (ABCDEF)
setup.benchmarks: classification accuracy, PPG-DaLiA regression loss

claims.claim: A single SSM block applied 6 times (AAAAAA) stays competitive with 6 independent blocks while reducing parameters 5.3-5.9x.
claims.evidence_quote: In particular, m = 1 (AAAAAA) reduces the total parameter count by 5.3–5.9× while remaining competitive across several datasets.

claims.claim: A simple prediction-change stopping rule selects 2-5 repetitions instead of the trained 6 while maintaining accuracy (stopping does not imply hidden-state convergence).
claims.evidence_quote: For the AAAAAA model, the stopping criterion typically selects between 2 and 5 repetitions, compared with the fixed 6 repetitions used during training, while maintaining classification performance.

numbers.what: Parameter reduction of fully shared SSM
numbers.quote: m = 1 (AAAAAA) reduces the total parameter count by 5.3–5.9× while remaining competitive across several datasets.

numbers.what: Reshaping gains (no recurrence): LRU Heartbeat, S5 MotorImagery
numbers.quote: most notably for LRUs on the Heartbeat dataset (71.3% → 75.5%), and for S5 on the MotorImagery dataset (54.4% → 61.8%).

limitations: Time-series tasks only; small models; neither supervision strategy dominates; stopping criterion heuristic.
survey_notes: Beyond-Transformer evidence that depth looping is architecture-agnostic (SSM blocks); cyclic periodic tying taxonomy parallels RINS signatures and MoEUT grouping (ABAB). Convergence-style stopping on output change is a cheap halting baseline.

title: Mixture of Universal Experts: Scaling Virtual Width via Depth-Width Transformation
relevance_reason: MoE whose layers share a pool of layer-agnostic 'universal experts' reused across depth (recursive expert reuse), with a trajectory-state router; cross-layer sharing rather than iterating a block.
one_sentence: MoUE adds a shared pool of universal experts reachable from multiple layers via a staggered rotational topology, with depth-aware load balancing and a router carrying a fast-weight trajectory state, converting depth into 'virtual width' and beating matched MoE by up to 1.3% (4.2% when converting checkpoints).
key_contributions: Universal expert pool reused across layers (virtual width) under fixed activated parameters
Staggered rotational connectivity, depth-aware exposure-corrected load balancing, and a dual-pathway router with an online fast-weight state over depth
Progressive conversion of existing MoE checkpoints into MoUE

setup.model_sizes: Qwen-3 style MoE-160M (12 experts, top-2) and MoE-700M (64 experts, top-8) backbones
setup.train_tokens_or_data: samples of OLMo 2 Mix 1124 at a fixed data-to-parameter ratio, sequence length 4096
setup.baselines: matched MoE baselines (iso-parameter and iso-compute)
setup.benchmarks: lm-evaluation-harness average

claims.claim: At matched activated and total parameters and tokens, MoUE beats matched MoE baselines by up to 1.3%; converting existing MoE checkpoints gives up to 4.2%.
claims.evidence_quote: consistently outperforms matched MoE baselines by up to 1.3% across scaling regimes, enables progressive conversion of existing MoE checkpoints with up to 4.2% gains

claims.claim: Under fixed compute budgets, width expansion via universal experts raises averages (12A2: 41.0 to 42.3; 64A8: 43.8 upward).
claims.evidence_quote: for MoE 12A2, Avg. improves from 41.0 to 42.3, and for MoE 64A8, from 43.8 to

limitations: Small backbones (160M/700M); gains of about 1 point; complex routing/topology machinery.
survey_notes: Hybrid on the sharing axis between MoE and MoEUT, close to MoRE 2609.18176 (adjacent-layer expert sharing) and Mobius 2608.14290 (global shared FFN). The router's fast-weight trajectory state is a cross-depth memory mechanism. Not a loop over a block, so loop-count claims do not apply.

title: Linear Reusable Neural Bases Architecture for Network Compression
relevance_reason: Represents each block's neurons as linear combinations of a shared set of neural bases (cross-layer basis reuse for compression); no block is iterated in depth and no loop count.
one_sentence: LRNBA builds attention and FFN blocks from coefficient-weighted combinations of shared reusable neural bases, enabling wider/deeper nets at a fixed parameter budget; on WikiText-2 an 8-layer variant reaches lower training loss with about 3/4 of the parameters but higher training time.
key_contributions: Neural-basis view of FFN blocks (sensor/response parameters) shared across blocks via coefficient tables
Extension to attention and projection blocks and sub-neural reuse
Small-scale function-fitting and WikiText-2 language-model experiments

setup.model_sizes: d=512, L=8, 8 heads (WikiText-2 base model)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: WikiText-2, sequence length 128, 800 epochs of 512 batches of 16
setup.baselines: standard Transformer
setup.benchmarks: training/test cross-entropy loss

claims.claim: On WikiText-2, the 6h6m LRNBA variant converges fastest and reaches the lowest training loss with about 3/4 of the standard Transformer's parameters, but training time grows with the number of bases.
claims.evidence_quote: achieves the fastest convergence and the lowest training loss while using only approximately 3/4 as many parameters as the standard Transformer.

limitations: Tiny experiments (WikiText-2, training loss emphasis); increased training time; no looping or test-time compute.
survey_notes: Out of scope for looped models; at most a footnote under 'cross-layer weight generation / basis sharing' alongside Basis Sharing 2410.03765 and Share Your Attention 2508.04581.

title: Depth-Recurrent Attention Mixtures: Giving Latent Reasoning the Attention it Deserves
relevance_reason: Fully depth-recurrent single-layer MoE LM with attention along depth (to earlier depth states) and expert attention; FLOP-, parameter- and memory-matched against layered MoE.
one_sentence: Dreamer makes the whole model one depth-recurrent layer combining sequence attention, depth attention (attending over the token's previous depth states to relieve the fixed hidden-size bottleneck) and sparse expert attention (MoE), and needs 2-8x fewer training tokens than matched layered MoE on math reasoning.
key_contributions: Depth attention: attention along the depth dimension over earlier recurrent states (history injection), analogous to sequence attention fixing RNN bottlenecks
Fully depth-recurrent design (no fixed prelude/coda) with sparse expert attention, depth-position-encoded routing and RMSNorm applied to the residual stream
Tightly FLOP-, parameter- and memory-matched comparison with a layered SOTA-style MoE at depth 16 (~1B) and 32 (~2B) on ~100B tokens

setup.model_sizes: depth 16 (~1B parameters) and depth 32 (~2B parameters)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: ca. 100B tokens of open instruction datasets with CoT traces removed; 25B-token ablations
setup.loops_train: fixed depth (16 or 32 recurrent applications)
setup.baselines: LA (layered non-recurrent MoE), DR without depth attention
setup.benchmarks: validation perplexity, math reasoning benchmarks (e.g. GSM8K)

claims.claim: At matched FLOPs, parameters and memory, depth recurrence with depth attention needs 2-8x fewer training tokens to reach the layered baseline's accuracy, and beats ~2x larger models at equal tokens.
claims.evidence_quote: our models require 2 to 8× fewer training tokens for the same accuracy as FLOP-, parameter-, and memory-matched SOTA, and outperform ca. 2× larger SOTA models with the same training tokens.

claims.claim: Naive weight reuse across depth breaks residual scale compatibility; normalizing the residual stream itself is needed, and forcing attention projections to be reused hurts unless re-parameterized.
claims.evidence_quote: However, when increasing the depth, the scales of residuals and their additive updates can become incompatible across depths, which prevents learning depth-generalized experts.

claims.claim: Depth-recurrent MoE shows 2-11x larger expert-selection diversity across depths than standard MoE.
claims.evidence_quote: We further present insights into knowledge usage across depths, e.g., showing 2 to 11× larger expert selection diversity than SOTA MoEs.

numbers.what: Model scales
numbers.quote: We compare three main architecture variants, at depth 16 (ca. 1B parameters) and depth 32 (ca. 2B parameters)

numbers.what: Training data
numbers.quote: As training data, we use ca. 100B tokens from a mix of openly available instruction datasets (Table 4).

limitations: Instruction-data mixture with CoT removed (not general web pretraining); math-focused evaluation; fixed depth; ~2B scale.
survey_notes: Design-space: argues against 'partially fixed layer stacks' (prelude/coda), contradicting sandwich advocates (Huginn, RINS, 2609.36636, CART); its whole-stack loop succeeds when combined with MoE (as MoEUT) and depth attention (history injection over depth, cf. CoTFormer's cross-repeat attention and MeSH memory). Rare tightly matched (FLOP/param/memory) comparison with a positive result for looping.

title: Mobius Learning: Cyclic Depth Folding in Transformers
relevance_reason: Looped Transformer variant where different data streams traverse the shared block groups in cyclically shifted orders, so each group serves shallow and deep roles.
one_sentence: Mobius Learning partitions a Transformer into P=4 block groups held by different workers and feeds each worker's data starting at its own group, so streams loop through cyclically shifted orders; at loop depths 6-15 on GPT-2 small it beats fixed-order looping at matched tokens and depth.
key_contributions: Cyclic depth folding: worker-indexed cyclic block orders make each block group act at every source-relative depth (depth-role superposition)
Matched comparison with ordered-loop training at the same loop depth L (K=4L block-group applications) and token budget
Distributed 'Mobius parallelism': each worker stores one block group and keeps raw data local

setup.model_sizes: modded GPT-2 small (124M)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 2.5B FineWeb tokens, Muon optimizer, four workers
setup.loops_train: fixed loop depths L (e.g. 6, 10, 15), K = 4L block-group applications
setup.baselines: ordered-loop (fixed-order looped) training at the same L
setup.benchmarks: FineWeb validation loss

claims.claim: At loop depths 6, 10 and 15, cyclic depth folding gives lower validation loss than ordered-loop training at the same token budget and loop depth.
claims.evidence_quote: At loop depths L = 6, 10, 15, this construction achieves lower validation loss than ordered-loop training under the same 2.5B-token budget and loop

claims.claim: The comparison is matched within each loop depth but not across depths, since compute grows with L.
claims.evidence_quote: Since K increases with L, the comparison is matched between methods within each row, not across loop depths.

numbers.what: Training budget and model
numbers.quote: in four-worker experiments with a modded GPT-2 small (124M) model trained on 2.5B FineWeb tokens using Muon

limitations: Single small model (124M), four workers, 2.5B tokens; preliminary version; gains only at larger loop depths; no downstream tasks.
survey_notes: Unique 'cyclic' topology entry: block order varies per data stream; challenges the assumption (used by prelude/coda designs) that shared blocks need fixed depth roles. Very small-scale, preliminary evidence; relevant to the systems/distributed angle of looped models.

title: Share Your Attention: Transformer Weight Sharing via Matrix-based Dictionary Learning
relevance_reason: Cross-layer sharing of attention projections via shared matrix-atom dictionaries; compression, not iterated depth; compares to repeat-all-over and sequential sharing.
one_sentence: MASA represents each layer's Q/K/V/O matrices as linear combinations of a shared dictionary of matrix atoms, cutting attention parameters by 66.7% at on-par quality and beating GQA, low-rank, repeat-all-over and sequential sharing at matched parameter budgets (100M-700M).
key_contributions: Matrix-atom dictionary shared across layers for attention projections (layer-specific coefficients)
Drop-in replacement trained with standard optimizers; also applied to ViT and to pretrained LLMs
Comparisons with repeat-all-over (MobileLLM) and sequential sharing at comparable parameter budgets

setup.baselines: GQA, low-rank, Repeat-all-over, Sequential sharing
setup.benchmarks: perplexity and benchmark accuracy; ViT image classification

claims.claim: At comparable parameter budgets, dictionary-shared attention beats GQA, low-rank and repeat-all-over/sequential layer sharing.
claims.evidence_quote: Experiments across scales (100M–700M parameters) show that MASA achieves better benchmark accuracy and perplexity than grouped-query attention (GQA), low-rank baselines and recently proposed Repeat-all-over/Sequential sharing at comparable parameter budgets.

numbers.what: Attention parameter reduction in a 700M model
numbers.quote: reducing the attention module's parameters by 66.7% (e.g., 226.5M → 75M in a 700Mparameter model) while achieving on-par performance.

limitations: Compression only; no extra effective depth; up to 700M from scratch.
venue: This work was accepted and presented at AAAI 2026
survey_notes: Peripheral: cross-layer weight sharing for memory, not compute-depth looping. Useful contrast: dictionary sharing beats whole-layer repetition (RAO) at matched parameters, consistent with ALBERT's finding that attention sharing is cheap.

title: AbbIE: Autoregressive Block-Based Iterative Encoder for Efficient Sequence Modeling
relevance_reason: Head/Body/Tail looped decoder LM (Body iterated r times) comparing plain chaining vs an inter-iteration residual for input injection; trained with 2 iterations, extrapolates at test time.
one_sentence: AbbIE splits a Transformer into Head, iterated Body and Tail; the AbbIE-D variant adds an inter-iteration residual (input re-injection) that converges to a fixed point while plain chaining (AbbIE-C) diverges, and with only 2 training iterations it extrapolates to more test iterations, improving perplexity up to 5% and ICL up to 12% at <=350M.
key_contributions: Head (token->concept space) / Body (iterated) / Tail decomposition, trained with r=2 iterations
Two injection variants: AbbIE-C (chain outputs) vs AbbIE-D (inter-iteration residual, diffusion-inspired); only AbbIE-D reaches a fixed point
Upward generalization to more test-time iterations without specialized data

setup.model_sizes: up to 350M
setup.train_tokens_or_data: compute-optimal budget of 20 tokens per parameter and multiples; sequence length 2048
setup.loops_train: 2 iterations
setup.baselines: standard Transformer (STD), Depth (path-independent recurrent baseline)
setup.benchmarks: perplexity, zero-shot ICL (HellaSwag, LAMBADA, ARC-Easy, CommonsenseQA)

claims.claim: Plain chaining of iterations (AbbIE-C) fails to converge; an extra inter-iteration residual (AbbIE-D) reaches a fixed point like the path-independent Depth baseline.
claims.evidence_quote: In contrast, AbbIE-C fails to converge after 32 iterations. This shows that the residual steam, present in the body of Transformer, is in itself not sufficient and an extra inter-iteration residual connection is needed.

claims.claim: At the same size and token budget, AbbIE beats the standard Transformer and Depth baseline in perplexity, but at a higher FLOP cost.
claims.evidence_quote: Across all configurations, AbbIE consistently outperforms both the standard Transformer and Depth baseline in terms of perplexity.

claims.claim: Training with only 2 iterations suffices for upward generalization, giving up to 12% ICL and 5% perplexity improvements when scaling test-time iterations.
claims.evidence_quote: We show that AbbIE upward generalizes (ability to generalize to arbitrary iteration lengths) at test time by only using 2 iterations during train time, far outperforming alternative iterative methods.

numbers.what: Gains from test-time iteration scaling
numbers.value: up to 12% zero-shot ICL, up to 5% perplexity
numbers.quote: gives it an up to 12% improvement in zero-shot in-context learning tasks versus other iterative and standard methods and up to 5% improvement in language perplexity.

numbers.what: Largest model size
numbers.quote: We perform all of our evaluations on model sizes up to 350M parameters.

limitations: Up to 350M; higher training FLOPs than standard Transformer (authors hypothesize convergence for very long runs); AbbIE-C discarded.
survey_notes: Injection-type evidence: an explicit inter-iteration residual (input injection) is required for convergence/extrapolation; supports Huginn-style injection and contrasts with 2609.36636 which finds lightweight initial-state injection gives negligible gains over no injection (but there the dense variant collapses). Training with only 2 loops and extrapolating is a cheap regime; compute-matching is absent (iso-param/iso-data only).

title: Intra-Layer Recurrence in Transformers for Language Modeling
relevance_reason: Per-layer recurrence: each layer re-applied r_l times via a reuse map, studying which layers benefit from looping.
one_sentence: ILR re-applies individual layers of a small LLaMA-style LM according to a reuse map (e.g. [4,2,1,1]) and finds that spending iterations on earlier layers lowers perplexity most, at extra compute and with no parameter increase (1.2M and 100M models).
key_contributions: Per-layer reuse map R=[r_1..r_L] as a finer-grained alternative to block looping
Finding that early-layer recurrence gives the largest perplexity gains
Tests with NoPE, ALiBi and other positional schemes at 1.2M and 100M

claims.evidence_quote: prioritizing early-layer reuse ([4, 2, 1, 1]) reduced perplexity from 16.57 to 14.62 (NoPE) and 14.38 to 13.63 (ALiBi) as shown in Table 1.

title: Implicit Language Models are RNNs: Balancing Parallelization and Expressivity
relevance_reason: Self-iterates a (single-layer/few-layer) SSM or transformer block to an approximate fixed point (DEQ-style, phantom gradients) and pretrains up to 1.3B on 207B tokens.
one_sentence: Implicit SSMs/transformers iterate a block with additive input injection until (approximate) fixed-point convergence, which theoretically yields RNN-like non-linear state transitions; a bounded-iteration curriculum with phantom gradients scales them to 1.3B/207B tokens, where they beat explicit counterparts and solve state tracking.
key_contributions: Theory: implicit (fixed-point) SSMs implement non-linear, non-diagonal state transitions like RNNs, solving the S5 word problem
Approximate convergence suffices: curriculum bounding iterations retains parallelism; phantom-gradient (truncated implicit) backprop
Largest self-iterated models with dynamic halting to date (implicit Mamba2 and Llama3 up to 1.3B on 207B D-Pile tokens), with length generalization and path independence

setup.loops_test: self-iterate until fixed-point convergence (dynamic halting); test-time iterations varied
setup.baselines: explicit Mamba2 and Llama3 (e.g. 16-layer Mamba2 vs 1-layer implicit), conventional SSMs/transformers on word problems
setup.benchmarks: S5 word problem, length generalization, downstream zero-shot tasks, perplexity

claims.evidence_quote: Empirically, we find that only approximate fixed-point convergence suffices, enabling the design of a scalable training curriculum that largely retains parallelization

Expressivity argument (beyond TC0 via iteration) complements theory sections. Code link in text is truncated (github.com/microsoft/...), so not recorded.

title: RingFormer: Rethinking Recurrent Transformer with Adaptive Level Signals
relevance_reason: One shared Transformer layer applied recurrently with depth-specific, input-dependent low-rank 'level signals' and unique LayerNorms per iteration.
one_sentence: RingFormer applies a single shared Transformer layer repeatedly (encoder-decoder for MT, ViT for images) and adds per-depth low-rank transformations of the input that generate level signals for Q/K/V and FFN plus per-iteration LayerNorm, matching vanilla Transformers on WMT14 De-En and ImageNet with fewer parameters and beating Universal Transformers.
key_contributions: Input-dependent level signals from depth-specific low-rank matrices injected into attention projections and FFN of a shared block
Per-level unique layer normalization

title: Hyperloop Transformers
relevance_reason: Middle-cycle looped Transformer (begin/middle x3/end) with loop-level hyper-connections (matrix-valued parallel residual streams) and loop position embedding.
one_sentence: Hyperloop allocates ~25%/50%/25% of parameters to begin/middle/end blocks, loops the middle block 3 times, and applies hyper-connections (4 parallel residual streams) only after each loop plus a loop position embedding; it beats depth-matched Transformers with ~50% fewer parameters at 240M-2B.
key_contributions: Loop-level hyper-connections: expand the residual stream into parallel streams mixed only at loop boundaries (150-300K extra parameters)

title: SpiralFormer: Looped Transformers Can Learn Hierarchical Dependencies via Multi-Resolution Recursion
relevance_reason: Middle-cycle (pre-loop-post) looped Transformer where each loop iteration runs the shared core at a different sequence resolution (coarse-to-fine chunk compression).
one_sentence: SpiralFormer runs a shared middle core over a coarse-to-fine resolution schedule (e.g. 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 1 of the token sequence via causal chunking), with Anchor or MeSH state topologies, and improves loss per FLOP over full-resolution looped models and Pythia at 160M-1.4B on 250B Pile tokens.
key_contributions: Multi-resolution recursion: each loop step executes the shared core at its own sequence resolution, compressing tokens into chunk-level latents with causal handling
Two variants: -B (same layer allocation as full-resolution LoopedFormer, fewer FLOPs) and -L (parameter-matched to Pythia, fewer FLOPs)
Recurrence-ratio study: loss is U-shaped in the fraction of layers in the shared core, minimum at 30-40%

title: MeSH: Memory-as-State-Highways for Recursive Transformers

key_contributions: Probing diagnosis: later loops contribute little (features stabilize prematurely) under naive/residual/anchor state passing
Memory-as-State-Highways: B-slot state buffer with step-wise learnable write and read routers, initial slot anchored to embeddings

title: What Makes Recurrence Effective in Looped Language Models?
relevance_reason: Controlled pretraining study of LoopLM design choices (physical depth vs loops, prelude/coda allocation, initial-state vs history-state injection, timestep conditioning) under under-unrolling, horizon and extrapolation.
one_sentence: Pretrains small LoopLMs (Llama3.1-1B / Qwen3-0.6B layer configs, FineWeb-Edu, Chinchilla tokens) under matched physical and effective depth and finds extra test-time loops help reasoning but hurt knowledge; coda helps under-unrolling, prelude helps extrapolation; history-state injection plus timestep gating beats initial-state injection.
key_contributions: Unified p + s x K + c (Prelude-Core-Coda) template with BaseLoop (p=c=0) vs CoreLoop, matched on physical depth, training effective depth, inference effective depth and training pipeline
Finding that test-time unrolling beyond the training horizon improves reasoning but degrades knowledge, and that the physical-depth/loop split matters beyond effective depth
History-state injection (difference-based, lag window w) and scalar Loop/Branch timestep gating; channel-wise history + timestep conditioning is the best pair, initial-state injection adds nothing

numbers.quote: BaseLoop 2 × 10, with a shallow physical core and many recurrent iterations, peaks early and degrades under further unrolling, whereas 10 × 2, with a deep physical core but few recurrent iterations, remains relatively flat during extrapolation

limitations: Small models (sub-1B layer configs) and Chinchilla-scale token budgets; fixed-K training only (no randomized or adaptive loops); timestep gating gains are configuration-dependent and not universal; absolute scores are low (reasoning ~30).
builds_on: Saunshi et al. 2025 (Reasoning with latent thoughts)
survey_notes: Key controlled evidence for the 'design space' section: it matches physical depth, training effective depth, inference effective depth and data. Contradicts Huginn's claim that dense initial-state injection is needed/safe for extrapolation (dense injection collapses knowledge here) and partly contradicts Huginn's warning against step conditioning: here timestep gating with rescaled time grid helps extrapolation, although configuration-dependent. Agrees with prelude/coda (sandwich) designs but adds nuance: coda for under-unrolling robustness, prelude for extrapolation. The reasoning-up/knowledge-down split under extra loops is a central caveat for 'loops as test-time compute'. Also: Huginn-style 1+2x5+1 failed to train with AdamW (optimizer sensitivity).

title: CoTFormer: A Chain-of-Thought Driven Architecture with Budget-Adaptive Computation Cost at Inference
relevance_reason: Weight-tied repeated block where each repeat's outputs are appended as new tokens that later repeats attend to; token-level adaptive repeats with budget control.
one_sentence: CoTFormer argues CoT differs from weight-tied depth because thought tokens attend to earlier intermediate states; it interleaves each repeat's representations into the attention context, beats Block Universal Transformers at equal size and repeats, and adds MoD-style per-repeat routing for inference-time budget control.
key_contributions: Distinguishes Block Universal Transformers (tied N-layer block repeated) from CoT: in CoTFormer later repeats attend to all tokens' representations from all previous repeats
LN-CoTFormer: reserved unshared beginning/final layers (2 -> 21x5 -> 1), layer norm after each repeat; 24x5 beats a 48-layer standard Transformer
Mixture-of-Repeats adaptive training: per-repeat routers with randomly sampled capacities, interpolation x(i+1)=(1-s)x(i)+s B(x(i)), and a depth embedding, enabling inference-time compute budgets

setup.model_sizes: 12- and 24-layer bases (hidden 768, 12 heads) repeated 2-5 times; standard 12/24/48-layer baselines (parameter counts not stated)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: OpenWebText2; 40k steps (60k for adaptive), batch 128 sequences of length 256
setup.loops_train: fixed nrepeat in {2,3,5}; adaptive model samples random per-repeat capacities with max 5 repeats
setup.loops_test: fixed repeats, or router-based capacity / threshold chosen at inference to set compute budget
setup.baselines: Block Universal Transformer (same layers and repeats), adaptive Block UT with Mixture of Repeats, standard 12/24/48-layer Transformers
setup.benchmarks: OpenWebText2 perplexity; MACs vs perplexity Pareto

claims.claim: At equal parameters and equal number of repeats, CoTFormer beats Block Universal Transformer in perplexity, and the gap widens with more repeats (at the cost of extra attention compute).
claims.evidence_quote: It can be clearly seen that CoTFormers significantly outperform Block Universal Transformers with the same size and the same number of repeated applications of the model.

claims.claim: At matched MACs, CoTFormer sits on the perplexity-compute Pareto front: a 12x3 CoTFormer is cheaper than a 12x5 Block UT of similar accuracy even at sequence length 8192.
claims.evidence_quote: It can be seen that even for sequences as long as 8192, the 12x3 CoTFormer's cost remains below that of 12x5 Block Universal Transformer.

claims.claim: With reserved unshared first/last layers and a layer norm after each repeat, a 24-layer CoTFormer with 5 repeats beats a standard 48-layer Transformer (24.11 vs 24.17 ppl); but matching deeper models needs more repeats than the depth ratio.
claims.regime: unmatched depth (24x5 vs 48x1; half the unique layers, more compute)
claims.evidence_quote: Most noticeably, after applying these changes, the performance of a CoTFormer with 24 layers and 5 repeats, surpasses the performance of a standard 48 layer Transformer.

claims.claim: Router-based token allocation gives a much better compute-accuracy trade-off than uniformly truncating repeats at inference; but adaptive training lags a fixed-5-repeat model at equal inference compute (23.83 vs 23.19).
claims.evidence_quote: For example, after 60k steps, the former reaches perplexity 23.83 while the latter achieves 23.19.

claims.claim: A depth embedding conditioning on remaining repeats is neutral at fixed repeats but helps in the adaptive case.
claims.evidence_quote: While the performance is similar on fixed number of repeats, a noticeable boost is observed in the adaptive case.

claims.claim: Alternative adaptive-training methods for Universal Transformers (ACT/PonderNet-style) did not outperform at small scale, so a Mixture-of-Repeats adaptive Block UT is used as baseline.
claims.evidence_quote: While alternative methods for adaptive training of Universal Transformers have been proposed in the literature, we could not obtain a better performance using those methods in small scale experiments.

numbers.what: Table 1 perplexities, 24-layer base: Standard 24 / BUT 24x2 / CoT 24x2 / BUT 24x3 / CoT 24x3 / BUT 24x5 / CoT 24x5 / Standard 48
Table 2 ablation: Standard 48x1 vs CoTFormer 24x5, + reserved layers (2->21x5->1), + layer norm
numbers.quote: Standard 48x1 24.17(0.00) 24x5 24.48(0.03) 24.51(0.01) 24.11(0.03) CoTFormer + Reserved Layers + Layer Norm

numbers.what: Adaptive vs fixed-5-repeat LN-CoTFormer perplexity at equal inference compute, 60k steps
numbers.quote: For example, after 60k steps, the former reaches perplexity 23.83 while the latter achieves 23.19.

numbers.what: Training setup
numbers.quote: We train the models for 40k steps using the AdamW [20] optimizer and apply linear warmup of the learning rate for the first 8000 steps.

numbers.what: Training-time cost of fixed 5 repeats vs adaptive
numbers.quote: For example, when training the model with fixed 5 repeats, the training takes roughly around 1.5x longer.

numbers.what: Repeats needed to beat a 2x deeper model
numbers.quote: For example, to get better performance than a 48 layer model using a 24 layer model, 5 repeats is needed whereas optimally we would need 2.

limitations: Small scale (OpenWebText2, 40-60k steps, seq length 256); attention cost grows with repeats; adaptive model underperforms fixed-depth at same compute; at zero repeats adaptive Block UT beats adaptive CoTFormer; needs more repeats than the depth ratio to match deeper dense models; LN-CoTFormer shows loss spikes.
survey_notes: Lineage: introduces cross-iteration attention (history injection through the KV context), a precursor to KV/trajectory-sharing designs, and an early prelude-core-coda variant (2 -> 21x5 -> 1) with LN after each repeat and a remaining-depth embedding. Contrasts with Huginn-style models that avoid step conditioning (depth embedding here helps only for adaptive routing). Comparison regimes: Table 1 is iso-param and iso-repeats (but not iso-FLOP: CoTFormer pays extra attention); the 48-layer win is at 5x repeats, i.e. more compute. Reports that matching a 2x deeper dense model needs 5 repeats: evidence that loops are less efficient than unique layers per FLOP.

key: t:moeut
title: MoEUT: Mixture-of-Experts Universal Transformers
relevance_reason: Shared-layer (UT) language model made parameter-competitive by MoE FFN and MoE attention inside the loop, with layer grouping and peri-layernorm.
one_sentence: MoEUT fixes the UT parameter-compute ratio by making the shared block a group of G=2-4 MoE layers (sigma-MoE FFN + SwitchHead attention) repeated 8-9 times with peri-layernorm, slightly beating parameter-matched dense Transformers up to 1B parameters at fewer MACs.
key_contributions: MoE FFN and MoE attention inside a shared layer to decouple parameters from compute in UTs
Layer grouping (ABAB stacking of G non-shared layers, G=2 best) and peri-layernorm (no layernorm on the residual/main data path) for shared-layer signal propagation
First UT to match or beat parameter-matched dense Transformers on LM (C4, SlimPajama, peS2o, The Stack), plus expert-reuse analysis across depth

setup.model_sizes: 44M to 1040M parameters (e.g. 44M, 126M, 244M, 319M, 728M, 1040M)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: C4, SlimPajama, peS2o, The Stack subset; batch size 64, context length 1024, 10^5 steps for all models
setup.loops_train: fixed: group of G layers (2-4) repeated, typically 8 or 9 recurrent steps
setup.baselines: parameter-matched pre-LN dense Transformer, non-shared sigma-MoE, Sparse Universal Transformer (SUT)
setup.benchmarks: perplexity on C4/SlimPajama/peS2o/The Stack; zero-shot LAMBADA, BLiMP, CBT, HellaSwag, PIQA, ARC-E

claims.claim: MoEUT slightly outperforms dense Transformers with the same parameter count (same d_model and number of layers, same training steps), and the gap grows with scale, while using fewer MACs.
claims.evidence_quote: slightly outperforms dense models with the same number of parameters (Fig. 4a), and the gap tends to grow with scale.

claims.claim: At equal total training MACs, MoEUT beats the dense baseline by a large margin.
claims.evidence_quote: Given equal amounts of compute, MoEUT outperforms other models by a large margin.

claims.claim: Group size G=2 is optimal at 244M parameter-matched: both a single shared layer (G=1) and no sharing (G=18) are worse, and ABAB stacking beats AABB.
claims.evidence_quote: In Fig. 6, we observe that G = 2 is optimal, and the recurrence in the layer dimension is indeed beneficial.

claims.claim: ACT halting is the main cause of SUT's poor LM performance; removing ACT improves it dramatically, though it still trails MoEUT and dense baselines.
claims.evidence_quote: we found that most of this poor performance comes from the ACT mechanism that the authors advertise as one of the main components of their model.

claims.claim: Peri-layernorm is best, but its advantage over post-layernorm diminishes at larger scale.
claims.evidence_quote: the gap between peri-norm and post-norm is marginal: 11.29 perplexity points compared to 11.32).

claims.claim: Contrary to Takase & Kiyono's large groups with few steps, smaller groups with more recurrent steps perform better.
claims.evidence_quote: However, they consider models with large group sizes (G = 6 for 12 layers) and few recurrent steps (2). We find that models with smaller G with more steps perform better.

numbers.what: Training protocol for all models
numbers.quote: All models are trained with batch size 64 and context length 1024, for 105 steps.

numbers.what: Group size and recurrent steps
numbers.quote: In our experiments, the group size is between 2 and 4, and the typical number of recurrent steps is 8 or 9.

numbers.what: Peri-norm vs post-norm perplexity at 719M
numbers.quote: the gap between peri-norm and post-norm is marginal: 11.29 perplexity points compared to 11.32).

numbers.what: Training slowdown vs FlashAttention dense Transformer
numbers.quote: Compared to the standard Transformer with FlashAttention [56], our MoEUT model trains 1.5–2x slower.

numbers.what: Largest scale tested
numbers.quote: outperforming standard Transformers with less compute and memory requirements on all scales on which we can afford to test (up to 1B parameters).

limitations: Modest training regime (10^5 steps, batch 64); suboptimal Triton MoE kernels make training 1.5-2x slower than dense; zero-shot differences vs baseline are marginal; no ACT studied.
venue: 38th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2024).
survey_notes: Key design-space entry for 'MoE-in-loop' sharing and for normalization as part of state carrying (peri-LN avoids residual norm growth across loop steps). Disagrees with Takase & Kiyono on grouping: small G with many steps beats large G with 2 steps. Contradicts ACT-based UTs (SUT) at LM scale: ACT hurt. Agrees with ALBERT that naive sharing is parameter-starved; resolves it with MoE. Regime is clean (parameter-matched, same steps), but only up to 1B and modest token budget.

title: LT2: Linear-Time Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Looped Transformers whose shared block uses linear/sparse/hybrid attention; studies interaction of the token mixer with looping and converts Ouro into a hybrid looped model.
one_sentence: LT2 replaces softmax attention in looped Transformers with linear (GDN, KDA), sparse (DSA, window) or hybrid mixers; looping refines linear-attention memory and expands sparse receptive fields, hybrids match or beat the full-attention loop at 5x decode throughput, and Ouro-1.4B converts with ~1B tokens.
key_contributions: Looped linear and sparse attention with theory: loops iteratively refine linear-attention memory; T loops of a window-w block reach as far as T stacked window layers
LT2-hybrid (GDN+DSA) matches the full-attention looped model without quadratic attention; (Full+GDN) at 1:4 ratio surpasses it
Distillation of Ouro into Ouro-hybrid-1.4B with ~1B tokens; SDPA output gate mitigates attention-sink amplification across loops

setup.model_sizes: 0.6B and 1.3B from scratch; Ouro-hybrid-1.4B converted
setup.train_tokens_or_data: FineWeb-Edu 100B tokens (from scratch); ~1B tokens continued training for conversion
setup.loops_train: fixed T=4 loops
setup.baselines: standard full-attention Looped Transformer; Ouro-1.4B teacher; industry 1B-4B models
setup.benchmarks: zero-shot downstream average, perplexity, synthetic recall and state tracking, prefill/decode throughput to 32k

claims.claim: At matched parameters, loops and data, LT2-hybrid (GDN+DSA) matches the full-attention looped Transformer's quality with ~5.7x higher decode throughput at 8k context; (Full+GDN) improves zero-shot by +2.1 points with ~5x throughput.
claims.evidence_quote: it improves average zero-shot performance by +2.1 points over the standard looped transformer (61.4% vs. 59.3%) while still achieving ∼5× higher decode throughput at the same setting

claims.claim: Looped GDN slightly trails the full-attention loop at 0.6B but surpasses it at 1.3B while keeping linear time.
claims.evidence_quote: At the smaller 0.6B scale, looped GDN still slightly trails the Looped Transformer; however, at the larger 1.3B scale, it surpasses the Looped Transformer while preserving linear-time complexity.

claims.claim: A pretrained looped model (Ouro) can be converted to a linear-time hybrid with ~1B tokens, retaining teacher quality; comparison to industry models is unmatched.
claims.evidence_quote: with only ∼1B tokens of continued training, our converted Ouro-Hybrid1.4B retains the quality of its full-attention teacher while inheriting LT2's linear-time efficiency.

claims.claim: Full-attention looped Transformers lose more than half of decode throughput from 4k to 32k because the KV cache grows per loop iteration; linear-time mixers keep a flat decode rate.
claims.evidence_quote: Looped Transformer loses more than half of its decode throughput between 4k and 32k because its KV cache keeps growing per loop iteration.

numbers.what: Pretraining setup
numbers.value: 0.6B and 1.3B, 100B FineWeb-Edu tokens, T=4 loops, 1:4 hybrid ratio
numbers.quote: We pre-train all models on FineWeb-Edu [46] at 0.6B and 1.3B parameters with a 100B-token budget, using T=4 loops for every looped variant.

numbers.what: Decode throughput at 8k context (GDN+DSA vs full-attention loop)
numbers.quote: delivering ∼5.7× higher decode throughput at 8k context (125 vs. 22 tokens/s, batch size 8), entirely without quadratic attention.

numbers.what: Perplexity GDN+DSA hybrid vs full-attention loop at 1.3B
numbers.quote: Looped Hybrid (GDN+DSA), which contains no full attention, matches the full-attention reference at both scales (9.72 vs. 9.87 PPL at 1.3B).

limitations: Fixed 4 loops; up to 1.3B from scratch; pure DeltaNet loops unstable; conversion compared against public industry models (unmatched).
survey_notes: Hybrid design-space entry (looping x token mixer): looped linear attention behaves like iterative memory refinement; KV cache of full-attention loops grows per loop iteration, which LT2 avoids (systems relevance). Reports that weight-shared loops mildly amplify attention sinks and that an output gate mitigates it. Released weights (Ouro-hybrid-1.4B).

title: Looped Transformers as Optimizers
relevance_reason: Frames loop transitions (state injection/update rules) as optimizer steps on a fast-weight state and derives a new transition; middle-loop MoE LMs at 5B/10B total parameters.
one_sentence: Treats the looped hidden state as a fast weight updated by local gradient steps, derives loop transitions from a projection, objective and optimizer, aligns Parcae/HyperLoop read-write maps, and proposes OperLoop (weight decay, adaptive step size, delta objective), beating looped and non-looped baselines at matched training FLOPs.
key_contributions: Optimization view: a loop transition = closed-form local optimizer update with read/write projections; reveals input-map mismatches in Parcae and HyperLoop
Input-map alignment (transpose read/write) improves existing transitions with fewer parameters
OperLoop transition (explicit weight decay, adaptive causal step size, delta objective) on middle-loop MoE LMs with 4 parallel streams

setup.model_sizes: non-looped baselines 5B total / 600M active (18 layers) and 10B / 900M active (32 layers); looped variants ~50% of parameters
setup.train_tokens_or_data: ~300B tokens (5B scale) and ~500B tokens (10B scale), sequence length 4096
setup.loops_train: 3 loops (Loop3); 6 loops in scaling study
setup.baselines: non-looped MoE baselines, Parcae, HyperLoop, aligned variants
setup.benchmarks: commonsense LL accuracy, Wikitext/Lambada PPL, math/code/reasoning generation (e.g. 8-shot CoT GSM8K)

claims.claim: At matched unrolled training FLOPs and effective depth with about half the parameters, OperLoop raises the generative EM average over the non-looped baseline by 1.69 and 1.04 points at the two scales.
claims.evidence_quote: Relative to the non-looped baselines in Table 3, OperLoop uses approximately half the parameters while improving the EM average by 1.69 and 1.04 percentage points at the two scales.

claims.claim: Input-map alignment, derived from the optimizer view, improves existing transitions (HyperLoop 58.93 to 59.47 commonsense average) with fewer transition parameters.
claims.evidence_quote: For example, HyperLoop improves average accuracy from 58.93 to 59.47 while using fewer transition parameters.

claims.evidence_quote: For OperLoop, the EM average rises from 25.58 to 31.90, with 8-shot CoT GSM8K improving from 17.13

claims.claim: Even with 6 loops OperLoop still trails the non-looped baseline on Wikitext PPL and LL accuracy (while surpassing it on Lambada PPL), whereas generative EM improves: the evaluation metric changes the conclusion.
claims.regime: iso_param (Loop6 uses more compute than baseline)
claims.evidence_quote: still trails the non-looped baseline on Wikitext PPL and LL accuracy while surpassing it on Lambada PPL.

claims.claim: At matched compute (Loop3), OperLoop exceeds the non-looped baseline in EM average despite worse PPL and LL accuracy.
claims.evidence_quote: OperLoop exceeds the non-looped baseline in EM average

numbers.what: Baseline model sizes
numbers.quote: Our non-looped baselines are an 18-layer, 5B-parameter model with 600M activated parameters and a depth-scaled 32-layer, 10B-parameter model with 900M activated parameters.

numbers.what: Training tokens
numbers.quote: The 18-layer 5B and 32-layer 10B baselines are trained on approximately 300B and 500B tokens over 67K and 120K updates, respectively.

numbers.what: Looped variant parameter share and matching
numbers.value: ~50% of parameters, matched unrolled training FLOPs
numbers.quote: each looped variant uses the middle-loop pattern and matches the unrolled training FLOPs of its non-looped baseline, with approximately 50% as many parameters.

limitations: Only middle-loop MoE backbones with 4 parallel streams; fixed loop counts; PPL and LL accuracy can lag non-looped baseline; theory is a design framework rather than guarantees.
survey_notes: Design-space: the injection operator I(s,e) as an optimizer update (state decay = weight decay, adaptive step size, delta rule). Provides one of the largest-scale iso-train-FLOP/iso-effective-depth comparisons (5B/10B MoE, 300-500B tokens) where looping with half the parameters beats the non-looped model on generation EM but not always on PPL: metric choice changes conclusions (cf. knowledge/reasoning split in 2609.36636). Builds directly on Hyperloop's middle-loop + parallel streams.

title: On the Chain-of-Thought Monitorability of Looped Language Models
relevance_reason: First systematic evaluation of CoT monitorability in looped LMs (Ouro loop-depth sweep; Nanbeige4.2-3B vs non-looped LMs).
one_sentence: Evaluates CoT monitorability (MonitorBench, 8 cue tasks, two stress tests) of Ouro-Thinking at loop depths 4/6/8 and of looped Nanbeige4.2-3B against non-looped LMs; deeper loops reduce monitorability on 3 of 8 tasks under stress tests only.
key_contributions: Controlled within-model sweep of loop depth T in {4,6,8} for Ouro-1.4B/2.6B-Thinking on 8 MonitorBench tasks under standard, Direct Concealment and Monitor-aware Evasion prompts, with CoT-only, action-only and all-message monitors.

Rules out pass rate, task difficulty and CoT length as sole explanations of the monitorability drop (Spearman tests over 32 cells); qualitative shift toward treating the cue as an independent check or omitting it.
Cross-model comparison: looped Nanbeige4.2-3B is not less monitorable than non-looped LMs matched on parameters, layer count or effective layers (confounded).

setup.loops_train: Ouro default T=4; Nanbeige4.2-3B applies its 22-layer stack twice

setup.benchmarks: MonitorBench: 5 Cue Answer (Logic, Health, Safety, Engineering, Science) and 3 Cue Condition (Knowledge, Preference, Law Judgment) tasks; GSM8K for Huginn; judge Qwen3.8-27B

claims.regime: iso_param (same Ouro weights, only test-time loop depth varied)
claims.evidence_quote: Controlled changes in loop depth reveal task-dependent reductions in CoT monitorability: From T = 4 to T = 8, Ouro-1.4B-Thinking drops from 77.9% to 41.8% on Logic, 40.8% to 23.6% on Science,

claims.claim: The monitorability decline is not explained by changes in verification pass rate across the 32 model x task x stress-test cells.
claims.evidence_quote: The Spearman correlation is ρ = −0.126 with the p-value p = 0.493, indicating no significant monotonic relationship between changes in verification pass rate and changes in CoT monitorability.

claims.claim: The decline is not explained by shorter CoTs; length changes are not significantly correlated with monitorability changes.
claims.evidence_quote: changes in average CoT length from T = 4 to T = 8 are not significantly correlated with changes in CoT monitorability (Spearman's ρ = 0.248, p = 0.172).

claims.claim: Qualitatively, deeper-loop Ouro models treat the user's cue as an independent check or omit it, rather than verbalizing reliance on it.
claims.evidence_quote: As the loop depth increases, models are more likely to frame the user's guess as an independent check on their own reasoning, or omit any explicit mention of it altogether under stress tests,

claims.evidence_quote: Despite these confounders, the results provide no evidence that adopting a looped transformer architecture alone necessarily makes models less monitorable.

claims.evidence_quote: Among questions with positive estimated treatment effects, explicit attribution of the successful answer to the supplied cue is rare under the MonitorBench rubric.

numbers.quote: and 54.4% to 43.6% on Engineering under Direct Concealment, while other tasks show weaker or qualitatively different trends.

numbers.quote: changes in average CoT length from T = 4 to T = 8 are not significantly correlated with changes in CoT monitorability (Spearman's ρ = 0.248, p = 0.172).

numbers.quote: Ouro-2.6B-Thinking contains 48 transformer layers, with a loop depth of 4, resulting in 192 effective transformer layers in total.

numbers.quote: Wrong → Correct questions Monitorability score 60 0% 135 0.74% 103 0.97% 108 0.69%

limitations: Loop-depth analysis limited to the Ouro family (1.4B/2.6B); unclear generalization to larger or other looped architectures; mechanism of the reduction not established; cross-model comparison not causal (different data, post-training, architectures, capability). vLLM ignores Ouro's dynamic gating, so all tokens run all loops. T=2 not evaluated due to repetition. Monitor is an LLM judge.
survey_notes: Anchor paper for safety section. The loop-depth sweep is iso-parameter but T=6,8 exceed Ouro's training depth of 4 (Table 1 of 2604.11791 lists Ouro train loops 4), i.e. it is an extrapolation regime where 2604.11791 shows Ouro does not reach a fixed point and its stages of inference drift; the monitorability drop could be tied to this out-of-training-depth instability rather than to 'more latent reasoning' (not tested by the authors). Effect is task-specific (3/8 tasks) and only under stress-test prompts; Cue Condition tasks show stable CoT monitorability but large drops in action-only monitorability (final answers shorten). Cross-model comparison is unmatched and finds no architecture-level penalty. Motivation cites speculation (Raschka blog) that GPT-6 Astra is looped; that is speculation, not evidence. Cites Kuhn et al. 2026 blog claiming deep recurrent models are less robustly CoT-monitorable in a toy setting (not read, not in corpus). No probe-based or latent monitors are tested; monitors read text only.

title: A Mechanistic Analysis of Looped Reasoning Language Models
relevance_reason: Mechanistic study of fixed points, cyclic trajectories and stages of inference in pretrained looped LMs (Ouro, Huginn, retrofitted Llama/OLMo).
one_sentence: Shows that in looped LMs each layer of the recurrent block converges to its own fixed point (a cyclic trajectory), attention patterns then freeze, and each loop re-enacts feedforward-like stages of inference; input injection and norm placement decide stability.
key_contributions: Propositions: a fixed point of the k-layer block implies cyclic fixed points for every layer; converging residual streams imply slowly changing attention patterns.

Empirical analysis of Ouro 1.4B/2.6B, Huginn-0125 and retrofitted Llama/OLMo/TinyLlama: per-layer fixed points (except Ouro), cyclic latent trajectories, and per-loop ColSum-concentration stages that mirror feedforward models.
Random-init and small from-scratch (3.7B-token) experiments isolating input injection, norm structure and block size; non-fixed-point orbits/sliders are rare.

setup.model_sizes: Ouro 1.4B, Ouro 2.6B, Huginn-0125 3.5B, retrofitted Llama 1B, OLMo-2 1B, TinyLlama 0.8B; small from-scratch models with d=512
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Analysis on 256 GSM8K test examples (plus HellaSwag); small models trained for 3.7B tokens (nanochat fork)
setup.loops_train: Ouro 4; Huginn and retrofitted models 32; small models constant 4
setup.loops_test: 8 loops for attention similarity; up to 128 recurrences for fixed-point and extrapolation analysis
setup.baselines: Feedforward Llama 3.2 1B, OLMo-2 1B, and a depth-12 feedforward control for small models
setup.benchmarks: GSM8K test subset, HellaSwag (stages of inference metrics, not accuracy)

claims.claim: Many looped LMs converge so that each layer in the cycle reaches a distinct fixed point, so the recurrent block traces a consistent cyclic trajectory in latent space.
claims.evidence_quote: we analyze cyclic recurrence and show that for many of the studied models each layer in the cycle converges to a distinct fixed point; consequently, the recurrent block follows a consistent cyclic trajectory in the latent space.

claims.claim: Ouro does not reach a fixed point, unlike Huginn-0125 and retrofitted Llama, consistent with input injection encouraging fixed-point convergence.
claims.evidence_quote: While Huginn-0125 and retrofitted Llama quickly reach a fixed point, Ouro does not - despite small successive differences evidenced by Fig. 3.

claims.claim: Each recurrent block re-enacts the stages of inference of feedforward models; retrofitted models do first and last stages once (prelude/coda) and repeat middle stages.
claims.evidence_quote: the retrofitted models closely follow the stages of inference of their associated base model, but the initial and final stages are performed only once by the prelude and coda respectively, while the "middle" stages are repeated in the recurrent block.

claims.claim: Huginn-0125 shows no clear stages of inference, attributed to its sandwich norm on the residual stream preventing residual-norm growth.
claims.evidence_quote: However, Huginn-0125 does not demonstrate clear stages of inference (Fig. 36). We suggest that this is likely due to the specific norm structures used by these models (Table 1).

claims.claim: Models without a fixed point (Ouro) show unstable stages of inference at unseen recurrence depths, whereas fixed-point models keep them; authors link this to Ouro's degradation when extrapolating loops.
claims.evidence_quote: models that do not reach a fixed point exhibit unstable stages of inference. Conversely, models with recurrent-block-wise stages of inference that also converge to a fixed point are guaranteed to keep enacting these stages of inference for arbitrary test time recurrences.

claims.claim: In random-init models, input injection yields stable fixed points for all norm types except Ouro's; without injection only pre-norm converges, to a degenerate shared fixed point.
claims.evidence_quote: We see that input injection results in stable fixed point behavior for all norm types other than Ouro, whereas omitting input injection means that only pre-norm reaches a stable fixed point.

numbers.what: Fraction of GSM8K tokens with non-fixed-point limiting behavior (no system prompt / long persona prompt)
numbers.quote: without a system prompt (the setting used throughout this paper) only approximately 0.02% of tokens exhibit non-fixed-point behavior. This percentage can be significantly increased with the longer system prompt, but these behaviors remain rare at 0.14%.

numbers.what: Small from-scratch looped models: width and training tokens
numbers.quote: For all experiments we use a model dimension (residual stream) of 512 (4 heads of dimension 128) and train for 3.7B tokens.

numbers.what: Analysis sample
numbers.quote: all results are visualized on the same random subset of 256 examples from the GSM8k test set;

numbers.what: Recurrences used to estimate approximate fixed point
numbers.quote: for each model we find an "approximate fixed point" per layer by iterating 128 times, then compute the norm of the difference

limitations: Only cyclic recurrence with a single looped block (not multiple sequential recurrent blocks); no analytical explanation of why architectures reach stable limiting behavior, nor whether stability helps or hurts reasoning; small from-scratch experiments at tiny scale; orbit/slider detection depends on hand-tuned hyperparameters.
survey_notes: Key mechanism paper: unifies fixed-point view with 'stages of inference'. Directly relevant to safety section because Ouro, the only model used in 2610.02741's loop-depth monitorability sweep, is shown here to lack fixed points and to drift beyond its 4 training loops; 2610.02741 evaluates T=6,8. Agrees with 2509.23314 on settling dynamics but studies one deep cyclic block instead of multiple 1-2 layer blocks. Contrasts with 2507.02199 (Lu et al.), which reports cyclic logit-lens behavior in Huginn. Claims about Ouro extrapolation and Huginn constant performance are cited from the original papers, not re-measured here. The fixed-point regime implies extra loops add nothing once converged, which bears on adaptive halting (convergence criteria).

title: Transformers Stop Thinking Too Early, and a Tiny LoRA Fixes It
relevance_reason: Mechanistic tracing of pointer-chasing in Ouro and Huginn; shows extra pretrained loops add little until a tiny single-layer LoRA starts a relay that later loops continue.
one_sentence: Frozen standard and looped LMs follow only ~1.4-3.6 reference-chain lines and extra loops barely help; a rank-8 single-layer LoRA starts a middle-layer relay that loops then extend (Ouro-1.4B: 60 lines at 4 loops, at least 160 at 8).
key_contributions: Measures short default reach on variable-chain programs across 13 standard models, Ouro-1.4B/2.6B and Huginn-0125; extra loops give diminishing returns.
A rank-8 residual LoRA at one early layer (32,769 params in Ouro-1.4B) makes extra loops useful; first-loop-only LoRA lets unmodified later loops continue the relay.

Causal account via linear readouts, attention knockout and causal tracing: relay advances within layers 7-15 of each Ouro loop; placement past a model-specific limit removes the benefit; gains transfer to MuSiQue.

setup.model_sizes: 13 standard base models (Qwen3, Llama, OLMo-3, Gemma-3), DeepSeek-V4-Flash 292B MoE; looped Ouro-1.4B, Ouro-2.6B, Huginn-0125
setup.train_tokens_or_data: LoRA trained on synthetic reference-chain programs (up to 20-40 lines) with KL penalty on WikiText-103
setup.loops_train: Ouro pretrained with four loops; Ouro LoRA trained with four loops (also 1 and 2); Huginn trained with 32 recurrences on average
setup.baselines: Frozen models; constant-vector control; LoRA at different layers; projection LoRA
setup.benchmarks: Synthetic reference-chain programs (choice/exact accuracy, reach at 80%); MuSiQue exact match

claims.claim: Extra loops in pretrained looped models add little reference-following reach: Ouro-1.4B plateaus at about 2.2 lines and Huginn at 1.4-1.6 lines regardless of recurrences.
claims.evidence_quote: Ouro1.4B's three-chain reach is 0, 1.6, 2.3, 2.2, and 2.2 lines after one through five loops. Ouro-2.6B follows the same pattern despite twice the layers per loop.

claims.claim: With a rank-8 single-layer LoRA applied in every loop, additional loops extend reach far beyond the training chain length.
claims.evidence_quote: Its longer-trained LoRA reaches 60 after four loops, about 146 after six, and at least 160 after eight (Fig. 3); 160-line accuracy is 87%, at four times the longest training chain.

claims.claim: A LoRA applied only in Ouro's first loop suffices for unmodified later loops to continue the relay to about 25 lines.
claims.evidence_quote: Ouro's first-loop-only LoRA reaches 9.5 lines after two loops, 21.5 after three, and about 25 after four through eight. Unmodified loops therefore continue the computation.

claims.claim: The relay is localized to a short band of middle layers repeated in each loop; linear readouts of chain identity show this progression per loop.
claims.evidence_quote: Ouro's relay advances almost entirely within layers 7–15 of each loop; with the longer-trained LoRA it reaches lines 4, 9, 25, and 40 after the first four loops (Fig. 2d).

claims.claim: Loop gains are bounded: both looped models lose reach when run well beyond their training loop counts.
claims.evidence_quote: Huginn's longer-trained LoRA reaches 31 lines after eight recurrences and 58 after sixteen (95% interval 37–64). These gains are not unlimited: both models lose reach when run well beyond their training loop counts.

numbers.what: Reliable reach across 13 frozen standard models
numbers.quote: Thirteen pretrained base models reliably follow only 1.4–3.6 lines (median 2.2).

numbers.what: Huginn-0125 frozen reach after 8/16/32 recurrences
numbers.quote: Huginn reaches only 1.4–1.6 lines after 8, 16, or 32 recurrences.

numbers.what: LoRA trainable parameters
numbers.quote: Only A, B, and s are trained: 65,537 parameters in Qwen3-8B, 32,769 in Ouro-1.4B, and 84,481 in Huginn.

numbers.what: Ouro WikiText perplexity change with LoRA at four loops
numbers.quote: WikiText perplexity changes from 10.14 to 10.148 in Qwen and 13.294 to 13.302 in Ouro at four loops: a measured control, not a general-behavior guarantee.

numbers.what: Ouro MuSiQue EM with layer-6 LoRA at four loops
numbers.quote: In Ouro, the layer-6 LoRA improves exact match on 300 development questions from 48.3% to 60.0% after four loops,

numbers.what: Last-loop-only LoRA reach, layer 6 vs layer 20, Ouro four loops
numbers.quote: layer 6 reaches 21.6 lines after four loops; layer 20 reaches 2.6, essentially the frozen 2.5.

limitations: Synthetic in-context tasks; MuSiQue only shows placement effects, not the same mechanism; detailed traces on Qwen3-8B and Ouro-1.4B; two looped families (Ouro-2.6B grown from 1.4B); LoRAs task-format specific; first-loop-only sufficiency shown to ~25 lines; algorithm not uniquely identified.
survey_notes: Important for 'do extra loops buy reasoning?': frozen Ouro/Huginn show saturating reach with loops (consistent with fixed-point/settling results in 2604.11791 and 2509.23314), but the capacity is latent and unlocked by a 0.002%-size edit. Interpretability: linear readouts of chain identity across loops plus attention knockout give causal per-loop evidence of an iterative relay. Safety relevance: tiny edits can greatly expand latent (unverbalized) multi-step computation in looped models, which is a concern for CoT monitorability (2610.02741), though the paper does not frame it that way. The 'code' URL is a project page.

title: Prediction Dynamics in Depth-Recurrent Language Models
relevance_reason: Analyzes how per-recurrence intermediate predictions of Huginn and Ouro evolve and why answers stabilize before scores do.
one_sentence: Derives an exact margin decomposition (translation, winner-directed motion, competitor pairing) explaining why intermediate answers of depth-recurrent LMs match the endpoint while scores keep changing; measured on Huginn-3.5B and Ouro-1.4B on ARC/MMLU with small samples.
key_contributions: Translation-invariant (oscillation-seminorm) margin hierarchy giving an ordering of earliest depths at which the endpoint answer is guaranteed.
Empirical decomposition on Huginn and Ouro trajectories: direction and pairing remove a further 22.5-34.4% of total depth beyond translation removal.
Shows retrospective geometric gains do not by themselves give a better online stopping policy (prefix study).

setup.model_sizes: Huginn-3.5B, Ouro-1.4B (plus archived RecurrentLlama trajectories)
setup.loops_train: Huginn trained at recurrence 32; Ouro four loops
setup.loops_test: Native endpoints T=32 (Huginn) and T=4 (Ouro); quarter-depth grid
setup.baselines: Raw magnitude bound, mean and LSE centering, coordinate-permutation references
setup.benchmarks: ARC-Challenge, MMLU (multiple-choice; N=32 or 128 questions per task; archive N=2,704 trajectories)

claims.claim: Accounting for update direction and competitor pairing substantially lowers the earliest depth at which the final answer is already guaranteed, beyond removing common translation.
claims.evidence_quote: Across Huginn-3.5B and Ouro-1.4B, accounting for update direction and competitor pairing reduces the mean earliest qualifying depth by a further 22.5–34.4% of the total depth beyond translation removal under full answer-text scoring.

claims.claim: Common and contrast score energies attenuate at different rates, so the share of preference-changing motion can grow while absolute updates shrink.
claims.evidence_quote: Common and contrast energies can attenuate at different rates, allowing a growing preference-change share to coexist with shrinking absolute updates.

claims.claim: Endpoint disagreement mixes corrections, degradations and wrong-to-wrong switches; many intermediate answer changes do not improve correctness.
claims.evidence_quote: At Huginn MMLU t = 4, (NW→C , NC→W , NW→W′ ) = (24, 7, 30): the net accuracy gain is 13.28 pp, while 30 answer changes leave the answer incorrect.

claims.claim: Retrospective geometric margins do not directly yield a better early-exit policy; quotient ranking trails mean centering in a prefix study.
claims.evidence_quote: Retrospective geometric gains therefore need a separate predictive evaluation before they can inform a stopping policy.

numbers.what: Endpoint accuracy under all-options answer-text scoring (Huginn ARC/MMLU, Ouro ARC/MMLU)
numbers.quote: Under full answer-text scoring, endpoint accuracy averaged over all arrangements is 49.22/43.75% for Huginn ARC/MMLU and 65.62/49.22% for Ouro.

numbers.what: Prefix early-exit work reduction at 2.5% target disagreement on Huginn (raw/mean/quotient)
numbers.quote: At the 2.5% target disagreement level, normalized work reductions are 21.72% for raw, 23.93% for mean-centered and 22.97% for quotient ranking,

numbers.what: Candidate depths and endpoints
numbers.value: T/4, T/2, 3T/4; T=32 Huginn, T=4 Ouro
numbers.quote: Candidate depths are T /4, T /2, 3T /4 with endpoint T = 32 for Huginn and T = 4 for Ouro; D = T if no earlier depth qualifies.

limitations: Multiple-choice only; three checkpoints in two families; small question samples (N=32 per task for main answer-text analyses); retrospective, completed-trajectory geometry is not an online stopping policy; no interventions on recurrent states; open-ended generation not covered. Ouro outputs are taken per recurrent depth without its gate mixture.
survey_notes: Per-token/per-question convergence of intermediate decoded predictions across recurrences (vocabulary-space readout at each depth). Supports the view that answers settle before the full budget (consistent with fixed-point findings in 2604.11791 and Huginn convergence analyses), but warns that retrospective convergence signals need predictive validation before use as halting criteria. Very small N; treat numbers as illustrative.

title: Interaction Locality in Hierarchical Recursive Reasoning
relevance_reason: Causal locality analysis (SAE ablations, finite-noise patching) of recurrent H/L states in HRM and TRM across recursion cycles.
one_sentence: Introduces interaction locality (does a perturbation's effect stay within task-defined neighborhoods) and finds that in HRM and TRM high-level states write local summaries that repeated recursion accumulates into global solutions; first-step decodes already contain much of the final structure.
key_contributions: Task-geometry-aware locality metric instantiated with SAE feature ablations and finite-noise activation patching (Jacobian/attention checks in appendix).
Across Maze-Hard, Sudoku-Extreme and ARC-AGI, within-H patching is at least as local as within-L in all six model-task cells, strongest in TRM.
Extension to MTU3D (3D scene grounding) shows locality concentrated at module boundaries instead of across recursion.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: Released HRM and TRM checkpoints; ScanNet scenes for MTU3D
setup.loops_test: HRM 2x2 H/L schedule; TRM three high phases with four (Maze/ARC) or six (Sudoku) low calls
setup.baselines: Geometry-matched random-neighborhood baseline
setup.benchmarks: Maze-Hard, Sudoku-Extreme, ARC-AGI (HRM on ARC-AGI-2, TRM on ARC-AGI-1); MTU3D on 30 ScanNet scenes

claims.claim: High-level recurrent states write information locally, while repeated recursive updates accumulate local writes into broader solution structure.
claims.evidence_quote: activation patching gives the clearest architectural fingerprint: high-level recurrent states tend to write information within nearby cells or same-segment units, while repeated recursive updates accumulate these local writes into broader solution structure.

claims.claim: Within-H locality is at least as high as within-L in every model-task cell and above a geometry-matched baseline; the contrast is largest in TRM on Maze.
claims.evidence_quote: The effect is clearest in TRM/Maze, where within-H is .580 while within-L is near baseline at .032, and it extends to ARC-AGI when connected objects define the neighborhood.

claims.claim: Most state change happens early; first-step decodes already contain recognizable final solution structure, though such decodes are observational only.
claims.evidence_quote: Step 1 already contains recognizable task structure across domains, supporting it as a solution-forming window.

numbers.what: TRM/Maze patching locality within-H vs within-L
numbers.quote: where within-H is .580 while within-L is near baseline at .032,

numbers.what: Finite-noise patching sample size
numbers.quote: Finite-noise patching uses n = 50 examples per

limitations: Compares released checkpoints rather than an accuracy-matched training sweep; ARC versions differ between HRM and TRM; neighborhood definitions are task-geometry specific and do not exhaust spatial relations; no training-dynamics analysis.
survey_notes: Mechanism of how recursion routes computation in HRM/TRM: local writes per cycle, globalization over cycles. Consistent with 2609.22197 (distributed computation, task-dependent H/L roles) and with early settling (most change in first step). Patching-based rather than probe-based evidence. Note the 'Finite-noise patching uses n = 50' quote is short (8 words).

title: From Growing to Looping: A Unified View of Iterative Computation in LLMs
relevance_reason: Pretrains looped and depth-grown LMs (360M/1.7B) and compares their depth-wise mechanistic signatures (tuned lens, residual interventions, layer swaps).
one_sentence: Shows looped and middle-layer-duplication depth-grown LMs share mechanistic signatures (late-layer reliance, 4-layer periodic sublayer patterns, aggregation layers), and that grown models can be looped at inference for up to 2x gains on reasoning primitives.
key_contributions: Benchmarks standard, looped (Loop(Lxk), Loop(e-Lxk-d)) and depth-grown (MIDAS, LIDAS) models at 360M and 1.7B on 22 tasks under iso-param, iso-inference and training-FLOP views.

Mechanistic diagnostics (depth score, tuned-lens early exit, residual-stream norm, local-effect interventions, layer swapping) show convergent block-periodic signatures; fully looped models are more order-sensitive.
Composability: inference-time looping of a middle block in grown models and retrofitting recurrence during cooldown.

setup.model_sizes: SmolLM-v1 360M and 1.7B configurations; looped variants e.g. Loop(4x6), Loop(4-4x4-4), Loop(12x2)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: approximately 200B (360M) and 400B (1.7B) tokens
setup.loops_test: Same as training; grown models looped at inference with extra repetitions of a 4-layer block
setup.baselines: Standard transformers at full depth (iso-inference) and at the same unique-layer count (iso-param); MIDAS, LIDAS
setup.benchmarks: 22 tasks: closed/open-book QA, Lambada, HellaSwag, SVAMP/ASDiv/MAWPS, reasoning primitives; held-out NLL

claims.claim: At the same number of unique parameters, looped models beat standard models on most task categories, with the largest gains on reasoning-heavy categories.
