Its re-evaluation of HRM-Text 1B differs from HRM-Text's self-reported numbers (e.g. DROP 78.1 vs 82.21, MMLU 58.7 vs 60.73, BoolQ 87.5 vs 86.18; HRM-Text paper Table 1), a harness-sensitivity contradiction to report. Mimir is not better than HRM-Text on every task: MATH 45.8 vs 56.0 and MMLU 57.5 vs 58.7 favor HRM-Text. Provides no evidence about recurrence per se (no non-recurrent control).

title: Hierarchical vs. Flat Iteration in Shared-Weight Transformers
relevance_reason: Adapts HRM's Fast/Slow shared-weight recurrence to autoregressive LM at ~1.2B parameters and compares to a parameter-matched flat Universal Transformer and standard Transformers.
one_sentence: HRM-LM replaces a Transformer stack with an input block plus a gated Fast block (every step) and Slow block (every T steps) iterated M=12 times; at ~1.2B on OpenWebText it reaches 4.18 nats while a parameter-matched flat Universal Transformer plateaus near 7.6.
key_contributions: HRM-style two-speed shared-weight recurrence for causal LM with GRU-style gated updates, fixed initial state, K-step truncated BPTT and output fusion.

Parameter-matched comparison of hierarchical (HRM, 1229M) vs flat (UniTF, 1218M) shared-weight iteration across five runs; equal-hyperparameter and budget-matched comparisons with Transformers L=4 and L=12.
Corrects an earlier claim: weight sharing does not shrink KV cache (O(M n d)), only stored weights; reports 2-5x slower per-token generation.

setup.model_sizes: ~1.2B (HRM NT=12: 1229M; UniTF 474M-1218M; Transformer L=4 and L=12).
setup.train_tokens_or_data: OpenWebText, GPT-2 tokenizer; 10,000 iterations of batch 12 x 1,024 tokens (some runs to 20k-60k).
setup.loops_train: M = N x T = 12 recurrent steps (N=4 base), S supervision passes, K-step TBPTT window (K=2 base; K=8 best in ablation).
setup.baselines: UniTF (flat shared block, M=12), Transformer L=4 (equal parameters), Transformer L=12.
setup.benchmarks: OpenWebText validation cross-entropy only (no downstream tasks).

claims.claim: At matched parameters, hierarchical Fast/Slow shared-weight iteration trains to 4.18 nats while flat shared-weight iteration (UniTF) plateaus at about 7.6 nats regardless of hyperparameters.
claims.regime: iso_param, iso_data, same recurrent step count M=12
claims.evidence_quote: flat shared-weight iteration (UniTF, same block repeated uniformly) consistently plateaus at ≈7.6 nats regardless of hyperparameter settings, while hierarchically structured shared-weight iteration (HRM, Fast/Slow two-speed) converges to 4.18

claims.claim: Under equal hyperparameters HRM NT=12 trails an equal-parameter Transformer L=4 by 0.20 nats; a single-seed budget-matched search reverses this by 0.23 nats.
claims.regime: iso_param, iso_data (HRM uses ~3x the per-token compute of T-L4)
claims.evidence_quote: Under standardized equal-hyperparameter evaluation (MultiSeed), HRM NT=12 (4.896) trails Transformer L=4 (4.697) by 0.20 nats under equal hyperparameters

claims.claim: Weight sharing reduces stored parameters but not KV cache; HRM-LM with M=12 uses 3x the KV cache of the equal-parameter 4-layer Transformer.
claims.evidence_quote: parameter sharing reduces stored weights but not inference KV cache, since each of the M steps attends over a distinct set of positions and must cache its own K/V tensors.

claims.claim: A longer TBPTT window helps: K=8 is the best ablation result with no sign of diminishing returns from K=4.
claims.evidence_quote: K = 8 achieves K/M = 67% gradient coverage and is the best single result in the ablation suite.

numbers.what: Budget-matched HP search: HRM best vs T-L4 best (single seed)
numbers.quote: A budget-matched grid search (HPSearch, 8 configurations each, seed=42) recovers HRM best (4.31) over T-L4 best (4.54) by 0.23 nats

numbers.what: UniTF 1218M plateau
numbers.quote: the same ceiling as at 820M—while HRM NT=12 converges to 4.177 at 10k steps. The 10k completion is ongoing; the plateau is stable throughout; final val CE 7.578 at 10k.

numbers.what: T-L12 at 60k steps vs HRM at 10k
numbers.quote: T-L12 at 60k (4.250) trails HRM NT=12 at 10k (4.177) by 0.073 nats; confirmed converged

numbers.what: Training budget
numbers.quote: Training runs for 10,000 iterations with batch size 12, sequence length 1,024, on 6 NVIDIA RTX 6000 Blackwell GPUs using DDP.

limitations: Single scale (~1.2B), single dataset, validation loss only, no downstream tasks; very short training (10k steps) with absolute losses far above typical converged LM losses; several key results single-seed; HRM loses to Transformer L=4 under equal hyperparameters.
survey_notes: Contested evidence for 'hierarchy matters' in LM: the flat UniTF baseline plateaus at ~7.6 nats at 1.2B after 10k steps (it needed width-dependent initialization fixes, App. B), far worse than flat looped LMs reported elsewhere (e.g. Huginn 2502.05171, Ouro 2510.25741 train to normal LM losses), so the 3.4-nat gap may reflect a failure of this particular UniTF configuration and very short training rather than a structural ceiling; the author argues gradient-norm analysis rules out optimization artifacts. The paper itself reports HRM trails an equal-parameter T-L4 under equal hyperparameters. Contrasts with 2609.39967 (a shared single module suffices on puzzles) and with HRM-Text 2605.20613 (separate H/L weights, 1B, strong downstream results). Useful correction on KV cache: sharing does not reduce KV memory when M >= L.

title: When to Re-Plan: Subgoal Persistence in Hierarchical Latent Reasoning
relevance_reason: Extends HRM's H/L recurrence with a feudal manager-worker subgoal interface and studies the persistence period P on ARC.
one_sentence: Adding to HRM a high-level directional subgoal that persists for P low-level steps plus a cosine alignment loss lowers training-set LM loss on augmented ARC at P=3 (1.544 vs 1.640 baseline), while P=1 is worse than no subgoal.
key_contributions: Subgoal-Augmented HRM: normalized subgoal emitted every P micro-steps, injected as additive bias into L updates, with cosine alignment loss on net L displacement and an optional commitment gate.
Sweeps of persistence P and alignment weight lambda (narrow optimum near 0.05); 5-seed replication of best configuration.
Controlled ablation at lambda=0.10 with random directions isolating learned directional structure as the source of interference.

setup.model_sizes: HRM backbone, hidden 512, 4 H and 4 L layers, 8 heads (parameter count not stated).
setup.train_tokens_or_data: ARC + ConceptARC with up to 1000 augmentations per puzzle (arc-aug-1000); ablation on num_aug=100; ConceptARC-mini held-out (~4,900 train, ~400 val).
setup.loops_train: Hcycles = Lcycles = 2, ACT up to 16 internal steps, deep supervision with detached state.
setup.baselines: HRM without subgoals; subgoal variants (no injection, no alignment loss, random directions).
setup.benchmarks: Training-set LM loss (primary), token and exact accuracy (secondary), ConceptARC-mini LM loss.

claims.claim: Subgoal persistence, not injection, drives the effect: P in [3,6] beats P=1 and the baseline, with a minimum at P=3.
claims.regime: iso_data, matched compute (metric is training-set LM loss)
claims.evidence_quote: moderate periods P ∈ [3, 6] consistently outperform both very frequent (P =1) and longer horizons, with a clear minimum LM loss at P =3 (1.544 vs. 1.674 at P =1 and a 1.640 baseline

claims.claim: The held-out ConceptARC-mini improvement is about 0.4% in LM loss, which the author treats as secondary evidence only.
claims.evidence_quote: The no-subgoal baseline achieves LM loss 2.316; SubgoalAugmented HRM at λ=0.05, P =3 achieves 2.308. The improvement is modest in absolute terms (∼0.4%)

numbers.what: 5-seed replication at lambda=0.05, P=3
numbers.quote: At λ=0.05, P =3: mean LM loss 1.595 (std 0.045, min 1.540, max 1.662).

numbers.what: Primary metric definition
numbers.quote: We report LM loss as the primary metric: tokenlevel stablemax cross-entropy, masked over valid output positions, computed on the training set at matched optimization steps.

limitations: Primary metric is training-set LM loss, not held-out ARC accuracy; held-out gain ~0.4%; 5-seed mean (1.595, std 0.045) is only one std below the single baseline value (1.640); ablation single seed; ARC only.
venue: Accepted to the 2nd Workshop on Compositional Learning at ICML 2026, Seoul, South Korea.
survey_notes: Weak evidence; useful only as an example of explicit H-to-L intent signalling in HRM. Not comparable to any benchmark accuracy table. Its premise that HRM's H/L interplay is the locus of planning is in tension with 2609.39967, TRM and 2605.17811, which find a single shared module suffices or that roles emerge without separate modules.

title: One Model, Two Roles: Emergent Specialization in a Shared Recurrent Transformer
relevance_reason: Controlled ablation of HRM/TRM two-state recurrence with one shared Transformer: which signals make two latent states specialize and how that affects Sudoku/Maze accuracy.
one_sentence: AIR shares one 4-layer Transformer for HRM's L and H updates with HRM's one-step gradient; asymmetric input injection (only L sees x) yields specialized committed zH / uncertain zL and ~59% vs ~51% Sudoku-Extreme accuracy for symmetric injection.
key_contributions: Minimal testbed: TRM-style shared weights for both updates, HRM-style one-step truncated gradient, CL=CH=2, ACT not analyzed.

Injection-asymmetry and level-token ablations (5 seeds) showing that a state-identity signal is needed for specialization and accuracy; a single-state model with periodic injection does no better than symmetric two-state.
Decoded rollouts, freeze experiments and attention locality analysis characterizing the zH (proposal) vs zL (scratchpad) roles.

setup.model_sizes: One shared 4-layer Transformer (about half of HRM's parameters per the paper).
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 1,000 puzzles with 1,000x augmentation for Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Hard; evaluation on full 422,786 Sudoku test and 1,000 Maze test.
setup.loops_train: CL = CH = 2 (L,L,H,L,L,H); gradient only through final L and H update; deep supervision as in HRM.
setup.baselines: Symmetric-injection variants, level-token variants, single-state variant, published HRM (55.0 / 74.5).
setup.benchmarks: Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Hard exact match.

claims.claim: Asymmetric input injection improves accuracy over symmetric injection with the same shared model: ~59% vs ~51% on Sudoku, ~73% vs ~70% on Maze.
claims.evidence_quote: On Sudoku, asymmetric configurations (∆ > 0) cluster around 59%, whereas symmetric ones (∆ = 0) fall to about 51%, an ∼8-point drop. On Maze, most asymmetric variants cluster around ∼73% versus ∼70% for symmetric ones.

claims.claim: A single shared model with two states matches or exceeds the two-network HRM baseline with about half its parameters.
claims.regime: unmatched (HRM number quoted from its paper; ~50% of parameters)
claims.evidence_quote: the best AIR variants are also comparable to—and on Sudoku even exceed—the original two-network HRM baseline (55.0% on Sudoku, 74.5% on Maze) with only 50% of the latter's parameters

claims.claim: Two latent states are needed: a single state with periodic input injection reaches only 51.1% on Sudoku vs 60.0% for the asymmetric two-state default.
claims.evidence_quote: The single-state model achieves 51.1% accuracy, on par with the symmetric two-states baselines and far below the asymmetric default (60.0%). This indicates that periodic input injection alone is not sufficient.

claims.claim: A prepended-then-stripped learned level token recovers most of the asymmetry benefit under symmetric injection (57.5%), whereas additive level vectors do not (50.0%).
claims.evidence_quote: Addition element-wise add 50.0±1.9 metric variants (47.8%). This + Prepend (strip) prepend, attend, strip 57.5±1.3

numbers.what: Default Lx_H (asymmetric) Sudoku accuracy, 5 seeds
numbers.quote: Symmetric two-state, (1, 1) Asymmetric two-state, (1, 0) (default) 52.1±1.6 60.0±2.0

numbers.what: Evaluation and training protocol
numbers.quote: Training data consists of 1,000 puzzles with 1,000× augmentation. All accuracy numbers report peak / early-stop exact-match accuracy on a held-out test set.

limitations: Two synthetic grid tasks; only a 4-layer shared block and CL=CH=2; reported accuracies are peak/early-stop on the test set (checkpoint selection on test); HRM baseline quoted, not rerun; mechanistic evidence strongest on Sudoku.
survey_notes: Clarifies the HRM vs TRM 'hierarchy' question: separate weights are unnecessary (consistent with 2609.39967, TRM), but two distinguishable state roles matter (single-state 51.1% vs two-state 60.0%), which partly reconciles TRM's (y, z) two-state design with HRM. Mixes TRM sharing with HRM one-step gradient, so its ~60% Sudoku is well below TRM's 87.4% (TRM backprops through a full recursion), indirectly supporting the importance of the gradient horizon (2609.39967). Uses peak test accuracy.

title: Tiny Autoregressive Recursive Models
relevance_reason: Tests whether TRM's nested two-stream refinement transfers to causal next-token prediction under block-pass-matched compute, via a one-mechanism-at-a-time ladder from dense Transformer to autoregressive TRM.
one_sentence: Holding block design, token stream and next-token loss fixed and matching decoder-block evaluations, a dense Transformer and a flat two-stream Dual UT generalize best on character-level copy/reverse/addition while the autoregressive TRM stays near chance.
key_contributions: Controlled ladder: Dense -> Iterative (tied) -> step embeddings -> UT with ACT -> Dual UT (two streams) -> Dual Nested UT -> Autoregressive TRM (Q-halt, terminal readout), each adding one mechanism at matched block passes.
Autoregressive projection of TRM: causal masking and re-initialized latent streams per forward pass (no cross-call carry).
Negative result: nested token-internal refinement gives no reliable gains; Dual UT avoids late-position collapse on addition.

setup.model_sizes: Tiny models (exact sizes not stated in main text); fixed block budget C (e.g. 12 block evaluations).
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Procedurally generated character-level algorithmic sequences (Copy, Reverse, Addition).
setup.loops_train: C block passes per token split across tied recurrence or nested inner/outer updates; gradient truncation scheme not stated in the text read; trained 1,000-5,000 gradient steps at lr 3e-4, batch 64.
setup.loops_test: Same C; ACT variants run in full-compute mode.
setup.baselines: Dense Transformer (untied), Iterative Transformer, Iterative Step Transformer, Universal Transformer, Dual UT, Dual Nested UT.
setup.benchmarks: Copy, Reverse, Addition with OOD length scaling: exact match, character accuracy, position-wise accuracy.

claims.claim: At matched block-pass compute, untied depth and a flat two-stream recurrent baseline generalize best; the autoregressive TRM gives no consistent benefit and often degrades sharply.
claims.evidence_quote: Across compute-matched experiments on character-level algorithmic tasks (addition, copying, reversing), untied depth and a flat two-stream recurrent baseline yield the strongest generalization per block evaluation.

claims.claim: Character accuracy (length 10): Dense and UT solve Copy and Reverse; on Addition Dense 80% vs UT 66%; autoregressive TRM ~10-12% on all three.
claims.evidence_quote: Addition remains more difficult and separates these two models (80% vs. 66%). The autoregressive TRM performs poorly on all three tasks, reaching only 12%, 11%, and 10% accuracy, respectively.

claims.claim: Single-stream recurrent variants collapse at late output positions on addition, while Dual UT stays stable; only Dense and Dual UT overcome the last-character bottleneck.
claims.evidence_quote: Only Dense and Dual UT reliably break through the final-character bottleneck, with lastcharacter accuracy rising sharply and reaching high values by the end of training.

limitations: Tiny models, small data, three character-level tasks only; authors note results could change at larger scale; TRM adapted with causal mask and no cross-call carry, which removes features of the original TRM.
venue: Published at ICLR 2026 Workshop on AI with Recursive Self-Improvement.
survey_notes: Negative evidence for bringing TRM-style nested refinement to autoregressive LM: under iso-block-evaluation compute, nesting hurts; untied depth wins over tied UT on addition (80 vs 66). Contrasts with HRM-Text (2605.20613), which reports HRM beating FLOP-matched Transformers at 1B on instruction data, but HRM-Text uses PrefixLM, separate H/L weights and truncated BPTT, and matches training FLOPs rather than block passes per token; these differences, not just scale, may explain the disagreement. Also contrasts with HRM-LM 2604.14442 (hierarchy helps vs flat UT).

title: BDH-CQ: In-Context Learning with Recurrent Latent Reasoning
relevance_reason: Recurrent latent reasoning over depth (H_{r+1}=F(H_r,S)) with in-context recurrent memory on ARC-AGI-1; architecture details proprietary.
one_sentence: BDH-CQ (150M, Dragon Hatchling family) ingests ARC demonstrations into a recurrent memory and iterates a latent workspace to answer the query, reaching 29.5% pass@2 on public ARC-AGI-1 at $0.0007 per task without task IDs or evaluation demonstrations in training.
key_contributions: Inductive (non-transductive) ARC protocol for a latent recurrent reasoner: no task identifiers, no evaluation-task demonstration pairs in training, no test-time parameter updates.
Cost-accuracy operating point: 29.5% pass@2 at about 0.85 H200 GPU-seconds per task, independently reproduced by a black-box audit.
ConceptARC concept-family capability profile and controlled ARC-like interventions on binding and extrapolation.

setup.model_sizes: 150M parameters.
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Private curated ARC-style data plus ARC-AGI-1 training set, RE-ARC, ConceptARC, ARC-Heavy, ARC-GEN100K, with augmentations.
setup.loops_train: R latent reasoning iterations (value not disclosed; implementation proprietary).
setup.baselines: ARC Prize leaderboard systems (costs from leaderboard).
setup.benchmarks: ARC-AGI-1 public evaluation (400 tasks) pass@1/pass@2; ConceptARC.

claims.claim: BDH-CQ reaches 29.5% pass@2 on ARC-AGI-1 public evaluation at a computed $0.00070 per task, beyond the leaderboard's previous cost-accuracy Pareto frontier.
claims.evidence_quote: At the default point, the 150M-parameter system reaches 29.5% pass@2 in approximately 0.85 H200 GPU-seconds per task. At $3 per H200-hour this gives a computed cost of $0.00070 per task

claims.claim: Unlike HRM/TRM ARC pipelines, neither task identifiers nor evaluation-task demonstrations are used in training.
claims.evidence_quote: Neither task identifiers nor evaluation-task demonstration pairs participate in training, and no parameters are updated at inference time.

numbers.what: Table 1 ARC-AGI-1 public: N tasks / test pairs, pass@1 tasks and pairs, pass@2 tasks

limitations: Dimensions, update rules, training recipe and inference pipeline (candidate construction, ranking) are proprietary, so the loop structure cannot be placed precisely in the template; ConceptARC is in the training mixture, so the ConceptARC profile is not a held-out evaluation; cost comparisons mix measured hardware time with leaderboard API prices.
survey_notes: Important as the only ARC entry in this group evaluated inductively (no puzzle IDs, no eval demonstrations in training): its 29.5% pass@2 must not be ranked against HRM 40.3 / TRM 44.6 / looped flows 58.8, which are transductive with puzzle embeddings and 1000-augmentation voting (2512.11847, 2609.39967 App. A.6). Proprietary details prevent verifying recurrence structure; treat as adjacent.

title: Self-Supervised Transformers as Iterative Solution Improvers for Constraint Satisfaction
relevance_reason: A Transformer trained (self-supervised) for one refinement step and applied iteratively at test time on CSPs; test-time iteration as depth, but no latent recurrence across steps.
one_sentence: ConsFormer trains a Transformer with differentiable constraint penalties to improve a random CSP assignment in one step, then iterates it thousands of times at test time, solving 77.74% of out-of-distribution hard Sudokus at 10k iterations.
key_contributions: Self-supervised training with continuous relaxations of discrete constraints, no feasible-solution labels.
Single-step training, iterative deployment: more test-time iterations solve harder OOD instances.
Results on Sudoku, Graph Coloring, Nurse Rostering and MAXCUT.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: 9K training instances per problem (SATNet Sudoku in-distribution; RRN test set as harder OOD).
setup.loops_train: Single refinement step.
setup.baselines: Learned CSP solvers including Yang et al. (2023) recurrent Transformer, ANYCSP; OR-Tools.
setup.benchmarks: Sudoku (in-distribution and OOD), Graph Coloring, Nurse Rostering, MAXCUT.

claims.claim: Iterating a one-step-trained refiner at test time solves out-of-distribution hard Sudoku, improving with more iterations (65.88% at 2k, 77.74% at 10k).
claims.regime: unmatched (vs published learned solvers); iso_param across iteration counts
claims.evidence_quote: ConsFormer achieves instance solve rates of 65.88% and 77.74% with 2k and 10k iterations, respectively.

claims.claim: Authors attribute better test-time scaling than a 32-iteration-trained recurrent Transformer to training for a single iteration.
claims.evidence_quote: This could be due to Yang et al. (2023)'s approach being trained for 32 iterations, while ConsFormer was trained for a single iteration, allowing it to generalize better when applied iteratively.

limitations: Sudoku benchmarks are SATNet/RRN sets, not Sudoku-Extreme; no hidden state carried across iterations (state is the assignment).
venue: Proceedings of the 42 nd International Conference on Machine Learning, Vancouver, Canada. PMLR 267, 2025.
builds_on: Yang et al. 2023 (looped Transformer on Sudoku)
survey_notes: Predecessor-style evidence that iterating a prediction-space refinement map scales with test-time compute; conceptually close to GFPR (2609.33540, state is the prediction) and RSM (2603.15641, depth-agnostic operator trained shallow). Not comparable to Sudoku-Extreme numbers.

title: G-RRM: Guiding Symbolic Solvers with Recurrent Reasoning Models
relevance_reason: Uses SE-RRM recurrent reasoning models as neural hint generators for backtracking/SAT solvers; application of looped reasoners rather than a new looped method.
one_sentence: G-RRM feeds SE-RRM full-assignment proposals as branching hints to backtracking and SAT solvers; on 9x9 Sudoku (SE-RRM 91.1% correct) backtracking speeds up 33.3x and Glucose 1.70x, while CaDiCaL, which cannot overwrite hints, gains nothing.
key_contributions: Neuro-symbolic pipeline: recurrent reasoning model proposals guide classical CSP/SAT solvers to guaranteed-correct solutions.
Identifies two conditions for speedups: large combinatorial search space and solvers that can overwrite imperfect hints.

setup.baselines: Unguided backtracking, Glucose 4.1, CaDiCaL 3.0.0.
setup.benchmarks: Sudoku 9x9 to 25x25 solver runtime and conflicts.

claims.claim: Neural guidance from SE-RRM yields large speedups for backtracking and Glucose on 9x9 Sudoku, but not for CaDiCaL whose runtime is overhead-dominated and which always respects hints.
claims.evidence_quote: on 9 × 9 Sudoku, where the SE-RRM correctly solves 91.1% of instances, backtracking accelerates by 33.3× and Glucose 4.1 by 1.70× (median, p < 0.001)

limitations: Read at abstract level only (priority 3).
survey_notes: Shows one practical use of recursive reasoners: correctness via symbolic verification/search, addressing the no-guarantee failure mode. Its 91.1% SE-RRM figure on 9x9 Sudoku differs from 93.73% (16 steps) in 2603.02193, likely different instances or settings; protocol not checked.

title: CosmicFish-HRM: Adaptive Reasoning via Hierarchical Recurrent Mechanisms in Compact Language Models
relevance_reason: Compact autoregressive LM with an HRM core iterating H/L cycles and a Q-style learned halting head.
one_sentence: An 82.77M LM with an HRM reasoning core and learned halting trained on 10B tokens allocates non-uniform reasoning steps but does not beat similar-size Transformers (GPT-2 Small, OPT-125M, Pythia-160M) on zero-shot HellaSwag/PIQA/WinoGrande.
key_contributions: HRM-style H/L recurrent core inside a GQA/RoPE/SwiGLU decoder with halt/continue head, exploration during training and inference halt bias.
Analysis of reasoning-step allocation across tasks and inputs.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: CosmicSet, 10B tokens (web, Wikipedia, code, math, papers).
setup.loops_train: H/L cycles up to a maximum number of reasoning steps with learned halting.
setup.loops_test: Learned halting with bias delta=0.35 toward early stopping.
setup.baselines: CosmicFish-90M/120M without HRM core; GPT-2 Small, OPT-125M, Pythia-160M.
setup.benchmarks: HellaSwag, PIQA, WinoGrande, TriviaQA, ARC-Easy, Natural Questions (zero-shot).

claims.claim: At compact scale the HRM core does not improve zero-shot accuracy over similar-size Transformers; authors hypothesize the overhead amortizes at larger scale (untested).
claims.regime: unmatched (different data; non-HRM CosmicFish variants differ in size)
claims.evidence_quote: At compact scale, CosmicFish-HRM does not outperform conventional transformers of similar size on these benchmarks.

numbers.what: Zero-shot HellaSwag/PIQA/WinoGrande: CosmicFish-HRM

limitations: Small scale, shallow benchmarks not designed for iterative reasoning; no matched non-recurrent control at the same size and data; scaling hypothesis untested.
survey_notes: Negative/neutral LM data point for HRM-style recurrence at <100M scale; contrasts with HRM-Text (1B, instruction data, strong gains) and is consistent with AR-TRM (2603.08082) finding no benefit for TRM-style nesting in small autoregressive models. Low evidential weight (single author, no controlled baseline).

title: Latent Recurrent Thoughts: Recurrent Refinement of Proposed Latents for Reasoning with Frozen LLMs
relevance_reason: Uses TRM's recursive module as a small recurrent refiner of latent thought vectors fed to a frozen Qwen3-8B; recursion lives in an auxiliary module, not the LM.
one_sentence: LRT trains a ~4.2M proposer and a ~7M TRM-style recurrent refiner to produce continuous latent thoughts for a frozen Qwen3-8B, beating frozen-decoder latent-reasoning baselines on Countdown-4, Sudoku, HumanEval, MBPP and StrategyQA at matched budget.
key_contributions: Frozen-LLM latent reasoning where the latents come from a tiny recurrent refiner (TRM recursion with input re-injection and bounded residual corrections).
Controlled comparison with identical frozen decoder, prompts, data and budget; refiner scaling 7M -> 28M improves Countdown-4 and HumanEval monotonically.

setup.model_sizes: Frozen Qwen3-8B; trainable ~11.2M (proposer ~4.2M, refiner ~7M; refiner scaled to 28M).
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Task answer supervision without reasoning traces.
setup.loops_train: Truncated-gradient unrolling following TRM.
setup.baselines: Direct, Zero-shot CoT, prior frozen-decoder continuous-space methods (e.g. EBM-CoT), prefix/P-tuning; reference: thinking mode, MGDM, TRM, EqR.
setup.benchmarks: Countdown-4, Sudoku, HumanEval, MBPP, StrategyQA.

claims.claim: Scaling only the recurrent refiner (7M to 28M) with the decoder frozen improves Countdown-4 from 56.7 to 69.1 and HumanEval from 37.8 to 46.1.
claims.evidence_quote: Countdown-4 rises from 56.7 to 66.3 to 69.1, and HumanEval from 37.8 to 44.0 to 46.1.

claims.claim: On Sudoku, thinking-mode Qwen3-8B fails (0.5) while the 7M refiner reaches 49.2; from-scratch symbolic solvers (TRM, EqR) remain far higher.
claims.evidence_quote: Sudoku, is exactly where it fails (0.5) while a 7M recurrent refiner reaches 49.2: token-space search is not a substitute for iterative computation on a constraint-satisfaction substrate.

limitations: Abstract-plus-scan reading (priority 3); Sudoku dataset may differ from Sudoku-Extreme (TRM listed at 97.2 in its reference table, vs 87.4 on Sudoku-Extreme in TRM's paper).
survey_notes: Hybrid: TRM-style recursion as a plug-in reasoning module for a frozen LLM, one route to bring recursive reasoners to language other than pretraining an HRM LM (HRM-Text, Mimir) or editing explicit candidates (R-Qwen 2608.01534).

title: Parameter-Efficient Quality Estimation via Frozen Recursive Models
relevance_reason: Applies TRM's shared-network recursion (internal L cycles, external refinement steps) to MT quality estimation on frozen embeddings.
one_sentence: On low-resource MT quality estimation for 8 language pairs, TRM's external iteration hurts and internal recursion helps only narrowly; a 7M TRM head on frozen XLM-R embeddings reaches Spearman 0.370, above an equal-depth standard Transformer (0.336).
key_contributions: Three-phase test of TRM mechanisms on a regression task (QE): external iteration steps 1-16 and L cycles 1-6.
Frozen pretrained embeddings match fine-tuned ones with 37x fewer trainable parameters.

setup.model_sizes: TRM-QE 7M trainable on frozen XLM-R (vs 262M fine-tuned).
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Low-resource QE dataset, 8 language pairs.
setup.loops_train: External iteration 1-16 steps, Lcycles 1-6 (ablation).
setup.baselines: Fine-tuned variants, equivalent-depth standard Transformer, MonoTransQuest (560M).
setup.benchmarks: Spearman/Pearson correlation for QE.

claims.claim: TRM's recursive mechanisms do not transfer to QE: single-step models are best on external iteration, and internal recursion gives only narrow benefits.
claims.evidence_quote: Contrary to intuitions from reasoning tasks, single-step models achieve the highest correlation (0.333 Pearson, 0.324 Spearman),

claims.claim: Frozen-embedding TRM-QE (0.370 Spearman) outperforms an equivalent-depth standard Transformer (0.336).
claims.evidence_quote: TRM-QE with frozen XLM-R embeddings achieves a Spearman's correlation of 0.370, matching fine-tuned variants (0.369) and outperforming an equivalentdepth standard transformer (0.336).

limitations: Abstract-plus-scan reading (priority 3); single regression task family.
survey_notes: Out-of-domain negative result: TRM's outer-loop refinement (deep supervision steps) does not help a non-search regression task; supports the view that recursive-reasoner gains are task-dependent (search/constraint tasks), cf. 2609.39967's domain-dependent test-time gains.

title: Selection, Reflection and Self-Refinement: Revisit Reasoning Tasks via a Causal Lens
relevance_reason: Single shared Transformer layer unrolled as a fixed-point latent refiner with input/feedback injection and periodic intermediate alignment; compared to HRM and recurrent-depth baselines on Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, ARC.
one_sentence: SR2 casts reasoning as selection over dense latent dependencies and implements reflective representation learning, dependency self-refinement with a single recurrent Transformer layer, and periodic intermediate alignment, reaching 66.63% Sudoku-Extreme and 93.7% Maze-Hard at 3.4M parameters.
key_contributions: Causal 'selection mechanism' view of reasoning tasks motivating latent feedback (reflection) and dependency self-refinement.
Flattened recurrent Transformer: one shared block unrolled as fixed-point iteration, with feedback injection and periodic intermediate supervision.
Comparison ladder on Sudoku-Extreme/Maze-Hard: Transformer, Block Universal Transformer, Recurrent Depth (input injection), Reflective Model, HRM, SR2.

setup.model_sizes: SR2 3.4M (single Transformer layer backbone); Transformer/HRM/Reflective 27.3M (8 layers).
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Hard following HRM configuration.
setup.loops_train: Unrolled fixed number of refinement steps with periodic intermediate alignment every M steps.
setup.baselines: Transformer, Block Universal Transformer, Recurrent Depth, Reflective Model, HRM (same optimizer, lr, batch).
setup.benchmarks: Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, ARC-1, ARC-2 (pass@1).

claims.claim: SR2 beats HRM by 11.6 points on Sudoku-Extreme and 19.2 on Maze-Hard with one eighth of the parameters.
claims.regime: iso_data, unmatched in parameters (3.4M vs 27.3M); HRM numbers equal HRM's published values
claims.evidence_quote: Moreover, SR2 surpasses HRM by 11.6% on Sudoku-Extreme and 19.2% on Maze-Hard, while using only one eighth of HRM's parameters.

claims.claim: A non-hierarchical Reflective Model matches HRM at equal parameters, suggesting the hierarchy is not necessary; input injection is what lifts a flat shared block (Block UT) to Recurrent Depth.
claims.evidence_quote: HRM achieves results comparable to the Reflective Model, suggesting that hierarchical recurrent structures are not strictly necessary for reasoning tasks of this type.

numbers.what: Table 1 (pass@1): Transformer, Block UT, Recurrent Depth, HRM, Reflective, SR2 on Sudoku-Extreme / Maze-Hard (/ARC-1/ARC-2 where reported)
numbers.quote: Block Universal Transformer 3.4M 0 30.4 Recurrent Depth 3.4M 42.52 48.4 HRM 27.3M 55.0 74.5 40.3 5.0 Reflective Model 27.3M 53.12 70.8 SR2 3.4M 66.63 93.7 44.3 6.7

limitations: ARC not evaluated for all baselines; HRM numbers coincide with HRM's published values (rerun vs copied unclear); priority-3 reading depth.
venue: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026
survey_notes: Another independent result that hierarchy is unnecessary (Reflective Model ~ HRM), and that input injection is critical for flat weight-tied recurrence (Block UT 0% Sudoku vs Recurrent Depth 42.52%), in line with 2609.39967; relevant to interpreting the flat-UniTF failure in 2604.14442. Maze-Hard 93.7% is the highest single-model Maze number in this group, above TRM 85.3, FPRM 87.0, GFPR 92.0.

relevance_reason: Title indicates a TRM training method (offline target planning and distillation); no abstract or full text available.
one_sentence: Title-only entry: a planning-and-distillation training scheme for Tiny Recursive Models; content not available for extraction.
survey_notes: No arXiv id, no abstract, no full text in the corpus; candidates metadata lists an ACL 2026 Findings DOI (10.18653/v1/2026.findings-acl.1350), unverified from paper text. Lead author should fetch it if the deep-supervision/distillation axis needs coverage.

title: U NROLLED P OLICY I TERATION FOR T INY R ECURSIVE M ODELS
relevance_reason: Title indicates a policy-iteration view/training of Tiny Recursive Models; no abstract or full text available.
one_sentence: Title-only entry: unrolled policy iteration for Tiny Recursive Models; content not available for extraction.
survey_notes: No arXiv id, abstract or full text. Possibly related to 'Latent reasoning in TRMs is secretly a policy improvement operator' (Asadulaev et al., 2026), cited by 2609.39967 and 2603.15641; not verified.

title: What Limits Recursive Reasoning Models: Optimization, Architecture and Test-Time Scaling
relevance_reason: Controlled re-implementation and one-factor-at-a-time ablation of HRM/TRM/URM recursive reasoners across six domains; identifies which components matter.
one_sentence: Retraining HRM, TRM and URM in one codebase across six domains, the paper finds an intermediate gradient horizon, large physical batches and bounded/gated state updates matter most, explicit H/L separation does not, and builds a 13.6M model beating all three.
key_contributions: Unified pipeline re-training HRM, TRM, URM with matched data representation, tokenization and evaluation on Sudoku, Maze, ARC-AGI-1/2, plus new Game of Life and Arithmetic tasks with controlled OOD splits.

Controlled ablations: gradient horizon (KL,KH) has an interior optimum; physical batch beats gradient accumulation at equal effective batch; shared vs separate H/L modules at matched parameters shows no consistent winner; cumulative stabilization (gate, clipping, consistent dropout, relative noise) mainly cuts seed variance.

A 13.6M shared-block recipe with (H,L)=(4,2) cycles, gradients through last (2,2) cycles, bounded+gated+normalized updates; reports compute accounting showing parameter sharing does not reduce sequential compute.

setup.model_sizes: Ours 13.6M (one shared 4-layer post-norm block, hidden 512); HRM 27M (4+4 layers), TRM 7M (2 layers), URM 7M (2-layer config) as retrained baselines; 8-layer dense control.
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Sudoku-Extreme full training split without symmetry augmentation; Maze-30x30-hard; ARC-AGI-1 combined with ConceptARC (transductive, 1000 augmentations per puzzle); ARC-AGI-2 separate; 200k Game of Life trajectories; RPN arithmetic split by operand multiset.
setup.loops_train: (Hcycles,Lcycles)=(4,2) per ACT step; ACT budget max 16 steps (8 for ARC-AGI-1) with detached carry; gradients through final (KH,KL)=(2,2) cycles.
setup.loops_test: Halting disabled, full ACT budget executed; test-time scaling by extending ACT budget.
setup.baselines: HRM, TRM, URM retrained in same codebase; dense non-recurrent control; Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.6-27B from released checkpoints without fine-tuning.
setup.benchmarks: Arithmetic ID/OOD, Game of Life ID/OOD, Maze, Sudoku (exact accuracy); ARC-AGI-1/2 pass@1 and pass@2 with augmentation voting.

claims.claim: Explicit hierarchy (separate H/L parameters) is not a universal source of improvement: at matched parameter count shared modules win on Maze and ARC-AGI-1, separate ones give small gains on Sudoku and Game of Life.
claims.evidence_quote: Shared modules perform better on Maze and ARC-AGI-1, while separate modules provide small gains on Sudoku and Game of Life; the two configurations are nearly identical on Arithmetic.

claims.claim: Gradient horizon through the nested recurrence has an interior optimum: (KL,KH)=(2,2) gives the best Arithmetic OOD accuracy while (1,3), with the same number of differentiated applications, overfits ID.
claims.evidence_quote: The intermediate setting (KL , KH ) = (2, 2) achieves the highest OOD accuracy of 71.16%, whereas (1, 3) reaches the highest ID accuracy of 99.60% but generalizes poorly, obtaining only 17.88% OOD.

claims.claim: Gradient accumulation does not reproduce a large physical batch for recursive models: at fixed effective batch 8192, Game of Life OOD drops sharply with accumulation.
claims.evidence_quote: OOD accuracy decreases from 63.16% with a physical batch of 8192 to 37.71% with four accumulation steps, while the mean pre-clipping gradient norm increases from 0.38 to 65.46.

claims.claim: Larger recurrent blocks and extra test-time ACT steps give only domain-dependent gains (largest on Arithmetic and Sudoku, limited on Game of Life, Maze, ARC).
claims.evidence_quote: Increasing the recurrent block from four to eight layers, increasing hidden size, or adding attention heads does not yield consistent accuracy gains across the tested settings.

claims.claim: On ARC-AGI-1 the non-recurrent dense control is already competitive with recursive models; recursion helps most on Sudoku and Maze.
claims.evidence_quote: ARC behaves differently: on ARC-AGI-1 the dense control is already competitive, while all systems remain limited on ARC-AGI-2.

claims.claim: Parameter sharing reduces parameter count but not sequential inference cost: TRM and the 13.6M model have similar recurrent compute per answer.
claims.evidence_quote: Parameter sharing therefore primarily reduces parameter count rather than sequential computation: TRM and our configuration have substantially different parameter counts but similar recurrent inference cost.

numbers.quote: ARC-AGI-1 is combined with ConceptARC, while ARC-AGI-2 is kept separate. We follow the same transductive training protocol used by these models

numbers.quote: Adaptive halting is disabled during the main evaluation, and all examples execute the full ACT budget. For test-time scaling, we extend this budget beyond its training-time value.

limitations: Results partly single-seed; reported accuracies are 'EMA best' over recorded evaluation checkpoints (Table 8 notes OOD split used for checkpoint selection), so numbers may be optimistic; ARC protocol is transductive with ConceptARC added; Sudoku trained on full split, so not comparable to 1000-example protocols; baselines retrained in authors' codebase may deviate from original recipes.
venue: Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027
builds_on: Asadulaev et al. 2026 (TRM as policy improvement)
survey_notes: Key ablation paper for 'which components matter'. Contradicts HRM's premise that the hierarchy is essential (consistent with TRM and 2605.17811) but also contradicts HRM/TRM's 1-step or last-step gradient: optimal is intermediate truncation (2,2), consistent with HRM-Text's warmup to K=5 (2605.20613). Its retrained HRM/TRM/URM numbers closely match the original papers on ARC-AGI-1 pass@2 (40.30/44.60/53.25) and on Sudoku for TRM/URM (87.40/77.60), but its own Sudoku 98.41% uses the full Sudoku-Extreme training split (not 1000 examples), so it is NOT comparable to HRM 55.0 / TRM 87.4 under the 1000-example protocol; a survey table must flag this. ARC-AGI-1 adds ConceptARC and uses augmentation voting with Q-head tie-break. Dense control nearly matches on ARC-AGI-1 (33.50 pass@2), echoing 2512.11847 that ARC gains rely on TTA/voting and puzzle IDs.

title: Probabilistic Tiny Recursive Model
relevance_reason: Inference-only test-time scaling for TRM via noisy parallel latent rollouts and Q-head selection; reports Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, ARC-AGI-2 and PPBench.
one_sentence: PTRM adds Gaussian noise to TRM's latent at every deep-recursion (supervision) step, runs K parallel rollouts and picks the answer with the highest Q-head value, lifting a pretrained TRM from 87.3% to 98.75% on Sudoku-Extreme without retraining.
key_contributions: Diagnosis: TRM failures are trajectories trapped in bad latent basins; the halting Q head tracks cell accuracy and separates correct from incorrect trajectories.
Width scaling: K noisy rollouts plus best-Q selection; pass@K vs best-Q@K gap under 1pp on PPBench validation; width gains exceed depth gains.
Results on PPBench golden set (62.6% to 91.2%), Sudoku-Extreme (to 98.75%), Maze-Hard (to 86.73% with mode@K), ARC-AGI-2 (pass@1 7.36% to 8.47%), and cost comparison to frontier LLMs.

setup.model_sizes: TRM-MLP 5M (Sudoku-Extreme), TRM-Att 7M (Maze-Hard, ARC-AGI-2, PPBench); direct-prediction baseline 27M.
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Standard TRM checkpoints and splits for Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, ARC-AGI-2; PPBench training set with 10x augmentation (trajectory sampling + dihedral).
setup.loops_train: Standard TRM: n latent updates then one answer update per latent recursion, T recursions per deep-recursion step (only last with gradient), up to Nsup=16 supervision steps.
setup.loops_test: D supervision steps (16-64) x K rollouts (25-100); e.g. Sudoku-Extreme K=100, D=64, sigma=0.3.
setup.baselines: Deterministic TRM (same checkpoint), published HRM/TRM/direct-pred numbers, frontier LLMs on PPBench (direct, agentic, oracle ensemble).
setup.benchmarks: PPBench golden set (sudoku, lightup, nurikabe, heyawake, tapa), Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, ARC-AGI-2 (pass@1/2/100 with augmentation voting).

claims.claim: On Sudoku-Extreme, noisy rollouts with Q-head selection lift the deterministic TRM checkpoint from 87.3% to 98.75% (best-Q@K), using K=100 rollouts and 64 supervision steps.
claims.regime: iso_param (same checkpoint; inference compute ~100x and 4x depth)
claims.evidence_quote: On Sudoku-Extreme, PTRM at K=100, D=64, σ=0.3 raises the deterministic baseline of 87.3% to 99.06% pass@K and 98.75% best-Q@K, achieving state of the art.

claims.claim: On Maze-Hard noise unlocks many correct rollouts (pass@K 95.63%) but the Q head selects them poorly (best-Q@K 85.17%, mode@K 86.73%).
claims.evidence_quote: On Maze-Hard, PTRM at K=100, D=16, σ=1.0 reaches 95.63% pass@K, an 11.83 point gain over the 83.8% deterministic baseline. mode@K gives the best PTRM accuracy here at 86.73%

claims.claim: On ARC-AGI-2, PTRM gives a small pass@1 gain and no pass@2 gain over deterministic TRM with augmentation voting.
claims.evidence_quote: With K=25 and σ=0.2, PTRM lifts pass@1 from 7.36% to 8.47% and pass@100 from 14.31% to 15.97% over our deterministic TRM baseline, while matching it at pass@2.

claims.claim: Width scaling dominates depth scaling: tripling depth at K=1 adds 3.1pp on PPBench validation while K=100 adds about 13pp.
claims.evidence_quote: On the deterministic baseline (K=1), tripling the depth from 16 to 48 steps raises PPBench validation accuracy from 76.4% to 79.5% (+3.1pp).

claims.claim: Against frontier LLMs on the PPBench golden set, PTRM (91.2%) beats the strongest direct-strategy LLM and an oracle ensemble of 7 LLMs; this is an unmatched comparison (task-trained 7M model vs general LLMs).
claims.evidence_quote: PTRM exceeds the strongest single LLM (direct strategy) by 57 points aggregate (91.2% vs. 34.7%), and exceeds the LLM ensemble by 36 points (91.2% vs. 55.1%)

numbers.what: TRM template as described by PTRM (co-authored by TRM's author): inner latent updates then answer update with one two-layer network
numbers.value: n z-updates + 1 y-update per latent recursion
numbers.quote: a single latent recursion consists of n updates to the latent state z followed by one update to the predicted answer y, all using the same two-layer network

numbers.what: TRM gradient: only the last of T latent recursions keeps gradients; deep supervision up to Nsup steps
numbers.quote: A deep recursion runs T latent recursions in sequence, with only the final one retaining gradients, allowing the model to leverage a large effective depth while keeping training efficient.

numbers.what: TRM inference does not use the Q head; runs all Nsup steps
numbers.quote: During inference, the Q head is not used, and the model performs Nsup supervision steps to maximize answer correctness.

Conclusion states 'ARC-AGI (from 7.8% to 8.47% pass@1)' although 7.8% is TRM's published pass@2 (Table 3) and the reproduced pass@1 baseline is 7.36%.
builds_on: Ren and Liu 2601.10679 (spurious fixed points in HRM)
Efstathiou and Balwani (noise on initial z)
survey_notes: Width-axis test-time scaling for recursive reasoners; co-authored by the TRM author. Compare with C-voting (2604.13521: random initial state + confidence selection), Speed-is-Confidence (2601.19085: halt-first selection), GFPR (2609.33540). Protocol: Sudoku-Extreme 98.75% uses 100 rollouts x 64 steps on the 1000-example-trained TRM-MLP checkpoint, so it is iso-param but ~400x the default inference compute; contrast 2609.39967's 98.41% which uses the full Sudoku training split. The ARC-AGI-2 pass@1 vs pass@2 mix-up in the conclusion is a precise inconsistency to flag. Reports Q-head-as-verifier works on Sudoku/PPBench but not Maze.

title: Less is More: Recursive Reasoning with Tiny Networks
relevance_reason: Single tiny weight-tied network recursed in depth (nested latent/answer recursion plus deep supervision); defines the TRM baseline for the recursive-reasoning line.
one_sentence: Simplifies HRM into one 2-layer network that recursively updates a latent z (n times) and an answer y, backpropagating through the full last recursion with deep supervision; beats HRM on Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard and ARC-AGI with 5-7M parameters.
key_contributions: Replaces HRM's two 4-layer modules, IFT 1-step gradient and Q-learning ACT with a single 2-layer net, backprop through one full recursion (n+1 calls) after T-1 no-grad recursions, and a single-pass BCE halting head.
Reinterprets HRM's z_H as the embedded current answer y and z_L as latent reasoning z; ablations show 2 features beat 1 or n+1.
Ablation table on Sudoku-Extreme isolating full-recursion gradients, layers, EMA, MLP-vs-attention, ACT; reports ARC-AGI-1 44.6% / ARC-AGI-2 7.8% (2 tries, public eval).

setup.model_sizes: 5M (TRM-MLP Sudoku), 7M (TRM-Att), 19M (TRM-MLP Maze/ARC); HRM 27M
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Sudoku-Extreme 1K train / 423K test, 1000 shuffling augmentations per example; Maze-Hard 1000 train / 1000 test, 8 dihedral augmentations; ARC-AGI-1 (800 tasks) and ARC-AGI-2 (1120 tasks) plus 160 ConceptARC tasks, 1000 augmentations per example
setup.loops_train: T=3 recursions of n=6 latent updates + 1 answer update (42 effective layers per supervision step); up to Nsup=16 deep-supervision steps with learned halting in training
setup.loops_test: Nsup=16 supervision steps (HRM protocol: full steps at test); ARC answers by majority vote over 1000 augmentations
setup.baselines: HRM 27M, direct prediction 27M (numbers copied from Wang et al. 2025), CoT LLMs (Deepseek R1, Claude 3.7, o3-mini-high, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Grok-4)
setup.benchmarks: Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard (30x30), ARC-AGI-1, ARC-AGI-2 public evaluation (pass@2)

claims.claim: Backpropagating through a full recursion process instead of HRM's 1-step gradient is the single largest gain (56.5% to 87.4% on Sudoku-Extreme).
claims.evidence_quote: Yet, we can still leverage multiple backpropagation-free recursion processes to improve (z L , z H ). With this approach, we obtain a massive boost in generalization on Sudoku-Extreme (improving TRM from 56.5% to 87.4%; see Table 1).

claims.claim: Fewer layers with proportionally more recursions generalizes better: 2 layers beat 4 layers at roughly matched emulated depth; adding layers overfits.
claims.regime: iso_data, approximately matched effective depth between TRM variants
claims.evidence_quote: In doing so, we obtain better generalization on Sudoku-Extreme (improving TRM from 79.5% to 87.4%; see Table 1) while reducing the number of parameters by half (again).

claims.claim: A single network can replace HRM's separate f_L and f_H; using separate networks is worse.
claims.regime: iso_data; single net has half the parameters
claims.evidence_quote: In doing so, we obtain better generalization on Sudoku-Extreme (improving TRM from 82.4% to 87.4%; see Table 1) while reducing the number of parameters by half.

claims.claim: HRM's fixed-point assumption behind the 1-step gradient is not satisfied in practice; residuals stay well above zero.
claims.evidence_quote: Thus, while the application of the IFT theorem and 1-step gradient approximation to HRM has some basis since the residuals do generally reduce over time, a fixed point is unlikely to be reached when the theorem is actually applied.

claims.claim: TRM-Att beats HRM on Maze-Hard, ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2 with a quarter of the parameters (HRM numbers copied from the HRM paper, same data/augmentation protocol).
claims.regime: iso_data; HRM numbers copied not re-run
claims.evidence_quote: TRM with selfattention obtains 85.3% accuracy on Maze-Hard, 44.6% accuracy on ARC-AGI-1, and 7.8% accuracy on ARCAGI-2 with 7M parameters.

claims.claim: Self-attention replaced by a sequence MLP helps only for small fixed context (Sudoku 9x9), and hurts on 30x30 tasks.
claims.evidence_quote: This worked well on Sudoku 9x9 grids, given the small and fixed context length; however, we found this architecture to be suboptimal for tasks with large context length, such as Maze-Hard and ARC-AGI (both using 30x30 grids).

claims.claim: Fixed-point iteration (TorchDEQ) instead of plain recursion slowed training and hurt generalization.
claims.evidence_quote: However, this slowed down training due to the fixed-point iteration and led to worse generalization. This highlights the fact that converging to a fixed-point is not essential.

claims.claim: Failed ideas: MoE MLPs in the loop and gradients through only the last k steps did not help; removing ACT entirely hurt.
claims.evidence_quote: We tried replacing the SwiGLU MLPs by SwiGLU Mixture-of-Experts (MoEs) (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022), but we found generalization to decrease massively.

claims.claim: Removing ACT (stopping only when solved) dropped generalization, attributed to too much time per sample.
claims.evidence_quote: We tried removing ACT with the option of stopping when the solution is reached, but we found that generalization dropped significantly.

limitations: Choices not guaranteed optimal across datasets (MLP mixer only helps Sudoku); no theory for why recursion beats a larger deeper network (suspected overfitting); deterministic supervised model, not generative; backprop through full recursion causes OOM for large n.
survey_notes: Template instance: one 2-layer net (attention or MLP-mixer), inner loop n=6 latent updates z<-f(x+y+z) then y<-f(y+z); middle loop T=3 (T-1 without grad, last with full BPTT through n+1 calls); outer deep supervision up to Nsup=16 with detached carry; BCE halting head used in training; ARC answers by majority vote over 1000 augmentations, pass@2, public eval, training includes ConceptARC. HRM baseline numbers are copied from 2506.21734, not re-run. Contradicts HRM's claimed necessity of hierarchy, two modules and fixed-point 1-step gradients; agrees with ARC Prize analysis that deep supervision (outer loop) drives gains. Comparison to LLMs is unmatched (task-specific training vs general models). Note HRM-vs-TRM 'effective depth matched' table (Table 3) is looped-vs-looped, not iso_effective_depth vs a dense model. Later papers (e.g. URM 2512.14693) report TRM 40.0 pass@1 under their own protocol, versus TRM's own 44.6 pass@2.

title: Universal Reasoning Model
relevance_reason: Universal (looped) Transformer with ACT outer loop and truncated backprop through inner loops on ARC-AGI/Sudoku; includes looped-vs-vanilla FLOP/parameter comparisons.
one_sentence: Ablates Universal-Transformer variants on ARC-AGI, attributes gains to recurrence plus strong nonlinearity, and adds ConvSwiGLU (depthwise short conv in the MLP) and truncated backprop through loops to reach 53.8% pass@1 ARC-AGI-1 and 16.0% ARC-AGI-2.
key_contributions: Looped-vs-vanilla Transformer table on ARC-AGI-1 at matched parameters and matched FLOPs: a 4-layer x 8-loop UT (40.0 pass@1) beats a 32-layer vanilla Transformer (23.75) at 32x FLOPs.
ConvSwiGLU: depthwise conv (kernel 2) after the MLP expansion; only this insertion point helps.
Truncated Backpropagation Through Loops: first 2 of 8 inner loops forward-only; ablations of nonlinearity (SwiGLU->SiLU->ReLU, softmax removal) show monotone degradation.

setup.model_sizes: 4 layers, hidden 512, 8 heads (absolute parameter count not stated)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Same datasets and augmented data as HRM/TRM (ARC-AGI-1, ARC-AGI-2, Sudoku)
setup.loops_train: inner loop 8 steps (first 2 forward-only), outer ACT loop up to 16 steps
setup.baselines: HRM and TRM re-run from official repositories; vanilla Transformers 2-64 layers
setup.benchmarks: ARC-AGI-1, ARC-AGI-2 (pass@1/10/100/1000), Sudoku

claims.claim: URM reaches 53.8% pass@1 on ARC-AGI-1 and 16.0% on ARC-AGI-2, above re-run TRM (40.0) and HRM (34.4).
claims.regime: iso_data (same data and augmentation; baselines re-run from official repos)
claims.evidence_quote: On ARC-AGI 2, URM obtains 16.0% pass@1, nearly tripling HRM and more than doubling TRM.

claims.claim: At equal FLOPs (32x), a weight-shared UT (4 layers x 8 loops) beats a 32-layer vanilla Transformer on ARC-AGI-1 pass@1 (40.0 vs 23.75); vanilla depth/width scaling saturates or degrades.
claims.regime: iso_infer_flop and iso_effective_depth (vanilla 32x vs UT 4x relative parameters)
claims.evidence_quote: At 32× FLOPs, reallocating computation from deep, non-shared layers to recurrent refinement improves pass@1 from 23.75 for vanilla Transformers to 40.0 for UTs.

claims.claim: Gains come from recurrence and nonlinearity, not elaborate hierarchy; weakening MLP activation or removing attention softmax degrades ARC-AGI-1 monotonically.
claims.evidence_quote: Among these components, the activation function in the MLP plays a particularly critical role: replacing SwiGLU with simpler nonlinearities such as SiLU or ReLU leads to substantial degradation, while completely removing the attention softmax results in a dramatic collapse in performance.

claims.claim: Truncating gradients through the first loops helps; text says 2 forward-only loops of 8 is best, though in Table 3 pass@1 is marginally higher at 3 forward-only loops (39.50 vs 39.13).
claims.evidence_quote: As shown in Table 5, when the total number of inner loops is fixed to 8, truncating gradients for the first two loops—i.e., running the initial two inner-loop iterations in forward-only mode—achieves the best performance.

claims.claim: Muon speeds convergence about twofold but does not improve final accuracy.
claims.evidence_quote: On ARC-AGI 2, the Muon-optimized model reaches a pass@1 accuracy of 11.5% in approximately 600,000 training steps, whereas the Adamatan2 baseline requires over 1,300,000 steps to achieve the same performance, corresponding to nearly a twofold speedup in optimization.

numbers.quote: This is because the teaser scores are taken directly from the official ARC-AGI leaderboard for rigor, whereas the scores in this table are reproduced from the official TRM and HRM repositories following their official evaluation procedures.

numbers.value: pass@1, single small model, no TTS/ensembling
numbers.quote: This comparison focuses on pass@1 score of single small models trained from scratch under the same data setting as HRM and TRM, excluding test-time scaling, ensembling, and visual methods such as VARC [10].

numbers.value: 4 layers, 512 hidden, 8 heads, 8 inner loops (2 forward-only), ACT max 16
numbers.quote: The inner loop runs for 8 steps, with the first two steps being forward-only, while the outer loop employs Adaptive Computation Time (ACT) [9] with a maximum of 16 steps.

Nonlinearity ablation ARC-1 pass@1: SwiGLU->SiLU, SiLU->ReLU, w/o softmax
Parameter-efficiency claim (UT 4x params vs vanilla up to 32x)
numbers.quote: With only 4× parameters, a UT achieves a pass@1 score of 40.0, dramatically outperforming vanilla Transformers that employ up to 32× more parameters yet remain markedly weaker.

limitations: Not stated as a section. Absolute parameter count, ARC split and how pass@n candidates are sampled are not specified; TBPTL ablation uses a 2-layer model without conv; RMSNorm and QK nonlinearity not ablated.
survey_notes: Template instance: single shared 4-layer block (decoder-only UT), inner loop 8 iterations with gradients only on the last 6 (TBPTL), outer ACT/deep-supervision loop max 16, EMA, AdamAtan2. Key protocol fact: Table 1 re-runs HRM/TRM from official repos and reports TRM ARC-1 pass@1 40.0 and Sudoku 66.8, below TRM's self-reported 44.6 (pass@2) and 87.4 (MLP variant) / 74.7 (attention variant); so URM's Sudoku 77.6 'surpassing TRM' holds against the re-run TRM, not against TRM-MLP's self-reported 87.4. Re-run HRM ARC-2 pass@1 (5.4) exceeds re-run TRM (4.6), contradicting TRM's ranking (HRM 5.0 vs TRM 7.8, pass@2). Internal inconsistency: Sec. 4.5 says pass@1 peaks at 2 forward-only loops, Table 3 shows 39.50 at 3 vs 39.13 at 2, and the text cites 'Table 5' for Table 3. Table 2 is one of the few iso-FLOP and iso-effective-depth looped-vs-dense comparisons in this subfield (4Lx8 loops UT 40.0 vs 32L vanilla 23.75 at 32x FLOPs; vanilla has 8x params). pass@n sampling mechanism is undefined for a deterministic model. Agrees with TRM/ARC Prize analysis that hierarchy is not essential.

title: Hierarchical Reasoning Models: Perspectives and Misconceptions
relevance_reason: Ablation/critique of HRM's hierarchy, one-step gradient and ACT halting; directly about which recursive-reasoning components matter.
one_sentence: Short MIT working paper re-running HRM: an 8-layer L-module-only model matches the 4+4-layer H/L HRM; HRM's one-step gradient is framed as latent consistency/diffusion training; using the learned ACT halting at inference does not beat running maximum steps.
key_contributions: Ablation removing the H-module (8-layer L-only, L-cycle=1) matches original HRM and trains faster.
Argues HRM's one-step-gradient training is equivalent to (latent) consistency/diffusion training, so its 'biological plausibility' is not unique.
Identifies train/test mismatch: HRM learns ACT halting in training but evaluates at the maximum number of steps; enabling learned halting at inference does not improve accuracy.

setup.model_sizes: original HRM (4-layer H + 4-layer L) vs 8-layer L-only
setup.train_tokens_or_data: HRM official setup (Sudoku shown in Figs. 2-5)
setup.loops_train: HRM default with ACT
setup.loops_test: fixed 1-16 reasoning steps, or per-sample halting by thresholding sigmoid(Q_halt) or sigmoid(Q_halt - Q_continue)
setup.baselines: original HRM
setup.benchmarks: Sudoku (HRM setup); no ARC-AGI numbers

claims.claim: Removing HRM's H-module and using an 8-layer L-module only performs similarly or slightly better than original HRM and trains faster.
claims.regime: iso_data; roughly iso_param (8 layers total in both)
claims.evidence_quote: The plain transformer/L-module-only setting performs similarly or slightly better than the original HRM while at the same time runs much faster (runtime 1h 48m vs. original HRM’s 4h 21m on a A100 GPU).

claims.claim: HRM's one-step gradient training is effectively the diffusion / latent consistency model training paradigm.
claims.evidence_quote: Second, the one-step gradient approximation employed by HRM is effectively equivalent to the training paradigm used in diffusion models.

claims.claim: Using HRM's learned ACT halting at inference does not improve accuracy; maximum steps is best.
claims.evidence_quote: Finally, our analysis indicates that ACT does not enhance inference performance; rather, running the model for the maximum number of reasoning steps yields the best results.

claims.claim: Released HRM code trains with ACT halting but evaluates at full maximum steps (train/test mismatch).
claims.evidence_quote: There is a critical mismatch in the original HRM implementation: while its ACT module learns to decide when to halt during training, evaluation ignores this policy and always executes the maximum number of reasoning steps.

numbers.what: Training runtime: L-only vs original HRM on one A100
numbers.quote: The plain transformer/L-module-only setting performs similarly or slightly better than the original HRM while at the same time runs much faster (runtime 1h 48m vs. original HRM’s 4h 21m on a A100 GPU).

numbers.what: Few-step solving on Sudoku
numbers.quote: As we will demonstrate later, a well-trained HRM on the Sudoku task also significantly reduces its inference steps, down to as few as 2 to 4 steps, which is surprising yet somewhat expected when viewing HRM as a LCM.

limitations: Working paper; results shown as training curves in figures without tables; single task (Sudoku) for halting analysis; no ARC-AGI evaluation; L-only model's outer ACT loop status not separately ablated.
venue: Working Paper
survey_notes: Agrees with TRM (2510.04871) and URM (2512.14693) that HRM's two-module hierarchy is not needed; agrees with ARC Prize analysis. Note the 'plain transformer' here is HRM's L-module with L-cycle=1 inside HRM's training pipeline; the paper does not say the outer deep-supervision/ACT loop was removed, so this is not evidence that recurrence is unnecessary. Its ACT finding (max steps best at inference) is consistent with HRM/TRM evaluating with all Nsup=16 steps. The diffusion/consistency framing is echoed by later denoising-recursion work (2604.18839, 2609.01449).

title: Latent Reasoning in TRMs is Secretly a Policy Improvement Operator
relevance_reason: Theory and training method for TRM-style recursive latent reasoning; analyzes dead compute in recursive steps and cuts recursion budget.
one_sentence: Formalizes one TRM latent step as a KL-regularized policy-improvement (CFG-like) operator and proposes Deep Improvement Supervision: per-step targets from a monotone discrete corruption schedule, which lets a TRM backbone use 18x fewer forward passes on ARC-AGI.
key_contributions: Policy-improvement view: pre- and post-reasoning logits of a TRM step define an advantage-like log-ratio; a step helps iff the ground-truth token has above-average advantage (Advantage Margin condition).
Deep Improvement Supervision (DIS): each of Nsup=6 supervision steps trained toward a progressively less-corrupted target, integer step index as input, no halting head, T=1, n=2.

title: Reasoning with Neural Cellular Automata
relevance_reason: Weight-tied local update rule iterated in time (recurrent depth) on maze/Sudoku/ARC; recursive reasoning without global attention, with depth and parallel-trial test-time scaling.
one_sentence: Neural cellular automata (strictly local 3x3 perception, shared MLP update, asynchronous stochastic firing) trained with BPTT plus sample replay solve mazes, Sudoku-Extreme and ARC-AGI-1, scaling at test time via longer rollouts, larger grids and many parallel stochastic trials.
key_contributions: Shows fully local recurrent cells reach 100% on mazes up to 201x201 (trained on small mazes), 75.6% Sudoku-Extreme (K=1) and 48.8% ARC-AGI-1 pass@2 with per-task TTT and 3264 rollouts.
Training ablation: sample replay, stochastic perturbations and asynchronous updates are critical for OOD generalization; test-time noise improves accuracy.
Niche-Capped Diversity Pruning for parallel trials and per-cell confidence-driven adaptive compute (about 30% fewer cell updates).

title: Equilibrium Reasoners: Learning Attractors Enables Scalable Reasoning
relevance_reason: Controlled study of weight-tied iterative (TRM-style) reasoners vs feedforward at matched layer evaluations, plus training interventions enabling depth extrapolation from 16 to 1,024 iterations.
one_sentence: Frames TRM-style iterative reasoners as learned attractor dynamics; a controlled feedforward-to-iterative construction path and two training interventions (random initial state, per-step noise with damping) let models trained with 16 iterations run 64-1,024 iterations and many restarts, reaching 99.8% on Sudoku-Extreme.
key_contributions: Construction path on Sudoku-Extreme at matched layer evaluations: 42-block feedforward (105.6M) 2.6% vs 2-block weight-tied (5.03M) 32.6%, then segmented online training + 16x depth 74.7%, hierarchy 76.5%, ACT 84.8%.

Randomized state initialization (RI) and noise injection (NI) shape attractor landscapes: Maze-Unique 44.9 to 82.2 at the same compute; fixed-point residual tracks error and serves as a verifier-free selection signal.
Two-axis test-time scaling (depth D, breadth B): Sudoku 86.4 (D=16) to 93.0 (D=64) to 99.8 (D=64, B=128); Mini-ARC 55.28 vs TRM 48.35.

Maze results are on a new Maze-Unique split (not Maze-Hard), so HRM 0.3 / TRM 44.9 there are not comparable to HRM 74.5 / TRM 85.3 on Maze-Hard. Agrees with Huginn-style random-init path independence. Two-latent (TRM y,z) structure helps with ACT (84.8 vs 73.9), consistent with TRM's single-z ablation (71.9). Headline 99.8 relies on breadth (B=128) and depth (D=64) beyond baselines; regime unmatched in inference FLOPs.

title: Diffusion as a Training Curriculum for Timestep-Free Iterative Reasoning
relevance_reason: Looped Transformer (shared block x8) inside a timestep-free recurrent diffusion denoiser with persistent hidden state; anytime solver whose accuracy rises with recurrent depth far beyond training.
one_sentence: Adds a persistent hidden state to a diffusion denoiser built from a looped Transformer block and removes timestep conditioning; trained with annealed corruption and 4-step truncated BPTT, it keeps solving more puzzles as inference depth grows (99.90% Sudoku-Extreme at K=10,000).
key_contributions: Timestep-free recurrent diffusion: shared block looped J=8 times per denoising step, hidden state carried across steps and never directly supervised; truncated BPTT through L=4 steps on staggered rollouts of K~Unif[20,160].
Inference needs no annealing: constant maximal noise on non-clue cells gives the best Sudoku solve rate (99.90%) and stable convergence, without parallel rollouts or selection heads.
Ablations: annealed-corruption training curriculum is critical (clean-only 0.00%); memoryless models are slower and lower; hidden-state interventions show it carries spatially structured progress.

title: Think Deep, Speak Once: Relit, A Recursive Latent Implicit Transformer Framework
relevance_reason: Transfers TRM-style recursion (y/z states, T-1 no-grad recursions, deep supervision, ACT) to language by putting a trainable recursive block on a frozen TinyLlama-1.1B.
one_sentence: Adds a trainable TRM-like recursive Transformer block (residual y/z updates, T-1 gradient-free recursions, deep supervision, BCE halting) on top of frozen TinyLlama-1.1B features and the frozen LM head, trained per GLoRE task with single-token answers.
key_contributions: TRM-to-language transfer: frozen LLM supplies anchor x; recursive block refines answer y and scratchpad z with residual updates and step embeddings; decoded via frozen LM head.
Recall-Then-Learn truncated backprop (gradient-free warm-up recursions then one gradient step) with deep supervision and ACT halting.
Reports 98.6% ProofWriter and 97.6% RuleTaker with per-task supervised training of the block (5,000 training examples each).

limitations: Single-token outputs only; frozen anchor is an information bottleneck (suggests LoRA or cross-attention); no ablation of recursion depth or a non-recursive head on the same frozen features; baselines are few-shot LLMs, not fine-tuned models.
venue: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026
survey_notes: One of the few attempts to bring TRM-style recursion to language: sandwich-like (frozen prelude = TinyLlama, recursive core = new block, frozen coda = LM head). Evidence is weak for recurrence per se: no non-recursive control head, no depth ablation, comparisons are to few-shot LLMs (unmatched), and per-task supervised training on 200-5,000 examples and the paper gives no simple supervised baseline on the same frozen features. Claim 'reasoning capability can be scaled efficiently through recurrent depth rather than parameter width' is not tested by an iso-param or iso-FLOP comparison. Useful in the survey's 'bringing recursive reasoning to LMs' paragraph with these caveats.

title: Energy-guided Recursive Model
relevance_reason: Test-time selection, sampling and depth control for a frozen recursive reasoner (EqR) via hand-specified Hopfield task energies; also a recurrent EBT LM experiment.
one_sentence: Scores K candidate trajectories of a pretrained EqR recursive reasoner with Hopfield-type energies built from known puzzle rules (plus global constraint penalties), matching candidate-pool oracle accuracy on Sudoku-Lite, PPBench and Maze-Unique and guiding early stopping; a continuation-memory variant cuts EBT perplexity 1.74%.
key_contributions: Training-free energy guidance for recursive models: lowest-energy candidate selection, parallel tempering over candidates, energy-plateau stopping.
Shows q-head, confidence and majority voting miss correct candidates that a rule-based energy recovers (Maze 99.30 vs 97.30 q-head at D=64, K=128).
Shows deeper recurrence is not monotonically better: Maze oracle 99.90 at D=16 vs 99.30 at D=64; energy stopping reaches 99.60 at mean depth 7.6.

setup.model_sizes: frozen EqR reasoner (size not restated); EBT 44.86M (6 blocks) for language
setup.train_tokens_or_data: no training; evaluation on Sudoku-Lite (2048), PPBench validation (301 puzzles, 5 types), EqR Maze-Unique (1000 test); RedPajama-V2 proxy of 33,000 documents / 7,397,883 target tokens
setup.loops_train: n/a (uses EqR checkpoints)
setup.loops_test: D<=64 recurrent depth, K=128 candidates (reasoning); K=8 (language)
setup.baselines: one rollout, whole-sequence majority, cell majority, EqR q-head, confidence selection, candidate oracle
setup.benchmarks: Sudoku-Lite, PPBench, Maze-Unique, RedPajama-V2 perplexity

claims.claim: With D<=64 and K=128, energy selection matches candidate-pool oracle accuracy on Sudoku, PPBench and Maze.
claims.regime: iso_infer_flop (same shared candidate pool; ERM adds only scoring)
claims.evidence_quote: With D ≤ 64 and K = 128, ERM matches the evaluated candidate-pool oracles on Sudoku, PPBench, and Maze, and supports early stopping.

claims.claim: Learned q-head halting and confidence saturate and select worse candidates on Maze than the rule energy.
claims.evidence_quote: On Maze, ERM reaches the 99.30% oracle, compared with 97.80% for majority and confidence and 97.30% for q-head.

claims.claim: Deeper recurrence does not guarantee better accuracy; energy-based stopping uses far fewer steps.
claims.evidence_quote: With K = 128 PT replicas and a maximum depth of 64, all 63 batches stop by this criterion at depths 6–11, averaging 7.60 steps, with 996/1000 = 99.60% exact accuracy (Table 4).

claims.claim: Hopfield continuation memory reduces perplexity of a fixed recurrent EBT, without establishing any advantage over a non-recurrent Transformer++.
claims.regime: iso_param (same frozen EBT, same K=8 candidates)
claims.evidence_quote: ERM reduces perplexity from 44.189 to 43.419 (Table 3), a 1.742% improvement (paired-document bootstrap 95% CI: 1.711–1.773%), and improves on candidate averaging by 1.649%.

numbers.what: Sudoku-Lite shared-pool selection
numbers.quote: On Sudoku, ERM selects all 2024/2048 correct answers available in the shared pool (98.83%), five more than confidence selection.

numbers.what: PT-ERM Sudoku, PPBench, Maze
numbers.quote: PT-ERM raises Sudoku accuracy from 98.83% to 98.97% (2027/2048), adding three solves, and preserves the PPBench and Maze results of 88.04% and 99.30% (Figure 3; Table 2).

numbers.what: PPBench selection gain over q-head
numbers.quote: PPBench shows the largest selection gain: ERM solves 265/301 puzzles, matching the oracle and exceeding q-head by 14 solves.

numbers.what: Maze at D=16, K=128
numbers.quote: D = 16 and K = 128 on the same 1000-example test split. ERM selects 999/1000 = 99.90% exact

numbers.what: EBT language model setup
numbers.quote: We use an S2 EBT with six blocks and 44.86M parameters, trained for 105,000 steps, and evaluate K = 8 shared trajectories on a frozen RedPajama-V2 proxy of 33,000 documents and 7,397,883 target tokens

limitations: Energies require known task rules (hand-specified memories and global constraints); local Hopfield terms not isolated from a discrete rule checker; one language corpus proxy; no comparison of the recurrent EBT to a non-recurrent Transformer++; stability of energy does not certify correctness; PT gain untested across seeds.
survey_notes: Not a new looped architecture; a test-time verifier for recursive reasoners. Protocol caution: the 'best accuracy in recursive modeling' claims (Sudoku 98.97, Maze 99.30) use rule-derived energies that encode the task's constraints (effectively a verifier), K=128 candidates, Sudoku-Lite (2048-example subset) and Maze-Unique, so they are not comparable to single-pass HRM/TRM numbers on Sudoku-Extreme/Maze-Hard. Useful evidence that (i) learned halting/q-heads are weak selectors and (ii) more recurrent depth can reduce accuracy on Maze (99.90 at D=16 vs 99.30 at D=64), consistent with 'overthinking' observations. Cites Fixed-point reasoners (2606.18206) and Solve the Loop (2605.12466) as related looped works.

title: Recursive Inference Machines for Neural Reasoning
relevance_reason: Generalizes HRM/TRM nested recursion as an inference machine and adds learned reweighting (gated/attentive state mixing) between recursive steps; evaluated on ARC-AGI, Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard.
one_sentence: Casts HRM/TRM as Sequential-Monte-Carlo-like inference machines with an identity reweighter and adds learned reweighters (input-dependent EMA gating, RIMA; attention over the latent history, RIMformer), improving over a re-run TRM on ARC-AGI-1 and Sudoku-Extreme; also a Gibbs-style TabPFN variant.
key_contributions: RIM template (Solver = f_L inner loop, Generator = f_H outer update, Reweighter); HRM = decoupled SimRIM, TRM = shared SimRIM with identity reweighter.
RIMA: learned input-dependent gate mixing candidate and previous state; RIMformer: Transformer reweighter attending over history (lookback max(N,T)).
TabRIM: Gibbs-sampling denoiser around TabPFN for noisy tabular data.

setup.model_sizes: 5.5M to 13.6M depending on backbone
setup.train_tokens_or_data: TRM data protocol: Sudoku-Extreme 1,000 train / 423,000 test; Maze-Hard 1,000/1,000; ARC-AGI-1/2; UCI Cleveland Heart and Ljubljana Breast Cancer with 25% corrupted test features
setup.loops_train: TRM schedule (T inner Solver steps, N outer Generator steps, deep supervision)
setup.baselines: SimRIM = TRM: re-run with authors' code for ARC-AGI-1 and Sudoku-Extreme; ARC-AGI-2 and Maze-Hard numbers stated to be taken from TRM paper; TabPFN
setup.benchmarks: ARC-AGI-1, ARC-AGI-2 (pass@1, pass@2), Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, two UCI medical datasets

claims.claim: Non-identity reweighters (RIMA, RIMformer) outperform TRM (identity reweighter) on symbolic benchmarks.

claims.evidence_quote: We observe that the RIMs with non-trivial Reweighters (RIMFormer and RIMA) consistently outperform the identity-reweighted RIM (SimRIM).

claims.claim: Fully dynamic (learned, input-dependent) reweighting beats static EMA coefficients, which hurt TRM on Sudoku-Extreme.
claims.evidence_quote: The results indicate that fully dynamic, neuraldriven reweighting consistently yields superior performance, suggesting that joint adaptation of both latent trajectories is essential for solving high-complexity reasoning tasks.

claims.claim: Longer lookback (attention over history) helps Maze-Hard but hurts Sudoku-Extreme.
claims.evidence_quote: We observe that increasing the lookback window size does not yield better performance in all cases. While it improves performance on Maze-Hard, it reduces performance on Sudoku-Extreme.
