survey_notes: Adds gated/attentive state passing (a GRU-like or history-attention reweighter) to TRM's recursion; related to the survey's state-passing axis. Baseline-provenance problem: the paper states ARC-AGI-2 TRM numbers come from the TRM paper, yet lists 4.6 (pass@1) / 7.4 (pass@2), whereas TRM's paper reports 7.8 (2 tries) and no pass@1; 4.6 and 7.4 coincide with URM's (2512.14693) re-run TRM ARC-2 pass@1 and pass@10. RIMA's large ARC-2 gain (+5.30 pass@1) is measured against these copied numbers, not a re-run. Re-run TRM on Sudoku-Extreme (87.16) closely matches TRM's 87.4, and on ARC-1 (44.38 pass@2) matches TRM's 44.6, unlike URM's and DIS's lower replications. RIMformer is worse on Sudoku (80.21) and ARC-2 pass@2 (7.1), so 'consistently outperform' holds only for RIMA.

title: Stream Recursion Model (SRM)
relevance_reason: HRM-derived recursive model with many latent streams and learned stream-wise attention, trained as a language model on OpenWebText with truncated backprop through recursive layers.
one_sentence: Generalizes HRM's two additive streams to many streams that exchange information via learned stream-wise attention, trains HRM-style recursive LMs on OpenWebText (~5B tokens), and finds SRM roughly matches GPT-2 loss with fewer parameters but several times more compute, while HRM fails on language.
key_contributions: Stream-wise attention connection function replaces HRM's additive stream coupling, allowing performance to scale with stream count.
Language-model test of HRM-family recursion: HRM 109M reaches training loss 4.93 vs GPT-2 124M 3.20; SRM-base 68M 3.18; SRM-large 454M 2.96 after 10k steps.
Interpretability analyses of stream routing and specialization.

setup.model_sizes: SRM-base 68M, SRM-med 134M, SRM-large 454M; GPT-2 124M; HRM 109M
setup.train_tokens_or_data: OpenWebText, 10k steps, batch 512, ~5B tokens (sweeps: ~0.5B tokens)
setup.loops_train: model depth of 8 recursive layers, backprop through the last 4; HRM baseline 3 H-cycles x 4 L-cycles
setup.baselines: GPT-2 (Hugging Face default config) and HRM trained with the same pipeline
setup.benchmarks: OpenWebText training loss

claims.claim: SRM-base matches GPT-2 loss with about half the parameters but about 7x the training time; SRM-med beats GPT-2 at similar parameters with about 6x compute.
claims.regime: iso_data (same tokens and config); not iso_train_flop
claims.evidence_quote: We see that SRM-base is able to achieve on par performance to GPT-2 with roughly half the parameters and 7 times the compute time.

claims.claim: HRM as originally designed fails on language modeling.
claims.regime: iso_data (but HRM trained with a different learning rate, 1e-4 vs 1e-3)
claims.evidence_quote: We demonstrated that HRM, as it was originally designed was incapable of performing on language datasets.

claims.claim: Backprop through more than 4 of 8 recursive layers gives diminishing returns.
claims.evidence_quote: Using a fixed depth of 8 layers we found that returns severely diminished when performing backpropagation through more than 4 layers.

numbers.what: OpenWebText after 10k steps: params, time, training loss for GPT-2, HRM, SRM-base, SRM-med, SRM-large
numbers.quote: #Params 124M 109M 68M 134M 454M Time 11h 22h 77h 68h 264h Training Loss 3.20 4.93 3.18 3.08 2.96

numbers.quote: For training, our batch size during training is 512, and we train for a total of 10k steps, resulting in using ∼ 5B training tokens.

numbers.what: HRM language baseline configuration
numbers.value: L-net 6 blocks, H-net 4 blocks, 3 H-cycles, 4 L-cycles, lr 1e-4
numbers.quote: For HRM specific parameters, the L-net had a depth of 6 transformer blocks, while the H-net was 4 blocks deep. We used 3 H-cycles and 4 L-cycles.

numbers.what: Compute budget
numbers.quote: Furthermore, we achieve the results in this work with only a single 4xL40s GPU cluster over the course of 2 months and ∼1000 GPU hours of external compute.

numbers.what: HRM baseline learning rate
numbers.quote: We used 3 H-cycles and 4 L-cycles. During training, we used a step size of 1e − 4, and used 1000 warm-up steps.

numbers.what: SRM learning rate
numbers.quote: We use a learning rate of 1e − 3, and a weight decay of 0.1.

limitations: Short training (~5B tokens) and only training loss reported (no held-out perplexity or downstream tasks); hyperparameter sweeps at 0.5B tokens; ACT omitted for causal LM; HRM baseline uses a different learning rate; compute per token much higher than GPT-2.
survey_notes: Rare direct test of HRM-family recursion as a causal language model. Result: original HRM is poor on LM (loss 4.93 vs GPT-2 3.20 at same tokens), SRM's many-stream attention coupling fixes this but at 6-7x training time, so no iso-FLOP advantage is shown; SRM-base's parity with GPT-2 at half the parameters is an iso_data/approximately-iso-loss parameter-efficiency claim only, and on training loss rather than validation. Disagreement noted in the paper about the optimal number of streams (HRM/TRM say 2; 2510.00355 finds 1 suffices; SRM finds more streams help once coupling is learned). Weight sharing: step-functions are reused within a layer by a hard-coded call order (e.g. ABCABC); the paper does not state explicitly whether the 8 layers share weights, so treat its 'recursion' depth with care.

title: Dynamical Systems Theory Behind a Hierarchical Reasoning Model
relevance_reason: Reformulates HRM/TRM recursion as neural ODE/SDE dynamics with explicit equilibrium/contraction losses; weight-tied recursive reasoner on Sudoku-Extreme and Maze.
one_sentence: Recasts TRM-style recursion as discretized neural ODEs/SDEs and adds equilibrium, Routh-Hurwitz stability and hyperspherical repulsion losses plus noise; a 5M Contraction Mapping Model reports 93.7% on Sudoku-Extreme and a weight-shared 0.26M model 85.4%.
key_contributions: Contraction Mapping Model (CMM): auxiliary losses enforcing convergence of the latent phase point to a stable equilibrium (equilibrium and Routh-Hurwitz terms) and repulsion on the hypersphere against collapse.
Stochastic variant (NSDE) with additive Gaussian noise (sigma=0.01) reduces overfitting; polynomial StableMax3/5 and AlgGradNorm loss balancing.
Hardware-constrained (16 GB VRAM, AMP) re-runs of HRM and TRM, showing lower Sudoku-Extreme accuracy than reported.

setup.model_sizes: 5M (D=512, MLP-mixer); 0.52M and 0.26M (D=128, weight-shared)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Sudoku-Extreme and Maze (HRM/TRM data protocol)
setup.loops_train: TRM schedule NH=3, NL=6 (best), Nsuper=16 deep supervision; gradient through Ngrad steps
setup.baselines: HRM, TRM numbers copied from papers and re-run under AMP / gradient accumulation
setup.benchmarks: Sudoku-Extreme, Maze (Maze-Hard)

claims.claim: A 5M CMM reaches 93.7% on Sudoku-Extreme, above HRM (55.0%) and TRM (87.4%) as reported in their papers.
claims.regime: iso_param vs TRM-MLP (5M), iso_data; baselines copied; against the authors' own TRM run (79.1%) the gap is larger
claims.evidence_quote: On the Sudoku-Extreme benchmark, a 5M-parameter CMM achieves a state-of-the-art accuracy of 93.7%, outperforming the 27M-parameter HRM (55.0%) and 5M-parameter TRM (87.4%).

claims.claim: Re-running HRM and TRM under a 16 GB / AMP budget lowers their Sudoku-Extreme accuracy, while TRM Maze reproduces.
claims.evidence_quote: While the reproduced TRM results for the Maze benchmark closely match the originally reported metrics, a noticeable performance drop is observed in the Sudoku-Extreme reproduction for both HRM and TRM.

claims.claim: Weight-sharing across recursive steps halves the tiny model to 0.26M parameters while retaining 85.4% Sudoku-Extreme and 82.2% Maze.
claims.evidence_quote: Remarkably, even when aggressively compressed to an ultra-tiny footprint of just 0.26M parameters, the CMM retains robust predictive power, achieving 85.4% on Sudoku-Extreme and 82.2% on the Maze benchmark.

claims.claim: Noise injection (NSDE) broadens the basin of attraction and counters overfitting of deterministic recursion.
claims.evidence_quote: The injection of noise creates a robust manifold of initial states, forcing the system to learn a broader basin of attraction towards the stable equilibrium.

numbers.what: Sudoku-Extreme baselines: copied (HRM 55.0, TRM-MLP 87.4, TRM-Att 74.7) and own runs (HRM 45.9, TRM 79.1)
numbers.quote: HRM (our run) TRM (our run) 45.9 79.1 27M 5M AMP AMP, MLP-mixer

survey_notes: Contrasts with TRM's 'no fixed point needed' by adding explicit equilibrium/contraction losses and reporting gains; consistent with EqR (2605.21488) attractor view and with noise-injection benefits (EqR, NCA 2609.36126, 2609.01449). Reproducibility data point: under 16 GB/AMP constraints, HRM Sudoku-Extreme 45.9 (vs 55.0 reported) and TRM 79.1 (vs 87.4), TRM Maze 84.2 (vs 85.3). The 93.7 headline is the best of several test-set-evaluated configurations; a selection effect cannot be excluded (no validation split mentioned). Sharing note: the 5M model follows TRM; 'weight-sharing across recursive steps' is introduced explicitly only for the 0.26M variant.

title: Tiny Recursive Reasoning with Mamba-2 Attention Hybrid
relevance_reason: Swaps the per-step operator inside TRM's recursion for a Mamba-2 + attention hybrid at parameter parity; ARC-AGI-1 pass@K, Sudoku, Maze.
one_sentence: Replaces TRM's Transformer blocks with a Mamba-2 -> Mamba-2 -> attention -> MLP hybrid at parameter parity (6.86M vs 6.83M), keeping TRM's recursion schedule, and finds +2.0 pass@2 on ARC-AGI-1 with pass@1 parity, attributed to more diverse candidates under augmentation voting.
key_contributions: First Mamba-2 hybrid operator inside a TRM recursive scaffold, parameter-matched to TRM-attn.
ARC-AGI-1 pass@K analysis: hybrid improves coverage (pass@100 +4.75) but not top-1 selection; vote statistics show more unique candidates and flatter votes.
Argues post-norm is essential for recursion stability because it bounds residual-stream growth over unrolled steps.

setup.model_sizes: TRM-attn 6.83M, TR-mamba2attn 6.86M, TRM-mlp-t 5M/19M, TR-mamba2mlpt 6.28M/13.24M
setup.train_tokens_or_data: TRM benchmark suite and augmentation protocol (ARC-AGI-1, Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-30x30-Hard)
setup.loops_train: TRM schedule: H_cycles=3 outer, L_cycles=4-6 inner, deep supervision with Q-halt head
setup.loops_test: TRM protocol; ARC test inputs expanded into ~880 augmentations, aggregated by vote count and confidence
setup.baselines: TRM-attn re-trained by the authors; TRM-mlp-t ARC number copied from TRM paper
setup.benchmarks: ARC-AGI-1 eval (pass@1..1000), Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-30x30-Hard

claims.claim: At parameter parity, the Mamba-2 hybrid improves ARC-AGI-1 pass@2 by 2.0 points with pass@1 parity.
claims.evidence_quote: On ARCAGI-1, we find that the hybrid improves pass@2 (the official metric) by +2.0% (45.88% vs 43.88%) and consistently outperforms at higher K values (+4.75% at pass@100), whilst maintaining pass@1 parity.

claims.claim: Operator choice is task dependent: MLP-t mixing best on Sudoku, fails completely on 30x30 Maze where the hybrid beats attention.
claims.evidence_quote: Maze (Table 3): In contrast to Sudoku, both MLP-t variants completely fail on the larger 30×30 grids (0.0% accuracy), whilst TR-mamba2attn achieves 80.6% versus 60.8% for TRM-attn.

claims.claim: Post-norm is needed for stability of unrolled recursion, independent of HRM's Q-learning motivation.
claims.evidence_quote: We argue that post-norm is essential for recursion stability itself, independent of Qlearning: it bounds the residual stream magnitude across recursive unrolling, preventing divergence.

Sudoku-Extreme: TRM-mlp-t, TR-mamba2mlpt, TRM-attn, TR-mamba2attn

venue: Latent & Implicit Thinking Workshop @ ICLR 2026
survey_notes: Operator-in-the-loop ablation at strict iso-param. Re-trained TRM-attn baselines: ARC-AGI-1 pass@1 40.75 / pass@2 43.88 (TRM paper 44.6 pass@2), Sudoku-Extreme 72.2 (TRM paper 74.7 for attention), Maze-Hard 60.8 (TRM paper 85.3): a further replication below TRM's reported Maze number. The +2.0 pass@2 gain is within the spread of independent TRM replications (40.4-44.4 pass@2 across 2511.16886, 2603.05234, this paper), and runs are single-seed, so the effect is weak evidence. The coverage vs selection result shows that pass@1 vs pass@2 vs pass@K choices change conclusions, which matters for comparing URM (pass@1) with TRM (pass@2).

title: Structured Sparse Memory for Recurrent Reasoning
relevance_reason: Decomposes from-scratch recurrent ARC systems (HRM/TRM/URM, 'XRM') into recurrent compute, task-embedding memory and synthetic data; includes iso-FLOP unique-layers vs recurrence sweeps.
one_sentence: Shows the per-puzzle-augmentation task-embedding table in HRM/TRM/URM holds ~448M parameters (30x the backbone), replaces it with a compositional sparse embedding (CoSE, 1/15 the parameters), adds Re-ARC/Re-ARC2 synthetic data and checkpoint/loop ensembling, reaching 84.0% ARC-AGI-1 and 46.7% ARC-AGI-2 pass@2.
key_contributions: Parameter accounting: XRM task tables are ~448M (ARC-AGI-1) and ~610M (ARC-AGI-2) learned parameters; shrinking them naively loses accuracy; CoSE (FiLM composition of puzzle/dihedral/color + low-rank residual) uses 1/15 the parameters and improves pass@2.
Synthetic, rule-preserving data (Re-ARC; new Re-ARC2 for ARC-AGI-2) is the largest measured driver of ARC-AGI-2 gains.
Iso-FLOP sweeps over unique layers U vs recurrence R and over truncated-BPTT horizon: balanced recurrence beats more unique layers; intermediate horizons beat H=1 (HRM) and full backprop.

setup.model_sizes: backbone 14M (URM-style, ConvSwiGLU); total 43-57M with CoSE vs 455-674M with full task tables
setup.train_tokens_or_data: ARC-AGI-1 / ARC-AGI-2 training tasks plus public-evaluation demonstration pairs (XRM protocol), dihedral and color augmentations, Re-ARC (ARC-AGI-1) or Re-ARC2 (ARC-AGI-2); 600k / 1M steps (best: 1.6M / 2.38M)
setup.loops_train: U unique layers repeated R times with truncated BPTT horizon H; outer refinement loop (ACT-style) as in XRM
setup.loops_test: ensemble of outer refinement loops of 16 and 24 iterations; votes over augmented views and recent checkpoints
setup.baselines: HRM, TRM, URM, VARC (numbers from papers); full-table ablations re-run
setup.benchmarks: ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2 public evaluation (pass@1, pass@2, pass@1000); cellular automata; nanochat language modeling with Engram memory

claims.claim: The task-embedding table, excluded from usual model-size counts, is an order of magnitude larger than the recurrent backbone in HRM/TRM/URM.
claims.evidence_quote: In existing XRM systems, the task embedding table can be more than 30 times larger than the backbone itself: ∼448M learnable parameters on ARC-AGI-1 and ∼610M on ARC-AGI-2.

claims.claim: At matched forward and backward FLOPs, more recurrence with fewer unique layers beats more unique layers (which overfit), up to a point; intermediate gradient horizons are best.
claims.regime: iso_train_flop, iso_infer_flop, iso_effective_depth (fixed L=U*R); not iso_param
claims.evidence_quote: At matched forward and backward FLOPs, too many unique layers overfit while too few provide insufficient capacity. At fixed forward configuration, intermediate learning horizons outperform both very short and full horizons.

title: Boosting Inference with Guided Reasoning: Stochastic Exploration for Recursive Models
relevance_reason: Inference-time stochastic exploration of a frozen TRM's recursive latent trajectories with Q-head-guided particle reweighting; diagnostics for when extra recursive compute helps.
one_sentence: Treats a frozen TRM's inference as approximate inference over latent trajectories: noise in the inner recursion proposes S=16 particle trajectories that TRM's Q-head reweights (Feynman-Kac tilt), lifting Sudoku-Extreme from 85.9% to 98.0% without retraining but not helping Maze-Hard.
key_contributions: Deterministic TRM recursion as the one-particle, zero-noise limit of a particle (SMC-like) procedure; Q-head reused as guide.
Label-free diagnostics (local stability, guide alignment / Q-spread bound, cloud-token entropy) that predict when exploration helps.
Sudoku-Extreme gain to 98.0% (oracle 98.0%); on Maze-Hard oracle headroom exists (90.9%) but the flat Q-head cannot select it.

setup.model_sizes: frozen TRM backbones (7M class; not restated)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: TRMs trained on Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Hard (standard data); evaluation on a 10,000-puzzle Sudoku-Extreme test split, 1,400-puzzle deterministic-failure split, 1,000 Maze-Hard test; 500-puzzle validation for tuning
setup.loops_train: TRM default
setup.loops_test: S=16 particles, N=48 outer steps, noise sigma 0.3 (Sudoku) / 0.5 (Maze)
setup.baselines: deterministic TRM (own checkpoint), unguided particles, post-hoc oracle particle
setup.benchmarks: Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard

claims.claim: Guided stochastic exploration raises Sudoku-Extreme exact solve from 85.9% to 98.0% without retraining.
claims.regime: iso_param, iso_data; not iso_infer_flop (16 particles x 48 steps)
claims.evidence_quote: On Sudoku-Extreme (Wang et al., 2025), our method improves exact-solve accuracy from 85.9±0.6% to 98.0±0.3%, solving previously out-of-reach failure cases and recovering baseline performance at much lower depths (Figure 1).

claims.claim: On Maze-Hard exploration exposes headroom but the Q-head guide is too flat to exploit it; the diagnostics predict this without labels.
claims.evidence_quote: On Maze-Hard exploration is stable but the Q-head guide is too flat: the spread bound flags this label-free, a priori (Figure 3), and evaluation confirms the predicted non-improvement (Table 1).

claims.claim: Recursive models leave trajectory-level headroom that requires both stable exploration and an aligned internal guide.
claims.evidence_quote: The lesson is that recursive models leave useful trajectory-level headroom, but recovering it requires both stable exploration and a ranking-aligned internal guide.

title: Flow Reasoning Models: Turning Flows Into Efficient Recurrent Reasoners
relevance_reason: Whole-network recurrence via self-conditioning of a flow model on its own outputs, trained with Fixed-Point Forcing; compared with HRM/TRM/EqR on Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique with FLOP accounting.
one_sentence: Self-conditions a continuous flow over discrete outputs on its previous prediction to make a recurrent refiner, and trains it on rollout-derived states (Fixed-Point Forcing) to remove exposure bias; reaches 99.5% Sudoku-Extreme (1K training puzzles) and 99.9% Maze-Unique, matching EqR's 98.7% with 44x fewer inference FLOPs.
key_contributions: FRM: flow-matching model whose input includes its own last prediction, giving recurrence without backpropagation through time.
Fixed-Point Forcing: train on states from the model's own inference dynamics; fixes confidently-wrong fixed points of plain self-conditioning (Sudoku 32.6% to 99.2% three-seed mean).
Accuracy-vs-inference-FLOP frontiers against HRM, TRM, EqR and masked diffusion models.

title: Compute Time Scaling with Recursive Models for Combinatorial Optimization
relevance_reason: Transfers TRM (weight-tied 2-block recursion, deep supervision, halting) to combinatorial optimization (TSP, MIS) and scales test-time depth and width.
one_sentence: Adapts TRM to TSP and MIS with graph-aware attention biases, lightweight decoders (2-opt edge insertion, peeling), problem-specific halting checks and noisy parallel rollouts; achieves the lowest learned-solver gaps on TSP-500/1000 and beats KaMIS on ER-[700-800] with 200 rollouts, plus self-relabeling training.
key_contributions: TRM4CO: 7M weight-tied TRM core (constant across problems) with problem embeddings and decoders; depth D and width K scale test-time compute, evaluation may run deeper than training.
Halting on a problem-specific solved check during training instead of a learned head; at test, selection by objective.
Self-relabeling: periodically replacing labels with the model's better solutions; can train MIS from scratch without solver labels.

title: Steering Recurrent Reasoners at Inference Time with Readout Feedback
relevance_reason: Training-free inference-time control of frozen recurrent reasoners (AKOrN, ItrSA++, TRM) by feeding readout probabilities back into the latent dynamics.
one_sentence: Readout Feedback converts a recurrent reasoner's intermediate token probabilities into pairwise coupling forces added to its latent updates; without retraining it improves 4 of 6 model-task pairs (including TRM on Sudoku-Extreme, 68.4% to 74.2%) at comparable FLOPs.
key_contributions: RoFB: closed-loop test-time steering using the model's own readouts, pulling same-class tokens together and pushing others apart in latent space.
Compute-matched comparison with longer rollouts and confidence-based voting: RoFB reaches operating points unattainable by either (e.g. ItrSA++ Maze 83.6% at ~100x less compute than baseline 81.7%).
Sign-flip intervention confirms the direction of feedback drives the gains.

title: One Step Forward and K Steps Back: Better Reasoning with Denoising Recursion Models
relevance_reason: Looped TRM transformer trained to undo diffusion corruption over k recursive steps; controlled TRM vs non-recursive and diffusion baselines on ARC-AGI-2 with matched FLOPs.
one_sentence: Denoising Recursion Models corrupt the target with masking noise and train a TRM to recover it over a k-step recursive window (no deep supervision), outperforming re-run TRM on ARC-AGI-2 at equal parameters (24.9% vs 21.8% pass@2 at 14M with NVARC pretraining) and showing non-recursive and diffusion baselines fail.
key_contributions: DRM: one forward corruption step then k recursive backward steps through a single gradient window; SPRM: noise in TRM latent states during training.
Controlled baselines inside the TRM codebase: stacked Transformer at matched FLOPs (70M) 25.5% vs TRM 45.7% on ARC-Easy; masked diffusion ~0-1%; TRM without deep supervision 34.7%.
Documents that TRM's released evaluation aggregates predictions across fine-tuning checkpoints as well as 1000 augmentations, and that training includes ARC2-Eval demonstration pairs.

title: Generative Recursive Reasoning
relevance_reason: Stochastic (latent-variable) version of HRM/TRM recursive reasoning with depth and width (parallel trajectory) scaling; Sudoku-Extreme, ARC-AGI, multi-solution tasks.
one_sentence: Makes each recursive latent transition of an HRM/TRM-style model stochastic (amortized variational inference with a truncated ELBO), enabling multiple hypotheses and width scaling with a latent process reward model for selection; improves Sudoku-Extreme, ARC-AGI and multi-solution puzzles over deterministic recursive baselines.
key_contributions: GRAM: stochastic transitions conditioned on input and state, trained by a truncated per-supervision-step ELBO (gradients stopped through earlier states), ACT for depth.
Width scaling: N sampled trajectories selected by majority vote or a Latent Process Reward Model value head.
Multi-solution coverage on N-Queens and Graph Coloring where deterministic recursion covers at most 36.1% of solutions; unconditional generation (Sudoku boards, MNIST).

setup.loops_test: 16 supervision steps; up to 320 iterations in scaling analysis; N up to 20-50 parallel samples

title: How Much Is One Recurrence Worth? Iso-Depth Scaling Laws for Looped Language Models
relevance_reason: Joint scaling law that measures the worth of one recurrence in unique parameters under matched effective depth and training FLOPs.
one_sentence: 116-run iso-depth (20 effective layers) sweep over r in {1,2,4,8} fits L = E + A(N_once + r^phi N_rec)^-alpha + B D^-beta, finding phi = 0.46: a recurrence is worth about half a unique block, so looping loses at matched compute.
key_contributions: Recurrence-equivalence exponent phi in a joint Chinchilla-style law; phi = 0.46 (95% CI [0.41, 0.53]) on a prelude-2/recur/coda-2 baseline with linear injection and full BPTT.
Delta-phi as a diagnostic: truncated BPTT lowers loss but drops phi to 0.38 (loop mechanism undertrained, wider optimum, higher inference cost); loop-boundary hyperconnections raise phi to 0.65.

Downstream five-axis suite: parametric knowledge tracks the capacity loss of looping, reasoning axes show no above-noise looped advantage at these budgets; gap persists at a ~4e20 FLOP, 47B-token extrapolation run.

survey_notes: Cleanest controlled evidence that looping costs quality at matched training FLOPs and matched effective depth (phi=0.46 < 1). Directly complements Parcae (2604.12946), which fixes unique parameters and lets depth/FLOPs/KV grow (iso-param): the two laws answer different questions and are not contradictory. Contradicts the strong reading of Ouro's 2-3x parameter-efficiency claim only in regime: Ouro compares unmatched public checkpoints. Agrees with Ouro App. D (non-looped with r-times layers wins). Its downstream finding (knowledge hurt, reasoning not helped at <=4e20 FLOPs) partially conflicts with Saunshi-style 'loops help reasoning' claims, but the authors attribute it to small scale. Contrasts with SMELT (2609.01343) and Looped-MoE scaling laws (2609.40316), which report net gains for looping in MoE settings under compute matching; difference is architecture (dense vs MoE, partial middle-layer loop) and the matching rule (SMELT also matches total params and KV). Truncated BPTT result is a warning for Huginn/Parcae/retrofit recipes that use it.

title: Scaling Laws for Looped Mixture of Experts
relevance_reason: Joint scaling law over model size, data, recurrence and MoE sparsity for middle-block looped (MoE) transformers, with a compute-matched trillion-token validation.
one_sentence: Fits a Chinchilla/MoE-style law with a bounded, sparsity-conditional effective-parameter mapping N_eff = N_act + kappa1(m) N_loop (1 - e^{-(R-1)/kappa2(m)}); recurrence gains saturate, sparsity raises the ceiling; a 1.3B-total looped MoE matches a 2.9B MoE on reasoning at matched training FLOPs.
key_contributions: Bounded recurrence mapping (finite asymptote kappa1 N_loop) that beats linear (Parcae-style) and power-law (Iso-Depth-style) mappings on held-out R=16, N and D; sparsity-conditional kappa_j(m) = kappa_j m^-theta.
Fitted law used for compute-optimal R* (grows with compute and sparsity, larger for smaller models) and memory-optimal expert count; tight memory favors recurrence, more memory favors sparsity.

Downstream (14 benchmarks): sparsity gives ~3x active-parameter efficiency overall, recurrence ~2x total-parameter efficiency on reasoning (BBH, GSM8K) at matched training FLOPs; ~3T-token LoopMoE (R=5) vs ~6T-token 2x larger MoE at ~1.5e22 FLOPs.

setup.model_sizes: sweep N_act in {0.3, 0.6, 1.0}B with E in {1,2,4,8,16}; trillion-token pair A0.3B-1.3B LoopMoE vs A0.6B-2.9B MoE
setup.train_tokens_or_data: sweep D in {100,...,500}B tokens of an open-licensed web-heavy mix; LoopMoE ~3T tokens vs MoE ~6T tokens (~1.5e22 FLOPs each)
setup.loops_train: R in {1,2,3,4,6,8} (R=16 held out); middle block looped with 2 prelude and 2 coda layers; LoopMoE R*=5 with per-loop supervision
setup.baselines: non-looped dense and MoE models at matched training FLOPs; 2x larger non-looped MoE
setup.benchmarks: BBH, GSM8K, ARC-C/E, OpenBookQA, HellaSwag, PIQA, SIQA, WinoGrande, BoolQ, DROP, MMLU, Natural Questions, TriviaQA

claims.claim: Recurrence adds effective parameters only up to a finite asymptote; MoE sparsity raises that asymptote and delays saturation (routing reaches different experts across passes).
claims.regime: iso_param; iso_data (fixed N_act and D in the sweep)
claims.evidence_quote: Finding: Scaling recurrence adds effective-parameter gain up to a finite, sparsity-dependent asymptote, while scaling sparsity raises and sustains this gain over more recurrent passes.

claims.claim: The bounded mapping extrapolates better to unseen R=16 than linear (overestimates) and power-law (overly optimistic) mappings used by prior looped scaling laws.
claims.evidence_quote: The linear mapping substantially overestimates the effective-parameter gain, while the power-law mapping captures diminishing gains but remains overly optimistic beyond the fitted range.

claims.claim: At matched training FLOPs (E=8), more recurrence lets a smaller model match a model with about 2x the total parameters on reasoning (GSM8K, BBH).
claims.evidence_quote: These recurrence gains can offset a ∼2× increase in total parameters on Reasoning: at 1021 FLOPs, the 0.3B model with R≥4 matches or exceeds the 0.6B model with R=1, while the 0.6B model with R≥3 matches the 1.0B model with R=1.

claims.claim: At trillion-token scale and matched training compute, a 1.3B-total looped MoE with law-derived recurrence matches a 2.9B-total non-looped MoE on reasoning but trails on the 14-benchmark overall score, and uses more inference compute.
claims.regime: iso_train_flop (not iso_data: ~3T vs ~6T tokens; not iso_infer_flop)
claims.evidence_quote: Despite using ∼2× fewer active and total parameters, A0.3B-1.3B LoopMoE at R ∈ {4, 5} matches A0.6B-2.9B MoE on reasoning tasks (BBH, GSM8K) by using more inference compute, while trailing on Overall performance.

claims.claim: Compute-optimal recurrence grows with training budget and sparsity; under fixed compute, tight weight-memory budgets favor recurrence and large budgets favor sparsity.
claims.evidence_quote: Finding: At fixed compute, tight memory favors recurrence, and more memory favors sparsity.

numbers.quote: varying recurrence from R=1 to R=5 raises inference compute from low to high and boosts Overall performance by a substantial +10.3 points (36.6 → 46.9; Table 2).

numbers.quote: at 5×1020 FLOPs, the 0.3B MoE models with E≥8 outperform the larger 1.0B dense model on both Overall and Reasoning.

limitations: Only middle-block looping studied; law asymptotes are properties within the observed R range (R<=8 fitted, R=16 held out); weight memory only (KV cache excluded); trillion-token LoopMoE trails the 2x MoE on overall score and needs up to 1.8x its inference compute; sweep models use last-pass loss only.
survey_notes: Third family of looped scaling laws: bounded (saturating) mapping vs Parcae's linear unrolled-parameter mapping and Iso-Depth's power law; argues both prior mappings are unbounded and over-predict at large R. Dense fitted asymptote kappa1 = 0.3682 (times N_loop), i.e. dense looping is worth little in the limit, consistent in direction with Iso-Depth phi=0.46 and with Sparse Layers (2605.09165) that dense looping scales poorly while Looped-MoE scales well. Positive downstream claims are iso_train_flop at fixed sparsity but the looped model uses more inference FLOPs (up to 1.8x) and fewer tokens; the reasoning-vs-overall split (matches 2x MoE on BBH/GSM8K, trails overall) supports the 'loops help reasoning more than knowledge' pattern (Ouro, Iso-Depth parametric-knowledge axis). Law-derived recurrence R*=5 contrasts with SMELT's choice of looping twice and LoopCoder-v2's saturation at 2 loops; different matching rules (SMELT matches total params and per-token FLOPs too).

title: SMELT: Scaling Laws for Compute-Matched MoE Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Multi-scale (to 54B total params) MoE looped Transformer study matching per-token FLOPs, total parameters and KV cache, with separate Chinchilla-style fits per architecture.
one_sentence: Loops the middle half of an MoE Transformer twice while matching per-token FLOPs, total parameters and KV cache (narrower width, more experts, smaller heads); across 100M-1.6B active (to 54B total) it saves 6.8-18.0% training FLOPs on the frontier.
key_contributions: Budget-matched recipe: loop middle 50% of layers twice, narrow hidden size, raise expert count to recover total params, adjust head size/GQA to hold KV cache, scale looped residual updates by 1/r.
4 scales x 4 sparsity grid (96 matched pairs, up to ~215B tokens) with separate surfaces L(F,S,D) = E + A(1-S)^b/F^a + K/D^c; SMELT has steeper frontier exponent (0.250 vs 0.237).
Downstream gains exceed what validation loss predicts and grow with scale; gains largest on Code, long samples and with more in-context examples; second visit reduces attention sink.

setup.model_sizes: active-parameter scales 100M, 200M, 600M, 1.6B (physical depth 10/12/20/30); up to 54B total non-embedding parameters at S ~ 97%
setup.train_tokens_or_data: internal corpus; 205B-token stable phase plus 10B-token cosine branches (longest ~215B tokens); identical token sequences per matched pair
setup.loops_train: middle 50% of layers looped r=2 (ablations r=1-4 at 200M)
setup.baselines: unlooped MoE Baseline matched on per-token FLOPs (+~3%), total non-embedding params (+~0.4%), KV cache (within ~4%)
setup.benchmarks: held-out validation loss (39 sources), DCLM Core (22 tasks), DCLM Completion, MMLU 5-shot

claims.claim: With per-token FLOPs, total parameters and KV cache matched, the looped MoE (SMELT) reaches lower loss than the unlooped MoE at every scale and sparsity level.
claims.evidence_quote: SMELT reaches lower loss than the Baseline at every scale and sparsity level.

claims.claim: On the fitted compute-optimal frontier SMELT saves 6.8-10.0% of training compute at 1e20 FLOPs and 14.7-18.0% at 1e21 FLOPs, with the saving growing with compute because its frontier exponent is larger.
claims.evidence_quote: At C = 1020 , SMELT saves 6.8–10.0% of training compute across sparsity levels. At C = 1021 , the range widens to 14.7–18.0%.

claims.claim: Downstream gains exceed what the validation-loss gap predicts, and this excess grows with scale; at 1.6B the largest excess shifts to Symbolic Problem Solving.
claims.evidence_quote: SMELT wins on DCLM Completion in 96 of 96 matched pairs, on DCLM Core in 83 of 96, and on MMLU in 29 of the 30 pairs whose Baseline scores at least 10 percentage points above chance

claims.claim: Under matched FLOPs, looping twice beats three or four loops because extra visits force a thinner model; looping the middle half beats full-stack looping.
claims.evidence_quote: Two visits win on all three metrics (Table 5); both a third and a fourth visit regress because the matched FLOPs cap forces a thinner model.

claims.claim: The looping gain is largest on Code and structured data, concentrates on long samples, and grows when in-context examples are provided.
claims.evidence_quote: CE Gain is positive on all five categories. Code leads at 20.4%; Finance and Math/STEM follow at 16.8% and 16.6%; Knowledge and Web sit at 14.9% and 14.8%.

numbers.what: largest scale

few-shot gap growth

numbers.quote: the mean normalized gain over the four longest buckets (512–4096 tokens) is 1.52× the mean over the four shortest (32–256 tokens).

limitations: Design ablations only at 200M active (3.9B total); each configuration trained once (no training-seed variance); only contiguous fully shared block looping; matching is on arithmetic FLOPs, params and KV size, not wall-clock; frontier gains at 1e22 are extrapolated; mechanism probes are descriptive.
survey_notes: Strongest controlled positive evidence for looping: matched per-token FLOPs (inference and training), total params, KV cache and identical data, up to 54B total params. Apparent contradiction with Iso-Depth (2604.21106, phi=0.46, looping loses at matched FLOPs): regime differs, since Iso-Depth holds width fixed and lets unique params shrink by up to 3.2x, whereas SMELT recovers total params via extra experts and narrows width; the authors explicitly argue Iso-Depth's deficit may reflect parameter loss. Also dense vs MoE: consistent with Sparse Layers (2605.09165) and Loop Scaling Laws (2609.40316) that sparsity rescues looping. Loop-count result (2 best under FLOP matching) agrees with LoopCoder-v2 (2606.18023, saturation at 2 loops, different mechanism) and with Gao et al. (cited, 2 loop steps optimal under wall-clock matching), but differs from Loop Scaling Laws' law-derived R*=5, which matches only training FLOPs and lets inference FLOPs grow. Gains on code and in-context learning are measured via loss and DCLM; no explicit reasoning benchmark like GSM8K at these scales.

title: Parcae: Scaling Laws For Stable Looped Language Models
relevance_reason: Stable prelude-recur-coda looped LM with iso-parameter isoFLOP training scaling laws over mean recurrence and a unified train/test-time recurrence law.
one_sentence: Recasts looping as a dynamical system, constrains injection spectral norm (negative diagonal A, ZOH) for stability, and derives iso-parameter scaling laws: compute-optimal training raises mean recurrence and data together; test-time looping saturates exponentially near training depth.
key_contributions: LTI analysis showing divergent looped runs learn rho(A) >= 1; Parcae parameterizes A = Diag(-exp(log A)) with ZOH discretization, normalizes the injected input, and samples depth per sequence.
Iso-parameter isoFLOP sweeps at 140M and 370M: optimal mu_rec ~ C^0.40 and tokens ~ C^0.78; looping frontier strictly below fixed-depth at matched params and FLOPs.

Test-time law L(T) = L_inf + Z exp(-zT) with L_inf equal to the training-law loss at T = mu_rec, unified as a training floor plus exp(-z T / mu_rec) decay; 1.3B/104B-token comparison with parameter- and data-matched Transformers.

setup.model_sizes: 140M, 370M, 770M, 1.3B (nanochat Transformer setup, middle third looped); 100M and 350M in RDM (Huginn) setup
setup.train_tokens_or_data: FineWeb-Edu; 11.2B/29.6B/61.6B/104B tokens for 140M/370M/770M/1.3B; isoFLOP budgets 1e18-6.4e19 (140M) and 3.2e19-1.28e20 (370M)
setup.loops_train: Poisson per-sequence depth with mean mu_rec (8 for main comparisons; 2-12 in sweeps), backprop through ceil(mu_rec/2)
setup.baselines: parameter- and data-matched Transformers (nanochat) and RDMs (Huginn-style recurrent depth models); fixed-depth (mu_rec=1) Parcae at matched params and FLOPs
setup.benchmarks: validation PPL, WikiText, Lambada, Core and Core-Extended (DCLM suites), HellaSwag, ARC, PIQA, BoolQ, SciQ

claims.claim: Instability of prior looped models (residual explosion) is tied to learning an injection transition with spectral radius >= 1; constraining it yields convergence across learning rates where baselines diverge.
claims.evidence_quote: Figure 3 and Table 2 confirm this empirically: divergent runs learn a spectral radius of ρ(A) ≥ 1, with convergent runs maintaining ρ(A) < 1, affirming that LTI stability constraints are necessary.

claims.claim: At matched unique parameters and training tokens (but more FLOPs for Parcae, mu_rec=8 on the middle third), Parcae beats Transformers on validation PPL and Core/Core-Extended at all four scales up to 1.3B.
claims.evidence_quote: Table 5 shows that Parcae reduces validation perplexity by 4.3–9.2% and improves Core and Core-Extended Scores by up to 2.99 and 1.18 points, respectively.

claims.claim: At fixed parameter count and fixed training FLOPs, the compute-optimal looped frontier (fewer tokens, more recurrence) achieves strictly lower loss and higher Core than fixed-depth models that spend the FLOPs on more data.
claims.evidence_quote: Figure 6 shows fixed-depth Parcae models without looping at each FLOP budget. The optimal curve achieves a strictly lower loss, which translates to 1.2-2.0 points higher Core scores (Table 6).

claims.claim: Compute-optimal training increases mean recurrence and data in tandem following power laws.
claims.evidence_quote: Our initial scaling laws suggest that looping and data should be increased in tandem, given a fixed FLOP budget.

claims.claim: Test-time looping does not extrapolate past training depth in language modeling: gains plateau near the training mean recurrence and follow a saturating exponential.
claims.evidence_quote: we observe that gains plateau near µrec , suggesting training depth determines the test-time scaling ceiling.

claims.claim: Truncating the sampling distribution by the backprop depth hurts extrapolation to lower and higher recurrences, and deeper test-time recurrence quality is coupled to the backprop depth.
claims.evidence_quote: This implies that the capabilities of looped models utilizing deeper recurrences are heavily coupled with µbwd .

limitations: Scaling laws fitted only at 140M and 370M with separate per-size fits (unique N fixed); main Transformer comparison is not FLOP-matched; test-time gains saturate at training depth; higher mu_rec requires more test-time steps for equal quality; no LR sweep for Parcae.
survey_notes: Key iso-parameter scaling-law paper. Its positive results hold at fixed unique parameters (iso_param) where looping adds FLOPs; at fixed params AND fixed FLOPs, looping beats spending compute on more data (iso_param + iso_train_flop), which is NOT the same question as Iso-Depth (2604.21106), which fixes effective depth and FLOPs and lets unique params vary and finds looping loses (phi=0.46). Both can be true: looping is a good use of extra FLOPs when parameters (memory) are capped, but a worse use than unique layers when they are not. Iso-Depth explicitly frames Parcae as complementary and notes Parcae uses truncated BPTT, which Iso-Depth finds lowers phi. Test-time result (saturation at mu_rec) agrees with Ouro (degradation beyond T=4) and contradicts strong extrapolation claims from synthetic tasks. The 'twice the size' claim compares a 770M looped model (8 middle-third loops, more FLOPs) to a 1.3B Transformer on the same data; FLOPs are not matched.

title: Nanbeige4.2-3B: Unlocking Agentic Capabilities in a Compact Model
relevance_reason: Open-weight 3B non-embedding looped Transformer (two passes over the full stack) pretrained from scratch on 28T tokens, then SFT and agentic RL.
one_sentence: Technical report of a 3B non-embedding two-pass looped Transformer pretrained on 28T tokens and post-trained for agents; reports wins over larger public models (Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma4-12B) on agentic benchmarks, with only qualitative loop ablations.
key_contributions: Largest-token-budget looped LM in the corpus: 28T tokens, whole-stack two-pass loop, released weights.

Qualitative design findings: from-scratch looping beats upcycling a pretrained dense model; two passes best (about 75% of standard-Transformer token efficiency); halving KV by sharing across passes costs performance.
Agentic SFT/RL pipeline (mixed-mode RLHF, length-controlled reasoning RL, agentic RL with process rewards) on top of the looped base.

setup.model_sizes: 3B non-embedding (4B total) parameters
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 28T tokens, increased math/code/synthetic QA weights plus some agentic trajectories
setup.loops_train: 2 passes through the full layer stack
setup.baselines: public checkpoints: Nanbeige4-3B, Qwen3.5-4B/9B, Gemma4-E4B/12B (different data and training)
setup.benchmarks: base: GSM8K, BBH, MBPP, MMLU-Pro, SuperGPQA, GPQA; post-trained: GDPval, AgentIF-Oneday, OfficeQA-Pro, PinchBench-V2, ClawGym, Claw-Eval, MCP-Atlas, SWE-Bench Verified/Pro, Terminal-Bench 2.0, HLE, SciCode, GPQA-Diamond, HMMT, IMO-AnswerBench, LiveCodeBench-V6, AA-LCR, IF-Bench

claims.claim: With 3B non-embedding parameters the post-trained looped model beats larger public models (Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma4-12B) on all reported general-agent and code-agent benchmarks; comparison is against checkpoints trained on different data and recipes.
claims.evidence_quote: With only 3B non-embedding parameters, Nanbeige4.2-3B achieves the best results on all reported general-agent and code-agent benchmarks, outperforming the larger Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma4-12B models.

claims.claim: Training the looped architecture from scratch performs significantly better than upcycling a pretrained standard Transformer into a looped one (no numbers reported).
claims.evidence_quote: In our experiments, the from-scratch approach performs significantly better, suggesting that the model benefits from adapting representations to repeated layer reuse throughout pre-training

claims.claim: Two passes give the best trade-off, retaining about 75% of a standard Transformer's token efficiency; more passes add little, slow training and destabilize optimization.
claims.evidence_quote: A two-pass configuration provides the most favorable trade-off in our experiments: relative to a standard Transformer, it retains approximately 75% of the token efficiency and provides a significant capacity gain.

claims.claim: Sharing the KV cache across loop passes halves KV memory but consistently yields lower gains than the full non-sharing loop, so it was not used.
claims.evidence_quote: Although the sharing configuration reduces the KV-cache by half, its performance gains are consistently lower than those of the full, non-sharing loop configuration.

claims.claim: The looped base model improves on the non-looped predecessor Nanbeige4-3B-Base and beats similar-size public base models, but the gain conflates the loop with a new 28T-token data recipe.
claims.evidence_quote: The results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining the Looped Transformer structure with the improved pre-training data recipe.

numbers.what: pretraining tokens and size
numbers.quote: Nanbeige4.2-3B is pretrained from scratch on 28T tokens with a Looped Transformer that reuses the layer stack to increase capacity without adding parameters.

numbers.what: base model scores (total, non-emb, GSM8K, BBH, MBPP, MMLU-Pro, SuperGPQA, GPQA)
token efficiency of two-pass loop vs standard Transformer
numbers.quote: relative to a standard Transformer, it retains approximately 75% of the token efficiency and provides a significant capacity gain.

numbers.what: weights URL
numbers.quote: further supports its use as a compact local personal assistant. The model checkpoint is available at https://huggingface.co/Nanbeige/Nanbeige4.2-3B.

limitations: No controlled looped-vs-dense comparison is reported; loop-depth, upcycling and KV-sharing ablations are described qualitatively without numbers or scale; benchmark comparisons are against public models with different data; some benchmarks are in-house (Recruit-Bench).
survey_notes: Instantiation-table row: largest training-token budget (28T) of any looped LM in this group, two passes over the whole stack, open weights. All capability claims are unmatched. The qualitative ~75% token-efficiency statement is consistent in direction with Iso-Depth (2604.21106: looping is worth less than unique depth) and with the 2-loop saturation found by SMELT (2609.01343) and LoopCoder-v2 (2606.18023). The 'from scratch beats upcycling' statement is relevant to retrofit papers (e.g. 2511.07384) but no numbers are given. KV-sharing finding contrasts with Ouro (2510.25741), which reports last-step KV reuse at decode costs <=0.3 GSM8K points; the settings differ (Ouro shares only at decode after training without sharing).

title: LoopCoder-v2: Only Loop Once for Efficient Test-Time Computation Scaling
relevance_reason: 7B Parallel Loop Transformer coders trained from scratch on 18T tokens at R=1-4 with matched SFT; non-monotonic loop-count effect with per-loop diagnostics.
one_sentence: Trains 7B Parallel Loop Transformer coders at R=1,2,3,4 on the same 18T tokens and SFT; R=2 sharply improves code and agentic benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified 43.0 to 64.4) while R>=3 regresses, explained by a fixed cross-loop-offset cost versus shrinking per-loop gain.
key_contributions: Large matched loop-count study: four 7B PLT models from scratch on 18T tokens (1:1 text:code), identical 6M-example SFT, evaluated at their training loop count.

Gain-cost diagnosis: loop 2 carries the productive refinement (effective rank peaks, largest output shift); later loops oscillate, and the CLP positional-mismatch cost stays roughly fixed and exceeds per-loop gain by 30-45x.
Thinking (explicit CoT) on top of the R=2 latent loop is super-additive on reasoning benchmarks (e.g. +26.9 on LiveCodeBench).

setup.model_sizes: 7B dense PLT
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 18T tokens internal text+code mixture (1:1), >100 programming languages; 6M SFT examples
setup.loops_train: R in {1,2,3,4} (separate models)
setup.baselines: non-looped R=1 7B with identical data and SFT; public open and proprietary code models (unmatched)
setup.benchmarks: HumanEval+, MultiPL-E, BigCodeBench, LiveCodeBench, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, Multi-SWE, Terminal-Bench v1/v2, Mind2Web, BFCL, SWE-bench-CC

claims.claim: With identical parameters, 18T-token pretraining data and SFT, the two-loop PLT improves broadly over the non-looped baseline on code generation, code reasoning, agentic SWE and tool use.
claims.regime: iso_param; iso_data (R=2 uses more FLOPs per token)
claims.evidence_quote: the two-loop variant delivers broad gains over the non-looped baseline across code generation, code reasoning, agentic software engineering, and tool-use benchmarks, improving SWEbench Verified from 43.0 to 64.4 points and Multi-SWE from 14.0 to 31.0 points.

claims.claim: Loop count is strongly non-monotonic: three or more loops regress, often below the non-looped baseline (R=3 drops to 27.6% on SWE-bench Verified).
claims.evidence_quote: the two-loop model improves broadly over the non-looped baseline, including a gain on SWE-bench Verified from 43.0% to 64.4%, while the three-loop model regresses on many tasks, dropping to 27.6% on SWE-bench Verified.

Agrees with SMELT (2609.01343), Nanbeige4.2 (2607.22083) and Ouro's 8->4 reduction that small loop counts (2-4) are what works at scale; disagrees with the law-predicted R*=5 of Loop Scaling Laws (2609.40316), but the regimes differ (PLT offset cost; LoopMoE was selected under training-FLOP matching). The magnitude of the SWE-bench jump (43.0 to 64.4) and collapse at R=3 (27.6) from single runs warrants caution: agentic benchmarks are high-variance and post-training interacts with the base. Latent loop + explicit CoT super-additivity is a capability claim with no FLOP matching.

title: Scaling Latent Reasoning via Looped Language Models
relevance_reason: Largest openly released from-scratch looped LM family (1.4B/2.6B, 7.7T tokens) with learned exit gate, synthetic knowledge-capacity/manipulation study and small-scale loop scaling laws.
one_sentence: Pretrains Ouro, weight-tied whole-stack LoopLMs (1.4B, 2.6B; 4 loops; 7.7T tokens) with an entropy-regularized exit gate; claims 2-3x parameter efficiency vs public dense checkpoints and attributes gains to knowledge manipulation, not storage.
key_contributions: Ouro-1.4B (24 layers x 4) and Ouro-2.6B (48 layers x 4, upcycled by layer duplication) trained on 7.7T tokens plus Thinking SFT variants, released openly.

Entropy-regularized (uniform-prior ELBO) exit-gate objective plus a Stage-II gate fine-tune using per-step loss improvement; Q-exit thresholding at inference; last-step KV reuse cuts decode KV memory 4x.

Capo/Mano/multi-hop-QA synthetic studies: looping leaves knowledge capacity at ~2 bits/param but improves knowledge manipulation; small-scale total-loss and step-wise-loss scaling laws (53M-1.36B, 20B tokens).

setup.model_sizes: Ouro 1.4B (24 layers, d=2048) and 2.6B (48 layers, d=2048); scaling-law sweep 53M-1.36B; synthetic GPT-2 style 1M-40M
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 7.7T tokens total (3T+3T stable, 1.4T CT annealing, 20B LongCT, 300B mid-training) from open datasets; scaling-law runs 20B tokens FineWeb-Edu
setup.loops_train: 8 recurrent steps in Stage 1a, reduced to 4 from Stage 1b onward
setup.loops_test: 1-8 (5-8 are extrapolation beyond trained T=4); adaptive early exit via Q-exit
setup.baselines: Public dense checkpoints: Gemma3 1B/4B/12B, Llama3.2 1.2B/3B, Llama3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 1.5B/3B/7B, Qwen3 1.7B/4B/8B, DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen 1.5B/7B; synthetic iso-param and iso-FLOP transformers
setup.benchmarks: MMLU, MMLU-Pro, BBH, ARC-C, HellaSwag, Winogrande, GSM8K, MATH500, HumanEval(+), MBPP(+); AIME24/25, OlympiadBench, GPQA, SuperGPQA, BeyondAIME, HLE; HEx-PHI; Capo, Mano, multi-hop QA

claims.claim: Ouro 1.4B and 2.6B (4 loops, 7.7T tokens) match 4B and 8B public dense transformers on most benchmarks, i.e. 2-3x parameter efficiency; baselines trained on different data (2T-36T tokens).
claims.evidence_quote: we demonstrate that 1.4B and 2.6B parameter LoopLMs match 4B and 8B standard transformers on most benchmarks, yielding 2-3× parameter-efficiency gains

claims.claim: Looping does not increase knowledge storage: looped and non-looped models of equal parameter count store about 2 bits per parameter on Capo synthetic biographies.
claims.evidence_quote: looping does not increase knowledge capacity nor improve capacity scaling. Models with and without loops all attain around a similar capacity ratio ≈ 2 bits/parameter.

claims.claim: On the Mano modular-arithmetic manipulation task, looped models beat iso-parameter non-looped models for all k and often beat the iso-FLOP (12-layer, iso-effective-depth) baseline.
claims.evidence_quote: given the same parameters, looped models always outperform their non-looped counterpart for all possible k ∈ {2, 3, 6}. Even with the same number of FLOPs in the model, the looped models can often perform better.

claims.claim: Test-time depth extrapolation beyond the trained 4 steps degrades benchmark accuracy for both base and Thinking models, although HEx-PHI safety keeps improving at steps 5-8.
claims.regime: not_applicable (test-time loop sweep on one model)
claims.evidence_quote: benchmark performance sees a moderate degradation when extrapolating, with a noticeable drop compared to the peak at T = 4.

claims.claim: In the small-scale controlled sweep (20B tokens), a standard transformer whose layer count is multiplied by the recurrent step always beats the LoopLM; the gap grows with loops and shrinks with model size.
claims.evidence_quote: Overall, the performance of the standard model exceeds that of LoopLM under the same conditions. This gap increases with the recurrent step and decreases with the model size.

claims.claim: Gains from loop 1 to loop 4 on MMLU concentrate on reasoning-heavy subcategories and are smallest on fact-retrieval subcategories.
claims.evidence_quote: The categories with the most significant improvements are those requiring logical, maths, or procedural reasoning; conversely, categories that depend more on retrieving specific, memorized facts or nuanced world knowledge showed the most modest gains.

limitations: Headline comparisons are against public checkpoints trained on different data (unmatched); no controlled same-data dense baseline at 1.4B/2.6B scale. 8-step training was unstable (reduced to 4). Accuracy degrades when extrapolating beyond trained depth. RL did not improve over SFT, partly because rollout engines assume a fixed execution path. Scaling-law constants are not reported (only R2).
survey_notes: Anchor model for the instantiation table. The 2-3x parameter-efficiency headline is unmatched (Qwen3 trained on 36T, Gemma3-4B on 4T vs Ouro 7.7T on a different mix); the paper's own controlled appendix (App. D, 20B tokens, up to 1.36B) shows a non-looped model with r-times more layers always wins, with the gap shrinking with size, i.e. looping loses at iso-effective-depth but the paper never reports an iso-train-FLOP dense baseline at scale. Knowledge storage vs manipulation claim is shown only at <=40M synthetic scale (iso-param), plus an MMLU-subcategory correlational analysis. Consistent with Iso-Depth phi=0.46 (2604.21106) in that loops are worth less than unique layers. Extrapolation: degrades beyond trained depth (contrasts with Huginn-style randomized-depth training and Parcae's saturating test-time curve, which use different training regimes). Ouro's 2.6B model is grown from the 1.4B by layer duplication, so 2.6B is not a from-scratch run.

title: Sparse Layers are Critical to Scaling Looped Language Models
relevance_reason: Controlled isoFLOP scaling comparison of dense, MoE, looped and looped-MoE transformers at matched effective depth, plus early exit at loop boundaries.
one_sentence: IsoFLOP study (5e16-1e18 FLOPs, 16 effective layers) shows dense looping strictly hurts at matched compute, while replacing dense FFNs by top-2-of-8 MoE lets a looped model beat the dense baseline; loop boundaries are better training-free early-exit points.
key_contributions: Four architectures (Base, MoE, Looped 8x2, Looped-MoE 8x2) with identical active parameters and effective depth, compared with muP-transferred isoFLOP scaling laws.
Mechanism: expert routing diverges across loop passes (25-53% of tokens get fully disjoint experts in most layers), recovering per-pass expressivity.
Entropy-based early exit: looped models degrade less per FLOP saved because each loop ends with the output-facing layers; more loops (2x8) improve the trade-off further.

setup.model_sizes: compute-optimal models up to 305M active / 711M stored parameters; at 1e18 FLOPs Looped 168M, Base 246M, Looped-MoE 216M, MoE 366M stored
setup.train_tokens_or_data: FineWeb-Edu 10B-token sample, GPT-2 tokenizer; D = C/(6 N_active)
setup.loops_train: 8 layers x 2 loops (scaling study); 4x4 and 2x8 for early-exit study
setup.loops_test: same; early exit only at loop boundaries
setup.baselines: Base (16 unique dense layers) and non-looped MoE at the same active parameters and effective depth
setup.benchmarks: test loss; AI2 OLMES Core 9 (ARC-E/C, BoolQ, CSQA, HellaSwag, OBQA, PIQA, SIQA, WinoGrande); perplexity vs FLOPs saved

claims.claim: At matched training compute and effective depth, dense looping scales strictly worse than the dense baseline, while Looped-MoE scales better than the dense baseline.
claims.evidence_quote: We find that Looped-MoE scales better than Base, while Looped models scale strictly worse (Figure 1, middle), supporting our hypothesis that sparse routing restores expressiveness lost to weight tying.

claims.claim: Looping the same architecture always reduces quality at matched compute: non-looped MoE beats Looped-MoE and Base beats Looped; all four share roughly the same slope and differ in offset.
claims.evidence_quote: MoE scales the best, followed by Looped-MoE, then Base and lastly Looped. Looping the same architecture seems thus to strictly reduce expressivity.

claims.claim: Downstream at 1e18 FLOPs, Looped-MoE has the highest OLMES Core 9 average with fewer stored parameters than Base; dense Looped is lowest; non-looped MoE is lowest overall despite best test loss.
claims.evidence_quote: Looped-MoE achieves the highest average score (39.6) across the Core 9 benchmarks, outperforming Base (38.7) despite storing fewer unique parameters (216M vs. 246M). Looped scores lowest (37.4)

claims.claim: MoE routing diverges across loop passes, so the same physical layer runs different expert sub-networks on each pass.
claims.evidence_quote: Across layers 1–6 and 8, 25–53% of tokens receive entirely non-overlapping expert assignments between passes, while only 4–14% receive identical assignments.

claims.claim: Looped models give better training-free early-exit compute-quality trade-offs than non-looped models, and more loops improve this further.
claims.evidence_quote: at 10% FLOPs saved, Looped and Looped-MoE reach perplexity 50.2 and 51.0, compared to 55.4 for Base and 75.7 for MoE.

claims.claim: Critique of Ouro: Ouro compares by unique parameters while giving its models 4x the effective depth (more compute) than the dense models it is compared to.
claims.evidence_quote: In their study, they compare performance by the number of unique parameters, but giving their models much more compute (4x the effective depth) than the models in their comparisons.

numbers.what: compute budgets
numbers.quote: Repeating this across four budgets C ∈ {5 × 1016 , 2 × 1017 , 5 × 1017 , 1018 } FLOPs yields a set of compute-optimal points

numbers.what: fitted loss-vs-parameter exponents
numbers.quote: Fitting a power law for Loss, L ∝ N −α through the compute-optimal points yields α = 0.076 (Base) and 0.077 (Looped-MoE), consistent with the 0.076 scaling exponent reported by Kaplan et al. [4].

numbers.what: OLMES Core 9 average
numbers.quote: Looped-MoE achieves the highest average score (39.6) across the Core 9 benchmarks, outperforming Base (38.7) despite storing fewer unique parameters (216M vs. 246M).

numbers.what: non-looped MoE OLMES average
numbers.quote: MoE scores lowest on average (36.4) despite achieving the best test loss.

numbers.what: early exit at 10% FLOPs saved with 2x8 Looped-MoE
numbers.quote: At 10% FLOPs saved, Looped-MoE 2 × 8 reaches perplexity 42.0 versus 55.4 for Base and 75.7 for MoE.

numbers.what: largest scale trained
numbers.quote: we did not scale our four architectures beyond 305M/711M (active/stored) parameters

numbers.what: MoE configuration
numbers.quote: For all MoE configurations in this study, we use k=2 active experts out of E=8 total, following Mixtral [15].

numbers.what: Table 6 stored params and ARC-E, ARC-C, BoolQ for Looped, Base, Looped-MoE, MoE

limitations: Scale capped at 305M active / 711M stored and 1e18 FLOPs; depth held fixed (muP does not transfer across depth); downstream OLMES scores near chance on several tasks; early-exit savings are theoretical FLOPs, no throughput measurement.
survey_notes: Important for the regime audit: at iso_train_flop + iso_effective_depth (same active params, same tokens), looping strictly lowers quality for both dense and MoE (Fig. 10); the headline 'Looped-MoE beats Base' is a cross-architecture comparison (MoE vs dense) where Looped-MoE stores fewer unique params than Base. Agrees with Iso-Depth (2604.21106). Contrasts with SMELT (2609.01343), where looped MoE beats unlooped MoE, but SMELT matches total params by adding experts and narrowing width rather than holding width fixed. Explicitly criticizes Ouro: Ouro compares by unique parameters while giving its models 4x the effective depth. Downstream differences are small and at tiny scale (e.g. Looped-MoE's advantage is driven largely by BoolQ 63.9 vs 51.4).

title: Looped Language Models Improve Compositional Tool Calling
relevance_reason: Evaluates native (Ouro) and retrofitted (McLeish et al.) looped LMs on BFCL, NESTful and API-Bank with matched SFT and inference-depth sweeps.
one_sentence: LoRA-SFTs Ouro-1.4B/2.6B, retrofitted looped Llama-3.2-1B/OLMo-2-1B and non-looped baselines on the same function-calling data; looped models gain most on multi-call and nested tool use, accuracy rises with inference depth, and Ouro's exit gate gives a better compute trade-off.
key_contributions: Matched-SFT comparison of looped vs non-looped models on BFCL v3, NESTful and API-Bank, separating compositional (multi-call, nested) from single-call tool use.
Inference-depth sweeps (Ouro 1-4, retrofits 1-8) showing gains concentrate on compositional categories and saturate (Ouro-2.6B near-saturated after 3 iterations).
Adaptive exit (Ouro gate, thresholds q) matches or slightly exceeds the best fixed depth on BFCL with fewer average iterations.

setup.model_sizes: Ouro-1.4B, Ouro-2.6B; retrofitted Llama-3.2-1B and OLMo-2-1B; baselines Qwen3-1.7B/4B, Llama-3.2-1B/3B, public instruct models up to 8B
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Hermes function-calling dataset, LoRA rank 32, 2 epochs (SFT only; pretraining from released checkpoints)
setup.loops_train: Ouro: Tmax=4 with exit-distribution objective; retrofits: Poisson-lognormal sampled depth
setup.loops_test: Ouro 1-4 fixed or adaptive (q in 0.1-0.8); retrofits 1, 2, 4, 8
setup.baselines: same-SFT non-looped Qwen3/Llama base models; non-looped parents of the retrofits with same SFT; released instruct checkpoints
setup.benchmarks: BFCL v3 (Simple, Multiple, Parallel, Parallel-Multiple; AST accuracy), NESTful (Win Rate), API-Bank (Call Correctness, Exact, Parse)

claims.claim: Under matched SFT, looped models do better on compositional (multi-call, nested) tool calling, while gains on isolated single API calls are smaller and model-dependent; the Ouro comparison is against non-looped models with different pretraining.
claims.evidence_quote: In both experimental settings, looped models perform better on compositional tool-calling tasks, whereas gains on isolated API invocation are smaller and model-dependent.

claims.claim: Holding the fine-tuned model fixed and only varying inference depth, BFCL accuracy rises with recurrent depth, mostly on compositional categories, before plateauing.
claims.evidence_quote: Figure 2 shows that BFCL accuracy generally rises with recurrent depth, with the largest gains on compositional categories.

claims.claim: Adaptive exit with Ouro's gate recovers most of the deep-recurrence gain with fewer iterations per token, matching or slightly exceeding the best fixed depth on BFCL.
claims.evidence_quote: On BFCL, adaptive stopping matches or slightly exceeds the best fixed-depth operating point while executing fewer recurrent iterations on average.

claims.claim: Retrofitted looped models improve several compositional categories over their parents but remain much weaker than natively pretrained looped models on deeply nested workflows.
claims.regime: unmatched (same SFT; retrofit adds recurrence training to the parent)
claims.evidence_quote: although post-hoc recurrence improves several compositional tasks, retrofitted models remain substantially weaker than natively recurrent models on deeply nested workflows

numbers.what: BFCL Ouro-1.4B Base vs SFT (Simple, Multiple, Parallel, Par.-Mult., Overall)
BFCL Ouro-2.6B Base vs SFT
BFCL Qwen3-1.7B Base/SFT/Instruct (same SFT recipe vs public instruct)
BFCL retrofitted OLMo-2-1B SFT vs Looped SFT (8 loops)

SFT recipe
numbers.value: LoRA rank 32, lr 2e-5, 2 epochs, 4,096 max length
numbers.quote: All experiments use a maximum sequence length of 4,096 tokens, a 90/10 train-validation split, two training epochs, AdamW with learning rate 2 × 10−5

limitations: No same-pretraining non-looped counterpart exists for Ouro, so native comparisons are unmatched; the shared LoRA SFT recipe appears to fail for Qwen3 bases on multi-call categories (e.g. Qwen3-1.7B SFT Parallel 3.0 vs its public instruct 83.5), inflating the looped advantage; extra loops raise per-token compute; single-turn static benchmarks only; single A100 runs, no seeds.
survey_notes: Capability evidence for compositional/agentic use of looped models, but regime is weak: Ouro vs Qwen3/Llama differ in pretraining, and the same-recipe SFT baselines underperform their own public instruct versions dramatically on multi-call tasks, while public Qwen3-1.7B/4B-Instruct exceed the SFT'd Ouro models on BFCL overall. The cleanest evidence is the within-model inference-depth sweep (depth helps compositional categories, saturating by 3-4 for Ouro-2.6B) and the adaptive-exit result. Consistent with Ouro's claim that loops help composition/manipulation more than retrieval, and with Nanbeige4.2/LoopCoder-v2 agentic claims, which are also unmatched or FLOP-unmatched. Retrofit vs native gap echoes Nanbeige4.2's statement that from-scratch looping beats upcycling.

title: Squeezing More from Limited Data with Recursive Transformers
relevance_reason: Whole-stack weight-shared causal LM (RecursiveGPT) as a compute-scaling axis under fixed 10M-100M word data budgets, compared with standard Transformers and FLOP-matched extra epochs.
one_sentence: Under fixed BabyLM-scale data (10M-100M words) where larger standard models overfit, a recursive decoder with per-step norms and factorized embeddings outperforms standard Transformers and FLOP-matched extra-epoch training.
key_contributions: Optimal-scale sweep of standard Transformers (13M-1.2B params, 10M-100M words, two corpora): optimum depends on data budget and downstream target; extra parameters overfit.
RecursiveGPT: one shared block applied R times with step-specific RMSNorm and biases, MLP expansion 16, factorized embeddings; depth sweep peaks at R=16.
Compute-matched control: spending the same FLOPs on more epochs (146 at 10M words, 50 at 100M) degrades the standard model, whereas recursion improves it.

setup.model_sizes: RecursiveGPT 27.6M (R=16), 124.0M and 404.1M (R=24); standard 13M-1.22B
setup.train_tokens_or_data: BabyLM baseline corpus and Nemotron-ClimbMix; 10M-100M words, 10 epochs
setup.loops_train: fixed R (4-32 swept; 16 and 24 used)
setup.baselines: standard 12-layer Transformers with/without factorized embeddings on the same data; standard models trained for more epochs to match FLOPs; BabyLM 2025 GPT-BERT and AMLM hard decay (unmatched recipes)
setup.benchmarks: BLiMP, COMPS, LAMBADA pass@5; BLiMP Supplement, EWoK, Entity Tracking

claims.claim: At a fixed 10M-word data budget, a 27.6M recursive model beats both the best standard model and an unfactorized standard model on all three evaluations (same data, fewer params, more FLOPs).
claims.evidence_quote: Overall, the recursive models are highly competitive; in the 10M-word setting, our recursive model outperforms both standard models on all three evaluations.

claims.claim: At 100M words, the 404M RecursiveGPT-Large reaches the best average score, above a 1.22B standard model trained on the same data, while the 124M recursive model trails the 1.22B model except on BLiMP.
claims.evidence_quote: Scaling the recursive model to 404.1M parameters yields RecursiveGPT-Large, which uses substantially higher compute and reaches the best average score among our models while still being smaller than the 1.22B standard baseline.

claims.claim: Allocating the recursive model's extra compute to more epochs over the same data instead degrades the standard model, so recursion is a better use of FLOPs when data is the binding constraint.
claims.evidence_quote: Additional epochs reduce the average score from 45.07 to 41.47 at 10M words and from 63.47 to 56.68 at 100M words.

claims.claim: The benefit of recurrent depth is non-monotonic: average score improves up to depth 16 and then declines slightly, attributed to optimization difficulty.
claims.evidence_quote: the average score across the three evaluations improves with recurrent depth up to depth 16 and then declines slightly.

Table 1 LAMBADA p@5 and average scores
best recursive depth-sweep score
numbers.quote: pared with 45.07 for the best standard model from Section 3 and 44.93 for an unfactorized standard model with the same hidden size.

numbers.quote: At 10M words, we train for 146 epochs, approximately matching the estimated training FLOPs of RecursiveGPT. At 100M words, we train for 50 epochs.

numbers.quote: model sizes from 13M to 1.2B parameters, across two corpora and multiple benchmarks.

survey_notes: Data-constrained regime evidence: when data rather than compute binds, recursion beats both adding parameters (overfits) and adding epochs at roughly matched FLOPs. This reconciles with Iso-Depth (2604.21106), which is data-abundant (FineWeb-Edu, tokens grow with compute) and finds looping loses at matched FLOPs: the sign of the looping effect depends on whether data is limited. Same direction as Ouro's 'data-constrained era' motivation and Parcae's iso-param results. Compare with Looped GPT-BERT (2609.09691) in the same BabyLM setting.

title: Beyond What Seems Necessary: Hidden Gains from Scaling Training-Time Reasoning Length under Outcome Supervision
relevance_reason: Theory plus a synthetic looped-Transformer experiment showing OOD accuracy keeps improving with training-time loop count after ID saturates; the other half is RL token budgets.
one_sentence: Shows theoretically and empirically that under outcome-only supervision OOD performance can keep improving as training-time reasoning length (loop count or RL token budget) grows after ID accuracy saturates; looped single-block Transformers on 4-hop induction gain OOD up to ~44 loops.
key_contributions: Theory: self-iteration strengthens inductive bias and, with regularization, reduces reliance on ID-only shortcuts as iterations grow.
Looped one-block Transformer on p-hop induction (p=4): ID saturates near 100% by ~2 loops while OOD keeps rising up to ~44 loops (robust to loop embeddings, ~36 loops).
Parallel finding for RL token budgets on math: OOD gains continue past the budget where ID saturates.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: synthetic 4-hop induction sequences (vocab 4, length 12), 20,000 steps, batch 256
setup.loops_train: k in {1,2,4,...,48}, each model trained and evaluated at its k
setup.baselines: same looped model at fewer loops
setup.benchmarks: ID vs OOD validation accuracy on p-hop induction (split by hop-index parity); math RL benchmarks

claims.claim: With parameters and data fixed, increasing training-time loop count keeps improving OOD accuracy long after ID accuracy saturates.
claims.evidence_quote: Increasing the loop count yields OOD gains up to around 44 loops, while ID accuracy saturates near 100% by around 2 loops.

claims.claim: The OOD gains from more loops persist when explicit loop-index embeddings are added, peaking around 36 loops.
claims.evidence_quote: ID accuracy saturates around 2 loops, while OOD accuracy continues improving up to around 36 loops.

claims.claim: Under outcome-only supervision, OOD robustness may require a larger reasoning-length budget than ID validation alone indicates.
claims.evidence_quote: This suggests that robustness may require a larger budget than ID validation alone would indicate.

numbers.what: loop counts swept
numbers.quote: To scale latent reasoning depth, the backbone is applied repeatedly for k ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 24, 28, 32, 36, 40, 44, 48} loops, with parameters shared across loops.

numbers.what: model size
numbers.quote: We use model dimension 256, with 8 attention heads and MLP hidden dimension 512.

numbers.what: task
numbers.quote: In our experiments, we set p = 4, the vocabulary size to 4, and the sequence length to 12.

limitations: Looped evidence is a single tiny synthetic task; OOD is defined by hop-index parity rather than longer horizons or depth extrapolation; each loop count is trained separately, so no test-time extrapolation is studied.
survey_notes: Supports 'more training-time depth helps generalization beyond what ID metrics show' but only on a synthetic task at iso_param (FLOPs grow with loops). Not evidence about test-time extrapolation beyond the trained horizon. Contrasts with LM-scale findings where loops beyond 2-4 regress under FLOP matching (SMELT 2609.01343, LoopCoder-v2 2606.18023): different regime (iso_param, synthetic, no FLOP matching).

title: Evaluating Tiny Recursive Models Across Training for Code Generation
relevance_reason: Autoregressive Tiny Recursive Model (shared 2-layer block, effective depth 20) for NL-to-Python, compared with iso-parameter and iso-depth Transformer controls across training.
one_sentence: A ~28M TRM-AR (2-layer block reused to effective depth 20) beats an iso-parameter 2-layer Transformer on fit and generated-code quality, but loses to an iso-depth 20-layer Transformer at its validation optimum; its edge is resistance to overfitting, at ~175x per-step cost.
key_contributions: Crossover-curve evaluation of teacher-forced fit vs free-running generation across 40 epochs and 3 seeds with iso-parameter and iso-depth controls.
At equal parameters TRM-AR recovers ~45% of the validation-loss gap and ~57% of the generation-quality gap between the two controls.
At equal effective depth the larger plain Transformer fits and generates better; recursion is parameter-efficient but not compute-efficient.

setup.model_sizes: ~28M parameters; vanilla-2L (iso-param) and vanilla-20L (iso-depth, 1.68x total, ~10x non-embedding params)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: tiny-codes corpus (NL-to-Python), 40 epochs

claims.evidence_quote: However, at equal effective depth, the larger transformer fits and generates better at its validation optimum, suggesting TRM-AR’s advantage lies in resistance to overfitting, not greater capability.

claims.claim: Recursion is parameter-efficient but not compute-efficient: per-step time is ~175x the iso-parameter control and ~2.4x the iso-depth control.
claims.evidence_quote: Realizing an effective depth of 20 by looping a two-layer block costs roughly 175× the per-step time of the iso-parameter control and about 2.4× that of the iso-depth control

numbers.quote: at roughly 175× the per-step cost of the parameter-matched control.

numbers.quote: vanilla-20L (iso-depth control): twenty independent layers, matching TRM-AR’s effective depth of 20 at 1.68× the total, or ≈ 10× the non-embedding, parameters [37].

Shows ranking flips across checkpoints, a methodological warning for single-checkpoint claims. Attributes the iso-param advantage to implicit regularization under limited data, consistent with RecursiveGPT (2608.26973).

title: LatentMT: Machine Translation with Latent Reasoning

key_contributions: First systematic study of looped LMs for MT across 32 directions (high, mid, low resource) with swappable LoRA adapters on one frozen looped backbone.
Recurrent-depth sweep with early exit disabled: large gain from u=1 to u=2, then saturation; hidden-state differences shrink across steps.
Same-protocol comparison against Qwen3-8B SFT, plus comparisons to specialized MT systems.
