limitations: Linear attention, realizable linear regression, isotropic-scaled covariances in experiments; robustness theorem needs right-spread-out training distributions.
survey_notes: Gives a theoretical reason for the OOD robustness of looped ICL observed empirically in 2311.12424: weight tying constrains the global minimizer to a single iterative update that extrapolates, while untied layers can overfit to training covariances. Also supports looped models for early exit (monotone loss). Uses iso-effective-depth comparisons (L loops vs L layers), so looped models have 1/L the parameters.

title: ALTA: Compiler-Based Analysis of Transformers
relevance_reason: Compiler from programs with loops to weight-shared / Universal Transformers; constructive length-invariant algorithms plus learnability analysis of looped models.
one_sentence: Introduces ALTA, a RASP-like language with loops that compiles to weight-shared/Universal Transformer encoders, constructing length-invariant parity and addition and a 100% SCAN solver, and shows end-to-end training fails to find these sequential algorithms even when expressible, preferring fewest-layer solutions.
key_contributions: ALTA language, interpreter and compiler to Transformers with layer-wise weight sharing and dynamic halting (Universal Transformers), with sparse MLP transition rules.

Constructive results: a weight-shared encoder with relative positions computes parity for any length with finite parameters; addition of unbounded integers in N+2 layers; SUBLEQ interpreter; SCAN shift-reduce parser at 100% accuracy (up to 512 layers).

Learnability tools: trace supervision and program minimality w.r.t. a training set; end-to-end trained models mimic the shallow Sum+Modulo parity program and deeper models (to 256+256 layers) do not improve SCAN generalization.

setup.model_sizes: Compiled models; SCAN model needs fewer than 2,000 MLP hidden dimensions; trained variants up to 256 encoder + 256 decoder layers
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Parity (train length <= 20, test 21-40), addition, SCAN splits
setup.loops_train: Layers = loop iterations of compiled program; dynamic halting for addition
setup.loops_test: N+2 layers for N-digit addition; up to 512 layers for SCAN
setup.baselines: End-to-end trained transformers with and without weight sharing; trace-supervised models
setup.benchmarks: Parity, multi-digit addition, SUBLEQ, SCAN (length and MCD splits)

claims.claim: Simulation: weight-shared / Universal Transformer encoders can express length-invariant algorithms for parity and addition and solve SCAN without scratchpad decoding.
claims.evidence_quote: ALTA allows us to constructively show how Transformers can represent length-invariant algorithms for computing parity and addition, as well as a solution to the SCAN benchmark of compositional generalization tasks, without requiring intermediate scratchpad decoding steps.

claims.claim: Resource bound: the compiled addition program needs N+2 layers (loop iterations) for N-digit inputs, and its minimal version trained on <=3-digit data generalizes to unbounded lengths.
claims.evidence_quote: The number of layers required to compute the sum is N + 2, where N is the number of digits in the larger of the two inputs.

claims.claim: Learnability gap: end-to-end trained weight-shared transformers behave like the shallow Sum+Modulo parity program (no generalization to more ones than seen), not the length-invariant sequential program, despite it being expressible.
claims.evidence_quote: However, in practice, all variants exhibit behavior similar to that of the minimal Sum + Modulo program, i.e., they exhibit some degree of length generalization but do not generalize to examples with more ones than were seen during training.

claims.claim: More layers do not help end-to-end SCAN generalization even up to 256 encoder and 256 decoder layers.
claims.evidence_quote: However, all generalize poorly on the test splits, and increasing the number of layers does not improve generalization.

numbers.what: Rule counts of minimal parity programs (Sequential Relative vs Sum+Modulo)
numbers.quote: While the minimal Sequential (Relative) program contains 7 rules and the minimal Sum + Modulo program contains 31 rules, our results show that end-to-end model behavior is more consistent with the Sum + Modulo program.

numbers.what: SCAN compiled model size
numbers.value: < 2,000 MLP hidden dims; up to 512 layers
numbers.quote: Because our ALTA program decomposes the task into many small steps, it can require up to 512 layers to handle the longest SCAN examples.

limitations: Limited numeric computation and no probabilistic outputs; compiled models may not reflect learned ones; encoder-only focus.
venue: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (2/2025)
survey_notes: Key 'expressible is not learned' evidence for looped models: the sequential length-invariant solution exists in a weight-shared encoder but end-to-end training picks the fewest-layer shortcut. Agrees with 2607.20594 (training selects mechanism, not expressivity) though the selected mechanism differs (ALTA: shallowest; 2607.20594: serial frontier priced by budget). Trace (step-level) supervision recovers the minimal program behaviour, contrasting with 2603.21676 where per-step supervision harmed extrapolation (different supervision target: full program trace vs final-answer readout at each step).

title: Bypassing the Exponential Dependency: Looped Transformers Efficiently Learn In-context by Multi-step Gradient Descent
relevance_reason: Construction showing a linear looped transformer performs T steps of gradient descent in-context with error exp(-T/(2 kappa)), removing an exponential sample requirement.
one_sentence: Shows a linear looped transformer can explicitly run multi-step gradient descent in its hidden state for in-context linear vector generation, with error at most |alpha| exp(-T/(2 kappa)) after T loops, so O(d) well-conditioned examples suffice instead of exp(Omega(T)).
key_contributions: Lemma 4.1 / Theorem 4.2: each loop of a linear looped transformer implements one GD step on the in-context least-squares objective.

Theorem 4.5: prediction error <= |alpha| * exp(-T/(2 kappa)); with constant condition number (n = O(d)) the error decays exponentially in loops, bypassing the n = exp(Omega(T)) requirement of prior work.
Numerical check of GD convergence rates for d=4, n in {16,...,128} against the bound.

setup.model_sizes: Linear looped transformer (constructed weights Q, P)
setup.baselines: Prior bound of Gatmiry et al. 2024 requiring exp(Omega(T)) examples
setup.benchmarks: Synthetic linear vector generation / regression, d=4

claims.claim: Optimization/simulation: linear looped transformers implement multi-step GD in-context with error decaying exponentially in loop count when the data are well-conditioned (n = O(d)).
claims.evidence_quote: Our results demonstrate that as long as the input data has a constant condition number, e.g., n = O(d), the linear looped Transformers can achieve a small error by multi-step gradient descent during in-context learning.

claims.claim: Resource bound: after T loops the prediction error is at most |alpha| exp(-T/(2 kappa)) where kappa is the condition number of X^T X.
claims.evidence_quote: the linear looped Transformer can predict a vector output with error ≤ |α| · exp(− 2κ ) by explicitly performing multi-step gradient descent in its hidden states.

claims.claim: Prior results needed an exponential number of in-context examples in the loop count; this work removes that dependency.
claims.evidence_quote: However, their theoretical results require an exponential number of in-context examples, n = exp(Ω(T )), where T is the number of loops or passes, to achieve a reasonably low error.

numbers.what: Average condition numbers for n=16,32,64,128 at d=4
numbers.quote: The average κ values for the different sample sizes are {4.57, 3.13, 2.07, 1.62}, corresponding to n = {16, 32, 64, 128} respectively.

limitations: Linear attention, constructed (not trained) weights; 'experiments' run plain gradient descent rather than a trained transformer, so they validate the GD bound, not learnability.
survey_notes: Expressivity-side complement to the learnability result of 2410.08292 (theory_a): once loops implement GD, accuracy is bought by loops at rate exp(-T/2kappa); 2410.21698 shows the kappa dependence is necessary in depth (log kappa lower bound with stronger algorithms, sqrt kappa restricted). Note the experiments do not train any transformer.

title: Transformers discover an elementary calculation system exploiting local attention and grid-like problem representation
relevance_reason: Universal (weight-shared, recurrent) transformer with local attention on a grid and learned halting for multi-digit addition extrapolation; small task-specific model.
one_sentence: A Universal Transformer with local (convolution-like) attention over a learned grid layout of the input and PonderNet-style halting learns multi-digit, multi-operand addition and extrapolates from 10-digit training operands to hundreds or thousands of digits, though extrapolation in number of operands is weaker.
key_contributions: Architecture: Seq2Grid preprocessing into a 2D grid, local attention heads, recurrent (weight-shared) Universal Transformer core and a halting transformer with an Explore-Reinforce regularizer.
Extrapolation: trained on up to 4 operands of up to 10 digits, reaches 0.99 sequence accuracy on 2-term 602-digit additions (noGroups variant) and 0.93 on 5-6 terms.
Ablations: a fixed 12-step variant degrades operand-count extrapolation; learned halting stabilizes in steps even when more terms need more computation; failures on long carries.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: Multi-digit addition problems with up to 4 operands, each up to 10 digits
setup.loops_train: Dynamic halting (PonderNet-style); fixedTime variant uses 12 recurrent steps
setup.baselines: Variants: noGroups, SASA local attention, fixedTime (12 steps), PonderNet KL regularization; prior Grid LSTM / Neural GPU results
setup.benchmarks: Addition with extrapolation in number of digits (15 to 4000) and number of operands (5 to 10)

claims.claim: Universal transformers with local attention and adaptive halting learn multi-digit addition and extrapolate outside the training distribution, discovering place-value alignment.
claims.evidence_quote: Here we show that universal transformers equipped with local attention and adaptive halting mechanisms can learn to exploit an external, grid-like memory to carry out multi-digit addition.

claims.claim: Fixing the number of recurrent steps (12, no halting) degrades extrapolation over number of operands relative to learned halting.
claims.evidence_quote: On the tasks requiring extrapolation over the number of terms Π([5, 6], [1, 10]) and Π([7, 10], [1, 10]), the original SASA variant is outperformed by our base model, and fixing the number of recurrent steps further degrades performances.

claims.claim: Perfect extrapolation on both digits and operands never happens; learned halting steps plateau as the number of terms grows, correlating with accuracy drops.
claims.evidence_quote: These results confirm that perfect extrapolation on both #digits and #terms never happens, and model components seem to specialize in tackling one of these two degrees of freedom.

numbers.what: Training distribution
numbers.value: up to 4 operands, up to 10 digits
numbers.quote: The model is trained on a set of multi-digit addition problems consisting of up to 4 operands, each composed by up to 10 digits

numbers.what: noGroups variant on 2-term additions with [2000,2000] and [4000,4000] digits (char / seq accuracy)
Base model on N-term 5-digit additions (Table IV right): seq accuracy for 5..10 terms

limitations: Task-specific architecture (grid preprocessing, local attention); failures on long carry chains and many operands; results depend on lucky initializations for some variants.
survey_notes: Early example (2022) that recurrent depth plus learned halting can give large length extrapolation in arithmetic, but with strong locality priors (cf. 2602.01651's locality postulate and 2607.20594's observation that conv locality protects frontiers). Learned halting plateauing on harder inputs mirrors 2603.21676's ACT saturation finding.

title: Graph Hierarchical Recurrence for Long-Range Generalization
relevance_reason: Weight-shared two-level (fine graph + coarsened graph) recurrence for GNNs, HRM-inspired; graph modality, not a looped LM.
one_sentence: GHR couples a weight-shared recurrent update on the input graph with message passing on a pooled coarse graph (nested two-level recurrence inspired by HRM), improving out-of-range generalization where test interactions span longer distances than training.
key_contributions: Formalizes in-range vs out-of-range (OOR) generalization by interaction distance for graph models.
GHR: global recurrent step with nested low/high-level recurrences, input features injected each iteration; augments any message-passing backbone.
Strong OOR gains on synthetic SSSP/eccentricity/diameter and competitive results on long-range benchmarks.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: Synthetic graph tasks (RGG-SSSP, ECHO-Synth) and long-range graph benchmarks
setup.loops_train: T_L low-level and T_H high-level iterations (e.g. T_L=4, T_H=3)
setup.loops_test: Same, or unrolled for more iterations
setup.baselines: A-DGN, DRew, GPS, GRIT, RecurrentGIN
setup.benchmarks: ECHO-Synth sssp/ecc/diam, RGG-SSSP, long-range graph benchmarks

claims.claim: Existing graph models degrade sharply out-of-range while GHR consistently strengthens every tested message-passing backbone, with the largest gains out-of-range.
claims.evidence_quote: Despite its minimal design, GHR consistently strengthens every tested messagepassing backbone, yielding robust performance on long-range dependencies and particularly pronounced gains in out-of-range regimes.

numbers.what: ECHO-Synth SSSP IR/OOR MAE rows for A-DGN, DRew, GPS, GRIT, GHR-GINE (Table 2); GPS OOR 7.101 vs GHR-GINE OOR 0.226

survey_notes: Graph-domain analog of hierarchical multi-timescale looping (HRM lineage); out-of-range generalization relates to depth extrapolation in looped transformers. Belongs in the beyond-language section rather than theory.

title: Logical Characterizations of Recurrent Graph Neural Networks with Reals and Floats
relevance_reason: Exact expressivity of recurrent (weight-shared, self-terminating) GNNs under float vs real arithmetic; graph analog of looped-model precision results.
one_sentence: Gives exact logical characterizations of recurrent GNNs that iterate a shared layer until designated termination features fire: with floats they equal the graded modal substitution calculus (GMSC), with reals an infinitary graded modal logic, and both coincide on MSO-definable properties.
key_contributions: Recurrent GNNs with floats = GMSC = R-simple aggregate-combine float GNNs (Theorem 3.2), an absolute characterization under natural float assumptions.
Recurrent GNNs with reals = omega-GML (infinitary graded modal logic).
Relative to MSO-definable properties, float and real recurrent GNNs are equally expressive; in general floats are weaker; links to distributed automata.

setup.loops_test: Iterate until termination signalled by designated feature vectors

claims.claim: Exact characterization: recurrent GNNs with floating-point numbers match a rule-based modal logic with counting; with reals, an infinitary modal logic with counting.
claims.evidence_quote: For floats, the formalism matching recurrent GNNs is a rule-based modal logic with counting, while for reals we use a suitable infinitary modal logic, also with counting.

claims.claim: Precision matters in general but not for MSO-definable properties: float and real recurrent GNNs coincide there, while floats are weaker in general.
claims.evidence_quote: This implies that recurrent GNNs with reals and floats have the same expressive power over MSO-definable properties

limitations: Graph neural networks rather than transformers; expressivity only.
survey_notes: Parallel to the precision theme in looped-transformer theory (2605.30523: constant precision gives AC^d, growing gives TC^d; 2605.10878: fixed precision is essential). Peripheral; cite in a precision remark.

title: Attending to Mathematical Language with Transformers
relevance_reason: Early comparison of Transformer, Universal Transformer and UT with ACT on character-level evaluation of math expressions; small-scale, in-distribution.
one_sentence: Trains a standard Transformer, a Universal Transformer and an adaptive (ACT) Universal Transformer with common hyperparameters on about 12 million generated arithmetic expressions with symbolic variables, reporting test accuracies of 76.1%, 78.8% and 84.9%.
key_contributions: Character-level sequence-transduction dataset of arithmetic expressions with symbolic variable assignments.
Recurrent depth (UT) improves asymmetric subtraction and multiplication; adding ACT gives the best overall accuracy.
Errors concentrate in middle output digits, differing by one or two characters.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: About 12 million unique generated expression samples
setup.loops_train: UT recurrence; ACT halting in the adaptive variant
setup.baselines: Standard Transformer with the same hyperparameters
setup.benchmarks: Test accuracy on generated expressions (in-distribution)

claims.claim: Under common hyperparameters, recurrence and ACT raise test accuracy from 76.1% (Transformer) to 78.8% (UT) and 84.9% (adaptive UT).
claims.regime: iso_data (same hyperparameters; parameter and compute matching not stated)
claims.evidence_quote: The models respectively achieved test accuracies as high as 76.1%, 78.8% and 84.9% in evaluating the expressions to match the target values.

numbers.what: Test accuracy: Transformer / UT / adaptive UT
numbers.quote: The models respectively achieved test accuracies as high as 76.1%, 78.8% and 84.9% in evaluating the expressions to match the target values.

limitations: No length extrapolation tested; parameter counts and compute not reported; single dataset.
survey_notes: Historical datapoint only (2018); in-distribution gains, regime not controlled. Contrasts with later findings that ACT halting fails to extrapolate (2603.21676, 2508.16745).

title: Rethinking Deep Thinking: Stable Learning of Algorithms using Lipschitz Constraints
relevance_reason: Recurrent (weight-tied) Deep Thinking networks with Lipschitz constraints giving convergence guarantees and stable extrapolation (abstract only).
one_sentence: Analyzes growth of intermediate representations in recurrent Deep Thinking networks and constrains the recurrent map to be Lipschitz (DT-L), giving fewer parameters, more reliable training, and a guarantee of convergence to a unique solution at inference; extrapolates to harder problems including TSP.
key_contributions: Diagnoses DT training instability via growth of intermediate representations.
DT-L: Lipschitz-constrained recurrence with guaranteed convergence of the learned iteration to a unique fixed point.
Robust extrapolation to harder instances and learning on TSP where DT fails.

setup.baselines: Deep Thinking (DT) networks
setup.benchmarks: Easy-to-hard algorithmic tasks; traveling salesperson problem

claims.claim: Lipschitz constraints on the recurrent block give guaranteed convergence of the learned iterative procedure to a unique solution at inference time.
claims.evidence_quote: Additionally our DT-L formulation provides guarantees of convergence of the learned iterative procedure to a unique solution at inference time.

claims.claim: DT-L learns algorithms that extrapolate to harder problems with fewer parameters and more reliability than DT, and learns TSP where DT fails.
claims.evidence_quote: We demonstrate DT-L is capable of robustly learning algorithms which extrapolate to harder problems than in the training set.

survey_notes: Abstract only (full text unavailable). Stability/contractivity route to extrapolation, complementary to input injection and progressive loss (2202.05826) and to the state-degradation failure analysis in 2609.33144. Fixed-point guarantee contrasts with overthinking reported for unconstrained loops (2604.07822, 2607.20594).

title: Recurrent Convolutional Neural Networks Learn Succinct Learning Algorithms
relevance_reason: Learnability theory for networks with recurrent (cross-layer) plus convolutional weight sharing; constant parameter count with huge unrolled depth (abstract only).
one_sentence: Exhibits a recurrent-convolutional architecture with a constant number of parameters that, trained in polynomial time, learns as well as any efficient learning algorithm describable by a constant-size program (e.g. matching Gaussian elimination on parity).
key_contributions: Learnability: an RCNN learns in polynomial time as well as any efficient learning algorithm with a constant-size description.
Parity: matches Gaussian elimination, a problem hard for standard networks.
Recurrent plus convolutional weight sharing reduces parameters to a constant while the unrolled network may have trillions of nodes.

setup.model_sizes: Constant parameter count; unrolled network may have trillions of nodes

claims.claim: Learnability: a network combining recurrent weight sharing across layers with convolutional weight sharing learns, in polynomial time, as well as any efficient learning algorithm describable by a constant-sized program.
claims.evidence_quote: We exhibit a NN architecture that, in polynomial time, learns as well as any efficient learning algorithm describable by a constant-sized program.

claims.claim: The constants in the analysis are too large to be practically meaningful.
claims.evidence_quote: While in practice the constants in our analysis are too large to be directly meaningful, our work suggests that the synergy of Recurrent and Convolutional NNs (RCNNs) may be more natural and powerful than either alone

limitations: Constants too large to be meaningful in practice (per abstract).
survey_notes: Abstract only (full text unavailable). One of the few learnability (not just expressivity) results for weight-tied depth: parameter-count-constant recurrence learns succinct algorithms like parity. Complements 2606.00605 (GD on looped LN transformer learns power method) and 2605.10878 (weight norm of looped nets ~ Kolmogorov complexity).

title: The Exact Expressive Power of Fixed-Precision Looped Padded Transformers
relevance_reason: Title-only entry (no arXiv id, abstract or full text available); title indicates exact expressivity of fixed-precision looped padded transformers.
one_sentence: No text available; only the title is known, so no claims are extracted.
survey_notes: Title-only; corpus sources list it as citing 2301.13196, 2502.17416 and others. Lead author should locate the arXiv id before citing. Likely related to the constant-precision AC^d result in 2605.30523 (which characterizes constant-precision looped padded transformers as FO-uniform AC^d); do not assume they are the same paper.

title: Context-free Recognition with Transformers
relevance_reason: Proves log-looped padded transformers recognize all CFLs with explicit padding/looping bounds; small iso-parameter experiments with looped vs fixed-depth models.
one_sentence: Shows O(log N)-looped AHATs with O(N^6) padding recognize every context-free language, unambiguous CFLs need O(N^3) padding with O(log^2 N) loops, unambiguous linear CFLs O(N^2) padding with O(log N) loops, and postfix Boolean formulas need no padding; small looped models modestly beat fixed-depth ones.
key_contributions: CFL is contained in log-looped, N^6-padded AHATs (Theorem 3.1) via a parallel item-based parsing algorithm with logarithmic alternating depth.

Resource trade-offs by grammar class: UCFL with O(N^3) padding and O(log^2 N) looping (Theorem 4.1); unambiguous linear CFL with O(N^2) padding and O(log N) looping (Theorem 4.2); BFVP with log looping and no padding (Corollary 4.1).
Experiments at a 1.2M parameter budget: log(N)-looped (and padded) transformers outperform fixed-depth ones by up to 8 points on postfix BFVP, with smaller or no gains elsewhere.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: 1 million samples with string length at most 50; test 2000 samples up to length 500

setup.benchmarks: Balanced counting, Dyck(1), Dyck(2), Palindrome, BFVP infix and postfix

claims.evidence_quote: In this work, we show that looped transformers with O(log(N )) looping layers and O(N 6 ) padding symbols can recognize all CFLs.

claims.claim: Grammar structure trades padding for looping: unambiguous CFLs need only O(N^3) padding but O(log^2 N) looping; unambiguous linear CFLs need O(N^2) padding and O(log N) looping.
claims.evidence_quote: In this section, we show that UCFLs can be recognized by transformers with less padding than arbitrary CFLs if slightly more depth overhead is allowed:

claims.claim: Unpadded log-looped transformers can evaluate any Boolean formula in postfix notation.
claims.evidence_quote: We have proven (Cor. 4.1) that logdepth and no padding suffice to recognize this language in postfix notation with causally-masked transformers.

claims.claim: Empirically, at equal parameters, looping (and padding) gives moderate gains over fixed depth, largest (+8 points) on postfix BFVP as predicted; negligible on Dyck(1), and looping alone slightly hurts infix BFVP.
claims.evidence_quote: Overall, we find that looping and padding offer moderate performance gains over fixed-depth transformers on a range of CFLs, with the largest gains on the theoretically motivated postfix BFVP language.

title: When and How Unlabeled Data Provably Improve In-Context Learning
relevance_reason: Theory shows multi-layer or looped linear attention implements EM-like polynomial estimators for semi-supervised ICL; the application loops a tabular foundation model at the prompt level, not in depth.
one_sentence: For semi-supervised in-context classification of binary GMMs, proves one-layer linear attention cannot use unlabeled demonstrations while L-layer or looped linear attention implements polynomial (EM-like) estimators sum_i a_i (X^T X)^i X^T y with degree up to O(3^L); looping TabPFN-v2 over pseudo-labels improves few-shot tabular accuracy.
key_contributions: Landscape result: the global minimum of one-layer linear attention under SS-ICL is the plug-in estimator X^T y, so it ignores unlabeled data (Theorem 1).

Depth/looping: L-layer linear attention expresses label-propagation products prod(I + c_l X^T X) or feature-propagation (X^T X)^{3^{L-1}-1}; a single layer looped L times reproduces label propagation (Proposition 2); L>=2 approaches Bayes error as n grows (Theorems 3-4).
LoopTabFM: iteratively pseudo-labeling and re-prompting TabPFN-v2 improves accuracy on most OpenML binary datasets with 10 labeled + 10 unlabeled examples; most gains in the first two iterations.

setup.model_sizes: Linear attention (theory, synthetic experiments with 1-5 layers); TabPFN-v2 (application)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Synthetic binary GMM prompts with partially missing labels; OpenML binary classification datasets
setup.loops_train: L layers or a single layer looped L times
setup.loops_test: Loop-0 to Loop-5 TabPFN pseudo-label iterations
setup.baselines: One-layer linear attention / plug-in estimator; single-pass TabPFN-v2 (Loop-0)
setup.benchmarks: Semi-supervised ICL classification error; OpenML tabular test accuracy (100 random splits)

claims.claim: Separation: one-layer linear attention recovers the optimal supervised estimator but cannot exploit unlabeled data; multilayer or looped transformers can, via implicit polynomial estimators.
claims.evidence_quote: The loss landscape of one-layer linear attention models recover the optimal fully-supervised estimator but completely fail to exploit unlabeled data; (2) In contrast, multilayer or looped transformers can effectively leverage unlabeled data

claims.claim: Resource bound: the leading polynomial power is exponential in depth (K = O(3^L)), so logarithmic depth or looping suffices; each layer mirrors an EM pseudo-labeling step.
claims.evidence_quote: Importantly, the leading polynomial power is exponential in depth, so mild amount of depth/looping suffices.

claims.claim: A single linear attention layer looped L times reproduces the multi-layer label-propagation estimator with equal constants.
claims.evidence_quote: There exists a single-layer linear attention model whose parameters can be constructed such that, when looped L times, its output reproduces that of (11), with cℓ ≡ c′ for some arbitrary constant c′ .

claims.claim: Prompt-level looping of TabPFN-v2 with pseudo-labels improves few-shot accuracy on several datasets by over 10% relative but hurts on some (31, 40900).
claims.evidence_quote: For instance, on OpenML datasets 1049, 1464, 40701, and 40983, accuracy improves by more than 10% over the baseline using only 10 additional unlabeled samples.

numbers.what: Labeled/unlabeled examples in LoopTabFM evaluation
numbers.quote: For each experiment, we randomly sample 10 labeled and 10 unlabeled examples, ensuring that the labeled set includes at least one example from each class.

numbers.what: Max polynomial degree expressible by L layers or loops
numbers.quote: Crucially, an L-layer (or looped) attention can express up to K = O(3L ) powers, highlighting that logarithmic depth suffices to represent high-degree monomials.

limitations: Linear attention and GMM setting; constructions rather than training dynamics for depth >1; tabular gains inconsistent across datasets; LoopTabFM is prompt-level iteration not depth looping.
survey_notes: Adds 'looped linear attention = EM / power-series estimator' to the looped-as-iterative-algorithm section, alongside power method (2606.00605), multi-step GD (2410.08292, 2410.11268) and Chebyshev iteration (2410.21698). Exponential-in-depth polynomial degree parallels the log(kappa) depth bounds of 2410.21698. LoopTabFM is not depth recurrence; do not count it as looped-model evidence.

title: When Does Recurrence Become an Algorithm? Convergence Selection in Weight-Tied Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Controlled population study of what algorithm SGD selects in weight-tied looped transformers, with tied vs untied controls at fixed effective depth and parameter count.
one_sentence: Weight-tied looped transformers trained on group word problems learn a serial 'linear computation frontier' whose speed equals training demand n/T (budget law); weight tying, not expressivity, selects it over parallel scans, and S5's learning wall is operator size, not NC1-hardness.
key_contributions: Budget law: frontier speed v tracks n_tr/T_tr with exponent 0.98+-0.04 (R^2=0.99, 23 models); extra test-time loops rescue late positions at fixed length; implies a halting rule T*=ceil(n/v).

Selection not expressivity: at fixed effective depth 12 with matched parameters, untying hurts extrapolation (S4) and blocks learning (A5, G>=3 groups); A5 (NC1-complete) is learned while S5 deadlocks until an operator-first curriculum.

Tail-saturation proposition: skip/similarity metrics are blind at fixed points; head instrument tau(n,i) (convergence-time scaling) predicts seed-level OOD generalization; replicates on easy-to-hard prefix sums with 4x extrapolation.

setup.model_sizes: Blocks of 2 or 4 pre-norm layers; S (2L, d=128), M (2L, d=256), L (4L, d=512); claims at <= 25M parameters
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Synthetic per-position tasks: prefix parity, increment-with-carry, prefix products over Z60, S4, A5, S5; easy-to-hard prefix sums (32-bit train)
setup.loops_train: T = ceil(log2 n)+3 (jittered), fixed T, or T proportional to n (T=2n, n, n/2, n/4); streaming T=n+2
setup.loops_test: Swept up to 48 loops; rule T*=ceil(n/v)
setup.baselines: Tying-degree ladder G in {1,2,3,4,6,12} at fixed effective depth 12, constant-width and parameter-matched; Deep Thinking conv nets (reported)
setup.benchmarks: Group word problems, parity, prefix sums (Schwarzschild et al. 2021)

claims.claim: Budget law: free training installs a linear frontier solving v positions per loop with v approximately n_tr/T_tr, exactly 1 under T=n training.
claims.evidence_quote: free training installs a linear computation frontier, a mechanism that solves v positions per loop, and prices its speed by the training contract: v ≈ ntr /Ttr , exactly unity under T =n training

claims.claim: At fixed effective depth 12 with parameters matched, the fully untied model is worst at length extrapolation and, on A5, untied/partially tied configurations with G>=3 fail to learn, while tied ones learn; with constant width (more params) untying looks mildly beneficial.
claims.regime: iso_param and iso_effective_depth (param-matched arm); iso_effective_depth only (constant-width arm)
claims.evidence_quote: with free parameters, untying appears mildly beneficial; with parameters matched, the fully untied model is worst at length extrapolation, and on A5 every configuration with G ≥ 3 fails to learn the task at all (9/9 seeds) while tied configurations learn it.

claims.claim: Learning walls track operator size, not circuit class: NC1-complete A5 generalizes, S5 deadlocks under the standard curriculum, and an operator-first curriculum cracks S5 in 10/10 seeds.
claims.evidence_quote: an operator-first curriculum—an extended n=2 stage that masters the composition table before any chaining—cracks S5 in every seed attempted (10/10 across two machines, exact match ≥ 0.92 at 2× training length).

claims.claim: Standard instruments (skip tolerance, cross-step similarity, attribution) are provably blind once loops converge to a fixed point; only head-of-trajectory measurements identify the algorithm.
claims.evidence_quote: any loop-mechanism claim based on skip tolerance, cross-step similarity, or shared-dictionary attribution is uninformative unless the measurement is localized to the head of the trajectory

claims.claim: On the open prefix-sums benchmark, looped transformers extrapolate to 4x training length but break between 128 and 256 bits, short of convolutional Deep Thinking nets' 512-bit extrapolation.
claims.evidence_quote: The frontier breaks between 128 and 256 bits (Table 9), well short of the 512-bit extrapolation that convolutional Deep Thinking networks achieve on this dataset (Bansal et al., 2022)

numbers.what: Budget law fit
numbers.quote: the measured v tracks ntr /Ttr with a power-law exponent of 0.98±0.04 (95% CI; R2 =0.99 over 23 models at 8 demand levels; Fig. 6, left)

numbers.what: A5 from-scratch seed lottery
numbers.value: roughly a third of 22 seeds crack chained A5
numbers.quote: across 22 seeds on two machines, roughly a third crack chained A5 ; the rest never pass the second position—a bimodal outcome stable across hardware and run order

numbers.what: Population spread in length generalization across 64 looped models
numbers.quote: the population spans length generalization 0.00–1.00, including a 0.10–0.95 spread across seeds of a single recipe.

numbers.what: Table 6 S4 per-token accuracy at n=64 for G=1,2,3,4,6,12 (const. width / param-matched pairs); G=1 tied 0.21/0.21, G=12 untied 0.26/0.15
Scale of claims
numbers.quote: Scope. Claims concern what end-to-end training selects in weight-tied loops on per-position algorithmic sequence tasks at ≤ 25M parameters.

limitations: Per-position synthetic tasks only; <= 25M parameters; budget law is an empirical regularity not a theorem; global-attention frontier is length-fragile; strong seed lotteries.
survey_notes: Key bridge between theory and practice: theory says Theta(log n) loops suffice for S5/A5 via scans (Merrill and Sabharwal), but SGD in tied loops picks a serial O(n) frontier, so expressivity results do not predict learned mechanisms. Strong iso-param+iso-effective-depth evidence that tying is an inductive bias that helps extrapolation, but untied with constant width (more params) looks slightly better: regime determines the conclusion. Table 6 numbers are low per-token accuracies at n=64 (2x the training length of 32), so the absolute effect is small; for A5 param-matched, G=2 (0.15) exceeds G=1 (0.10). Overthinking appears only for tight-budget models. The proposition on tail blindness is relevant to mechanistic studies of Huginn/Ouro.

title: Neural Weight Norm = Kolmogorov Complexity
relevance_reason: Theory result stated for looped (iterated-until-halt) fixed-precision networks; concerns weight-decay priors rather than looped LM design.
one_sentence: Proves that for fixed-precision looped networks iterated until a halt channel fires, the minimum number of non-zero parameters (hence any Lp weight norm) needed to output a string equals its Kolmogorov complexity up to a log factor, so weight decay approximates Solomonoff's prior.
key_contributions: Sandwich bound N(s) <= K(s)+c_U and K(s) <= c_d N(s) log N(s) for fixed-precision looped networks (Theorem 4), tight at both ends (permutation witness).
Lp collapse: in fixed precision every Lp^p norm equals the non-zero parameter count up to constants, so the result is norm-agnostic.
Corollary: L2 weight decay induces an output prior matching Solomonoff's universal prior up to a polynomial factor; fixed precision is essential (real weights are super-Turing).

setup.model_sizes: Constant-size universal looped network in fixed precision (ternary, b-bit integer or dyadic weights)
setup.loops_test: Iterate x_{t+1} = f_theta(x_t) until halt channel fires (unbounded)

claims.claim: Simulation/complexity: in fixed precision, the minimum weight norm of a looped network that halts and outputs a binary string equals the string's Kolmogorov complexity up to a logarithmic factor.
claims.evidence_quote: We prove that, in any fixed-precision regime, the smallest weight norm of a looped neural network outputting a binary string equals the Kolmogorov complexity of that string, up to a logarithmic factor.

claims.claim: Fixed precision is necessary: with infinite precision, networks encode non-computable functions and weight norm loses meaning.
claims.evidence_quote: The fixed-precision assumption is essential: with infinite precision, neural networks can encode non-computable functions and the weight norm loses its relevance.

claims.claim: The result concerns minimum-norm networks, not what gradient descent finds, and is not validated experimentally.
claims.evidence_quote: Corollary 7 concerns the induced output prior Q(s), not what gradient descent finds; closing the gap between minimum-norm networks and trained networks is the natural next step. The theorem and its predictions are not validated experimentally.

numbers.what: Sandwich bound (Theorem 4)
numbers.value: N(s) <= K(s)+c_U; K(s) <= c_d N(s) log2 N(s) + c_d
numbers.quote:
N (s) ≤ K(s) + cU ,
(2)
K(s) ≤ cd · N (s) log2 N (s) + cd .

limitations: Asymptotic with large constants; single-string generation from zero state rather than supervised learning; no link to trained networks; no experiments.
survey_notes: Uses looping (iterate-until-halt) as the Turing-complete substrate; relevant to the survey only as a statement that, under fixed precision, parameter count of a looped network is a description-length measure. Its 'looped network' is any iterated feedforward block, not a looped transformer LM. Untested empirically.

title: Emergent Models: Intelligence from Tiny Substrates
relevance_reason: Cellular-automaton substrates iterating a fixed local rule for an adaptive number of steps, trained by evolutionary search; iteration-for-extrapolation lineage, not neural looped models.
one_sentence: Proposes Emergent Models, fixed-rule dynamical substrates (e.g. cellular automata) iterated for an adaptive number of steps and trained by evolutionary search, proves some are latent-universal (any partial computable function via the initial state), and shows tiny instances extrapolate exactly on simple arithmetic.
key_contributions: Latent universality (Theorem 1): with fixed update rule and interface, varying only the finite-support initial program state realizes any partial computable function.
Zoo of minimal EMs (tens to hundreds of parameters) learned by genetic algorithms; perfect extrapolation on all one-input arithmetic tasks tested (train [0,30], test [30,1000]).
Conjecture that adaptive iteration, not a single forward pass, enables extrapolation, governed by the ratio of parameters to temporal depth.

setup.model_sizes: 20-300 parameters
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Integer arithmetic on [0,30]; CartPole; MetaLife control
setup.loops_train: Adaptive (halting condition on substrate state)
setup.benchmarks: Integer functions (e.g. x mod 4, multiplication), CartPole, MetaLife

claims.claim: Universality: some Emergent Models are latent-universal, realizing any partial computable function with the rule and interface fixed and only the initial latent state varied.
claims.evidence_quote: Theoretically, we prove that some EMs are latent-universal: with the update rule and interface held fixed, they can realize any partial computable function by varying only the initial condition of the latent state.

claims.claim: Tiny iterated substrates extrapolate exactly on simple one-input arithmetic functions in all runs.
claims.evidence_quote: Perfect extrapolation is observed, in all runs, for all oneinput tasks considered.

numbers.what: Arithmetic train vs extrapolation ranges
numbers.quote: Training is performed on inputs in [0, 30], while extrapolation is evaluated on [30, 1000].

limitations: Evolutionary search, not gradient training; simple tasks; two-input multiplication and harder tasks largely fail; robustness limitations in control.
survey_notes: Peripheral to looped LMs; shares the thesis that iterating a small fixed rule with adaptive halting drives extrapolation (cf. 2602.01651, 2606.20325). Exclude from quantitative comparisons.

title: Simulation of Graph Algorithms with Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Constructive simulation of classic graph algorithms by constant-width looped transformers with adjacency-aware attention heads.
one_sentence: Proves by construction that a looped transformer with extra adjacency-multiplied attention heads and O(1) width simulates Dijkstra, BFS, DFS and Kosaraju's SCC (and a multitask model) for graphs of any size up to finite-precision limits, is Turing complete with constant width, and that the constructed parameters are hard to recover by training.
key_contributions: Constant-width looped transformers simulate Dijkstra (17 layers, 3 heads), BFS (17 layers), DFS (15 layers), Kosaraju SCC (22 layers, 4 heads); a 19-layer multitask model runs BFS, DFS and Dijkstra.
Parameter count independent of graph size; graph size bounded by O(1/delta_hat) and O(Omega) from finite precision.
Turing completeness with O(1) width via Graph-SUBLEQ (11 layers, 3 heads); ill-conditioning analysis shows constructed solutions are hard to reach by gradient training.

setup.model_sizes: 15-22 layers per loop body, 3-4 heads, O(1) width
setup.benchmarks: CLRS-style algorithms (Dijkstra, BFS, DFS, SCC); training-recovery experiments in Appendix B.4

claims.claim: Simulation: a looped transformer of constant width with adjacency-aware heads simulates Dijkstra's algorithm on rational-weighted graphs up to O(1/delta_hat) nodes.
claims.evidence_quote: There exists a looped-transformer hT in the form of (2), with 17 layers, 3 attention heads, and layer width O(1) that simulates Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm for weighted graphs with rational edge-weights

claims.claim: Parameter count does not grow with graph size, but finite precision limits the simulable graph size.
claims.evidence_quote: The number of parameters in the networks does not increase with the input graph size, which implies that the networks can simulate the above algorithms for any graph. Despite this property, we show a limit to simulation in our solution due to finite precision.

claims.claim: Universality: the architecture is Turing complete with O(1) width via an 11-layer, 3-head SUBLEQ simulation.
claims.evidence_quote: with 11 layers, 3 attention heads, and layer width O(1) that simulates SUBLEQ.

claims.claim: Learnability caveat: constructed parameters require approximating discontinuous functions, causing ill-conditioning that makes gradient-based recovery hard, worsening as tolerances shrink.
claims.evidence_quote: Despite demonstrating the existence of parameters capable of simulation, discovering them through gradient-based training is challenging.

numbers.what: Kosaraju SCC simulator size
numbers.quote: Theorem 6.4. There exists a looped-transformer hT in the form of (2), with 22 layers, 4 attention heads, and layer width O(1) that simulates Kosaraju's Strongly Connected Components algorithm

limitations: Constructive only; requires a non-standard attention head multiplied by the adjacency matrix; finite precision bounds graph size; training to recover the construction is ill-conditioned.
survey_notes: Anchor for 'looped transformers as algorithm executors' (graph section); extended to hypergraphs by 2501.10688. Explicitly flags the expressivity/learnability gap via ill-conditioning, consistent with 2410.18077 and 2607.20594.

title: Transformers Can Do Arithmetic with the Right Embeddings
relevance_reason: Main contribution is a digit positional embedding; looped transformers with input injection are a secondary, controlled ablation for length generalization.
one_sentence: Abacus positional embeddings (per-digit significance) let small transformers trained on 20-digit addition reach up to 99% on 100-digit addition; looped transformers with input injection and progressive loss further cut OOD error at fixed effective depth.
key_contributions: Abacus Embeddings: learned per-digit significance embeddings with random offset, giving 6x length extrapolation on addition (trained <=20 digits, tested to 120).

Controlled recurrence ablation at fixed effective depth 16 (16x1 to 1x16): 8x2 looped model best on OOD addition; looped model with input injection + progressive loss beats standard models with ~10x fewer parameters.
Extends to multiplication (15 digits, looped 4x4) and sorting, where looped models are best only at min-element extrapolation, not full sorting.

setup.model_sizes: 12M (1 layer x 16 recurrences) to 122M (16x1) parameters with Abacus + input injection (Table 3)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 20 million samples per training set; cramming budget of 8 exaFLOP (one RTXA4000, 24 h); 64 exaFLOP for multiplication
setup.loops_train: Effective depth 16 split as 16x1, 8x2, 4x4, 2x8, 1x16; progressive loss mixes nominal and random fewer recurrences
setup.baselines: Standard transformer (ST), ST with input injection, FIRE / NoPE / RoPE embeddings, index hints
setup.benchmarks: Multi-digit addition (ID <=20, OOD <=100, 100+ OOD to 160 digits), subtraction, multiplication up to 15 digits, array sorting

claims.claim: Abacus Embeddings with looped transformers and input injection raise OOD addition accuracy from 92.9% to 99.1% (87% error reduction) relative to the embeddings with standard architectures.
claims.regime: iso_effective_depth (effective depth 16), same data and 8 exaFLOP budget; looped model has fewer parameters
claims.evidence_quote: We show that when we combine Abacus Embeddings with input injection and looped transformers performance further improves, increasing from 92.9% to 99.1% in out of distribution accuracy, an 87% reduction in error

claims.claim: At fixed effective depth 16, an 8-layer block looped twice (8x2) halves the OOD error of the non-recurrent 16x1 model with input injection.
claims.evidence_quote: We see that a recurrent model with eight layers in the recurrent block and two recurrences is the most accurate of all effective depth 16 models, halving the error rate of a standard model with input injection in the OOD evaluation.

claims.claim: With FIRE or NoPE on 40-digit training data, the looped transformer (input injection + progressive loss) has the best OOD addition despite ~10x fewer parameters.
claims.evidence_quote: Despite having approximately 10× fewer parameters than the other models, we see that the looped transformer (recurrent, with input injection and progressive loss), achieves the best out of distribution performance using either position embedding.

claims.claim: Looping does not uniformly help: on sorting, the standard transformer has the best exact-match accuracy, while the looped transformer is best only at identifying the minimum element.
claims.evidence_quote: For sorting, different architectures appear to be better suited to different types of extrapolation, for example the looped transformer is best at extrapolating for finding the minimum element but not for sorting the whole array.

claims.claim: Length generalization reaches 6x the training length (20 to 120 digits), versus 2.5x for prior state of the art.
claims.evidence_quote: models trained with at most 20 digit operands can generalize to problems with 120 digit operands. This represents a state-of-the-art generalization factor of 6×, with the previous state of the art being only 2.5×.

numbers.what: Max OOD addition accuracy at 100 digits, trained on 20 digits, 1 GPU-day
numbers.quote: We find that training on only 20 digit numbers with a single GPU for one day, we can reach state-of-the-art performance, achieving up to 99% accuracy on 100 digit addition problems.

numbers.what: OOD addition accuracy: standard architecture with Abacus vs looped + input injection
numbers.quote: increasing from 92.9% to 99.1% in out of distribution accuracy, an 87% reduction in error compared to using the embeddings with standard architectures alone.

numbers.what: Training budget per addition run
numbers.quote: limit each training run to 8 exaFLOP of compute (a single Nvidia RTXA4000 GPU for 24 hours); for multiplication results we allow 64 exaFLOP (eight Nvidia RTXA4000 GPUs for 24 hours).

numbers.what: Input injection error reduction over Abacus baseline
numbers.quote: We find that incorporating input injection—skip connections inserted between the input layer and each decoder layer—can reduce generalization errors by 50% over the Abacus Embedding baseline.

numbers.what: Training set size
numbers.quote: For this study all training sets have 20 million samples and i = j, hence we can use one number to define the dataset

numbers.what: Total compute for main-paper results
numbers.quote: An estimate of the total compute required for all of the results presented in the main paper is 10, 039 GPU hours.

numbers.what: Parameters by configuration at effective depth 16 (16x1, 8x2, 4x4, 2x8, 1x16)

limitations: No natural-language tasks; compute-constrained from-scratch training; Abacus is absolute-style, so generalization is bounded by the offset range k; looped models not uniformly best (sorting).
venue: 38th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2024).
builds_on: Looped Transformers are Better at Learning Learning Algorithms (2311.12424)
survey_notes: One of the cleanest iso-effective-depth ablations: same effective depth 16, same 8 exaFLOP budget, varying block size vs recurrence. Optimum is a mild recurrence (8x2), not maximal (1x16), matching the 'partial sharing' finding elsewhere. Looped models are not uniformly best (sorting). Note iso-effective-depth here is not iso-param: 16x1 has 122M vs 12M for 1x16. Uses Bansal et al. progressive loss (randomized loops in training) and input injection; gradient scaling by recurrences for multiplication.

title: Encode, Think, Decode: Scaling test-time reasoning with recursive latent thoughts
relevance_reason: Re-runs OLMo-2 1B mid-training with a looped subset of middle layers (encoder / recursive block / decoder) chosen by angular-distance analysis.
one_sentence: Loops 4 reasoning-relevant OLMo-2-1B layers (7-4*k-5, chosen by Kneedle on layer-to-layer angular distance) during a re-run of the 50B-token mid-training, improving reasoning benchmarks with no new parameters or data; adds an ACT router variant.
key_contributions: Interpretability-guided layer selection: Kneedle knee points on mean angular distance between consecutive layers define the encoder (first 7 layers) and decoder (last 5 layers); the 4 middle layers are looped.
Mid-training re-run (same data, hyperparameters, parameter count) with fixed k=2..5 iterations; gains concentrate in math and reading comprehension, with little change on factual knowledge.
At equal FLOPs, selective looping beats looping all layers (0-16*2-0) or Huginn-style middle-12 looping (2-12*2-2); an ACT router allows adaptive per-token depth (max 10).

setup.model_sizes: OLMo-2 1B base (16 layers); configuration 7-4*k-5
setup.train_tokens_or_data: OLMo-2 stage-2 mid-training mixture (5e10 tokens), initialized from stage-1 checkpoint
setup.loops_train: fixed k in {2,3,4,5}, one model per k; adaptive ACT variant with Nmax=10
setup.loops_test: same k as training; adaptive variant per-token
setup.baselines: OLMo-2 1B mid-trained identically without recursion (k=1); alternative recursive configs 2-12*2-2 and 0-16*2-0 at matched FLOPs
setup.benchmarks: 17 tasks: TriviaQA, NQ, BoolQ, OpenBookQA, DROP, CSQA, HellaSwag, SocialIQA, WinoGrande, ARC-E/C, MMLU, MMLU-Pro, AGIEval, BBH, GSM8K, MATH

claims.claim: Looping the selected middle layers during mid-training improves the identically mid-trained non-recursive OLMo-2 1B, most on math and reading comprehension; iteration count and FLOPs grow with k (not FLOP-matched to a deeper dense model).
claims.evidence_quote: ETD models yield substantial gains on 17 reasoning benchmarks, including +28.4% relative accuracy improvement on GSM8K and +36% on MATH with the OLMo-2 1B Base model.

claims.claim: Which layers to loop matters: at equal FLOPs, looping the 4 knee-selected layers beats looping all layers or the middle 12 layers.
claims.evidence_quote: Our approach consistently outperforms these alternatives under equal compute. For example, the 2–12*2–2 setup is FLOP-equivalent to our 7–4*4–5 configuration, yet yields lower accuracy.

claims.claim: The best block position depends on task category: 7-4*2-5 is best for math, while an earlier block (3-4*2-9) is best for reading comprehension.
claims.evidence_quote: Interestingly, for reading comprehension, the 3-4*2-9 configuration performs best.

claims.claim: An ACT-style router trained end-to-end gives adaptive depth that tracks the fixed-depth accuracy-iteration trade-off and beats fixed k=5 on DROP and OpenBookQA with fewer average iterations.
claims.evidence_quote: we see that adaptive-depth ETD outperforms the ETD with fixed k=5 iterations. Moreover, it also achieves this with fewer iterations on average.

numbers.what: mid-training share of total tokens
numbers.quote: We evaluate the ETD approach by integrating it into the mid-training stage which uses only 1.25% of the total pretraining tokens.

numbers.what: GSM8K accuracy for OLMo-2 1B (k=1) and ETD k=2,3,4 (Table 3), then relative gains k=2..5 and MATH k=1,2
GSM8K at k=5
math reasoning category relative gain at k=2
numbers.quote: The largest improvement is observed on Mathematical Reasoning tasks, with an average relative increase of 16.3%.

numbers.what: selected configuration
numbers.value: 7 encoder layers, 4 recursive layers, 5 decoder layers
numbers.quote: Hence, we set the configuration to 7-4*k-5, i,e. 7 layers in latent encoder, 4 layer in recursive block, and 5 layers in latent decoder respectively

numbers.what: ACT halting threshold and cap
numbers.quote: Computation for a token is stopped once Ht ≥ 1 − ϵ, with ϵ is a small constant (e.g. 0.01), and the maximum possible number of iterations is Nmax =10.

numbers.what: MATH accuracy and relative change at k=2,3,4,5 (Table 3; base 4.57)

limitations: Only OLMo-2 1B base; one data order per configuration; each k trained separately; no FLOP-matched deeper dense baseline; MATH gains are on a very low base (4.57%) and reverse at k=4-5; instruct/post-training integration left to future work.
builds_on: Gromov et al. 2024 (layer pruning, angular distance)
survey_notes: Key (d) evidence on which layers to loop. Caveat for the survey: the headline +36% MATH is relative on a 4.57% base (5.45 at k=2, 6.22 at k=3) and MATH falls below baseline at k=4 (3.73) and k=5 (4.33), so the MATH claim is fragile; GSM8K gains are monotone (44.05 to 56.56). Regime: iso-param + iso-data vs the same OLMo-2 mid-training; the looped model uses more inference FLOPs and there is no deeper dense baseline. Agrees with 2511.07384 that looping middle/late layers with fixed prelude/coda works, but disagrees on details: ETD keeps all layers, uses no input injection, fixed k; 2511.07384 drops middle layers, loops later layers, and uses Huginn's concat adapter with a random initial state. ETD's layer-choice criterion (angular-distance knee) contrasts with 2511.07384's small search and 2610.00673's whole-stack looping.

title: Bridging the Gap Between Latent and Explicit Reasoning with Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Fine-tunes pretrained Llama/GPT-2 models into looped padded Transformers (whole model iterated R times over latent blocks) with parallel CoT-token supervision.
one_sentence: LOTUS turns a CoT-finetuned LM into a looped padded Transformer: K=6 latent blocks refined in parallel for R=6 full-model iterations, supervised post-loop against gold CoT tokens through the LM head; matches explicit CoT on GSM8K at 3B with 2.5x faster thinking.
key_contributions: Post-training recipe: learnable padded latent blocks, input-injected loop of the whole pretrained LM with gradients through all R iterations, cross-entropy of post-loop latents against gold CoT-step tokens plus answer loss (lambda_step=0.05), with a Coconut-style curriculum that grows latent blocks and loops together.

At Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, GSM8K within about 1.5 points of explicit CoT and better out-of-domain average, where prior latent-CoT methods trail by up to 9.2 points; thought-phase latency 2.5x (math expressions) to 6.9x (natural language) lower.

Ablations: post-loop readout beats per-iteration readout for direct LM-head supervision; accuracy rises steeply with trained loop depth R (14.6% at R=2 to 70.0% at R=6) and running more loops than trained does not help.

setup.model_sizes: GPT-2 124M, Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct
setup.train_tokens_or_data: GSM8k-Aug (385k samples); natural-language GSM8K-Aug for the stress test; 30 epochs
setup.loops_train: R=6 (curriculum R_e = K_e grows with converted CoT steps); ablation R=2..6
setup.baselines: Explicit CoT and No-CoT on same backbone and data; CODI, CODI+SIM-CoT, Coconut, PCCoT, KaVa
setup.benchmarks: GSM8K (in-domain), GSM-Hard, MultiArith, SVAMP

claims.claim: At 3B, the looped padded model with parallel gold-CoT supervision brings latent reasoning to within about 1 point of explicit CoT on GSM8K (same backbone, same data), unlike prior latent methods whose gap widens with scale.
claims.regime: iso_param + iso_data (explicit CoT uses more sequential decoding)
claims.evidence_quote: on L LAMA -3.2-3B-I NSTRUCT, it brings the GSM8K test accuracy to within 1 point of explicit CoT and surpasses explicit CoT on the out-ofdomain math average.

claims.claim: For direct LM-head supervision, reading only the post-loop latents beats supervising every iteration; the auxiliary-decoder variant prefers per-iteration readout.
claims.evidence_quote: LOTUS performs best with post-loop readout (70.0% vs. 68.2% per-iter), which lets the early latent blocks refine fully until the end of the loop.

claims.claim: Trained loop depth matters strongly and extra test-time loops beyond the trained depth do not help.
claims.evidence_quote: Accuracy climbs with R (22.7% at R“1 to 70.0% at R“6), peaks at the trained R“6, and dips slightly at R“7 (69.3%).

claims.claim: The looped padded backbone helps even without latent supervision, and gold-CoT supervision adds further gains.
claims.evidence_quote: Without any latent supervision, the looped backbone alone (63.3%) already exceeds CODI + SIM-CoT (62.3%, Table 1), which uses a single latent per step

numbers.quote: LOTUS is on par with explicit CoT in accuracy (68.13 vs. 68.41) while cutting thought-phase latency from 963.6 ms to 140.8 ms with a 6.9ˆ speedup.

numbers.what: trained loop depth ablation
numbers.quote: accuracy rises steeply with R (from 14.6% at R“2 to 70.0% at R“6), with gains continuing through R“5 (68.1%) before nearly saturating at R“6.

survey_notes: Belongs in (e) post-training/SFT into a looped model and (c) supervision design. Loops the entire pretrained LM over a padded latent workspace (looping is over depth, applied to latent positions only, with the question prefix KV-cached once). Full BPTT through R=6 iterations of a 3B model. Supervision finding (post-loop readout beats per-iteration readout for the LM-head route) is a counterpoint to per-loop/deep-supervision objectives used by Ouro-style training (2510.25741, 2610.00673); 2606.24898 in this group studies readout too. Uses a curriculum that grows loops with latent blocks (Coconut-style). Regime: vs explicit CoT on the same backbone and data (iso_param, iso_data); inference compute is not matched (LOTUS is cheaper in latency). No extrapolation beyond trained R, consistent with many fixed-R looped models.

title: Architectural Sampling: Test-Time Scaling via Computational Diversity in Frozen Vision Language Models
relevance_reason: Training-free repetition of a contiguous decoder-layer window in frozen VLMs, used to diversify sampled candidates rather than to deepen a single answer.
one_sentence: Builds a pool of candidates from a frozen Qwen VLM by repeating different contiguous decoder-layer windows r times (each window/r pair is one computation path); pass@9 rises 6.58 points over temperature sampling, best with early-layer windows.
key_contributions: Training-free candidate generation from distinct computation paths (window location x repetition count) with no weight updates or added parameters.
Early-layer windows give the largest gains; jointly reprocessing visual and language tokens is best; gains hold under greedy decoding.
Architectural rollouts replace temperature rollouts in label-free GRPO test-time RL (TTRV) and improve pass@1.

setup.model_sizes: Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-2B/8B, Qwen3.5-VL-2B/4B
setup.train_tokens_or_data: none (training-free); TTRV uses 20 unlabeled samples with LoRA
setup.loops_test: window repeated r times, up to depth 4 in the cost analysis
setup.baselines: temperature sampling, beam search, top-k, top-p from the same frozen model at equal candidate count
setup.benchmarks: 12 multimodal benchmarks incl. AI2D, ScienceQA, CV-Bench, MMStar, BLINK, A-OKVQA

claims.claim: At equal candidate count (9), candidates from repeated-layer paths cover more correct answers than temperature samples of the standard path; per-candidate compute is higher, so not FLOP-matched.
claims.regime: iso_param (same frozen checkpoint), equal candidate count, not iso_infer_flop
claims.evidence_quote: Across five Qwen checkpoints and twelve multimodal benchmarks, architectural sampling improves pass@9 over standardpath temperature sampling by 6.58 percentage points on average at the same ninecandidate budget.

claims.claim: Which layers to repeat: early windows give the highest pass@9; gains fall as the window moves deeper.
claims.evidence_quote: Every region improves over temperature sampling, but the gain falls as the window moves deeper. Reusing the early layers gives the highest pass@9 on all five benchmarks

numbers.what: largest and smallest checkpoint-level pass@9 gains
numbers.quote: The largest checkpoint-level gains are observed for Qwen3VL-8B (+12.43 points) and Qwen3.5-VL-4B (+9.13 points), while the smallest gain is +1.10 points for Qwen3.5-VL-2B.

numbers.what: latency overhead of recursion
numbers.value: roughly 1-2 s more, up to depth 4
numbers.quote: the overhead is marginal (roughly 1–2 seconds more, depending on recursion depth, up to depth 4)

limitations: Higher per-candidate forward cost than temperature sampling; requires access to internal layers (not usable for API-only models).
builds_on: 2507.07996 (CoLa, Skip a Layer or Loop it)
survey_notes: (d) training-free looping: here layer repetition is used as a diversity source for best-of-n and test-time RL, not as a single-answer improvement; claims are pass@k at equal candidate count, not FLOP-matched. Its finding that early-layer windows work best contrasts with retrofit papers that loop middle/late layers (2510.07358 ETD loops the middle block; 2511.07384 loops later layers) and should be noted as task/objective-dependent (diversity vs accuracy).

title: Don't Commit Alone: Joint Token Commitment in Diffusion Language Models
relevance_reason: Re-applies the last n layers of a diffusion LM once (a single partial extra pass) to coordinate jointly committed tokens; layer reuse, not iterated recurrence.
one_sentence: For LLaDA2.1-mini, a marker vector flags the tokens to be committed and the backbone's last n=3 layers are re-applied once to coordinate them before writing; with LoRA and markers trained on 50k FineWeb-Edu documents, 5 of 7 benchmarks improve.
key_contributions: Frames parallel-commit error as conditional total correlation and adds a marker-gated coordination pass that reuses the last n layers.
Re-applying layers without the marker reduces accuracy; deeper coordination (n=6, 9) gives no consistent gain over n=3.

setup.model_sizes: LLaDA2.1-mini (frozen backbone + LoRA + marker vectors)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 50k FineWeb-Edu documents
setup.loops_train: one extra pass over last n=3 layers (ablation n=6, 9)
setup.baselines: released LLaDA2.1-mini factorized decoder; same weights with Stage B disabled
setup.benchmarks: GSM8K, CMATH, DROP, PIQA, GPQA, HumanEval+, MBPP+

claims.claim: Extra layer reuse helps only with the marker signal: re-applying the last n layers without the marker lowers GSM8K accuracy, so the gain is not just added depth.
claims.evidence_quote: Re-applying the last n layers without a marker reduces accuracy by 0.76 points, indicating that the marker announcement contributes beyond additional depth.

claims.claim: Re-applying more layers does not help: n=3 beats n=6 and n=9 on average.
claims.evidence_quote: Averaged over the seven benchmarks, n=3 scores 78.72, compared with 77.50 for n=6 and 77.65 for n=9.

numbers.what: per-benchmark gains over released decoder
numbers.quote: Table 1 shows that C O C OMMIT improves code generation (HumanEval+ +5.49, MBPP+ +1.33), physical commonsense (PIQA +3.70), graduate-level science QA (GPQA +3.03), and grade-school math (GSM8K +1.52).

numbers.what: decomposition of gain on GSM8K
numbers.quote: With Stage B disabled, our weights improve by 1.14 points over the released model, capturing the effect of the adapters and CPT data. Enabling Stage B at the same weights adds another 0.38 points.

limitations: Single dLLM checkpoint; most of the GSM8K gain comes from adapter training rather than the coordination pass; deeper reuse not beneficial.
survey_notes: Peripheral to (d): shows one extra pass over the last layers can be trained cheaply with LoRA, but the decomposition attributes only +0.38 of the GSM8K gain to the extra pass, and raw layer re-application without the learned marker hurts. Not a recurrent-depth model; cite at most in a footnote on layer reuse in diffusion LMs.

title: Port-Hamiltonian Latent Deliberation: Mitigating the Deliberation Drift Cliff in Test-Time Compute Scaling
relevance_reason: Constrains an iterated continuous latent 'thought' vector with dissipative Hamiltonian/Helmholtz-Hodge flows to stop drift beyond the trained horizon; toy-scale, not a looped transformer LM.
one_sentence: Shows unconstrained recurrent latent deliberation collapses when iterated far beyond training horizons (drift cliff) and proposes dissipative geometric flows (DG-HHD) that keep accuracy at deep steps, on synthetic graphs and a tiny ProofWriter model.
key_contributions: Names the 'deliberation drift cliff': gains at K<=4 collapse at K>=16 for unconstrained recurrent latent models.
Trade-off: strictly conservative (curl-free) flows suppress drift but cap accuracy; DG-HHD decouples a dissipative potential part from circulation.

setup.model_sizes: compact deliberation models, Dmodel 128-256
setup.train_tokens_or_data: synthetic relational multi-hop graphs; ProofWriter
setup.loops_train: short horizons (K<=4 cited for gains)
setup.baselines: unconstrained recurrent baselines, conservative HHD, autoregressive baseline
setup.benchmarks: synthetic multi-hop graphs; ProofWriter

claims.claim: Unconstrained recurrent latent updates diverge out of distribution when iterated well past the training horizon; dissipative constraints prevent this.
claims.evidence_quote: an unconstrained baseline (B0-Naive) suffers a catastrophic drop from a peak of 96.60% at K = 4 down to 34.13% at K = 64 (∆ = −62.47%).

numbers.what: conservative vs unconstrained flows trade-off
numbers.value: conservative: 3.40% cliff, 32.73% peak; unconstrained: 82.33% peak, 36.87% cliff
numbers.quote: completely suppressing long-range drift (cliff 3.40%) but bottlenecking peak reasoning accuracy at 32.73% ± 1.10%

limitations: Compact models (Dmodel 128-256) on synthetic deduction tasks; single continuous thought vector, not token-sequence recurrence; scaling to LLMs left open. Survey caution: unconventional reporting (e.g. '22-round investigation', 'certified invariants') and large seed variance (+-13.61, +-14.93).
survey_notes: (b) stability: supports the general finding that unconstrained recurrence drifts beyond the trained horizon and contractive/dissipative structure fixes it at some cost in expressivity (cf. STARS 2605.26733 spectral-radius penalty, 2607.10681 spectral margin). Toy-scale with high variance; cite only as weak corroboration.

key: t:layer duplication in llms
title: Layer Duplication in LLMs
relevance_reason: Abstract only: duplicates early self-attention layers of pretrained LLMs once or twice, with or without fine-tuning; a shallow form of layer reuse.
one_sentence: Per the abstract, duplicating the initial multi-head self-attention layers of LLMs once or twice often gives a significant performance boost, with or without fine-tuning; attention analysis explains the gain.
key_contributions: Early-layer attention duplication (1-2 copies) as a training-free or fine-tuned enhancement (abstract only).

setup.loops_test: initial layers duplicated once or twice

claims.claim: Duplicating the initial self-attention layers once or twice often improves performance.
claims.evidence_quote: The re-sults demonstrate that duplicating the initial layers once or twice often yields a significant performance boost.

venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (Findings, 2025; from corpus metadata, DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.findings-emnlp.967)
survey_notes: Full text and arXiv id unavailable; abstract only. Its early-layer preference agrees with 2610.01687 (early windows best for candidate diversity) and contrasts with retrofit work that loops middle/late layers (2510.07358, 2511.07384) and with 2602.14759 (best loop region roughly 40-60% depth). Venue comes from corpus metadata, not from paper text.

key: t:lsrl process supervised grpo on latent recurrent states improves mathematical reasoning
title: LSRL: Process-Supervised GRPO on Latent Recurrent States Improves Mathematical Reasoning
relevance_reason: Title only (no abstract or full text); per RLTT (2602.10520) it applies process-supervised GRPO to Huginn's latent recurrent states.
one_sentence: No abstract or full text available; the title indicates process-supervised GRPO over latent recurrent states for math reasoning.
venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (Findings, 2025; from corpus metadata, DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.findings-emnlp.669)
survey_notes: Not readable here (no arXiv id, abstract is empty). The RLTT paper (2602.10520, its Sec. 1/related work) describes LSRL as scoring Huginn's per-depth latent states with GPT-4.1 nano as process rewards for GRPO and reports its GSM8K/MathQA gains; that quote is stored in the 2602.10520 record. Relevant to (e) RL with latent trajectories; lead author should obtain the ACL Anthology PDF.

title: MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers
relevance_reason: Training-free task-level layer routing (skip, repeat, residual add) over frozen pretrained LLMs; repeats layers but is not a trained weight-tied recurrent model.
one_sentence: Learns one task-level Markov policy over skip/repeat/add-hidden-state layer moves on a frozen LLM via cross-entropy-method search on ~1000 training examples, decodes top-k routes with Viterbi, and improves accuracy over the unrouted model and Dr.LLM.
key_contributions: Layer routing as a context-dependent Markov policy (layer, budget phase, displacement, op context) searched without gradients or weight updates.
Exact top-k Viterbi decoding plus validation selection replaces per-example search and router training.
Gains are largest on weak/small models; routes partly transfer across related math tasks.

setup.model_sizes: Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B (4-bit), Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct (4-bit), DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B; Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct in appendix
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Per benchmark: 1,000 training examples for route search plus 100-200 validation examples; no weight updates
setup.loops_train: Routes capped at 40-52 block calls (e.g. 40 for Qwen3-1.7B with 28 layers); local move radius r=5
setup.loops_test: One fixed searched route per task (e.g. 33 block calls on Qwen3-1.7B GSM8K route)
setup.baselines: Unrouted forward pass, Dr.LLM, Dr.LLM with MACRO action space
setup.benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH500, MedQA, OpenBookQA, SciQ, MMLU-Pro, SVAMP, ASDiv, MAWPS, GSM8K-Hard, GSM8K-Plus, multistep arithmetic, object counting

claims.claim: Task-level routing of a frozen LLM improves average accuracy over the unrouted model and over Dr.LLM while cutting route-search time.
claims.regime: iso_param vs unrouted same model; inference FLOPs not matched (routes can be longer than the standard pass)
claims.evidence_quote: MACRO achieves a +5.0% average accuracy improvement over the unrouted baselines, with largest gains on small models. We outperform the best dynamic routing approach Dr. LLM by +7.2%, while reducing route-search time 9.4× (from 14.8 to 1.6 hours).

claims.claim: Gains shrink as the base model gets stronger: large on Qwen3-1.7B and the R1-distilled model, under 1 point on Qwen3-8B/14B.
claims.evidence_quote: its margin over the unrouted baseline is widest exactly where that baseline is weakest, narrowing to a smaller but consistent gain once the model is already strong

claims.claim: The action space (including residual addition of earlier hidden states) matters more than the router: Dr.LLM's skip-and-repeat space often falls below baseline, while the same routers with MACRO's action space are much stronger.
claims.evidence_quote: indicating that the action space itself is a decisive part of what makes layer routing help rather than hurt

claims.claim: Logit-lens analysis suggests routing exposes an answer already computed internally rather than adding new reasoning.
claims.evidence_quote: this suggests that routing improves how an already-computed answer is exposed rather than changing the reasoning itself

numbers.what: Single route on Qwen3-1.7B GSM8K (L3-L7 executed twice, 33 block calls) vs baseline
numbers.quote: rewinding Qwen3-1.7B from layer 7 back to layer 3 and replaying five blocks raises test accuracy from 43.4% to 69.5%, without changing a single weight

numbers.what: Mean improvement over baseline per model (Table 3): Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, 8B, 14B-4bit, Mixtral-4bit, R1-Distill-Llama-8B
numbers.quote: Qwen3-1.7B Qwen3-4B Qwen3-8B Qwen3-14B (4-bit) Mixtral-8x7B (4-bit) DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B +12.68 +1.50 +0.76 +0.78 +1.33 +13.04

numbers.what: Average gain over unrouted, over Dr.LLM, and search-time reduction
numbers.quote: yielding a +5.0% average accuracy improvement over the nonrouted baseline, +7.2% over Dr. LLM, and +1.5% over Dr. LLM with an equivalent action space, while reducing the route-search computational cost by 9.4×

numbers.what: One shared route trained on 8 in-domain tasks, Qwen3-1.7B out-of-domain mean accuracy baseline vs MACRO
Search budget
numbers.value: 10 iterations x 30 candidate programs; route length cap 40 for Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B
numbers.quote: The main experiments use 10 search iterations with 30 candidate programs per iteration.

numbers.what: Inference cost of a revisited block
numbers.value: T applied steps cost as a T-block tied-weight network
numbers.quote: a route of T applied steps has the cache and decoding cost of a T -block network with tied weights

limitations: Routes are task-level (not input-dependent) and need labeled training/validation examples; per-token compute and KV cache grow with route length; the authors argue gains may come from eliciting an internally present answer rather than new capability; no gain on the reasoning-distilled model versus Dr.LLM+Ext.
survey_notes: Section (d) training-free looping: frozen Qwen3 gains from replaying a contiguous mid-stack block (L3-L7 of 28) agree with ETD/ inner-loop papers that a middle block is the right segment to loop. Comparison is iso-param but not iso-inference-FLOP; gains are task-specific and need labeled data for search, and vanish on strong models (<1 pt on 8B/14B), so 'training-free looping helps' is a weak-model, task-tuned result. The residual 'add earlier hidden state' action resembles input/history injection in trained looped models (Huginn) and is what makes Dr.LLM's routers useful in this paper.

title: Skip a Layer or Loop It? Learning Program-of-Layers in LLMs
relevance_reason: Training-free looping/skipping of contiguous segments of frozen pretrained LLMs, with a learned 2.1M-parameter program predictor; direct evidence on which layers to loop in pretrained models.
one_sentence: MCTS over skip/repeat programs of frozen LLM layers shows better programs exist for most inputs (oracle), then a small predictor trained on MCTS traces outputs per-input segment skip/keep/repeat programs that beat standard inference and dynamic-depth baselines on math.
key_contributions: Oracle MCTS study: joint skip+loop programs beat skip-only or loop-only; valid programs are mostly short contiguous segments repeated at most once.

PoLar predictor (frozen Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B encoder + layer-query cross-attention, ~2.1M params) predicts segment boundaries and skip/keep/repeat labels per input, supervised by MCTS-found valid programs.
Gains at pass@1 and pass@k over sampling, with lower latency on average and OOD transfer to ASDiv, MAWPS, MMLU-Pro.

setup.model_sizes: LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B-Chat, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B (all frozen)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Predictor trained on MCTS-derived valid programs for DART-Math: 4,130 training, 826 validation, 1,651 test examples
setup.loops_train: Segments of at most Kmax=4 contiguous layers; repeat = one extra pass of a segment
setup.loops_test: Per-input predicted program; top-k beam candidates for pass@k
setup.baselines: Greedy and sampled base model, ShortGPT, MindSkip, FlexiDepth, Dr.LLM
setup.benchmarks: DART-Math DM-1..DM-5 (in-distribution); ASDiv, MAWPS, MMLU-Pro subjects (OOD)
