claims.claim: In an oracle MCTS search (validity judged by answer correctness), allowing layer recurrence beats skip-only, and joint skip+loop is best in every setting.
claims.regime: iso_param (same frozen model); oracle uses ground-truth correctness, so this is an upper bound, not a deployable method
claims.evidence_quote: Layer recurrence-only performs better than layer skipping-only, but combining the two complementary operators produces the best program-of-layers.

claims.claim: Useful programs in pretrained models are local: mostly single-layer or two-layer contiguous segments, repeated at most once; deep iterative reuse is rare.
claims.evidence_quote: Valid execution programs are predominantly composed of contiguous layer segments and typically require at most a single recurrence per segment.

claims.claim: The learned predictor outperforms sampling-based inference of the same frozen model at pass@1 and pass@5, often with fewer unique layers.
claims.regime: iso_param; not iso-inference-FLOP per program but average executed layers is below full depth
claims.evidence_quote: Base (sampling) improves from 32.8% at pass@1 to 43.8% at pass@5, while P O L AR improves from 35.1% to 51.2%.

claims.claim: Pretrained models' training objective favors only short-range local reuse, limiting how much looping a frozen model can exploit.
claims.evidence_quote: their training objectives favor short-range, local reuse over rich program composition

numbers.what: Oracle MCTS gain of Skip&Loop over base at 115% depth budget (LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen1.5-MoE, Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen3-8B)
numbers.quote: gain@115%: +47.3pp gain@115%: +37.2pp Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct Qwen3-8B gain@115%: +63.7pp gain@115%: +53.4pp

numbers.what: Fraction of inputs with shorter valid programs (oracle): initially correct / initially wrong
numbers.quote: solved correctly by standard inference (C→C), 71.9% admit shorter valid programs. Even for inputs initially solved incorrectly (W→C), 34.0% admit shorter programs that correct the model's prediction.

numbers.what: Share of segments that are a single layer in valid programs
numbers.quote: Figure 7(a) shows that 57.7% of segments consist of a single layer, and over two-thirds contain at most two consecutive layers

numbers.what: LLaMA-3.2-3B DART-Math macro pass@1 / pass@5: Base sampling vs PoLar
numbers.quote: Base (sampling) improves from 32.8% at pass@1 to 43.8% at pass@5, while P O L AR improves from 35.1% to 51.2%.

numbers.what: Relative end-to-end runtime on Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B (24 layers), easier vs harder inputs
numbers.quote: Consequently, P O L AR reduces end-to-end latency while improving accuracy: it achieves 0.83× the base runtime on easier inputs and 0.95× on harder inputs.

numbers.what: Predictor size
numbers.quote: it contains approximately 2.1M parameters, corresponding to only 0.01%–0.06% of the base LLM size

numbers.what: Accuracy gain at those runtimes (Table 4: DM-1, DM-5) with avg layers 23.30 and 23.76 of 24

limitations: MCTS findings are oracle (validity = correct answer) and the predictor is supervised by these traces; only one extra repeat per segment; evaluated mainly on math (DART-Math) with OOD transfer at pass@1; in-distribution numbers were revised after deduplication of DART-Math.
venue: Proceedings of the 43 rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea. PMLR 306, 2026.
builds_on: Looped transformers (Fan et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2023)
survey_notes: Section (d): strongest evidence that frozen pretrained LLMs tolerate only local, shallow looping (single/two-layer segments, at most one repeat), which contrasts with retrofit papers (2511.07384, ETD 2510.07358) that loop a multi-layer middle block many times after continued training; the gap suggests training is required for deep recurrence. Big MCTS gains (+37 to +64pp) are oracle upper bounds using answer correctness and must not be cited as deployable gains; the deployable predictor gives +5.7 to +9.4 points at pass@1. Successor/sibling of CoLa (2507.07996, same authors) and companion to 2609.31360.

title: Programs-of-Layers in LLMs through the Lens of Cortical Areas
relevance_reason: Independent reproduction and audit of training-free skip/repeat programs over frozen LLM layers (PoLar, 2606.06574) across 5 models up to Qwen3-32B.
one_sentence: Reproduces PoLar's MCTS diagnostics on 5 frozen LLMs (repeat beats skip, both together best, harder inputs need more repeats) but fails to reproduce the learned router: its top-1 program always collapses to the identity forward pass.
key_contributions: Releases a reconstructed MCTS over skip/keep/repeat programs and reproduces PoLar findings F1-F3 on Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, Qwen2.5-3B/7B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B.
Shows the PoLar router's pass@1 gain does not replicate (identity collapse), while its pass@5 gain comes from a small fixed menu of programs from beam search.
Finds error-correcting programs are fragile and MMLU-Pro rescuing programs overfit to answer position.

setup.model_sizes: Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B-Chat, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B (LLaMA-3.2-3B excluded from MCTS/router track); all frozen
setup.train_tokens_or_data: DART-Math difficulty 1-5 and a 6-domain MMLU-Pro subset; router trained on MCTS-discovered programs (1,250-question train slice)
setup.loops_train: Segment repeat (re-run a contiguous block once more) or skip
setup.loops_test: Per-input MCTS program (oracle) or router-predicted program
setup.baselines: Standard forward pass (identity program); PoLar's published numbers
setup.benchmarks: DART-Math DM-1..DM-5, MMLU-Pro subset

claims.claim: Oracle search reproduces PoLar's ordering: repeat-only beats skip-only and combined skip&repeat beats both, on every model and difficulty.
claims.regime: iso_param (same frozen model, oracle program selection using correctness)
claims.evidence_quote: skip and repeat combined beat either alone, on every model and every DART-Math difficulty level, with repeat the stronger of the two mechanisms on its own.

claims.claim: The learned single-shot router does not reproduce: its top-1 program is always the identity forward pass, even with PoLar's own code and many anti-collapse fixes.
claims.evidence_quote: On every model, difficulty split, and training-data treatment tested, the router's top-1 decode is always the literal identity program, both for our own reimplementation and for Li et al.'s own unmodified training code run on our data

claims.claim: A single well-chosen middle block repeated once, with no training, improves Qwen3-8B on MMLU-Pro; blocks straddling an early boundary (layer 6) collapse accuracy.
claims.evidence_quote: Simply repeating a well-chosen middle block (layers 18–22), no retraining, no other intervention, already improves Qwen3-8B's accuracy on a 6-domain subset of MMLU-Pro

claims.claim: Error-correcting programs are brittle and MMLU-Pro rescuing programs track answer position, not content, suggesting oracle program gains partly reflect overfitting.
claims.evidence_quote: MCTS-discovered rescuing programs substantially overfit to the correct answer's position, not its content.

numbers.what: PoLar's published router gain that this paper fails to reproduce at pass@1
numbers.quote: Li et al. (2026)'s headline router claim is a real, if modest, pass@1 gain over Base (41.6% → 43.2%, +1.6pp), growing to +14.0pp by pass@5.

numbers.what: Share of identity programs in router training data
numbers.quote: nor is it a majority-class artifact of the training data (table 3: identity examples are only 2.4–7.0% per model)

numbers.what: Break rate when reverting one edit in a rescuing program
numbers.quote: it is roughly flat across DM-1–DM-5 within every model, ranging 52.5% (Qwen3-32B) to 72.3% (Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B) pooled over difficulty

numbers.what: Segments using at most one recurrence
numbers.quote: pooling the "0" and "1" extra-repetition bins in fig. 7b, 73–86% of segments across all 5 models use at most one recurrence

numbers.what: Single-layer segment share reported by PoLar (not reproduced: 4 of 5 models fall below)
numbers.quote: Li et al. report that 54.5% of segments in valid programs touch only a single layer, and over two-thirds touch at most two.

limitations: Could not evaluate the router OOD because it always collapsed to identity; several MCTS numbers do not match PoLar precisely; operator set limited to skip/keep/repeat of whole layers; neuroscience analogy is interpretive.
survey_notes: Key contradiction for section (d): directly contradicts PoLar's (2606.06574) headline router claim (pass@1 gain) and its segment-length statistic, while confirming the oracle MCTS findings. Note version drift: this paper quotes PoLar's single-layer share as 54.5% and router pass@1 41.6->43.2, while PoLar v2 (our fulltext) reports 57.7% and different pass@1 numbers after a DART-Math deduplication revision. Oracle gains from searching layer programs with answer correctness should be treated as upper bounds with overfitting risk (position overfitting on MMLU-Pro, brittle edits). The Qwen3-8B middle-block result (layers 18-22 of 36 helpful, mixing across layer 6 harmful) agrees with retrofit/ETD-style evidence that middle layers are the loopable region.

title: Skip a Layer or Loop it? Test-Time Depth Adaptation of Pretrained LLMs
relevance_reason: Per-sample test-time search over skipping and repeating layers of frozen pretrained LLMs (training-free looping of pretrained layers).
one_sentence: Uses per-input MCTS with gold-answer reward to find chains of skipped/repeated layers of frozen LLaMA-3 and OLMoE models, showing large oracle accuracy gains and that most inputs admit shorter layer paths.
key_contributions: Defines chain-of-layers (CoLa): per-sample paths that skip or repeat contiguous blocks (k, r in 1..4) of a frozen pretrained model.
MCTS (200 simulations per input, length penalty) with correctness reward finds better or shorter paths for most samples.
Layer-usage analysis: early layers are always kept, middle layers are most often skipped in small models; larger and instruction-tuned models use layers more uniformly.

setup.model_sizes: LLaMA-3-3B, LLaMA-3-8B, OLMoE-1B-7B, base and instruction-tuned variants (frozen)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: No training; 500 sampled instances per dataset; MCTS feedback from gold answers
setup.loops_train: n/a
setup.loops_test: Repeat a block of k layers r times, k, r in {1,2,3,4}; path length constrained
setup.baselines: Original forward pass; skip-only and recurrence-only search spaces
setup.benchmarks: ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, DART-Math levels 1-5

claims.claim: With per-sample oracle search, shorter paths exist for most correctly answered samples and correcting paths exist for most wrongly answered samples.
claims.regime: iso_param; oracle (MCTS uses gold-answer correctness on the evaluated input), so an upper bound
claims.evidence_quote: For >75% of samples with correct predictions by the original LLM, we can find shorter CoLa, suggesting a large space for improving inference efficiency; (2) For >60% of samples with originally incorrect predictions, we can identify CoLa achieving correct predictions

claims.claim: Joint skip+recurrence search beats skip-only and recurrence-only on all datasets and models; skip-only is stronger on easy ARC tasks, recurrence-only on harder DART levels for instruct models.
claims.evidence_quote: Our full method, which searches over both skipping and recurrence decisions, consistently achieves the highest accuracy on all datasets and models.

claims.claim: Recurrence-only gains come with increased depth; error-correcting paths are often shorter than the full model, suggesting 'overthinking' in depth.
claims.evidence_quote: Recurrence-only strategies achieve moderate gains over the pretrained baseline, but do so by increasing the overall depth

claims.claim: Early layers are kept; skipping concentrates in middle layers, most sharply in small pretrained models.
claims.evidence_quote: CoLa models consistently keep early layers but exhibit an elevated skip rate of middle layers.

numbers.what: LLaMA-3-3B base ARC-E accuracy, original vs skip-only (oracle)
numbers.quote: For example, on LLaMA-3B, accuracy on ARC-E improves from 27.8% to 75.4%, showing that reducing computation depth can be beneficial

numbers.what: LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct DART-2: skip-only, recurrence-only, full CoLa (oracle)
numbers.quote: on DART-2, the LLaMA-3-8B-Instr model improves from 25.2% (skip-only) and 22.0% (recurrence-only) to 66.2% with the full space

numbers.what: MCTS budget and length penalty
numbers.quote: We use 200 simulations per input in our MCTS implementation for optimizing CoLa, balancing search quality and runtime.

numbers.what: LLaMA-3-3B base, original / skip-only / recurrence-only / CoLa (oracle): ARC-E then ARC-C
numbers.quote: Original +Skip-only +Recurrence-only +CoLa (Skip+Recurrence) 27.80 75.40 65.40 95.80 20.80 75.60 54.80 98.20

limitations: Search uses the gold answer of each test input as reward (oracle, not deployable as-is); 200 MCTS simulations per input; evaluated on 500 samples per dataset with zero-shot prompts and very low baseline accuracies for base models (e.g. 1.4% on DART-5), which inflates relative gains.
survey_notes: Section (d): precursor to PoLar (2606.06574) and MACRO (2608.05872). All headline gains are per-sample oracle search with test labels, so they measure the existence of better paths, not a method. Contradiction: CoLa Table 1 often has skip-only > recurrence-only (e.g. ARC and base-model DART), whereas PoLar Finding 1 and RE-PoLar (2609.31360) report recurrence-only > skip-only on DART-Math; CoLa's text also says DART-2 recurrence-only is 22.0% while its Table 1 lists 20.80. Baseline accuracies of base models are near floor (zero-shot formatting), so oracle path search partly fixes output formatting.

title: Inner Loop Inference for Pretrained Transformers: Unlocking Latent Capabilities Without Training
relevance_reason: Training-free middle-block looping of frozen pretrained LLMs (Gemma 2, Llama 3) with hidden-state interpolation to stabilize repeated application.
one_sentence: Re-applies a selected middle block of frozen Gemma 2 and Llama 3 models at inference; naive looping always hurts, while interpolating looped states with cached/baseline states gives small gains on Gemma and inconsistent results on pre-norm Llama.
key_contributions: Middle-looping of a frozen model (prelude once, block s..e-1 repeated R times, coda once) with representation interpolation (uniform average, moving average to baseline, auto-alignment softmax) to limit distribution shift.
Shows naive looping of a pretrained block degrades accuracy for every start-end configuration on Gemma2-2B WinoGrande.
Best loop region sits at roughly 40-60% relative depth; matched-magnitude noise control underperforms structured looping.

setup.model_sizes: Gemma 2 2B and 9B, Llama 3 8B (frozen)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: No training; loop region selected by sweeping on WinoGrande
setup.loops_train: n/a
setup.loops_test: Naive sweep uses loop count 3; one model-specific loop region (e.g. Gemma 2-2B layers 10-13) fixed across tasks
setup.baselines: Same frozen model without looping; matched-magnitude noise injection
setup.benchmarks: WinoGrande, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, GSM8K, HellaSwag, MMLU (lighteval)

claims.claim: Naively repeating a block of a frozen pretrained model degrades accuracy for every tested start-end configuration, some collapsing toward chance, consistent with distribution shift of activations.
claims.regime: iso_param (same frozen model, more inference FLOPs)
claims.evidence_quote: All looped configurations perform worse than the baseline accuracy, with some settings collapsing to near-chance performance.

claims.claim: Interpolating looped states (uniform averaging of cached loop states) yields modest gains on Gemma models; Llama-3-8B (pure pre-norm) responds inconsistently.
claims.evidence_quote: this yields modest but consistent accuracy gains for Gemma models, while Llama 3–8B responds less reliably, due to architectural differences.

claims.claim: The best loop region is in the middle of the network (about 40-60% depth).
claims.evidence_quote: the selected intervals consistently fall within comparable relative depths, roughly 40–60% of the network, matching the stage-wise inference dynamics reported in [2].

claims.claim: Normalization placement matters for stability of repeated application: pre-norm is described as less stable under repetition than Gemma 2's pre+post norm.
claims.evidence_quote: most modern LLMs rely on pre-layer normalization, which improves optimization during training but is known to be less stable when blocks are repeatedly applied

numbers.what: Gemma 2-2B WinoGrande (5-shot): baseline vs Uniform interpolation
Gemma 2-2B GSM8K (5-shot): baseline, Uniform, Moving Average, Auto-Align, Noise
Llama 3-8B MMLU (5-shot): baseline vs Uniform (looping hurts)
Best loop region for Gemma 2-2B
numbers.quote: In the case of Gemma 2-2B, the best configuration corresponds to looping layers 10–13 (see Figure 1).

limitations: Gains are small and mostly within the reported standard errors; loop region tuned on WinoGrande; Llama 3-8B gains are unreliable; only three models up to 9B; no wall-clock or FLOP accounting.
builds_on: Saunshi et al. Reasoning with latent thoughts
survey_notes: Section (d) and (b): direct evidence that naive training-free looping of a pretrained block is harmful (distribution shift), which agrees with retrofit papers that require continued training (2511.07384, ETD 2510.07358) and with RE-PoLar/PoLar that at most one repeat of short segments helps. The fix here is a training-free analogue of stabilizing state passing (averaging/interpolating with the non-looped state, akin to damping or residual scaling). Effect sizes (<1 point mostly, within ±1-3.6 std errors) are much smaller than MACRO/PoLar task-tuned gains; the middle-depth loop region (40-60%) agrees with RE-PoLar's best repeat block (layers 18-22 of 36 on Qwen3-8B, 2609.31360), while MACRO's example GSM8K route replays earlier layers (L3-L7 of 28, 2608.05872).

title: Training-Free Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Loops a contiguous mid-stack window of frozen pretrained LLMs at inference with no training.
one_sentence: Inference-time wrapper re-applies a mid-depth window of a frozen checkpoint as damped Euler / Runge-Kutta sub-steps rather than naive repetition; naive looping degrades, damped sub-stepping gives small gains (about +1 to +2.6 pp) on knowledge MC benchmarks across 7 families.
key_contributions: Views each pre-norm block as a forward Euler step at h=1; replaces naive K-fold looping with K damped sub-steps (h=1/K) that target the same endpoint the post-loop layers were trained on.
Block-mode vs layer-mode iteration; layer-mode needed on MoE checkpoints to avoid expert-routing thrash.
Depth-fraction rule for which layers to loop (window center at about 0.45-0.60 of depth) across dense and MoE models from 16 to 48 layers.

setup.model_sizes: Qwen3 0.6B/1.7B/4B (base and instruct), Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct, Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B-Chat, Llama-3.2 1B/3B-Instruct, DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat, Moonlight-16B-A3B-Instruct
setup.train_tokens_or_data: none (frozen checkpoints)
setup.loops_train: n/a (not trained with loops)
setup.loops_test: K in {1..24} in ablations; out-of-the-box recipe uses K-stage Runge-Kutta on the mid 4 layers (K=2-3)
setup.baselines: same frozen checkpoint without looping; naive K-fold looping; uniform loop of Inner Loop Inference (2602.14759); Anderson, heavy-ball, Aitken, higher-order RK solvers
setup.benchmarks: lm-eval-harness knowledge MC (MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Main, MMLU, ARC-Challenge, CommonsenseQA, OpenBookQA) plus a 16-task macro suite

claims.claim: Naive K-fold reapplication of a mid block in a frozen model degrades accuracy almost universally, because post-loop layers were trained on the one-pass endpoint.
claims.regime: iso_param (same frozen checkpoint, extra inference compute)
claims.evidence_quote: But the post-loop layers are not trained to receive the trajectory at t=K, and empirically, naive K-fold looping degrades performance almost universally (Section 3).

claims.claim: Damped sub-stepping (K Euler steps of size 1/K, or K-stage RK with anchor) keeps iterates in the trained regime and improves over the unlooped checkpoint on most cells.
claims.evidence_quote: The principled goal of g (K) is therefore not to advance integration to t=K, but to better approximate the same endpoint x(t=1) that the unmodified network already targets.

claims.claim: Which layers to loop: the optimal window sits at a stable fractional depth across architectures; MoE models need layer-mode iteration.
claims.evidence_quote: A universal depth-fraction rule places the optimal window at fractional depth ≈0.45–0.60 across dense and MoE architectures from 16 to 48 layers.

claims.claim: Higher-order solvers and fixed-point accelerators do not beat simple damped sub-stepping, suggesting the looped middle of a pretrained transformer is not contractive.
claims.evidence_quote: find none robustly beats K-stage Runge–Kutta, suggesting the looped middle of a pretrained transformer [35, 77, 5] is not contractive in any useful sense

numbers.what: Headline gains over the unlooped frozen checkpoint
numbers.quote: our method improves Qwen3-4B-Instruct by +2.64 pp on MMLU-Pro, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct by +1.14 pp on CommonsenseQA

numbers.what: Share of (model, benchmark) cells non-negative under the fixed recipe
numbers.quote: 87% of cells across seven model families and our benchmark suite are non-negative under the fixed out-of-the-box recipe with no per-cell hyperparameter tuning.

numbers.what: Cell breakdown: positive vs neutral
numbers.quote: resulting in 27 positive (∆ > +0.3 pp, 60%) and 12 neutral (|∆| ≤ 0.3 pp, 27%) cells.

numbers.what: Naive looping collapse on 16-task macro (Qwen3-1.7B-Base)
numbers.quote: The naive loop variant degrades monotonically, falling to 37.89% at K=6 (-17.71 pp).

numbers.what: Toy model MSE: naive K=8 looping vs damped sub-step
numbers.quote: at K=8 this degrades to a MSE of 335 versus the sub-step value of 1.04 (≈ 320× gap).

numbers.what: Compute used for experiments
numbers.quote: Approximately 20,000 NVIDIA H100 HBM3-80GB GPU hours were used for the experiments.

limitations: Gains are small (roughly +1 to +2.6 pp) and concentrated on knowledge-heavy multiple-choice benchmarks; negatives concentrate in sub-3B distilled checkpoints; MLA-based MoE models show 3-4x smaller gains; Table 3 reports the best loop configuration per model family, so headline cells involve configuration selection (Table 4 is the leakage-free check).
survey_notes: Training-free retrofit (sub-theme d). Key message for the survey: post-loop layers expect the one-pass endpoint, so naive repetition fails and looping must be damped (convex mix x <- (1-1/K)x + (1/K)g(x)); this is the inference-time analogue of residual scaling / damping fixes used in trained loops. Directly contradicts the simple uniform repetition of 2602.14759, which they report fails to scale after K>=6. Depth-fraction rule (middle layers ~0.45-0.60) agrees with ETD (2510.07358) and other papers that loop middle 'reasoning' layers. Regime is iso_param with more inference FLOPs, not iso_infer_flop. Gains are modest and selection-sensitive.

title: Entropy-Gated Latent Recursion
relevance_reason: Training-free re-application of a frozen LLM's top-L decoder layers at high-entropy tokens, used as a deterministic sampling axis.
one_sentence: At high-entropy tokens a frozen LLM re-applies its top-L layers to an anchor-fused, norm-matched state until the next-token distribution converges; varying L gives deterministic rollout diversity that, aggregated by majority vote, beats greedy and FLOP-matched beam search on math.
key_contributions: Training-free top-L layer recursion gated by token entropy (about 5% of tokens trigger) with KL-based early exit and Kmax=3.
Stabilization of training-free recursion by fusing the refined state with the layer N-L anchor (small alpha) and norm-matching; large alpha collapses accuracy.
Layer span L as a deterministic sampling axis complementary to temperature; EGLR-SC majority vote over L.

setup.model_sizes: 8 frozen instruction-tuned models 0.5B-14B (Qwen2.5-0.5B/3B/7B/14B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B/7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: none (frozen)
setup.loops_train: n/a
setup.loops_test: Kmax=3 iterations of top-L layers, L in {1..10}, KL early exit
setup.baselines: greedy decoding of same model, self-consistency at matched samples, beam search B=4 and B=11 (FLOP-matched to full L sweep)
setup.benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH-500, MinervaMath, AMC23, AIME24, AIME25

claims.claim: Majority vote over the L-axis rollout pool improves over greedy decoding of the same frozen model on almost all cells, and beats FLOP-matched beam search.
claims.regime: iso_param vs greedy (about 11x more compute); iso_infer_flop vs Beam-11
claims.evidence_quote: EGLR-SC improves over greedy on 44/48 (model, dataset) cells across 8 instruction-tuned models and 6 math reasoning benchmarks, and outperforms FLOP-matched beam search on 11/12 cells.

claims.claim: Single-configuration recursion is not reliably beneficial; gains come from aggregation over configurations.
claims.evidence_quote: A single L without aggregation sometimes degrades accuracy (e.g., Qwen2.5-3B / MATH-500 at L = 10: 61.6% vs. greedy 64.6%). The reliable gain comes from aggregating over the L-axis pool via EGLR-SC.

claims.claim: Training-free recursion must stay close to the anchor state: a small fusion weight is stable, large weights collapse because drift compounds.
claims.evidence_quote: drops sharply at α = 0.5 (56.6%, −8.4 pp), and collapses at α ≥ 0.7 (near-zero at 0.9). Large α erases the anchor signal; the recursion then compounds drift errors.

numbers.what: MATH-500 oracle accuracy, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct: joint LxT vs T-only vs L-only
numbers.quote: on MATH-500 with Qwen2.53B-Instruct, the joint L×T oracle reaches 91.6%, +8.2 percentage points beyond the temperature-only oracle (83.4%)

numbers.what: EGLR-SC gain over greedy on MATH-500 across models
numbers.quote: On MATH-500, gains range from +1.8 pp (Qwen2.5-Math-7B) to +13.2 pp (Llama-3.1-8B), a universal, training-free lift from the L axis alone.

numbers.what: Kmax ablation on MATH-500 (Qwen2.5-3B, L=4)
numbers.quote: Accuracy rises from Kmax = 1 (63.2%) to Kmax = 3 (65.0%) then plateaus at Kmax = 4, 5 (64.8%, 64.6%).

numbers.what: Worst-case per-token overhead of a single EGLR run
numbers.value: below 5% over greedy (rho 0.05, Kmax 3, L 10, N 36)
numbers.quote: For ρ ≈ 0.05, Kmax = 3, L = 10, N = 36, worst-case overhead is below 5% over greedy.

numbers.what: Hyperparameters
numbers.quote: We use α = 0.2, Kmax = 3, τKL = 5×10−4 throughout.

numbers.what: Compute of FLOP-matched beam baseline
numbers.quote: Beam-11 is FLOP-matched to the full L = 0, . . . , 10 EGLR sweep (∼11.2× greedy).

limitations: Single L configurations show mixed gains (can degrade); KL early exit saturates at Kmax=3 and extending Kmax gives over-refinement; LxT pool analysis only on one model-dataset pair.
survey_notes: Training-free retrofit (sub-theme d). Loops the TOP-L layers (not middle layers), unlike 2605.23872 and ETD (2510.07358) which place the loop at mid-depth; a contrast for the 'which layers to loop' question. Stabilizes training-free recursion via anchor fusion (alpha<=0.2) and norm matching, analogous to the damped sub-stepping of 2605.23872: both find that the refined state must only nudge, not replace, the one-pass state. The headline gains rely on self-consistency over ~10 configurations (~11x compute); single-config recursion is near-neutral (65.0 vs 64.6 on MATH-500). Possible use as a rollout-diversity source for GRPO is proposed but not tested.

title: GramLoop: Training-Free Gram-Gated Replay for Robust Dense Prediction
relevance_reason: Training-free replay of a short block window in a frozen vision backbone (DINOv3), not a language model.
one_sentence: Replays blocks [21,23] of a frozen 40-block DINOv3 ViT-7B twice and gates each patchwise update by final-layer cosine-Gram drift from the standard trajectory, giving small robustness gains on shifted detection and segmentation benchmarks.
key_contributions: Training-free window replay in a frozen vision foundation model, controlled by a patchwise gate computed from final-layer Gram drift.
Separates where reliability is measured (final layer) from where the update is applied (loop endpoint); this placement is best in ablation.
At matched update strength, patchwise gating preserves Gram consistency better than uniform replay.

setup.model_sizes: DINOv3 ViT-7B/16 (40 blocks), frozen
setup.train_tokens_or_data: none (frozen backbone and heads)
setup.loops_train: n/a
setup.baselines: paired frozen DINOv3 baseline; uniform-gated replay; alternative gate/update placements
setup.benchmarks: COCO-O, COCO-P, COCO-C, ADE20K-C, ADE20K-P, clean ADE20K

claims.claim: Gram-gated replay of a mid window of a frozen DINOv3 improves every shifted benchmark over the paired baseline, at about 2x inference time.
claims.regime: iso_param (same frozen model, more inference compute)
claims.evidence_quote: GramLoop improves over the paired DINOv3 baseline on every shifted benchmark. Although the gains on the -C and -P suites are modest, they are obtained without training or parameter updates

claims.claim: Measuring drift at the final layer and applying the update at the loop endpoint is the best placement; naive replay can disrupt the relational structure the suffix expects.
claims.evidence_quote: Table 4 shows that measuring Gram consistency at the final layer while applying the accepted update at the loop endpoint performs best.

numbers.what: COCO-O gains (mAP, Effective Robustness)
numbers.quote: On COCO-O, it improves mAP by +0.252 and Effective Robustness by +0.250, while preserving clean ADE20K performance.

numbers.what: Replay configuration
numbers.quote: GramLoop replays blocks [21, 23] for K = 2 additional replays and measures each proposal's cosine-Gram drift at the final block.

numbers.what: Inference cost
numbers.quote: Table 5 reports 1.96× GPU-equivalent inference time with unchanged peak memory, making runtime the main trade-off.

numbers.what: Clean ADE20K change
numbers.quote: GramLoop also improves clean ADE20K by +0.165 mIoU.

limitations: Gains on corruption/perturbation suites are modest (fractions of a point); runtime roughly doubles; fixed K with no adaptive replay.
survey_notes: Vision analogue of training-free looping (sub-theme d). Loops a mid-depth window (blocks 21-23 of 40, ~0.55 depth), consistent with the depth-fraction rule of 2605.23872, and again needs a control mechanism (Gram gate) because naive replay disrupts what the frozen suffix expects. Gains are small (+0.25 mAP on COCO-O). Comparison is same-model iso_param with ~2x inference compute; no FLOP-matched baseline.

title: Hopping Too Late: Exploring the Limitations of Large Language Models on Multi-Hop Queries
relevance_reason: Interpretability analysis; its back-patching (re-feeding a later-layer state into an earlier layer) is a one-off, oracle-selected training-free loop, motivating looping of pretrained layers.
one_sentence: Shows two-hop queries are resolved sequentially (bridge entity early, second hop late) so later layers may lack needed knowledge; patching a later-layer hidden state back into an earlier layer fixes up to 66% of failures with oracle layer choice.
key_contributions: Two-hop query dataset and Patchscopes-based localization of a sequential latent reasoning pathway.
Back-patching: re-running part of the forward pass from an earlier layer with a later-layer state, giving the model more layers without parameters or training.
Identifies that the second hop starts too late in depth, a mechanistic motivation for extra depth or looping.

setup.model_sizes: LLaMA 2 7B and 13B, LLaMA 3 8B and 70B, Pythia 6.9B and 12B
setup.train_tokens_or_data: none (frozen models)
setup.loops_train: n/a
setup.loops_test: one back-patch from source layer to an earlier target layer (oracle over source-target pairs)
setup.baselines: same model without back-patching
setup.benchmarks: authors' two-hop query dataset

claims.claim: Re-running layers by patching a later-layer state into an earlier layer corrects a large share of previously incorrect two-hop answers, but only with oracle choice of layers.
claims.regime: iso_param (same frozen model, oracle layer selection)
claims.evidence_quote: correctly answering between 32%-66% of incorrect cases while keeping the correct cases at 100% across models and token positions.

claims.claim: Back-patching is not a practical inference method because the right source/target layers must be chosen a priori.
claims.evidence_quote: our current proposed method is not a practical inference method, as only a subset of back-patches generate the correct answer.

numbers.what: Share of incorrect cases fixable by some back-patch (oracle)
numbers.quote: We find that in up to 66% of previously incorrect cases there exists a back-patch that results in the correct generation of the answer

limitations: Back-patching success requires choosing optimal source/target layers (oracle over pairs); only two-hop queries; mechanistic decoding methods are approximations.
survey_notes: Motivational evidence for sub-theme d (training-free looping of pretrained layers): extra passes through earlier layers can recover failed compositional reasoning, but the 66% figure is an oracle over source-target layer pairs, not a deployable method. Not a looped model; do not cite as a looped-LM result.

title: ScaleNet: Scaling up Pretrained Neural Networks with Incremental Parameters
relevance_reason: Depth-expands pretrained ViTs (and Llama-3.2-1B) by reusing each pretrained layer's weights with per-instance parallel adapters, a relaxed retrofit loop; mainly vision.
one_sentence: Doubles the depth of pretrained ViTs by inserting layers that share weights with existing layers plus small per-instance parallel adapters, then continues training; beats stacking/interpolation baselines and from-scratch training of the deeper model at lower training cost.
key_contributions: Weight-sharing depth expansion of a pretrained model: new layers tie to original layers via a layer mapping (interleaving or cyclic stacking).
Per-instance adjustment parameters (LoRA or parallel adapter) so each reuse of a shared tensor can specialize; without them gradient norms grow and fluctuate.
Ablations on reuse count (2 best, 3 worse), placement (interleave best for isotropic DeiT, stacking at tail for hierarchical Swin).

setup.model_sizes: DeiT-Small/Base, Swin-Tiny/Small/Base (vision); Llama-3.2-1B (language)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: ImageNet-1K continued training (100 epochs typical); Llama-3.2-1B scaled model trained 3 epochs on Stanford Alpaca
setup.loops_train: each pretrained layer reused 2x (2x depth); 3x in ablation
setup.baselines: Random, Stack (StackBERT), Interpolate, SWA expansion baselines; deeper model trained from scratch; original pretrained model
setup.benchmarks: ImageNet-1K top-1, COCO detection, ADE20K segmentation, zero-shot commonsense (BoolQ, PIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC, OBQA)

claims.claim: A 2x depth-scaled DeiT-Base built by weight sharing plus adapters beats training the deeper model from scratch with a third of the epochs (excluding the cost of the source checkpoint).
claims.regime: iso_effective_depth vs from-scratch deep model; training compute not matched (source pretraining excluded)
claims.evidence_quote: With a 2× depth-scaled DeiT-Base model, ScaleNet achieves a 7.42% accuracy improvement over training from scratch while requiring only one-third of the training epochs

claims.claim: Reusing layers twice helps but three reuses hurts, suggesting a limit on how often a shared pretrained layer can be reused.
claims.regime: iso_param across reuse counts is not held (params grow with adapters); same data
claims.evidence_quote: increasing the reuse time to three leads to a performance drop, with DeiT-Base dropping to 82.27% and Swin-Base to 83.58%. This suggests that reusing the same parameters too many times can constrain ability of the model

claims.claim: Per-instance adjustment parameters stabilize training of the weight-shared expanded model; without them gradient norms increase and fluctuate.
claims.evidence_quote: when layer adjustment is not applied to the model, the gradient norms increase significantly, with fluctuations observed in the initial layers.

claims.claim: Which layers / ordering: interleaving reused layers is best for isotropic DeiT, stacking at the tail is best for hierarchical Swin.
claims.evidence_quote: For DeiT-Base, interpolating layers yields the best performance, achieving a Top-1 accuracy of 82.53%, compared to 82.23% for stacking layers

numbers.what: DeiT-Small ScaleNet vs from-scratch 24-layer model (ImageNet top-1, training hours)
numbers.value: 81.13% in 15.8 h vs 79.31% in 47.3 h (300 epochs from scratch)
numbers.quote: using ScaleNet with DeiT-Small for just 100 epochs achieved a top-1 accuracy of 81.13%, surpassing the accuracy of the fully pretrained model, while also reducing the training time to just 15.8 hours.

numbers.what: From-scratch 24-layer DeiT-Small at 300 epochs
numbers.quote: When pretrained for 300 epochs, the model's accuracy increased to 79.31%, but this came at a significantly higher cost of 47.3 hours.

numbers.what: Scaled DeiT-Base and Swin-Base top-1
numbers.quote: the scaled DeiT-Base model reaches 82.53% Top-1 accuracy, surpassing the strongest baseline while maintaining the lowest parameter overhead among expansion methods.

numbers.what: Llama-3.2-1B 2x scaled (Alpaca, 3 epochs) vs original, zero-shot commonsense average
numbers.quote: Overall, the scaled model achieves an average performance improvement of 0.92%. This experiment further demonstrates the generalizability of ScaleNet.

limitations: Doubling depth doubles inference FLOPs; three-fold reuse degrades; training-efficiency comparisons exclude the source model's pretraining; the LLM experiment compares an Alpaca-finetuned scaled model against the original checkpoint (no identically finetuned unlooped control stated).
survey_notes: Sub-theme d (upcycling dense checkpoints into weight-shared deeper models), vision-first. Same recipe family as Relaxed Recursive Transformers (shared layers + per-instance LoRA), but used to grow rather than compress. The 7.42% headline is vs a from-scratch deep model and excludes source pretraining cost, so it is not iso_train_flop. The Llama-3.2-1B result (+0.92% avg) lacks an identically finetuned unexpanded control as far as stated, so treat as unmatched. Reuse-count saturation (2 good, 3 worse) is consistent with retrofit papers that find limited benefit from many repeats of pretrained layers without training.

title: Speeding up Deep Model Training by Sharing Weights and Then Unsharing
relevance_reason: Trains BERT as a fully weight-tied (looped) stack for the first ~10% of steps, then unties; the final model is not looped, but it is a weight-sharing curriculum.
one_sentence: Pretrains BERT with weights shared across all layers for the first ~10% of iterations, then unties and trains to convergence; the untied model beats standard BERT at equal iterations and reaches baseline quality in about half the steps for some sharing units.
key_contributions: Share-then-unshare schedule: weight-tied (ALBERT-like) training first learns a common component, then layers specialize.
Untying point ablation: about 10% of total steps is best; sharing throughout (ALBERT) or never are both worse.
Sharing-unit ablation (A layers shared B times, e.g. 1x24, 2x12, 4x6) and simplified-model theory.

setup.model_sizes: BERT-large (24 layers) and BERT-base (12 layers), alternative embedding sizes
setup.train_tokens_or_data: English Wikipedia + BookCorpus, and XLNet pretraining data; 0.5M or 1M iterations at batch 512, sequence length 512
setup.loops_train: 24 tied applications (1x24) during the first 10% of steps; also 2x12, 4x6 units
setup.baselines: standard untied BERT trained for the same iterations (24x1)
setup.benchmarks: MLM accuracy, SQuAD v1.1/v2.0, GLUE

claims.claim: Sharing weights for the first ~10% of steps then untying improves BERT over the standard untied baseline trained for the same number of iterations.
claims.regime: iso_param, iso_data, iso_train_flop (same architecture, data and iterations)
claims.evidence_quote: Our experiments show that oftentimes under various settings, the best result is given by sharing weights for the first 10% of the total number of iterations.

claims.claim: Keeping weights tied throughout (ALBERT-style) is much worse; never sharing generalizes worse; untying around 10% is best.
claims.evidence_quote: If weights are shared throughout the entire pre-training process, the final performance will be much worse than without any form of weight sharing

claims.claim: With multi-layer sharing units, half the iterations match the baseline trained for full iterations.
claims.evidence_quote: SWE 4x6 and 2x12 trained for a half million iterations achieve similar fine-tuning results compared to the non-SWE baseline trained for one million iterations.

numbers.what: Untying point used
numbers.quote: untying at around 10% of the total number of training steps lead to the best performance.

numbers.what: Table 1 Wiki+Books (Baseline 0.5M, SWE 0.5M, Baseline 1M, SWE 1M): MLM acc, SQuAD avg, GLUE avg
Training schedule
numbers.quote: We adopt the training procedure in the TensorFlow official implementation in which a BERT model is trained for 1 million iteration steps

limitations: Only BERT (encoder MLM) studied; final model is untied so there is no inference-time looping or parameter saving; gains are small (e.g. about 0.7 pt SQuAD average at 1M steps).
survey_notes: Sub-theme a/d bridge: a weight-tied looped phase used as an initialization/curriculum for a dense model (the reverse direction of retrofitting dense -> looped). In BERT, tying for all of training (ALBERT-style) is reported to be much worse than untied at equal unique parameters, a useful iso-param data point against pure looping when depth is equal. Comparison is cleanly matched (same architecture, data, iterations). The paper text says 'Submitted to ICLR 2021', not an acceptance, so venue is null.

title: Retrofitting Recurrent Depth into a Pretrained Language Model: Installation, Extrapolation, Transfer, and Retention at Two Parameter Budgets
relevance_reason: Retrofits a pretrained dense LM (Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct) into a prelude/weight-tied recurrent block/coda model.
one_sentence: Converts Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct into a prelude/12-layer looped block/coda model with an identity-preserving gated re-entry bridge; per-loop intermediate-state supervision installs a stepwise operator (full-block 180M or 6M LoRA) that extrapolates about 1.5x its trained depth on a synthetic pointer-chasing task.
key_contributions: Identity-preserving retrofit: one-loop path reproduces the base exactly; split re-entry bridge re-injects the prelude output on loops 2..T under an identity-biased live gate.

Installation at two budgets (180.6M full-block vs 6.01M rank-16 LoRA over frozen base) with exact per-loop intermediate-state supervision followed by outcome-only annealing; adapter matches full block in-support, full block wins far tail.

Engineering lessons: per-parameter learning rates need separate tensors/optimizer groups (slice-gradient scaling is cancelled by Adam and Muon); zero-gate identity init is self-locking; learned halting fails.

setup.model_sizes: Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (24 layers; prelude 0-5, recurrent block 6-17, coda 18-23); dense controls 0.5B and 1.5B
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Synthetic scrambled rule-table composition task (depth 1-14 eval, 1,792 frozen rows); controlled verbal relay/pointer renderings; token counts not reported
setup.loops_train: forced loops = task depth; supports 4, 6, 8 (N16) and 12 (N24)
setup.baselines: Dense Qwen2.5-0.5B direct-answer SFT, 0.5B serialized-scratchpad SFT, 1.5B direct-answer SFT; adapter-budget recurrent arm
setup.benchmarks: synthetic composition depth family; ARC-Easy/ARC-Challenge at loop 1 (preservation); verbal relay/pointer surfaces

claims.claim: Prelude re-injection is required; without it iterated pretrained layers drift off-manifold within a few loops.
claims.evidence_quote: The re-injection is essential: without fresh access to the Prelude representation, iterated application drives states off the pretraining manifold within a few loops

claims.claim: A 6.01M-parameter LoRA retrofit over frozen base weights matches the 180.6M full-block retrofit overall (identical protocol), better in-support, worse beyond depth 11.
claims.regime: same surgery, same staged protocol and steps, different trainable-parameter budget (within-method ablation)
claims.evidence_quote: The adapter matched the full block overall (83.8% versus 84.0%), led through depth 11, and trailed beyond.

claims.claim: The recurrent retrofit beats a same-size scratchpad CoT SFT model overall and especially beyond its horizon, and is faster at batch 1; but training lineage, tokens and inference compute are not matched (system comparison).
claims.regime: iso_param on base checkpoint (0.5B vs 0.5B) but training history/FLOPs/inference compute unmatched; 1.5B arm unmatched
claims.evidence_quote: The recurrent model won overall, 84% versus 72%, retained 53% versus 2.5% beyond depth 10, and answered 7.6 times faster in fewer output tokens.

claims.claim: Differential learning rates for new retrofit parameters must be implemented as separate tensors in their own optimizer group; gradient-slice scaling silently fails under AdamW and Muon.
claims.evidence_quote: when retrofitting a recurrent bridge into a pretrained transformer, any parameter that needs its own learning rate must be a separate tensor in its own optimizer group.

numbers.what: trainable parameter budgets of the two retrofits
numbers.quote: installs at two budgets: 6M trained parameters over frozen base weights and 180M full-block.

numbers.what: layer split of Qwen2.5-0.5B (prelude/recurrent/coda)
numbers.quote: RoPE; RMSNorm; tied embeddings), split at a = 6 and b = 18. The Prelude computes an input-grounded representation p.

numbers.what: per-token FLOPs relative to base at T loops
numbers.quote: T loops cost (1 + T)/2 of a base forward pass, or 1.00x, 2.50x, 4.50x, and 6.50x base-model FLOPs per token at T = 1, 4, 8, and 12.

numbers.what: depth extrapolation frontier / supervised support
numbers.quote: The converted model learns a persistent loop-indexed state transition whose validity frontier scales at 1.44 to 1.50 times its supervised support.

numbers.what: extrapolation accuracy
numbers.quote: the operation extrapolates to roughly 1.5 times its supervised depth, holding 70% accuracy through depth 18.

numbers.what: persistence of stepwise states after 1,000 outcome-only steps (full block)
numbers.quote: after a final training phase which no longer graded them: 625 of 640 still held the correct intermediate answer, showing

numbers.what: off-task degradation with more forced loops on ARC-Challenge (earlier checkpoint)
numbers.quote: degraded progressively at deeper forced loops, decisively so by loop 8 (71 versus 155, p = 3.8e-14). Off task, extra loops are not free.

numbers.what: learned halting head accuracy over a working mechanism
numbers.quote: a halting head trained with supervised cross-entropy to the stated depth selected correctly on only 70/768 rows (9.11%)

numbers.what: installed vs fresh adapter at matched verbal training
numbers.quote: adapter verbal training begun from the installed mechanism outpaced matched fresh training by 18.6 points, including on a held-out test set.

numbers.what: retired eval-only stability damper effect
numbers.value: tail trace ratio 33.65 -> 2.91, 52 rescued vs 67 harmed
numbers.quote: at full strength it reduced the loop-8 tail trace ratio from 33.65 to 2.91 on a 512-row ARC-Challenge sweep without a clean answer-selection gain (52 rescued versus 67 harmed)

limitations: Single 0.5B substrate; synthetic/templated tasks only; dense comparison does not match training tokens, optimizer history, FLOPs or inference compute; single seeds for N24 and adapter arms; forced depth (learned halting failed); no external benchmark superiority; catastrophic interference when adding a second (inverse) operation at both budgets.
builds_on: Bae et al. 2024 relaxed recursive transformers
survey_notes: Retrofit sub-section (d). Agrees with Huginn/McLeish that input (prelude) re-injection is needed when looping pretrained layers; adds that a zero-initialized gate is self-locking (dead gradients) so identity init must stay 'live'. Retrofit is installed by per-loop intermediate-state supervision (deep supervision) on a synthetic task, not general LM data, so it is not comparable to McLeish/ETD/Closing-the-Loop LM benchmarks. Loop-1 non-inferiority on ARC but degradation at deeper forced loops off-task (extra loops are not free) echoes overthinking findings. Learned halting (supervised and PonderNet) failed, contrasting with exit-gate successes in Ouro/Closing the Loop at scale. Dense comparison is explicitly a system comparison, not iso-FLOP or iso-data. Optimizer lesson (Adam/Muon cancel slice gradient scaling) is relevant to any retrofit using per-group LRs. Single-author, unreviewed.

title: LoopUS: Recasting Pretrained LLMs into Looped Latent Refinement Models
relevance_reason: Post-training conversion of pretrained dense LLMs into encoder / looped reasoning block / decoder models.
one_sentence: Recasts Qwen3 (1.7B-8B), TinyLlama and Phi-4 into a shallow encoder, looped middle block and late decoder with a Mamba-style decay gate, random deep supervision with per-step detachment, a monotonicity loss and a confidence exit head, trained on 3B FineWeb-Edu tokens.
key_contributions: Block decomposition from layer-wise cosine-distance dynamics: tiny encoder (1-6 layers), 1 decoder layer, nearly the whole middle stack looped.
Input-dependent exponential-decay gate h' = a*M(h) + (1-a)*h as a damped, contraction-like update to limit hidden-state drift; SiLU monotonicity loss penalizes loops that raise next-token loss.
Random deep supervision: unroll B=20 loops, supervise K=5 uniformly sampled steps, detach between steps; reported to beat TBPTT in loss and cost.

setup.model_sizes: Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Phi-4 (14B), TinyLlama 1.1B
setup.train_tokens_or_data: FineWeb-Edu, 3B tokens, context 1024
setup.loops_train: B=20 loop steps, K=5 supervised depths per batch
setup.loops_test: max recursion budget 8 with confidence stopping (default); depth sweeps to 100
setup.baselines: Original backbone without adaptation; McLeish et al. 2025 and Bae et al. 2025 numbers copied from their papers
setup.benchmarks: WikiText, LAMBADA ppl; MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC-E, ARC-C, PIQA, WinoGrande, OBQA (zero-shot)

claims.claim: LoopUS-adapted checkpoints improve average zero-shot accuracy over the original backbones by +1.6 to +2.2 points (1.7B-14B), mostly on ARC-C/OBQA; MMLU/HellaSwag flat.
claims.regime: unmatched: adapted model (3B extra tokens, up to 8 loops of almost the whole stack) vs untouched base; no continued-pretraining control at equal tokens; inference FLOPs not matched
claims.evidence_quote: yields consistent gains across models, reducing WikiText and LAMBADA perplexities and improving average downstream accuracy by +1.6 to +2.2 points, with the clearest gains on ARC-C and OBQA.

claims.claim: On TinyLlama, LoopUS reports a larger gain (+6.3) with 3B tokens than McLeish et al. (-2.9 at 52B) and Bae et al. (+3.5 at 60B), but numbers are copied from the respective papers and the authors call it non-controlled.
claims.regime: unmatched (cross-paper numbers, different base checkpoints and token budgets)
claims.evidence_quote: Since prior results are drawn from the corresponding papers, we treat this comparison as an adaptation-efficiency reference rather than a fully controlled head-to-head benchmark.

claims.claim: Random deep supervision with per-step detachment beats truncated BPTT: TBPTT costs more and plateaus at higher LM loss; removing the selective gate also gives higher loss.
claims.evidence_quote: TBPTT [59] incurs higher computational cost while plateauing at a substantially higher LLM than the standard LoopUS training recipe, indicating lower efficiency and worse performance in this setting.

claims.claim: The gated loop extrapolates stably to far more loops than trained (no divergence up to 100 iterations), with gains saturating after a few iterations.
claims.evidence_quote: This stability extends well beyond the training regime: the checkpoint continues to behave robustly even at unseen recursion depths such as 40, 80, and 100.

numbers.what: training data budget and context
numbers.quote: streaming training on FineWeb-Edu with the CC-MAIN-2025-26 configuration [47], a total budget of 3B tokens, and sequence length 1024.

numbers.what: loop training configuration
numbers.quote: The loop-specific configuration uses 20 total reasoning steps with deep supervision on 5 loop positions per example, a training stopping threshold of 0.55, and the all stopping mode.

numbers.what: learning rate and warmup
numbers.quote: The reference script uses AdamW with a learning rate of 5 × 10−5 , one epoch over the token budget, bf16 mixed precision, FlashAttention-2 [60], cosine scheduling, 300 warmup steps

numbers.what: layer split for Qwen3-8B and Phi-4
numbers.quote: Qwen3-8B: Encoder layers 0–5, Decoder layer 35. • Phi-4: Encoder layers 0–5, Decoder layer 39.

numbers.what: TinyLlama adaptation-efficiency headline
numbers.quote: yielding a 14.6% relative gain on TinyLlama with 17–20× fewer training tokens than existing looped baselines.

numbers.what: TinyLlama average delta vs prior retrofits (cross-paper)
numbers.quote: LoopUS achieves the largest average gain (∆= + 6.3), compared with ∆= − 2.9 for McLeish et al. [10] and ∆= + 3.5 for Bae et al. [11], while using fewer additional training tokens.

numbers.what: average halting depth with confidence head (Qwen3-4B)
numbers.quote: With adaptive stopping enabled, the same checkpoint halts after 3.39 iterations on average out of a maximum budget of 8, yet remains close to the best observed performance.

numbers.what: per-depth KV cache speedup at 1024 generated tokens
numbers.quote: At 1024 generated tokens, KV caching yields a 1.64× speedup for Qwen3-1.7B, a 2.31× speedup for Qwen3-4B, and a 2.49× speedup for Qwen3-8B.

limitations: Text-only; moderate 3B-token post-training budget; no math or long-context evaluation (context 1024); no instruction tuning/RL; comparisons to prior retrofits are cross-paper; no equal-token continued-pretraining control and inference FLOPs not matched.
survey_notes: Retrofit (d) and gradients (c). Key design contrast: loops almost the entire stack (e.g. Qwen3-1.7B encoder 0-1, decoder 27) rather than a small middle block (ETD, McLeish), and uses no prelude re-injection, only a decay gate; contrasts with 2608.11233 and McLeish/Huginn which deem input injection necessary. Its per-step-detached random deep supervision is a one-step gradient variant; it reports TBPTT worse, while McLeish/Huginn use truncated BPTT successfully. The headline -2.9 for McLeish et al. on TinyLlama is a cross-paper number against the original checkpoint and should not be read as McLeish failing under its own matched control. Main Table 1 compares against the untouched base (no 3B-token continued-training control), so gains may partly reflect extra training; inference compute per token is multiplied by up to 8 loops of nearly the whole model. Project page URL in abstract: https://thrillcrazyer.github.io/LoopUS.

title: Penelope: Localized Latent Recurrence for Efficient Structured Reasoning
relevance_reason: Retrofits a pretrained decoder (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3.5-0.8B) with weight-shared recurrence over a selected layer interval for latent reasoning.
one_sentence: Runs the lower decoder prefix once, then recurs a shared late layer interval only over 8 memory and 2 readout slots (GRU/time-modulated updates, prompt KV cached), trained with a CoT-to-latent curriculum; matches Coconut accuracy on structured reasoning with lower latency.
key_contributions: Localized recurrence: only a 5-layer interval of Llama-3.2-1B ([11,16)) is re-applied, and only to fixed-size memory/readout positions against a cached prompt KV, so marginal cost per loop is r layers instead of L.
Progressive CoT-to-latent curriculum (Coconut-style): each stage removes one visible reasoning step and adds one latent refinement, K=1..6 then consolidation at K=6.

Matched-source comparison with Coconut/CODI/visible CoT (same source checkpoint, data, update count) plus a placement control showing early/middle/late/full intervals give statistically indistinguishable accuracy.

setup.model_sizes: Llama-3.2-1B (L=16); Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base cross-backbone control
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Deep ListOps (4,800 train), ProsQA (17,886 train), PrOntoQA (9,000 train); 1,500 or 3,000 optimizer updates
setup.loops_train: curriculum K=1..6, then fixed K=6
setup.loops_test: validation-selected fixed K (e.g. 5,4,2 on Deep ListOps; 1,1,6 on ProsQA)
setup.baselines: Visible CoT, Coconut, CODI, full-decoder recurrence, K=0 boundary-only diagnostic
setup.benchmarks: Deep ListOps, ProsQA, PrOntoQA (exact match), latency

claims.claim: Under matched source checkpoint, data and optimizer-update count, Penelope is within about 0.5 point of Coconut on Deep ListOps while cutting latency; parameter counts and training FLOPs are not matched (75.35M vs 11.28M trainable).
claims.regime: iso_data (same source, data, update budget); not iso_param, not iso_train_flop; inference compute favors Penelope
claims.evidence_quote: Under matched optimizer-update and data-exposure budgets, Penelope reaches 52.25 ± 0.72% EM, within 0.54 point of Coconut, while exceeding Visible CoT and CODI by 0.98 and 1.08 points, respectively.

claims.claim: Which layers are looped barely matters: early, middle and output-side 5-layer intervals are within 0.19 point; full-decoder recurrence is only 0.27 point better at 2.51x the layer calls.
claims.regime: within-method placement control (same source, curriculum, data, update budget, seeds; K=6)
claims.evidence_quote: Early, middle, and output-side recurrence lie within 0.19 point, while full-decoder recurrence is only 0.27 point above the outputside interval despite 2.51× more sequential decoder-layer applications.

claims.claim: Recurrence contributes only a small gain over the same checkpoint run with K=0 (boundary only).
claims.evidence_quote: K = 0 obtains 51.56 ± 0.81% pooled test EM, whereas independently validation-selected depths obtain 52.25 ± 0.72%.

numbers.what: recurrent interval and interface size
numbers.value: Llama-3.2-1B, L=16, interval [11,16), 8 memory + 2 readout states
numbers.quote: The experiments use Llama-3.2-1B (Dubey et al. 2024) with L = 16, the recurrent interval [ℓs , ℓe ) = [11, 16), eight latent interface states, and two readout states.

numbers.what: trainable parameters
numbers.quote: Runtime auditing gives Coconut 11.28M trainable parameters, while Penelope uses 11.27M LoRA plus 64.08M recurrent-module parameters (75.35M total).

numbers.what: LoRA and learning rates
numbers.value: rank 16, alpha 32; LR 2e-5 adapters, 1e-4 new modules
numbers.quote: The source uses rank-16 LoRA (Hu et al. 2022) (α = 32, dropout .05) on all attention and MLP projections. Penelope and Coconut continue these adapters at learning rate 2 × 10−5

numbers.what: curriculum schedule
numbers.value: K=u=1..6 in first half, then fixed K=6
numbers.quote: The first half of training traverses K = u = 1, . . . , 6 in equal update blocks; the second half fixes K = 6 and consolidates answer-only generation.

numbers.what: ProsQA EM
numbers.quote: On ProsQA, Penelope obtains 78.27±0.90% EM compared with Coconut's 79.87±1.80% and CODI's 78.27 ± 1.10%

numbers.what: Deep ListOps latency vs Coconut
numbers.quote: Their synchronized complete-subset means are 99.82 ± 0.65 and 188.15 ± 1.02 ms, a 46.9% reduction.

numbers.what: marginal sequential layer cost per extra refinement
numbers.quote: Equation 15 makes the marginal cost of one additional refinement r rather than L, and

numbers.what: replacing gated GRU transition with direct overwrite
numbers.quote: while retaining boundary memory and recurrent readout, lowers test EM from 52.25 ± 0.72% to 51.44 ± 0.35%.

numbers.what: Deep ListOps EM vs Coconut under matched updates and data
numbers.quote: Under matched optimizer-update and data-exposure budgets, Penelope reaches 52.25 ± 0.72% EM, within 0.54 point of Coconut

limitations: Only three synthetic structured-reasoning tasks at 1B scale; fixed validation-selected depth (no online halting); methods not parameter- or training-FLOP-matched; gains over the K=0 boundary are small and non-monotonic in K; latency at batch size 1 on one GPU.
survey_notes: Retrofit (d) / post-training (e). Training recipe is a Coconut-style CoT-to-latent curriculum on top of a LoRA-tuned visible-CoT checkpoint, i.e. distillation of explicit steps into loops; closest in spirit to LOTUS (2606.31779). Its placement control (early/middle/late/full intervals within noise at fixed K) contradicts the strong 'loop the middle reasoning layers' layer-selection arguments of ETD (2510.07358) and LoopUS (2605.11011), though only on synthetic tasks at 1B. The K=0 vs selected-K gap is only 0.69 point, so most of the accuracy comes from the boundary/curriculum, not from extra loops; not evidence of test-time depth scaling (authors say so). Recurrence is over memory slots, not token states: an architecture between looped transformers and latent-token methods.

title: SCOUT: Teaching Pre-trained Language Models to Enhance Reasoning via Flow Chain-of-Thought
relevance_reason: Fine-tunes a pretrained LLM (Qwen2.5-0.5B) into a head/recursive-block/tail looped model with per-iteration distillation.
one_sentence: Retrofits Qwen2.5-0.5B into a head / weight-tied recursive block / tail model run for T=3 iterations, supervising each iteration by KL to a progressively larger teacher (1.5B, 3B, 7B) and fusing the previous iterate via cross-attention; small average gains over SFT.
key_contributions: Progressive distillation: iteration t is supervised by a capacity-matched teacher (weaker teachers for early loops), versus uniform hard-label or fixed-teacher per-loop supervision.

Retrospective cross-attention module: self-attention over the initial state z(0), cross-attention over the previous iterate z(t-1); compared against init, additive, concat-project, gate and AdaLN-style injection.
Partition ablation: half of the layers as head and half as recursive block (tail = output projection) beats a 1/3-1/3-1/3 split by about 15 points under per-step SFT.

setup.model_sizes: Qwen2.5-0.5B student; teachers Qwen2.5-1.5B, 3B, 7B
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Instruction mix: Alpaca GPT4, Alpaca CoT, WikiQA, CodeAlpaca, MathInstruct; 2 epochs, LR 2e-5
setup.baselines: SFT, distilled SFT (7B teacher, no recursion), recursive hard-label SFT, recursive distillation with equal/increasing weights, reversed teacher order
setup.benchmarks: OpenBookQA, GSM8K, MBPP, ARC-e, ARC-c, TruthfulQA, CoQA, GLUE

claims.claim: SCOUT gives monotonic per-iteration gains over SFT on the same data (+0.23, +1.05, +1.81 average), the best among recursive variants; gains are small and no variance is reported.
claims.regime: iso_data and near iso_param (same 0.5B student plus cross-attention modules); inference compute and training FLOPs (teacher passes) not matched
claims.evidence_quote: SCOUT outperforms all baselines, with monotonic improvement across iterations (+0.23 → +1.05 → +1.81), and highest final performance (e.g., 35.5 on GSM8K, 52.4 on GLUE).

claims.claim: Uniform per-loop supervision (same hard labels or same 7B teacher at every iteration) stagnates or regresses with more iterations; reversing teacher order collapses at iteration 3.
claims.evidence_quote: R-SCOUT, which reverses teacher order (7B → 3B → 1.5B), initially achieves strong results (+1.47) but collapses in later steps (–0.42), confirming the necessity of aligning teacher strength with iteration depth.

claims.claim: Naive state-integration choices (init injection, additive, concat-project, gate, AdaLN modulation) degrade with more iterations when retrofitting; only cross-attention stays flat.
claims.regime: within-method ablation under per-step hard-label SFT
claims.evidence_quote: Naive fusion strategies such as Init, Add, and CatProj show diminishing returns with deeper iterations, suggesting limited support for long-horizon reasoning.

numbers.what: student, iterations and per-iteration teachers
numbers.quote: For progressive distillation, we assign Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen2.5-3B, and Qwen2.5-7B as teacher models for reasoning iterations 1, 2, and 3, respectively.

numbers.what: fine-tuning schedule
numbers.quote: We fine-tune the model for 2 epochs with a learning rate of 2 × 10−5 using the LlamaFactory framework [40].

numbers.what: headline gain
numbers.quote: Experiments across eight reasoning benchmarks show that SCOUT consistently improves both accuracy and explanation quality, achieving up to 1.8% gains under fine-tuning.

numbers.what: uniform fixed-teacher recursive distillation trajectory
numbers.quote: performance stagnates or regresses in later steps (R-Distill-EQ: +1.23 → –0.04 → +0.15).

numbers.what: average accuracy by iteration 1/2/3 (Table 2): Init, Add, CatProj injection
average accuracy by iteration 1/2/3 (Table 2): Gate, ModInj, XAttn (ours)
partition ablation: half-half split vs 1/3 split
numbers.quote: Consequently, iteration 1 already outperforms the entire Case-1 trajectory by +14.5–14.8 points.

limitations: Fixed T=3 and manually chosen teachers; single 0.5B student; small gains without variance; recursion adds inference compute not matched by baselines; layer-allocation space not explored beyond two splits.
builds_on: Looped transformers (Giannou et al.; Yang et al.)
survey_notes: Post-training/distillation (e) and retrofit (d). Per-loop supervision with a teacher-strength curriculum over depth is a distinctive deep-supervision variant; uniform per-loop targets were found to hurt later loops, consistent with the 'readout'/over-supervision concerns elsewhere but contrasting with Ouro/Huginn which use the same next-token target at every exit. Its partition result (no coda: half head, half looped, tail = only output projection) runs against McLeish/ETD/Huginn designs that keep a multi-layer coda, but evidence is weak (0.5B, garbled table, single seed). Additive input injection (Huginn-style) degraded sharply by iteration 3 in this retrofit, a contradiction with from-scratch findings that additive injection works at small scale. All gains are within ~2 points and the recursive model uses ~2x inference compute; treat as weak evidence.

title: LayerNorm as Implicit Gain Control in Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Stability analysis of the recurrence in Parcae-style gated looped transformers (pre-LN block, constrained diagonal carry).
one_sentence: Shows analytically and at toy CPU scale that pre-LayerNorm inside a looped block couples its Lipschitz constant inversely to activation scale, making the recurrence Jacobian non-normal; the spectral margin, not operator norm, is the stability budget, and Parcae's carry constraint stabilizes rather than stores memory.
key_contributions: Pre-LN acts as implicit gain control: block Lipschitz constant scales as 1/||h||; Jacobian is non-normal (operator norm > 1, spectral radius < 1 at fixed points), and the spectral margin shrinks as carry rho -> 1.
Identifies an activation-implosion failure mode (small activations -> Lipschitz spike -> divergence) and recommends monitoring per-token activation spread and max carry during training.

Shows gradient descent routes depth-memory through the nonlinear block rather than the constrained linear carry on cross-channel tasks; removing the carry constraint lets rho exceed 1 at high learning rate with state explosion hidden by the coda LayerNorm.

setup.model_sizes: toy: d = 8-32, 2-4 heads, CPU only
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Tiny Shakespeare (char-level), copy / windowed-copy synthetic tasks; e.g. 120-150 steps
setup.loops_train: T = 4 or 8 fixed loops
setup.loops_test: same as training (fixed-point analysis at init and after training)
setup.baselines: Parcae-constrained carry vs unconstrained free scalar carry; carry-ablated variants
setup.benchmarks: Tiny Shakespeare loss, synthetic copy tasks; Jacobian spectral radius / operator norm

claims.claim: The relevant stability budget of a pre-LN looped block is the spectral margin of the recurrence Jacobian, not an operator-norm bound, because LayerNorm makes the Jacobian non-normal.
claims.evidence_quote: it renders the recurrence Jacobian non-normal—asymptotically contractive at every verified fixed point even where its operator norm exceeds 1—so the true stability budget is the spectral margin, not an operator-norm bound.

claims.claim: A diagonal carry constraint rho < 1 (Parcae) is necessary but does not certify convergence of the full nonlinear recurrence; some initializations never reach a fixed point.
claims.evidence_quote: so the diagonal carry constraint is necessary but not sufficient for convergence of the full recurrence.

claims.claim: Without the carry constraint, gradient descent drives the carry above 1 at higher learning rates and the hidden state explodes; the coda LayerNorm keeps loss finite so loss curves can hide the failure.
claims.regime: ablation: constrained vs unconstrained carry, same model/data/steps
claims.evidence_quote: the loss stays finite even while the state explodes, because the Coda’s LayerNorm normalizes hT before the unembed—loss curves alone can hide this failure mode.

claims.claim: Small activations are the dangerous regime: activation implosion raises the block Lipschitz constant and leads to divergence, a failure mode distinct from residual explosion.
claims.evidence_quote: This predicts a failure mode distinct from residual explosion: activation implosion followed by divergence.

claims.claim: On cross-channel tasks gradient descent stores depth-memory in the nonlinear block and leaves the constrained carry at rest; the carry is recruited only on axis-aligned per-channel tasks.
claims.evidence_quote: gradient descent routes memory through the block’s more expressive nonlinear recurrence and leaves the stability-constrained carry at rest—the carry’s role is stabilization, not memory.

numbers.what: spectral margin 1 - rho_spec collapse as carry increases
numbers.quote: collapsing monotonically from 0.159 at ρ = 0.3 to 0.012 at ρ = 0.95

numbers.what: fraction of untrained instances that never converge to a fixed point
numbers.quote: a minority of untrained instances never converge to a fixed point at all (1/10 at low carry, 2/10 from ρ = 0.7;

numbers.what: unconstrained carry value and state norm at high LR
numbers.quote: gradient descent drives ρ past 1 at higher rates (1.20 at lr=3 × 10−2 , 1.84 at lr=10−1 ), with the state norm exploding to ∼9,570.

numbers.what: Lipschitz constant vs activation norm
numbers.quote: Small activations → dangerous. Lip(f ) spikes (∼17 at ∥h∥ ≈ 2 vs. ∼0.1 at ∥h∥ ≈ 218)

numbers.what: experimental scale
numbers.quote: All results are derived analytically and verified empirically at small scale (d = 8–32, 2–4 heads, sequence lengths 1–32, CPU only)

numbers.what: observed contraction threshold vs Banach bound (tanh toy)
numbers.quote: the observed threshold sits roughly 2× above the Banach sufficient condition.

limitations: All experiments at d <= 32, at most 4 heads, CPU; non-normality gap after training and at scale untested; training experiments use LayerNorm only; post-LN would lack the gain control; windowed copy only to k = 6.
builds_on: Saunshi et al. 2025 (Reasoning with latent thoughts)
survey_notes: Toy-scale theory complement to Parcae (2604.12946, assigned to scaling group): Parcae's spectral constraint on the diagonal carry plus prelude normalization; this paper adds pre-LN in-block gain control as a third stabilizer and brackets the stable regime (activations not too small: LN gain control; not too large: Parcae's prelude-norm growth at 1.3B). Practical diagnostics for the recipe table: monitor max carry, per-token minimum activation spread; loss curves can hide state explosion. No large-scale evidence; treat as mechanism hypothesis.

title: Simply Stabilizing the Loop via Fully Looped Transformer
relevance_reason: Diagnoses and fixes training instability of from-scratch looped LMs as loop count grows.
one_sentence: Identifies gradient oscillation and residual-state explosion as causes of looped-LM training collapse at high loop counts and fixes them parameter-free by feeding the previous loop output to every layer as the attention query (Attention Injection), training stably to 12 loops.
key_contributions: Diagnosis: at 12 loops a vanilla looped transformer hits a high-loss plateau with growing residual-state norm and oscillating early gradients, despite per-layer RMSNorm.

Fully Looped Architecture (previous-loop output available to every layer) plus Attention Injection (previous-loop state used as query, current stream as keys/values, reusing self-attention weights), no new parameters.
At 127M and 318M with Chinchilla 20 tokens/param on FineWeb-Edu, FLT trains stably to 12 loops where LT, input-injection LT and first-layer-AI LT collapse; +4.82 avg points over LT at 6 loops (base).

setup.model_sizes: small 127M (6 layers), base 318M (12 layers)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: FineWeb-Edu, 20 tokens per parameter (Chinchilla)
setup.loops_train: 3, 6, 9, 12 (fixed per model)
setup.baselines: vanilla Looped Transformer (LT), LT with input injection (LTi), LT with first-layer attention injection (LTai), FLT with residual-addition fusion (FLTres)
setup.benchmarks: WikiText-2 PPL, validation BPB, DCLM CORE, LAMBADA, PIQA, HellaSwag, OpenBookQA, ARC-E, ARC-C

claims.claim: Looped-LM training instability at high loop counts has two components: early gradient oscillation and residual-state explosion; per-layer RMSNorm alone does not prevent the explosion.
claims.regime: diagnostic, same backbone and setup across loop counts
claims.evidence_quote: Although all of our models already incorporate RMSNorm [Zhang and Sennrich, 2019] in each layer to regulate the output residual states, residual explosion still occurs.

claims.claim: FLT trains stably to 12 loops while other looped baselines collapse.
claims.regime: iso_param + iso_data + same loop count (looped vs looped variants)
claims.evidence_quote: enabling the Fully Looped Transformer to be trained stably up to 12 loop iterations, whereas other baseline looped models collapse in this regime.

claims.claim: At base size vanilla LT gets worse with more loops and collapses at 9, whereas FLT improves monotonically with loops; but at small size input-injection LT is best, so the gain is scale-dependent.
claims.regime: iso_param + iso_train_flop + iso_data (same params, loops, tokens, hyperparameters)
claims.evidence_quote: The original LT drops from 40.52 to 36.56 between 3 and 6 loops and collapses at 9 loops, while LTi and LTai show only fluctuating or saturated gains.

claims.claim: Fully looped connectivity with plain residual fusion only attenuates residual explosion; attention-based injection is needed for stable training.
claims.regime: ablation at matched params and loops
claims.evidence_quote: This indicates that FLA attenuates residual amplification, but is not sufficient by itself to guarantee stable training.

claims.claim: Models trained with fixed loops benefit from more test-time loops only within the training range; beyond it performance fluctuates.
claims.regime: same model evaluated at different loop counts
claims.evidence_quote: When the loop count at inference exceeds the maximum used during pretraining, performance begins to fluctuate, indicating that the model struggles to adapt to excessive computational resources.

numbers.what: FLT vs LT downstream average at 6 loops, base size
numbers.quote: In particular, at 6 loops, FLT outperforms the original LT by 4.82 absolute points, corresponding to a relative improvement of about 13.2%.

numbers.what: FLT base: WikiText-2 PPL and CORE from 3 to 9 loops
numbers.quote: At the base size, its Wiki2 PPL decreases from 40.47 to 38.44, its Core Metric rises from 15.37 to 16.16, and its validation BPB improves from 0.898 to 0.892.

numbers.what: FLT base downstream average at 9 loops
numbers.quote: FLT is the only variant whose downstream-task average consistently increases, reaching 41.72 at 9 loops

numbers.what: LT small: downstream average from 3 to 9 loops
numbers.quote: At the small size, its downstream-task average drops from 32.57 to 30.22, while Wiki2 PPL, validation BPB, and the Core Metric also worsen.

numbers.what: best small-size average (input-injection LT, 6 loops)
numbers.quote: LTi obtaining the best small-size average of 33.35 at 6 loops; LTai fails to converge in this setting.

numbers.what: model scales
numbers.quote: All baselines are trained at two scales: the small size (127M parameters, 6 layers) and the base size (318M parameters, 12 layers).

numbers.what: training data budget
numbers.quote: we scaled the number of training tokens used proportionally to the total number of model parameters, using 20 tokens per parameter.

numbers.what: loss / gradient choice
numbers.quote: Following Geiping et al. [2025], we use the standard next-token prediction loss, supervising only the last step.

limitations: Only 127M and 318M models; single run per configuration with no error bars; no non-looped dense baseline in main table; extrapolation beyond training loop count unstable.
survey_notes: Stability (b): residual-norm growth with loops persists despite per-layer RMSNorm, consistent with Parcae's norm-growth diagnosis; the fix is architectural (attention-mediated injection), not a spectral constraint. Input injection (LTi) is competitive at 127M but not sufficient at 12 loops/318M. Comparison is looped-vs-looped only at matched params, tokens and loops; no dense baseline reported in Table 1, so the paper does not show looping beats an iso-param or iso-depth dense model. Single seed. Recipe details: muP LR scaling, Muon + AdamW, zero-init output projections, last-step loss (as in Huginn). Extrapolation failure beyond training loops agrees with other fixed-loop papers.

title: On the Residual Scaling of Looped Transformers: Stability and Transferability
relevance_reason: Derives residual-branch scaling and learning-rate transfer rules specific to weight-tied looped Transformers, tested in LM pretraining.
one_sentence: Shows that weight sharing makes residual updates correlated across loops so the residual stream grows as Theta(N); the correct branch scale is 1/N (or lambda/(N sqrt L) for L-layer blocks), which bounds norms and makes the optimal learning rate independent of loop count.
key_contributions: Theory: with shared weights, per-loop residual updates align, so squared norm grows Theta(N^2) instead of Theta(N); 1/sqrt(N) depth scaling is insufficient and 1/N is required.
