Factored parameterization eps = lambda/(N sqrt L) separating loop correlation (1/N) from across-layer variance (1/sqrt L); stable LR depends only on unique depth L.
Experiments (L = 12/24/48, N = 1-8, up to 438M params, 10B FineWeb-Edu tokens): 1/N scaling keeps norms bounded, lowers loss at N = 8, and transfers the LR tuned at N = 1.

setup.model_sizes: Llama-style pre-norm, L = 12/24/48 unique layers; largest 438M parameters
setup.train_tokens_or_data: FineWeb-Edu, 10B tokens (20,000 steps, 0.5M-token batch)
setup.loops_train: N in {1, 2, 4, 8} for training; up to 64 in initialization diagnostic
setup.baselines: no residual scaling (eps=1), sqrt scaling (eps=1/sqrt N), linear scaling (eps=1/N); non-shared deep stacks as control
setup.benchmarks: FineWeb-Edu validation loss; residual-stream norm; cosine similarity of loop increments

claims.claim: Standard 1/sqrt(depth) residual scaling fails for looped networks because shared weights make residual updates correlated; 1/N scaling is required to keep the residual stream bounded.
claims.regime: same looped model, different residual scaling rules (initialization diagnostic and training)
claims.evidence_quote: We show that this is insufficient for looped architectures: weight sharing makes residual updates correlated across iterations, requiring the stronger scaling ε = 1/N .

claims.claim: With 1/N scaling the optimal learning rate depends only on unique depth L, not loop count N, so LR tuned at N = 1 transfers to larger N.
claims.regime: iso_param, iso_data LR sweeps across N
claims.evidence_quote: A key consequence is that the optimal learning rate depends only on the number of unique layers L, not on the loop count N , enabling direct hyperparameter transfer from small to large N without retuning.

claims.claim: Linear residual scaling gives lower loss than sqrt scaling at 8 loops.
claims.regime: iso_param + iso_data + iso_train_flop (same model and tokens, only eps changes)
claims.evidence_quote: at N = 8, linear scaling achieves a lower minimum loss than sqrt scaling (a reduction of 0.025 nats), indicating better trainability at larger loop counts.

claims.claim: Loop-step increments remain positively correlated after full training, so the mechanism persists beyond initialization.
claims.evidence_quote: the pairwise cosine similarities between loop-step increments decrease after full training, but the correlation matrix remains positive for most loop-step pairs across all three depths

numbers.what: loss reduction of linear vs sqrt residual scaling at N = 8
numbers.quote: linear scaling achieves a lower minimum loss than sqrt scaling (a reduction of 0.025 nats)

numbers.quote: The largest model trained in this work has 438M parameters and is trained for 10B tokens

numbers.value: 20,000 steps, 0.5M-token batch, WSD with 500 warmup steps
numbers.quote: Training uses FineWeb-Edu for 20,000 optimizer steps (10B tokens, 0.5M-token global batch), AdamW [14] with

numbers.quote: For L=48 with N =8, base learning rates above 2×10−3 cause divergence, consistent with the tighter stability margin at large effective depth.

numbers.quote: with early and middle iterations concentrated in the 0.3–0.6 range; only the latest steps show near-zero or mildly negative values

numbers.what: loop counts in initialization diagnostic
numbers.quote: We vary the number of loop iterations N ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64} and compare

limitations: Theory models the block as a shared-weight ReLU MLP without attention; finite set of sizes (<= 438M) and loop counts (<= 8 in training); single seed per configuration; Post-Norm and multi-stage looped architectures not covered; no downstream benchmarks.
builds_on: Saunshi et al. (Reasoning with latent thoughts)
survey_notes: Key recipe item for (a)+(b): scale each residual branch in the looped stack by lambda/(N sqrt L); then LR transfers across loop counts (contrast muP-style depth scaling used by FLT 2605.18797 and others). Diagnoses the same residual-norm growth with loops that FLT (2605.18797) and Parcae (2604.12946) report, but fixes it by parameterization rather than architecture or spectral constraint. Cites Ouro [31] for training instability at large N. Evidence is LM loss only (no downstream), <= 438M, 10B tokens, N <= 8, single seed. Gradient: end-to-end backprop through all N passes is implied; truncation not discussed. Compare with Training-free looped transformers (2605.23872), which uses inverse-loop-count step scaling for frozen models (as described here).

title: Stability and Generalization in Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Fixed-point theory and small-scale experiments on which recurrence design choices (recall/input injection, outer normalization) give stable, extrapolating looped transformers.
one_sentence: Frames looped-network stability as reachability, input-dependence and geometry of fixed points; proves autonomous (no-recall) loops have countable fixed points, and shows recall plus outer normalization gives reachable, input-dependent fixed points that extrapolate better on chess, sudoku and prefix sums.
key_contributions: Three 'axes of stability' (reachability, input-dependence, geometry) for fixed-point iteration; proof that autonomous looped networks have countable fixed points and no spectral regime gives a useful input-gradient.
Shows recall (input injection) plus outer normalization yields fixed points that are reachable, smooth in the input, and independent of the initial iterate; introduces 'internal recall' placement.
Single-layer looped transformers (~1M params) trained with truncated progressive loss on chess, sudoku, prefix sums: normalized recall models beat unnormalized and autonomous ones on harder OOD data.

setup.model_sizes: single-layer looped transformer, hidden 256; 0.98M-1.39M params; fixed 15-layer baselines 11.9M-17.8M
setup.train_tokens_or_data: prefix-sums (32-bit train, 512-bit test), sudoku, Lichess chess puzzles (40,000 train examples for sudoku/chess)
setup.loops_train: up to T = 30 iterations, progressive loss with random N no-grad + K grad iterations
setup.baselines: autonomous (no recall) looped models, external vs internal recall, outer-norm variants (none/pre/post/peri/GRU), fixed-depth 15-layer transformers
setup.benchmarks: validation (easy) and hard (OOD) exact-match accuracy on prefix-sums, sudoku, chess

claims.claim: Looped networks without input recall have countable fixed points and cannot achieve strong input-dependence; recall plus outer normalization yields reachable, locally smooth fixed points with stable backpropagation.
claims.evidence_quote: prove that looped networks without recall have countable fixed points and cannot achieve strong inputdependence at any spectral regime, while recall combined with outer normalization reliably produces a regime in which fixed points are simultaneously reachable

claims.claim: For autonomous networks no Jacobian spectral regime gives a useful training signal: contractive vanishes the input-gradient, expansive fails reachability, critical explodes parameter gradients.
claims.evidence_quote: We find that no regime provides useful training signal: ρ(J) < 1 causes the input-gradient to vanish exponentially, ρ(J) > 1 fails reachability, and ρ(J) = 1 induces exploding parameter gradients.

claims.claim: Outer normalization on recall models improves hard (OOD) accuracy over the best unnormalized recall model.
claims.regime: iso_data, near iso_param (looped variants differ only in normalization/recall)
claims.evidence_quote: The best normalized model performs 12 and 2 percentage points better on hard data than the best un-normalized model on sudoku and chess, respectively

claims.claim: Recall looped models (about 1M params) beat fixed-depth 15-layer models with an order of magnitude more parameters on sudoku and prefix sums and match them on chess.
claims.evidence_quote: If they were, fixed-depth models – which have an order of magnitude more parameters – would dominate across tasks, yet they are outperformed by recall variants on sudoku and prefix-sums, and only match them on chess

numbers.what: hard-data gain of best normalized vs best unnormalized model
numbers.quote: The best normalized model performs 12 and 2 percentage points better on hard data than the best un-normalized model on sudoku and chess, respectively

numbers.what: autonomous networks on prefix sums
numbers.quote: Notably, prefix-sums is the only problem on which autonomous networks achieve 0% accuracy across all configurations.

numbers.what: looped model parameter count
numbers.quote: Looped models with GRU had 0.98M parameters, while models without it had 1.39M.

numbers.what: fixed-depth baseline size
numbers.quote: Fixed (non-looped) models used 15 layers and had 11.9M parameters without GRU and 17.8M parameters with it.

numbers.what: progressive (truncated) loss
numbers.value: N no-grad iterations then K grad iterations; T = 30
numbers.quote: The model runs N iterations without gradients followed by K iterations with gradients; loss is computed and backpropagated only over the final K iterations.

numbers.what: optimizer stabilizers
numbers.value: gradient clip 1, exponential warmup over 10 epochs
numbers.quote: We apply an exponential warmup over the first 10 epochs, reaching 63% of the target learning rate by epoch 9

limitations: Only small single-layer transformers on three algorithmic tasks; axes of stability are closer to necessary than sufficient; best normalization/recall placement varies by task; no language modeling.
builds_on: Yang et al. 2024 (looped transformers learn learning algorithms)
survey_notes: Theory backing for two recipe items widely used empirically: input injection (recall) and outer normalization between loops; cites Huginn as finding outer normalization necessary and notes post-norm token clustering can cause the representation collapse Geiping et al. report. Gradient recipe: truncated progressive loss (random no-grad prefix, grad over last K) with alpha = 1 largely prevents overthinking beyond training depth. Learning rate drives the recall matrix spectral radius above 1 and into instability (same LR-instability link as LayerNorm-gain paper 2607.10681 and residual-scaling paper 2606.18524). Toy scale only; looped vs fixed-depth comparison is param-unmatched (fixed has ~10x params).

title: Stabilizing Recurrent Dynamics for Test-Time Scalable Latent Reasoning in Looped Language Models
relevance_reason: Diagnoses divergence of looped LMs beyond the training loop horizon and adds a Jacobian spectral-radius regularizer to stabilize recurrence, tested on Ouro-1.4B.
one_sentence: Shows looped LMs (incl. Ouro-1.4B) peak at some loop depth then collapse; normalization placement trades stability against effectiveness, and STARS (Jacobian spectral-radius regularization via one-step JVP power iteration plus random loop sampling) curbs degradation beyond the training horizon.
key_contributions: Diagnosis on 4-digit addition with a single looped block: pre-norm (internal) lets hidden-state norm grow without bound and diverge past the training horizon; post-norm (external) stays bounded but settles in poor attractors; prelude/coda layers and L2 state-difference regularization do not fix this.
STARS: regularize squared Jacobian spectral radius (single-step power iteration with JVP) at a randomly sampled loop depth, combined with log-normal random loop sampling.
On Ouro-1.4B fine-tuned on 400K NuminaMath samples, STARS keeps 65.55% average at 8 loops vs 52.97% for plain SFT, and raises the 4-loop peak, at about 2x training cost.

setup.model_sizes: toy single GPT block (d_model 512, 8 heads, d_ff 1024); Ouro-1.4B
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 100,000 4-digit addition samples; 400K-sample subset of NuminaMath-1.5 for Ouro fine-tuning (one epoch)
setup.loops_train: fixed T_train = 4 (diagnostics); log-normal random loops (range [1,100] toy; [1,16] Ouro)
setup.loops_test: swept beyond training horizon; 2, 4, 8 for Ouro benchmarks
setup.baselines: Ouro-1.4B base, Ouro-1.4B-SFT (same data), Ouro-Random Loop, Ouro-JSRR ablations; Recurrent-Llama-3.2 / Recurrent-OLMo-2 (McLeish et al.); Qwen/Llama/Gemma public models
setup.benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH500, ASDiv, SVAMP, AMC23; multi-digit addition accuracy

claims.claim: Normalization placement, not the normalizer type, determines looped dynamics; pre-norm lets the hidden-state norm grow without bound beyond the training horizon while post-norm stays bounded but ineffective.
claims.evidence_quote: Without a constraint mechanism after the residual addition, the norm of the hidden state tends to grow without bound.

claims.claim: Prelude/coda layers (Huginn-style) do not change the stability tendencies of the recurrence.
claims.regime: ablation, same task and loop count
claims.evidence_quote: Finding 3: The inclusion of Prelude and Coda layers does not alter the system’s dynamical tendencies.

claims.claim: Random loop sampling improves performance retention beyond the training loop count but does not fix effective stability and is sensitive to the sampling range; L2 regularization between consecutive states adds almost nothing.
claims.evidence_quote: Finding 4: Overall, sampling loop counts during training significantly enhances performance retention and generalization capabilities. However, it does not fundamentally transform the effective stability of the system and is sensitive to the size of the sampling range.

claims.claim: STARS fine-tuning of Ouro-1.4B reduces accuracy collapse when running more loops than trained and improves the peak over SFT on the same data.
claims.regime: iso_param + iso_data vs Ouro-1.4B-SFT (STARS uses ~2x training compute)
claims.evidence_quote: on GSM8K, while Ouro-1.4B experiences a 20.47% drop from its peak performance after 8 recurrent steps, our method degrades by only 8.26%.

numbers.quote: on GSM8K, while Ouro-1.4B experiences a 20.47% drop from its peak performance after 8 recurrent steps, our method degrades by only 8.26%.

numbers.quote: Moreover, our approach improves peak performance by 4.01% on GSM8K at the same time.

numbers.quote: peaking at an average accuracy of 74.18% at 4 recurrent steps

venue: Proceedings of the 43 rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea. PMLR 306, 2026.
survey_notes: Stability (b) + post-training (e): contractive (spectral-radius) regularization applied at fine-tuning time to a pretrained LoopLM. Contrasts with Parcae (2604.12946) which constrains only the linear carry by construction, and with LayerNorm-gain paper (2607.10681) which argues spectral margin is the right budget. Reports Ouro-1.4B degrades past 4 loops (Ouro trained with 4 loops), consistent with 'no extrapolation beyond training horizon' in FLT (2605.18797). Disagrees with Huginn-style intuition that prelude/coda help stability (toy evidence only). Comparisons to Qwen/Llama/Gemma in Table 2 are unmatched; the clean comparison is STARS vs SFT on the same 400K data and base, but STARS costs ~2.04x training compute. Single-step JVP power iteration keeps memory modest; no truncated-BPTT.

title: LoopMTP: A looped transformer guided by latent multi-token prediction
relevance_reason: From-scratch whole-stack looped LM with per-loop auxiliary (latent MTP) supervision and gated state aggregation.
one_sentence: LoopMTP loops a 12-layer 260M model, aligns loop t's hidden state (cosine) with the embedding of token t steps ahead, and aggregates all loop outputs with learned gates; it beats a parameter-matched non-looped model and LoopFormer at 6.8B tokens.
key_contributions: Latent soft multi-token prediction: per-loop cosine alignment of hidden state t to the (stop-gradient) output embedding of token i+t, a cheap per-loop auxiliary loss.
Gated softplus aggregation over all loop outputs (initialized to favor loop 1) plus a ponder KL-to-uniform regularizer, instead of overwriting the state.
Loop-LNS: fixed 1/T residual-branch scaling and per-iteration LayerNorms for stable training up to 15 loops without per-loop LR/WD/warmup tuning.

setup.model_sizes: LoopMTP 260M (L=12, d=1024); non-looped baseline 266M; LoopFormer 280M
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 6.8B tokens of Nemotron-CC-v2 high-quality subset + Nemotron-CC-Math-v1 (Sec. 5 expert: ~6.8B tokens of Nemotron-CC-Math-v1)
setup.loops_train: T in {3,5,7,9} (main); T in {3,7,9,11,13,15} (math expert)
setup.baselines: parameter-matched non-looped transformer (same depth, wider FFN); LoopFormer (2602.11451) with per-loop-count grid search
setup.benchmarks: PPL on FineWeb-Edu/OpenWebText; ARC-C/E, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, SIQA, PIQA, LAMBADA (OLMES); math suite BPB; HumanEval/MBPP BPB; GSM8K 8-shot

claims.claim: LoopMTP beats a parameter-matched non-looped model trained on the same 6.8B tokens on nearly every benchmark; it costs 2.49-7.05x the FLOPs, so the comparison is iso-param/iso-data, not iso-FLOP.
claims.evidence_quote: Despite being slightly smaller, L OOP MTP outperforms the non-looped baseline on nearly every benchmark: not only on reasoning-based tasks, but also on perplexity, general tasks, and QA suites.

claims.claim: Without the latent MTP auxiliary loss, math BPB degrades monotonically as loop count grows; with it, performance improves with loops.
claims.evidence_quote: The effect is most pronounced on math, where step-by-step reasoning is required: without MTP, increasing the loop count causes performance to degrade monotonically.

claims.claim: Residual scaling by running depth (1/((t-1)L+l)) shrinks later-iteration updates so much that their gradient contribution vanishes; a fixed 1/T factor is used instead.
claims.evidence_quote: yields tiny factors for later iterations of deep unrollings, which we found empirically neutralizes their gradient contribution.

claims.claim: LoopFormer training diverged from gradient explosion unless LR/WD/warmup were grid-searched per loop count, whereas LoopMTP trains stably with one fixed configuration.
claims.evidence_quote: LoopFormer's grid search targets training stability: without the right combination training diverges due to gradient explosion.

numbers.what: General-task average accuracy, LoopMTP (T=9) vs non-looped baseline
numbers.quote: it improves average accuracy by up to 8.08% over the non-looped baseline (50.02% vs. 46.28%)

numbers.what: Training data
numbers.quote: and Nemotron-CC-Math-v1 (Mahabadi et al., 2025) for 6.8B tokens.

numbers.what: Perplexity improvement over non-looped baseline
numbers.quote: improves perplexity by 10.5% on FineWebEdu and 11.2% on OpenWebText.

numbers.what: Math-expert GSM8K 8-shot, LoopMTP vs non-looped at matched params (~260M)
numbers.quote: our model reaches 19.03% accuracy on GSM8K. At matched parameter count, the non-looped baseline achieves only 7.05%

numbers.what: Training FLOPs relative to LoopFormer at matched T and tokens
numbers.quote: L OOP MTP requires only 0.59–0.60× the training FLOPs of LoopFormer, while achieving better performance.

numbers.what: FLOP cost relative to same-size non-looped baseline
numbers.quote: Relative to the non-looped baseline of the same size, L OOP MTP costs 2.49–7.05× the FLOPs at both training and inference for T =3–9.

numbers.what: Effect of weight decay on looped-model GSM8K
numbers.quote: Weight decay (WD) alone accounts for relative differences of up to 53% between the best- and worst-performing settings at a fixed number of iterations.

numbers.what: Max stable loop count
numbers.quote: improves average accuracy by up to 8.1% (relative) over the non-looped baseline, with training remaining stable for up to 15 loops.

limitations: Small scale (~260M, 6.8B tokens); math-expert runs single seed; only math domain for expert models; diminishing and non-monotonic gains at higher loop counts; not FLOP-matched to the dense baseline.
survey_notes: Training-recipe evidence: (a) per-loop auxiliary loss (latent MTP) as deep supervision; (b) stability via per-iteration LayerNorm + fixed 1/T residual scaling (Loop-LNS) + gate init favoring loop 1 (starts as a non-looped net); weight decay strongly matters for looped models (App. C; low WD gives vanishing grad norms). Reports LoopFormer instability (divergence) needing per-loop LR/WD/warmup sweeps, consistent with Closing the Loop 2610.00673 emphasizing warmup. Comparison is iso-param/iso-data only; looped model uses 2.49-7.05x FLOPs. Aggregating all loop outputs rather than last-state readout addresses 'latent overthinking'; relates to readout concerns in 2606.24898. MTP helps at small scale here, contrary to Gloeckle et al., per the authors.

title: DeepLoop: Depth Scaling for Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Residual-scaling/initialization rule for training stability of weight-tied looped transformers, with LM pretraining ablations.
one_sentence: DeepLoop shows weight tying makes shared updates aggregate across loop visits, derives a loop-aware DeepNorm rule (alpha=(2N)^1/2, beta=(8N)^-1/2), and improves looped GPT-2 small/medium validation loss at every R>=3 and HRM on ARC-AGI-1.
key_contributions: First-order perturbation bound for tied depth with a visit-alignment coefficient kappa_R; recovers DeepNorm p=1/4 for decorrelated visits and requires p=1/2 in the aligned fixed-physical-depth regime.
DeepLoop: Post-LN sandwich block with branch-input norm and alpha=(2N)^1/2, beta=(8N)^-1/2; no gates or auxiliary losses.
Extends to truncated-gradient hierarchical reasoners (HRM) by counting gradient-visible visits; +3.25 pp ARC-AGI-1 two-vote accuracy.

setup.model_sizes: GPT-2 small (124M) and GPT-2 medium (350M) looped backbones; HRM
setup.train_tokens_or_data: FineWeb-Edu 50B tokens (100K steps, context 1024, batch 480); HRM on arc-aug-1000
setup.baselines: same looped model with standard pre-LN block and standard init (no residual scaling); vanilla HRM
setup.benchmarks: FineWeb-Edu validation loss; lm-eval-harness 8 tasks (ARC-C/E, HellaSwag, OpenBookQA, PIQA, SciQ, SIQA, WinoGrande) 0/1-shot; ARC-AGI-1

claims.claim: At matched loop count, params, data and compute, DeepLoop's residual parameterization is neutral at R=1 and beats the pre-LN looped baseline in validation loss at every R>=3 at both scales (single seed).
claims.regime: iso_param + iso_data + iso_infer_flop (looped vs looped, same R)
claims.evidence_quote: DeepLoop is effectively tied with the baseline at R=1 and improves over it in these single-seed runs at R=3, R=5, and R=7 at both scales.

claims.claim: Weight tying changes residual scaling: the conservative aligned regime needs exponent p=1/2 rather than DeepNorm's 1/4 as loop count grows at fixed physical depth.
claims.evidence_quote: The bound recovers the DeepNorm exponent when visits decorrelate, but in the conservative aligned regime it requires the exponent to increase from 1/4 to 1/2 as loop count grows at fixed physical depth.

claims.claim: Empirical p-sweep at R=3: training escape from the unigram floor is unreliable through p=0.50 and universal only from p=0.55; smaller p gives lower loss when it trains.
claims.evidence_quote: escape is the minority outcome in the clearly sub-threshold region p ≤ 0.40, remains unreliable through p = 0.50, and becomes universal from p = 0.55.

claims.claim: Truncating gradients to the last outer cycle (HRM) puts the truncated module in the untied-DeepNorm regime; analysis counts only gradient-visible visits.
claims.evidence_quote: The truncation thus places H in the untied-DeepNorm regime even though H is

numbers.quote: The GPT-2 small runs use a GPT-MHA-RoPE model trained on FineWeb-Edu for 50B tokens (100K optimizer steps, context length 1024, global batch size 480)

numbers.what: Validation loss GPT-2 medium R=7: baseline vs DeepLoop
numbers.quote: at the medium scale the gap widens monotonically through R=7, reaching −0.028 nats.

numbers.what: Validation loss gap at small scale
numbers.quote: DeepLoop pulls ahead by −0.016 nats at R=3, the gap peaks at −0.023 nats at R=5, and remains open

numbers.what: GPT-2 medium 1-shot average downstream accuracy, DeepLoop R=7
numbers.quote: the best Avg cell in the table is DeepLoop R=7 in both shot settings, headlined by 55.20 % on 1-shot.

numbers.what: HRM ARC-AGI-1 two-vote accuracy, vanilla vs DeepLoop
numbers.quote: DeepLoop improves the paper-protocol two-vote accuracy from 36.50% to 39.75% (+3.25 pp) and improves every column of the voting ladder.

numbers.what: Per-seed escape fractions in p-sweep (p=0.30..0.60)
numbers.quote: the per-seed escape fractions are 0/5, 1/5, 2/5, 2/5, 3/5, 5/5, and 5/5 for p = 0.30, . . . , 0.60

limitations: Single-seed LM runs; only up to 350M and R=7; p-sweep is short-horizon (step 2000) and shows p=1/2 itself only 3/5 seeds escape; baseline is pre-LN, so architecture placement and exponent are changed together in main table; kappa_R not measured directly.
survey_notes: Stability sub-theme (b): residual-scaling rule specific to weight tying. Comparison is looped-vs-looped at same R (not looped vs dense). Note p-sweep shows the default p=1/2 is itself unreliable (3/5 seeds escape) at R=3 short horizon, so 'stability' is a soft threshold. Contrasts with LoopMTP 2608.03624 (fixed 1/T branch scaling under pre-norm) and with residual-scaling work 2606.18524; the sandwich norm it adopts comes from Huginn. Also treats truncated BPTT (HRM last-cycle gradient) as reducing the effective visit count, linking (b) and (c).

title: Scheduling Recursive Reasoning in Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Adaptive per-loop update step size (relaxation) for looped/recurrent models (TRM, Ouro, Huginn, training-free looped Qwen3), plus a training-time trajectory regularizer.
one_sentence: TAPS replaces the unit recurrent update X_{k+1}=X_k+Delta with an online-adapted step size driven by a persistent-progress vs fluctuation decomposition; it raises terminal accuracy of frozen TRM, Ouro, Huginn and looped Qwen3, and a co-design regularizer adds gains on Sudoku/Maze.
key_contributions: Exact decomposition of the temporally averaged loss sensitivity to recurrent step size into persistent-progress and centered-fluctuation terms.
TAPS: training-free online step-size controllers (six estimators) that need no labels; sufficient conditions for reaching a target loss in fewer loops.
Training-inference co-design: penalty mu*sum ReLU(S_k - kappa P_k) added to the task+ACT loss during SFT of a TRM checkpoint.

setup.model_sizes: TRM (Sudoku/Maze); Ouro-1.4B, Ouro-2.6B, Huginn-0125; Qwen3-4B-Instruct with training-free intermediate-layer recurrence
setup.train_tokens_or_data: no pretraining; co-design SFT from a pretrained Sudoku TRM checkpoint on Sudoku-Extreme
setup.loops_train: as released checkpoints; TRM horizons H=32 (Sudoku), H=16 (Maze)
setup.loops_test: fixed horizon K; Qwen3 intermediate-layer loop K=3
setup.baselines: unit-step inference (eta=1); constant eta=0.8/1.2; fixed-point inference; task-only SFT
setup.benchmarks: Sudoku-Extreme, Maze; MMLU, ARC-C, HellaSwag, GSM8K (Ouro/Huginn); CommonsenseQA, GPQA-Main, MMLU-Pro (Qwen3)

claims.claim: Adaptive step-size control improves terminal accuracy of frozen recurrent models without retraining, while fixed rescaling is inconsistent.
claims.regime: iso_param, same model and loop horizon
claims.evidence_quote: Table 1 shows that all six variants improve terminal accuracy and reach the unit-step baseline's terminal performance in less wall-clock time on both tasks.

claims.claim: On recurrent LMs (Ouro-1.4B, Huginn-0125) all TAPS variants improve average accuracy over unit steps; fixed rescaling can substantially degrade performance.
claims.evidence_quote: all six TAPS variants improve average accuracy over unit-step inference on both models, although the gains vary across tasks. In contrast, fixed rescaling is sensitive to the chosen scale and can substantially degrade performance

claims.claim: A training-time penalty on fluctuation exceeding progress (co-design SFT) reduces late-stage loss variability and improves held-out accuracy at matched training loss.
claims.evidence_quote: Co-design leaves the final training loss largely unchanged, but reduces its late-stage variability by 10.3%. At matched training loss, it lowers held-out terminal loss by 5.9%

numbers.what: Co-design best controller vs unit-step (Sudoku, Maze)
numbers.quote: the best controller reaches 91.39% accuracy at 1.300× speedup on Sudoku and 79.90% accuracy at 1.561× speedup on Maze, compared with 89.67% and 78.80% under unit-step inference.

numbers.what: Ouro-1.4B GSM8K row then Avg row across TAPS variants (unit-step Avg 61.10)
Co-design regularizer hyperparameters
numbers.quote: We use µ = 10−3 and κ = 4 in all co-design experiments.

numbers.what: Fixed-point inference comparison
numbers.quote: the accuracy that fixed-point inference attains after 1,000 updates is matched within roughly 260.

limitations: Theory rests on conditions linking trajectory statistics to task loss; controllers use local proxies; co-design is only a small SFT study on TRM Sudoku; LM gains vary by task and are small on Huginn.
survey_notes: Mainly an inference-time technique (update-scale / relaxation as a third control axis next to architecture and loop count); training relevance is limited to a small co-design regularizer (sub-theme a/b: trajectory-smoothness regularization during SFT). Related to stability-by-damping work (training-free looping uses smaller fixed steps; 2605.23872) and residual scaling (2606.18524, 2607.13491). Gains on Huginn are small (Avg ~38.87 to ~39.15); comparisons are same-checkpoint, so iso-param and iso loop count.

title: Loop Dropout: Regularizing Shared Updates in Looped Language Models
relevance_reason: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning rule for pretrained looped LMs (Ouro, Huginn, LoopUS) that targets per-loop imbalance of a shared LoRA update.
one_sentence: Standard LoRA on looped LMs is late-loop biased; Loop Dropout masks whole adapter applications per loop with inverse-survival rescaling, improving GSM8K/MATH-500 fine-tuning of Ouro-1.4B/2.6B and depth extrapolation, at no inference cost.
key_contributions: Diagnostic: a LoRA adapter trained on Ouro-1.4B reduces loss 32% when applied only at loop 4 but 12% when applied only at loop 1 (late-loop bias).
Loop Dropout: Bernoulli masks over complete adapter applications at each loop (p=0.5) with division by survival probability; plain masking without rescaling does not help.
Gains over LoRA, LoRA+, CoTo, LoRA Dropout on Ouro; shared adapters with Loop Dropout beat per-loop independent adapters; larger gains when evaluated at more loops than trained.

setup.model_sizes: Ouro-1.4B, Ouro-2.6B (4 loops); also LoopUS-Qwen3-4B (8 loops) and Huginn (32 loops)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: MetaMathQA 100k GSM-type examples, one epoch; Tulu 2 100k for instruction tuning; direct GSM8K recipe
setup.loops_train: 4 (Ouro default); also 6
setup.baselines: LoRA, LoRA+, CoTo, LoRA Dropout, rsLoRA; unscaled masking; per-loop independent adapters
setup.benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH-500, HumanEval+/MBPP+ (EvalPlus), MMLU, BBH, TruthfulQA, IFEval

claims.claim: With all four loops active, a standard shared LoRA update is much more effective at later loop positions than earlier ones.
claims.evidence_quote: For Ouro-1.4B fine-tuned on GSM8K with standard LoRA, loss reduction falls from 32% when the update is applied at the fourth loop to 12% when applied at the first, relative to the same frozen model.

claims.claim: Randomly omitting adapter applications alone does not help, because it shrinks the expected training update relative to inference; inverse-survival rescaling is required.
claims.evidence_quote: Randomly omitting adapter applications alone, however, does not improve task performance; it reduces expected update strength during training while leaving inference unchanged.

claims.claim: Loop Dropout improves math fine-tuning at both Ouro sizes versus LoRA under matched examples, steps and LR-search budget.
claims.evidence_quote: On Ouro-1.4B, GSM8K accuracy increases by 1.19 percentage points over LoRA, while MATH-500 rises from 38.87% to 47.53%, an 8.67-point gain. On Ouro-2.6B, the corresponding gains are 1.11 and 4.33 points.

claims.claim: Adapters trained at 4 loops transfer better to deeper recurrence with Loop Dropout; advantage grows with evaluation depth.
claims.evidence_quote: For adapters trained at four loops, Loop Dropout exceeds LoRA by 2.98 and 4.75 percentage points on GSM8K when evaluated at six and eight loops, respectively.

numbers.what: GSM8K at 8 loops (trained at 4), Loop Dropout vs LoRA
numbers.quote: At eight loops, Loop Dropout achieves 75.6% accuracy, compared with 70.8% for LoRA.

numbers.what: Single-loop loss reduction range with Loop Dropout
numbers.quote: Figure 1b shows that Loop Dropout maintains loss reductions of 31–36% across all four loops, narrowing the disparity between early and late applications.

numbers.what: Trainable adapter parameters
numbers.quote: giving 15.1M trainable parameters on Ouro-1.4B and 30.3M on Ouro-2.6B. Loop Dropout uses p = 0.5.

numbers.what: MATH-500 gain from masking: shared vs independent per-loop adapters
numbers.quote: On MATH-500, the gain is 11.40 points with shared adapters, compared with 4.80 and 4.40 points with independent rank-four and rank-sixteen adapters.

numbers.what: LoopUS-Qwen3-4B gains over LoRA
numbers.quote: on LoopUS-Qwen3-4B, the gains are 1.59 percentage points on GSM8K and 6.20 points on MATH-500.

numbers.what: Instruction tuning gains on Ouro-1.4B
numbers.quote: On Ouro-1.4B, Loop Dropout improves HumanEval+ by 2.24 points and TruthfulQA MC2 by 0.87 points over LoRA.

limitations: LoRA-only post-training (no full fine-tuning or pretraining); fixed loop count Ouro checkpoints; modest GSM8K gains (~1 pt) versus larger MATH-500 gains; three seeds.
survey_notes: Post-training sub-theme (e): PEFT of looped LMs. Key fact: a shared adapter learns mostly a late-loop update; randomizing which loops apply it (with rescaling) helps, analogous to Ouro/Huginn randomizing loop count in pretraining. Shared+masked beats per-loop independent adapters, so parameter-untying across loops is not what helps. Comparison is adapter vs adapter on the same frozen looped backbone (iso-param/data/inference FLOPs). Also evaluates Huginn (32 loops) and LoopUS-Qwen3-4B. Backprop through all 4 loops implied (LoRA on the shared block, final-loss training).

title: Dense Supervision Is Not Enough: The Readout Blind Spot in Looped Language Models
relevance_reason: Controlled study of per-loop (dense) cross-entropy, readout normalization, and hidden-state norm drift in looped LMs.
one_sentence: Per-loop cross-entropy through scale-invariant (RMSNorm/LayerNorm) readouts trains usable early exits but cannot see hidden-state scale, so norms drift to tens of thousands in pre-norm loops; raw readouts, norm penalties, or inter-loop normalization fix it.
key_contributions: Readout blind spot: dense CE controls only the state variables the readout exposes; normalized readouts give ~zero radial gradient while pre-norm residual recurrence carries and updates scale.
2x2 ablation {terminal-only, per-loop CE} x {RMSNorm, raw readout} at 44M/129M plus norm-penalty and final-only-norm controls.

Norm drift makes models nearly K-invariant (extra loops barely change the normalized state), so its cost appears in the depth dimension; scale-controlled variants give a better PPL-throughput frontier.

setup.model_sizes: 44M and 129M looped transformers (controlled); 1.4B Ouro-scale sanity check
setup.train_tokens_or_data: WikiText-103, 4 epochs, 3 seeds; 1.4B check on FineWeb ~1.3B tokens (50,000 steps)
setup.baselines: terminal-only CE; per-loop CE with RMSNorm readout; raw readout; final-only norm; norm penalty (lambda=0.01); inter-loop normalization
setup.benchmarks: WikiText-103 validation PPL and final-loop hidden-state norm; throughput; 1.4B downstream evaluation

claims.claim: Per-loop CE through RMSNorm readouts still lets final hidden-state norms drift into the tens of thousands in loops without inter-loop normalization; scale-visible readouts and norm penalties keep norms in the tens.
claims.evidence_quote: The key negative result is per-loop + RMSNorm: it receives a CE loss at every loop, yet reaches final-loop norms of 39,207 at 44M and 56,051 at 129M. Raw readouts keep norms in the tens under both terminal-only and per-loop CE.

claims.claim: Dense supervision trains exits; scale control needs a scale-visible loss or removing scale from the loop (inter-loop normalization).
claims.evidence_quote: The resulting design rule is simple: dense supervision trains exits; recurrent scale control requires either making scale visible to a loss or removing it from the loop.

claims.claim: Norm drift costs depth use: RMSNorm per-loop models become nearly K-invariant (additional loops barely change the normalized state), whereas scale-controlled variants improve with more loops and achieve lower PPL at matched K/throughput.
claims.evidence_quote: with final-loop norms in the tens of thousands, angular updates shrink like 1/sk , so additional loops barely change the normalized state the readout sees.

claims.claim: At 1.4B Ouro-scale with inter-loop RMSNorm, both checkpoints are essentially K-invariant after ~1.3B tokens, consistent with inter-loop norm bounding scale.
claims.regime: near-matched tokens, not a controlled ablation
claims.evidence_quote: Both checkpoints are essentially K-invariant on this slice (CE varies by less than 0.01 nats across K=2,3,4), which is consistent with Ouro's inter-loop RMSNorm bounding in-loop scale

numbers.what: Norm penalty with RMSNorm readout: final-loop norms
numbers.quote: even with the same RMSNorm readout, an explicit scale-visible loss collapses norms to 17–27.

numbers.what: PPL gap raw readout vs RMSNorm readout at matched K
numbers.value: 0.30 PPL lower at K=1 (~80k tok/s); 0.42 at K=4 (~21k tok/s)
numbers.quote: At equal throughput (K = 1, about 80k tokens/s), raw readout is 0.30 PPL lower than RMSNorm. At full depth (K = 4, about 21k tokens/s), the gap is 0.42 PPL.

numbers.what: 1.4B sanity-check training tokens
numbers.quote: corresponding to near-matched training token counts: 1.321B tokens for the baseline and 1.303B tokens for the no-readout-norm checkpoint.

numbers.what: Per-token heavy-tail of norm drift
numbers.value: median 12-21x smaller than mean; 1% tokens reach 10^5+
numbers.quote: RMSNorm-readout drift is concentrated in a heavy tail of outlier tokens, especially under per-loop CE: the median is 12–21× smaller than the mean

limitations: Main evidence at 44M/129M on WikiText-103 with inter-loop normalization deliberately removed; architectures with inter-loop normalization, gating or clipping may avoid the failure; 1.4B check not a controlled ablation; teacher-forced scoring rather than autoregressive serving.
survey_notes: Links (b) stability and (c) deep supervision: per-loop CE (as in Ouro's exit-weighted per-loop loss) does not by itself prevent hidden-state norm growth; inter-loop normalization (Ouro, LoopMTP per-iteration LN) or a norm penalty does. Explains why some looped models become K-invariant (extra loops do nothing) despite dense supervision; relevant to 'depth extrapolation' claims. Complements Fully Looped Transformer 2605.18797 (residual explosion) and STARS 2605.26733 (Jacobian spectral radius). Small-scale; 1.4B check shows both variants K-invariant at 1.3B tokens, which also cautions that short-horizon Ouro-style training may not yet exploit loops.

title: What Makes Looped Transformers Perform Better Than Non-Recursive Ones
relevance_reason: Loss-landscape explanation of looped vs non-looped training dynamics plus a depth curriculum (train non-looped, then switch to looping).
one_sentence: Argues looping induces steep V-shaped valleys in a River-Valley loss landscape that let optimization keep progressing on complex patterns, and proposes SHIFT: train the single-pass model first, then switch to looping, matching looped accuracy with ~1.26x faster training on a toy task.
key_contributions: Empirical observations: looped attention shows a two-phase simple-to-complex learning curriculum and a three-phase Hessian eigenspectrum evolution (collapse, diversification, stabilization); single-pass and deeper non-looped (Deep-Attn) models stay static.

Extended River-Valley landscape theory distinguishing U-shaped (flat) and V-shaped (steep) valleys; theorems on deeper river exploration and positively aligned gradients between single-pass and looped models (shared river upstream).
SHIFT depth curriculum (T=1 then T>1) with a plateau-plus-patience switch criterion (SCP).

setup.model_sizes: toy single-attention-layer models; GPT-2-style blocks with embedding dim 256 for algorithmic tasks
setup.train_tokens_or_data: synthetic Markov language dataset; Parity, Addition, Copy, Binary Sum, Unique Set (from Fan et al. 2025); 50,001 steps
setup.loops_train: fixed loops in toy model; FOP-Loop-Adaptive (T loops for length-T sequences) on algorithmic tasks
setup.loops_test: adaptive stopping for longer sequences (length generalization)
setup.baselines: Single-Attn (same block, one pass); Deep-Attn (3 untied attention layers) for Hessian analysis; pure Looped-Attn
setup.benchmarks: training/validation accuracy, length generalization accuracy, training time

claims.claim: Looped attention follows a simple-to-complex two-phase curriculum while the single-pass model stalls after simple patterns, attributed to a V-shaped-valley landscape bias.
claims.regime: iso_param (same block, looped vs single pass)
claims.evidence_quote: we conjecture that the recursive architecture of Looped-Attn induces a landscape-level inductive bias towards River-V-Valley.

claims.claim: A non-recursive 3-layer model (Deep-Attn) shows the same static Hessian spectrum as single-pass, so the effect is attributed to recursion, not depth alone.
claims.evidence_quote: We find that the spectral shape and evolution of Single-Attn (Figure 8) and Deep-Attn (Figure 10∼12) are nearly identical.

claims.claim: SHIFT (single-pass first, then looped) reaches comparable final performance to pure looped training with less training time; the switch point matters (too early suboptimal, too late fails to converge).
claims.regime: same model and data, training-time comparison
claims.evidence_quote: SCP selects a shift point between 100 and 150 epochs. This achieves a training speedup of approximately 1.26× without compromising final performance

numbers.what: SHIFT training speedup vs pure Looped-Attn (Markov dataset)
numbers.quote: This achieves a training speedup of approximately 1.26× without compromising final performance (Figure 5(b)).

numbers.what: Algorithmic-task training setup
numbers.value: dim 256, AdamW lr 1e-4, 50,001 steps, one RTX 3090
numbers.quote: We use the AdamW optimizer with a learning rate of 1e-4. All models are trained for a total of 50,001 steps.

numbers.what: Max Hessian eigenvalue Single-Attn vs Deep-Attn (value matrix)
numbers.quote: with maximum eigenvalues of a similar small magnitude (e.g., λmax ≈ 0.83 for Single-Attn and λmax ≈ 0.28 for Deep-Attn Layer 1).

limitations: Theory on simplified linear-attention models; landscape properties are conjectures from empirical observation; only toy/synthetic algorithmic tasks; on GPT-2-based tasks accuracy collapses temporarily at the switch.
builds_on: Looped Transformers for Length Generalization (Fan et al. 2409.15647)
survey_notes: Sub-theme (a) curriculum over depth: SHIFT is an extreme depth curriculum (T=1 then T>1), consistent in spirit with retrofit curricula (2511.07384 schedules recurrence) and with the claim that non-recursive pretrained models can be turned into looped ones by fine-tuning. Evidence is toy-scale only; speedup ~1.26x and switching causes a temporary accuracy collapse on GPT-2-based tasks. Iso-param looped vs single pass; Deep-Attn used only for Hessian comparison. Loss computed only at the final loop (no deep supervision) in the algorithmic setup.

title: LoopRPT: Reinforcement Pre-Training for Looped Language Models
relevance_reason: RL objective applied directly to the latent loop steps and exit gate of Ouro looped LMs (1.4B, 2.6B).
one_sentence: Applies reinforcement pre-training to Ouro LoopLMs: entropy-selected hard tokens, per-loop rewards (log-prob gain vs EMA teacher minus time penalty), Gaussian-noise latent rollouts with GRPO on the exit step; small gains and fewer average loops.
key_contributions: Dense per-loop reward: student log-prob of the true next token at loop k minus EMA-teacher log-prob at the teacher's exit step, minus a difficulty-scaled time penalty.
On-policy exploration in latent space via Gaussian noise injected into recurrent hidden states; GRPO over sampled exit steps plus a step-weighted next-token representation loss.
Reduces average exit loops (e.g. 3.51 to 2.28 on hard tokens, Ouro-2.6B) with small benchmark gains over its own Ouro starting checkpoint.

setup.model_sizes: Ouro-1.4B and Ouro-2.6B (initialized from the released Ouro checkpoints)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: OMNI-MATH: 4,428 competition problems with solutions (200 held out), 3 epochs, max length 4096
setup.loops_train: K = 4 latent loops with Ouro exit gate
setup.loops_test: K = 4 (Peak) or adaptive early exit; forced depth 1-4
setup.baselines: Ouro-1.4B/2.6B (authors' reimplementation of evaluation), Qwen3-1.7B vanilla and CoT, public 1-12B dense models (numbers copied from Ouro paper)
setup.benchmarks: Next-token reasoning on OMNI-MATH held-out (easy/medium/hard entropy buckets); MMLU, MMLU-Pro, BBH, ARC-C, HellaSwag, Winogrande, GSM8K, MBPP(+), HumanEval(+)

claims.claim: Per-loop RL on the latent steps improves hard-token next-token-reasoning accuracy while cutting average loops versus the same Ouro checkpoint without LoopRPT.
claims.regime: iso_param (same Ouro checkpoint before vs after LoopRPT; no equal-data NTP/SFT control)
claims.evidence_quote: On Ouro-2.6B, LoopRPT boosts Hard Peak accuracy by +3.58 while reducing average steps from 3.51 to 2.28.

claims.claim: Standard output-token RLVR is mismatched to looped models because Ouro's dynamic early exit causes instability and credit-assignment problems; LoopRPT moves reward to latent steps.
claims.evidence_quote: the dynamic early-exit mechanism—which adaptively determines computation depth—introduces instability and credit assignment issues for standard RLVR alignment.

claims.claim: Downstream gains over Ouro are small on general tasks and largest on math/code (e.g. GSM8K 81.76 to 85.36 at 2.6B); comparisons to Qwen/Gemma/Llama use numbers copied from the Ouro paper.
claims.regime: iso_param vs own Ouro checkpoint; unmatched vs public dense models
claims.evidence_quote: At the 2.6B scale, GSM8K accuracy increases from 81.76 to 85.36, alongside improvements in HumanEval+

claims.claim: Forcing more loops does not monotonically help: forced-depth accuracy can drop for medium and hard tokens, because later loops are not trained to refine monotonically.
claims.evidence_quote: forced-depth accuracy is not guaranteed to improve monotonically as depth increases, and may even degrade for Medium and Hard buckets.

claims.claim: Ablation: removing the representation loss plus exit-entropy bonus hurts most; removing Gaussian latent noise or PG+KL also raises average exit steps.
claims.evidence_quote: Removing Lrep + Lent yields the largest degradation in both accuracy and efficiency, underscoring that representation regularization and entropy shaping are vital for learning effective latent transitions.

numbers.what: Hard-token Peak accuracy gain and average loop reduction, Ouro-2.6B
numbers.quote: On Ouro-2.6B, LoopRPT boosts Hard Peak accuracy by +3.58 while reducing average steps from 3.51 to 2.28.

numbers.quote: At the 2.6B scale, GSM8K accuracy increases from 81.76 to 85.36, alongside improvements in HumanEval+

numbers.quote: LoopRPT delivers consistent gains over Ouro, particularly in coding (MBPP+ +2.91) and mathematical reasoning.

numbers.quote: O MNI -M ATH contains 4,428 competition-level mathematical problems paired with solutions, among which 200 examples are held out as the validation set.

numbers.what: Training compute
numbers.quote: Each training run takes approximately 2 hours for Ouro-1.4B and around 4 hours for Ouro-2.6B.

numbers.what: Epochs and sequence length
numbers.quote: We train for 3 epochs with a maximum sequence length of 4096 and use the AdamW optimizer.

numbers.quote: For each training example, we independently sample 8 times from an isotropic Gaussian distribution

numbers.what: EMA teacher momentum
numbers.quote: The teacher parameters are maintained as an exponential moving average of the current student parameters (momentum 0.995)

limitations: Only two Ouro scales and one small math dataset (OMNI-MATH, 3 epochs); no equal-data next-token/SFT fine-tuning control, so RL vs plain continued training is not separated; public dense baselines copied from the Ouro paper; gains on general benchmarks are below 1 point; forced extra loops can hurt. Authors list larger scales, broader data mixtures, and early-exit robustness under distribution shift as future work.
survey_notes: Post-training (e): RL whose actions are latent loop/exit decisions, not tokens. Credit assignment: per-loop reward table R(k) = (student log-prob at loop k minus EMA-teacher log-prob at teacher exit step) minus time penalty; policy gradient over sampled exit steps from noise-perturbed recurrences (score-function, reward not backpropagated), plus a dense step-weighted per-loop NTP loss (deep supervision over loops; whether gradients are truncated across loops is not stated). Despite the name, it is a small fine-tuning stage on 4,428 math problems from Ouro checkpoints, not pretraining. Main regime is iso_param before/after on the same checkpoint with no equal-data NTP control. Agrees with Ouro's statement that its early exit complicates RLVR. Forced-depth non-monotonicity agrees with reports that looped LMs do not extrapolate past the training depth unless trained for it.

title: Prioritize the Process, Not Just the Outcome: Rewarding Latent Thought Trajectories Improves Reasoning in Looped Language Models
relevance_reason: RLVR post-training of Ouro looped LMs, spreading the policy-gradient credit over every loop's next-token distribution.
one_sentence: Replaces GRPO's final-loop log-probability with a weighted sum of per-loop log-probabilities (exit-probability, progressive or uniform weights); on Ouro-1.4B/2.6B-Thinking it beats GRPO on math and transfers to non-math benchmarks.
key_contributions: RLTT: drop-in GRPO replacement whose policy gradient uses the weighted sum over loops of log P^(t)(y_j), so the outcome reward reaches every loop's readout.
Same-data, same-step, same-rollout comparison against GRPO on Ouro-1.4B/2.6B-Thinking, with paired significance tests and per-loop (1-4) evaluations.
Shows the only extra cost is memory, which grows linearly with loops (per-loop log-probs are kept); RLTT gives shorter responses and 10% less training time.

setup.model_sizes: Ouro-1.4B-Thinking and Ouro-2.6B-Thinking; non-looped baselines Qwen3-1.7B/4B + GRPO, DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B/7B
setup.train_tokens_or_data: MATH training split; 140 optimization steps, prompt batch 32, 8 rollouts per prompt, max generation length 2048
setup.loops_train: 4 loop iterations
setup.baselines: GRPO on the same Ouro checkpoints (matched data/steps/rollouts); SFT (loop-level table); Qwen3+GRPO trained on same MATH data; DeepSeek-R1 distills (public)
setup.benchmarks: MATH-500, AIME24, AIME26, BeyondAIME, GSM8K, ARC-C, MMLU-ST, GPQA, MBPP

claims.claim: Spreading reward over the latent trajectory beats terminal-loop GRPO on hard math, with matched base checkpoint, data, steps and rollouts.
claims.regime: iso_param + iso_data + matched training steps (GRPO vs RLTT from same Ouro checkpoint); decode budgets differ (GRPO allowed longer math outputs)
claims.evidence_quote: RLTT yields statistically significant improvements over GRPO on challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks, improving mean accuracy over MATH500, AIME24/26, and BeyondAIME by +5.8% on the 1.4B scale, and +10.9% on the 2.6B scale.

claims.claim: The authors attribute earlier failures of RLVR on LoopLMs to terminal-only credit assignment: GRPO rewards only the last latent state.
claims.evidence_quote: standard policy-gradient objectives such as GRPO only reward the last latent state before token emission, implicitly assuming a single-step decision process.

claims.claim: The gain is not sensitive to the per-loop weighting scheme (uniform, progressive, exit-probability), so exposing all loops to the reward matters more than the schedule.
claims.evidence_quote: RLTT’s performance is largely insensitive to the precise loop-weighting strategy used to distribute credit

claims.claim: RLTT's extra cost is memory, which grows linearly with loop count; tokens packed per GPU had to be halved compared with GRPO.
claims.evidence_quote: The practical overhead is instead memory, which scales linearly with the number of loops because RLTT must retain per-loop log-probabilities to form the trajectoryweighted objective.

claims.claim: RL-tuned Ouro beats Qwen3 + GRPO trained on the same MATH data, but the base models were pretrained differently, so this comparison is unmatched.
claims.regime: unmatched (different pretrained base models; same RL data)
claims.evidence_quote: Ouro1.4B+RLTT reaches 46.0% mean benchmark accuracy, outperforming both Qwen3-1.7B+GRPO (27.2%) and Qwen34B+GRPO (31.7%), while Ouro-2.6B+RLTT further improves to 51.2%

limitations: Only Ouro-Thinking checkpoints (the paper says Ouro is the only open-source LoopLM it knows of); a single short RL run (140 steps, MATH only); math evaluation decode budgets differ between GRPO (3072) and RLTT (512-3072); the Qwen3 baselines use a different learning rate (1e-4 vs 1e-6) and different pretraining; memory grows with loop count. No explicit limitations section.
venue: Proceedings of the 43 rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea. PMLR 306, 2026.
survey_notes: Post-training (e). Credit assignment over loops: policy gradient = sum over loops t of w_t * grad log P^(t)(y_j) * advantage, so every loop's readout is trained toward the rewarded token (a policy-gradient form of per-loop deep supervision); KL only on the terminal loop. Strongest controlled RL-on-loops evidence: same Ouro checkpoint, data, steps and rollouts (iso_param/iso_data/iso_train). Caveats: GRPO gets a larger decode budget on math; Qwen3+GRPO uses lr 1e-4 vs 1e-6 for Ouro. Internal inconsistency to flag: Table 2 GSM8K at 2.6B is 93.9 (GRPO) vs 94.0 (RLTT), but the loop-level Table 9 reports +34.3 at 4 loops on GSM8K, so the Table 9 evaluation setting (likely budget or checkpoint) differs and should not be mixed with Table 2. Agrees with Ouro that terminal-only RLVR gives little gain on LoopLMs; complements LoopRPT (2603.19714), which also gives dense per-loop RL signal but over exit decisions with an EMA teacher. Cites LSRL (Huginn + GPT-4.1-nano per-depth process rewards) as an expensive alternative.

title: Latent Thinking Optimization: Your Latent Reasoning Language Model Secretly Encodes Reward Signals in Its Latent Thoughts
relevance_reason: Trains a reward model on Huginn-3.5B's per-recurrence latent states and uses it to select latent trajectories; the LM weights are not updated.
one_sentence: Shows Huginn-3.5B latent trajectories from correct and incorrect answers are separable, trains a small Latent Reward Model on them, and uses KL-regularized rejection sampling over random-init trajectories to beat majority voting at equal sample budget.
key_contributions: Analysis: Huginn-3.5B recurrent-step trajectories (T=32) that lead to correct answers are compact and convergent, while incorrect ones are dispersed; a classifier on the first few steps already predicts correctness.

Latent Reward Model (a 2-layer transformer encoder over the stacked latent states) plus LTO, an acceptance-rejection sampler for the KL-regularized optimal latent policy (best-of-N in the beta -> 0 limit).
Gains over majority voting and verbal or confidence self-correction at N=20 samples on math, commonsense and code; also applied to non-looped LLMs by treating layers as latent steps.

setup.model_sizes: Huginn-3.5B (main); OLMo-7B, Llama-2-7B/13B, Mistral-7B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen-3-4B (layer-wise latents)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: LRM trained on 5 sampled trajectories per training problem (50 for MBPP) from GSM8K, SVAMP, CommonsenseQA, MBPP train splits
setup.loops_train: Huginn not retrained; LRM trained on T=32 recurrent steps (also 16/24 in ablation)
setup.loops_test: T = 32 default; 16 and 24 in Table A3
setup.baselines: Base model, majority voting, self-correction with confidence or verbal evaluation, CoE-R/CoE-C latent correction, LRM-weighted majority voting; all with N=20 samples
setup.benchmarks: GSM8K, GSM-Symbolic, SVAMP, CommonsenseQA, MBPP

claims.claim: A lightweight classifier on Huginn's recurrent latent trajectory predicts answer correctness well (near-perfect on SVAMP, about 0.8 ROC-AUC on MBPP).
claims.evidence_quote: On SVAMP, it achieves an ROC-AUC score close to 1.0, while on MBPP it achieves an ROC-AUC score of around 0.8.

claims.claim: At equal sampling budget (N=20), LRM-guided selection of latent trajectories beats majority voting and text-space self-correction on Huginn-3.5B on all five datasets.
claims.regime: iso_infer_flop approx. (same model, same N=20 candidate trajectories; LRM scoring adds small cost)
claims.evidence_quote: Across all datasets, LTO consistently outperforms both the base model and the best baseline for thinking correction.

claims.claim: With more recurrence steps (16 to 32), LTO's gain shrinks because random-init trajectories become less diverse, leaving fewer problems with mixed correct and incorrect samples.
claims.evidence_quote: This is attributed to the reduced diversity in the sampled latent thoughts and answers when longer thinking steps are used.

claims.claim: LTO only resamples and does not change the policy, so it cannot help when every sampled latent trajectory is wrong; the authors suggest moving the LRM signal into RL or preference optimization.
claims.evidence_quote: LTO cannot improve the latent thinking processes, since every generated latent thinking trajectory remains incorrect.

numbers.quote: Base Model Majority Voting Self-Correction w. Confidence Score Self-Correction w. Verbal Evaluation Latent Thinking Correction w. CoE-R Latent Thinking Correction w. CoE-C 0.326

numbers.what: Huginn-3.5B GSM8K: LRM-weighted majority voting and LTO
numbers.quote: Weighted Majority Voting w. LRM Latent Thinking Optimization w. LRM 0.375∗ 0.385∗

numbers.quote: On SVAMP, it achieves an ROC-AUC score close to 1.0, while on MBPP it achieves an ROC-AUC score of around 0.8.

numbers.what: Max relative gain of LTO on general (non-looped) LLMs
numbers.quote: LTO achieves substantial performance gains across diverse datasets, with an improvement of up to 103% over the base model, even with a modest sampling budget (N = 20).

numbers.quote: We adopt the default setting with sampling budget N =20 and latent thinking steps T =32

numbers.quote: For LTO and the baselines, we allocate a sampling budget of N =20 per problem.

limitations: Test-time selection only (no LM parameter update), so it fails when every sampled trajectory is wrong; the reward is binary correctness only; the Huginn base accuracy is low (GSM8K 0.326) and absolute gains are a few points; trajectory diversity, and so the headroom, shrinks with more recurrence steps.
venue: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026
survey_notes: Belongs under (e) post-training / test-time reward modeling over loop states, not RL training: LTO is reward-guided rejection sampling over Huginn trajectories (diversity comes from random initial-state seeds), with a 2-layer transformer latent reward model on all T steps. Regime: same model and equal N=20 candidates for all methods (approximately iso inference). Useful evidence that per-loop latent states carry a correctness signal, which motivates per-loop process rewards (compare RLTT 2602.10520 and LoopRPT 2603.19714, which turn per-loop signals into training gradients). The Table A3 finding (diversity across random initial states falls as recurrence steps grow) is consistent with Huginn's path-independence claim. Non-looped LLM results treat layers as latent steps, so they are not evidence about recurrence.

title: Energy-Entropy Regularization: The True Power of Minimal Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Training regularizer for a tiny single-head looped transformer on a synthetic induction-head task; no language-model scale.
one_sentence: Adds Tsallis-entropy (attention contraction) and Hamiltonian kinetic/potential penalties to the loss so a d=8 single-head looped transformer learns induction heads and generalizes from training length 16-64 to length 1000.
key_contributions: Entropy-based contraction bound for single-head looped attention, motivating a Tsallis-entropy penalty that keeps the recurrence contractive.
Energy-entropy regularized objective (task + kinetic + potential + entropy terms) that reshapes the loss landscape to train a minimal looped model.
d=8 single-head looped model with T=25 loops reaches length-1000 induction accuracy beyond a larger FOP-Looped-Adaptive baseline.

setup.model_sizes: single-head looped transformer, d = 8 (baseline FOP-Looped-Adaptive, d = 64, 4 heads)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: synthetic induction-head sequences, lengths 16-64; 20k training steps
setup.baselines: FOP-Looped-Adaptive (Looped GPT-2, Fan et al.), different size, steps and learning rate
setup.benchmarks: induction head task, length generalization up to L = 1000

claims.claim: The energy-entropy regularized d=8 looped model length-generalizes to L=1000 and beats a much larger looped baseline; the baseline differs in size, heads, steps, learning rate and loss, and there is no same-model cross-entropy-only ablation.
claims.evidence_quote: The EER framework achieves successful length generalization up to L = 1000, significantly outperforming the baseline despite having less than 0.02% of its parameter count

claims.claim: Training shows a phase transition: length-1000 accuracy jumps as the kinetic-energy penalty damps the latent dynamics.
claims.evidence_quote: the model undergoes a distinct phase transition around epoch 500, where the accuracy of length 1000 (Acc L1000) jumps from 33.5% to 79.2%.

numbers.what: Length-1000 accuracy before and after the phase transition
numbers.quote: the model undergoes a distinct phase transition around epoch 500, where the accuracy of length 1000 (Acc L1000) jumps from 33.5% to 79.2%.

numbers.what: Training lengths and loop count
numbers.quote: we train our d = 8 model on sequence lengths L ∈ [16, 64] with Ttrain , Teval = 25

numbers.what: Regularizer coefficients
numbers.quote: Following empirical tuning, we set λP = 0.1, λK = 0.001, λS = 0.02, q = 1.5 and η = 0.

limitations: One synthetic task (induction head) and one tiny model; the baseline is not matched in size, steps, learning rate or loss, and there is no same-architecture cross-entropy ablation; results appear to come from a single run, and the author reports sensitivity to hardware numerical noise (TF32 vs FP32).
survey_notes: Relevant only to (b) stability: explicit contractivity of the recurrence via an attention-entropy penalty plus damping of latent velocity. It is evidence that contractive regularization helps tiny looped models optimize and length-generalize, but it is weak (unmatched baseline, one task, single run). Do not cite it as evidence at LM scale. Agrees in spirit with the fixed-point/contraction view of stable looping (DEQ-style).

title: Closing the Loop: Practical Training Recipes for Looped Language Models
relevance_reason: From-scratch and dense-to-loop training recipes for Ouro-style whole-stack looped LMs with controlled dense twins.
one_sentence: Two-stage 310B-token recipe for a 1.4B Ouro-architecture LoopLM (warmup plus larger exit-gate KL coefficient), a one-scalar dense-to-loop conversion of Qwen3-1.7B, and controlled dense twins matched in parameters, data, or inference compute.
key_contributions: From-scratch recipe: one 210B-token pretraining run plus 100B-token response-only mid-training at fixed T=4; LR warmup prevents early exit-gate collapse and beta=0.15 lets it recover; about 3% of Ouro's training compute.
Dense-to-loop conversion with one learned input-mixing scalar and an epsilon-smoothed exit loss; step-specific LoRA is optional.

Controlled comparisons: dense twins share data, stages and tokens, matched in parameters (1.4B) or in inference compute (3.9B); ablations of normalization placement, embedding injection, and RL (RLTT).

setup.model_sizes: 1.4B LoopLM (24-layer shared block, Ouro-1.4B architecture); dense twins 1.4B (24 layers) and 3.9B (72 layers); Looped Qwen from Qwen3-1.7B-Base (28 layers) vs Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base continued
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 210B pretraining + 100B mid-training (HRM-Text mixture, response-only loss); conversion 60B curated instruction tokens or 84B web-scale tokens
setup.loops_train: T=4 (from scratch); T=3 (conversion)
setup.loops_test: fixed exit at 1-4 iterations (k=3 is the inference-matched point); Looped Qwen fixed exit after 2 of 3 steps
setup.baselines: dense-ouro-1.4B, dense-ouro-3.9B (same data and stages); Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base continued on identical data; published models (Ouro-1.4B, Huginn-3.5B, Qwen, Llama, Gemma) as context only
setup.benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH, MATH500, DROP, MMLU, MMLU-Pro, ARC-C/E, HellaSwag, Winogrande, CRUXEval-I/O

claims.claim: At equal parameters and identical data/stages, 4-step LoopLM-1.4B beats its dense twin on all 12 benchmarks (training compute is about 4x the dense twin's, so not iso-training-FLOP).
claims.evidence_quote: At equal parameter count, four-step LoopLM outperforms dense-ouro-1.4B on all 12 benchmarks.

claims.claim: At matched inference compute (3 loops vs a 72-layer dense twin on the same data), the dense model is ahead or level on every benchmark; the looped model's advantage is parameter count.
claims.evidence_quote: At equal inference compute the larger dense model is ahead or level on every benchmark, and the advantage of LoopLM at this point is its size.

claims.claim: Without Ouro's staged schedule the exit gate collapses to exit-after-loop-1; LR warmup prevents the early collapse and a larger KL/entropy coefficient beta lets the gate recover; LM loss does not reveal the collapse.

claims.claim: Normalization placement around the shared block matters: post-norm and sandwich-norm fail to train because gradients vanish through the block; a final norm before the LM head removes loss spikes.
claims.evidence_quote: Post-norm and sandwich-norm fail because gradients vanish through almost the entire decoder block, and this failure persists across warmup lengths, batch sizes, and normalization parameterizations.

claims.claim: Naively looping a pretrained decoder degrades later steps; one learned embedding-mixing scalar plus a smoothed exit loss yields refinement, and per-step LoRA adds little.
claims.regime: iso_param + iso_data (vs Qwen3-1.7B-Base continued on same data for same steps)
claims.evidence_quote: We show that looping the pretrained decoder as it is degrades the representation, that one learned scalar stops this degradation and that adapters are optional.

Training FLOPs are never matched (LoopLM costs 1.4x dense-3.9B per token). Contradictions: (1) sandwich-norm, used by Huginn (2502.05171), fails to train in this Ouro-style whole-stack setup; (2) concatenation input injection (Huginn-style) hurts from scratch (+0.12 nats), yet for conversion of a pretrained decoder an input-mixing scalar is required; (3) step-specific LoRA (Relaxed Recursive Transformers 2410.20672) unnecessary; (4) Ouro reported no RL gain, here RL helps only at mid solve rates; (5) Think-at-Hard (2511.08577) gains not reproduced. title: Teaching Pretrained Language Models to Think Deeper with Retrofitted Recurrence
relevance_reason: Converts pretrained fixed-depth LMs into Huginn-style prelude/recurrent-block/coda models via continued pretraining with a recurrence curriculum.
one_sentence: Performs model surgery on TinyLlama, OLMo-2 and Llama-3.2 1B models (drop middle layers, loop later layers with a concat adapter), trains with a curriculum over mean recurrence, and beats the parent model on math per training FLOP.
key_contributions: Pretrained-weight initialization of a (2,4,2) recurrent model beats random init per training FLOP; extrapolated loss curves cross only at roughly 950B tokens.
Curriculum that linearly or 1-sqrt schedules the mean of the Poisson-Lognormal recurrence distribution; scheduling max backprop depth is cheaper per FLOP but worse per step.
Recipe details: early layers as prelude, later layers as core and coda, Muon instead of AdamW, and a two-phase data curriculum with a FineWeb-Edu healing phase before high-quality data.

setup.model_sizes: ~1B parents (TinyLlama-1.1B-3T, OLMo-2-0425-1B, Llama-3.2-1B); recurrent (4,8,4) TinyLlama ~700M and (4,6,4) OLMo ~900M unique params
setup.train_tokens_or_data: ~120B FineWeb-Edu (init study); ~50B Nemotron-CC-Math-v1 (math runs); 26B or 52B (two-phase) FineWeb-Edu + Nemotron-Pretraining-SFT mixes
setup.loops_train: Poisson-Lognormal with mean 4, 8, 16 or 32 (curriculum-scheduled); backprop through last 8 recurrences
setup.baselines: non-recurrent parent model post-trained on the same data in the same order; random-init recurrent model; Huginn-0125 published numbers
setup.benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH, Arc-E/C, HellaSwag, Winogrande, MMLU, PIQA, OpenbookQA

claims.claim: Initializing the recurrent model from pretrained layers is far more efficient than random initialization (same architecture, same data).
claims.evidence_quote: We show that initializing parameters of recurrent models from those of a pretrained fixed depth model is significantly more efficient than using a random initialization (Figure 2).

claims.claim: A curriculum that slowly raises the mean recurrence keeps loss while reducing training cost; scheduling the max backprop depth instead is FLOP-efficient but worse per step.
claims.regime: iso_data and iso_train_flop curves (recurrent vs recurrent)
claims.evidence_quote: We propose a curriculum over recurrent depths, slowly increasing the average number of recurrent iterations during training to maintain performance while improving training speed (Figure 3).

claims.claim: At equal training FLOPs on the same data order, retrofitted recurrent models with fewer unique parameters beat the non-recurrent parent on GSM8K/MATH, and keep improving where the parent plateaus.
claims.regime: iso_train_flop + iso_data (recurrent has fewer unique params than the parent)
claims.evidence_quote: In all cases, under the same training FLOP budget, depth-recurrent models with fewer parameters can achieve higher accuracy on math problems than the non-recurrent parent model.

claims.claim: Muon is more stable than AdamW (including Huginn's AdamW variant) for recurrent training; AdamW loss spikes to NaN.
claims.evidence_quote: Muon is the most stable and achieves the lowest loss for recurrent models. Note, the AdamW line ends early as the loss spikes and becomes NaN.

claims.evidence_quote: We find taking early layers for the prelude, and later layers for the recurrent block and coda to be best.

claims.claim: A healing phase on web text before high-quality data recovers general LM ability lost to surgery.
claims.regime: iso_param + iso_data within recurrent model (single vs two phase)
claims.evidence_quote: for our depth-recurrent model, two phase training provides an increase of 5% on Arc-C, demonstrating that the initial 26 billion token healing period is effective

numbers.quote: We see the depth-recurrent model with two phase training can use recurrence to extend its accuracy to 37.7% by utilizing more FLOPs during inference.

survey_notes: Anchor for (d) retrofitting and (a) depth curricula. Unlike Relaxed Recursive Transformers it uses no LoRA and no distillation, and it benefits from more test recurrences. Regime nuance: the recurrent model has fewer unique params than the parent, and comparisons are per training FLOP with identical data order (so at equal FLOPs the recurrent model has seen fewer tokens); the parent is evaluated at its single fixed depth. Huginn comparison is unmatched (published numbers, different eval). Contrasts with ETD (2510.07358): ETD keeps all layers, no input injection, fixed recurrence; this paper drops middle layers and uses Huginn's concat adapter plus random initial state. Contrasts with 2610.00673: that paper keeps the whole decoder looped with a scalar embedding mix and finds AdamW with warmup stable; here AdamW spikes to NaN and Muon is needed. Truncated BPTT (last 8) inherited from Huginn.

title: CHERRY: Compressed Hierarchical Experts with Recurrent Representational Yield
relevance_reason: Mostly a Korean sovereign-LM recipe paper; one component compresses a 48-layer model into a few weight-tied blocks unrolled recurrently (RDT).
one_sentence: Among many components, a heal-after-merge recurrent depth transformation merges a 48-layer model's layers into few unique blocks and unrolls them (e.g. 6 layers x 8), recovering loss after short selective-token fine-tuning.
key_contributions: Recurrent depth transformation (RDT): merge layers of a trained dense model into fewer unique layers, heal with selected-token supervision, then unroll the shared block.
Ordering matters: unrolling a freshly merged, untrained model raises loss sharply; healing first, then unrolling, lowers it.
Compressed looped configurations reach similar loss to each other across 227M-566M, but well above the uncompressed 48-layer original.

setup.model_sizes: 1.019B 48-layer source; compressed 24Lx2 (566M) to 6Lx8 (227M)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: short SGT fine-tuning (500 steps on a 12,800-example set)
setup.loops_train: n=2..12 unrolls depending on configuration
setup.baselines: other compressed/unrolled configurations; uncompressed 48L model
setup.benchmarks: eval loss

claims.claim: A 6-layer block unrolled 8 times matches the loss of a 24-layer block unrolled twice at 2.5x fewer parameters; note both are compressed looped variants, and the uncompressed 48-layer original is much better.
claims.regime: iso_data among compressed variants; not iso_param vs the dense original
claims.evidence_quote: 6L×8 (227M, loss 2.934) ≈ 24L×2 (566M, loss 2.926). Parameter reduction: 2.5× at identical performance.

claims.claim: Recurrent unrolling must follow healing: unrolling a freshly merged model raises loss, so train then unroll.
claims.evidence_quote: Applying recurrent loop unrolling to an untrained, freshly-merged model increases loss by 212–346%

numbers.what: uncompressed reference
numbers.value: 48L original at 1,019M has much lower loss
numbers.quote: The 48L original at 1,019M achieves much lower loss through full-capacity SGT training.

numbers.value: best at n=8 (34 effective layers), degrades at n=10, 12
numbers.quote: Performance improves monotonically up to n=8 (34 effective layers), then degrades slightly at n=10 and n=12.

limitations: Recurrent compression evaluated on eval loss only after very short fine-tuning on a small dataset; frontier-scale recurrent compression is projected, not measured.
survey_notes: (d) compressing a dense model into shared recurrent blocks. The abstract's 'near-dense parity' (2.934 vs 2.926) is against the 24Lx2 configuration, which is itself compressed and looped; the uncompressed 48L original reaches much lower loss (0.994 in the same table). Weak evidence; loss-only and tiny fine-tuning budget. Finding that unrolling a merged model before healing hurts parallels 2610.00673 and 2608.11233, where naive looping of pretrained weights degrades representations.

title: ConceptMoE: Adaptive Token-to-Concept Compression for Implicit Compute Allocation

key_contributions: Learnable chunking compresses sequences by ratio R; saved compute is reallocated so activated FLOPs and total parameters match the MoE baseline.
Under matched FLOPs and parameters, spending saved compute on looping intermediate layers beats spending it on more activated experts in continual-training conversion.

setup.benchmarks: Open Benchmark (reasoning, math, code), in-house, long context

title: The Tell-Tale Norm: $\ell_2$ Magnitude as a Signal for Reasoning Dynamics in Large Language Models
relevance_reason: Interpretability paper whose one application is training-free, l2-norm-triggered re-application of a single layer of pretrained reasoning LLMs.
one_sentence: Hidden-state l2 norm tracks reasoning intensity; Adaptive Layer-wise Reasoning Recursion re-applies a layer in place when its norm peaks (until convergence or Kmax), improving frozen Qwen3 and R1-Distill-Llama reasoning models training-free.
key_contributions: l2 norm of hidden states as an intrinsic signal of reasoning, linked to SAE reasoning features.
Training-free per-layer recursion at norm peaks; one extra loop helps, many loops hurt; norm grows quickly with repeated application.

setup.loops_test: adaptive per layer until convergence or Kmax; Loop-1 vs Loop-8 ablation

setup.benchmarks: AIME24, GSM8K, GSM-Plus, MMLU-Pro and others

claims.evidence_quote: A single refinement loop (Loop-1) already achieves significant gains over the base model (e.g., AIME24: 60.00 → 66.67), indicating that lightweight, one-step refinement suffices to capture the benefit.

claims.claim: Repeating one layer of a pretrained model makes the activation norm grow rapidly, so only a few loops are safe.
claims.evidence_quote: the norm grows rapidly as the loop count increases; in our estimate, looping up to 3 times is relatively safe, while 4 loops is likely to exceed the current maximum norm observed in

relevance_reason: Training-free duplication of a layer range (traversed twice) in a frozen vision transformer; vision, not language.
one_sentence: Applies LLM 'circuit duplication' (a layer range traversed twice) to frozen DINOv3 embeddings for marine species classification, choosing the circuit globally or per class on a validation pool; improves over the standard forward pass.
key_contributions: First application of circuit duplication to a vision transformer.
Class-specific circuit selection preferred by most classes.

setup.model_sizes: DINOv3 ViT (12 layers)
setup.baselines: standard frozen forward pass; fully supervised ConvNeXt reference
setup.benchmarks: AQUA20

title: Refine Thought: A Test-Time Inference Method for Embedding Model Reasoning
relevance_reason: Re-runs a whole text-embedding model several times with previous pooled states appended to the input; iteration over full forward passes, not looping of layers in depth.
one_sentence: Training-free test-time method that re-encodes a query T times with Qwen3-Embedding, feeding back mean-pooled embeddings from earlier passes; small BRIGHT gain, large gains on a person-job matching benchmark, saturating at T=2-3.
key_contributions: Iterative re-encoding of queries with prior pooled states as extra input, no parameter changes.
Gains peak at T=2-3; decoder-only embedders benefit much more than encoder-only ones.

setup.model_sizes: Qwen3-Embedding-8B; bge-large-zh-v1.5
setup.baselines: single forward pass of the same embedding model
setup.benchmarks: BRIGHT, C-MTEB, PJBenchmark
